title: ‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to play | Activism | The Guardian
description: Ten years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rights
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Ten years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rights
Content: Colin Kaepernick, photographed in August this year.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick, photographed in August this year.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianActivism‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to playTen years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rightsSteve RoseSat 26 Sep 2026 06.59 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTShareColin Kaepernick still gets up at 4.30am every morning to train. “Strength training, speed training, position training – still do all of the same type of workouts I did while I was playing,” he says cheerily. “And then go about the rest of my day.” It is almost 10 years since Kaepernick last played a game of top-flight football. His career was abruptly and cruelly cut short just as it was peaking, after the National Football League (NFL) effectively closed ranks and shut him out for being too political. Now, at 38 years old, he is well aware that his chances of a return are dwindling by the day, but he remains as game-ready as ever. “I stay relentless at it,” he continues in his easy drawl. “I look at it from the perspective of, ‘What are the things that I can control?’ And what I know I can control is being prepared for when opportunity knocks, and to also continue knocking, on my end, looking for ways and opportunities … just staying resilient and focused and disciplined – that is what’s gotten me to this point in my life.”Kaepernick’s story is defined by the events of late 2016, when he repeatedly refused to stand for the pre-game national anthem – resulting in a chorus of booing on the pitch, insults and outrage off it, and exclusion from the sport he still loves. He was one of the biggest names in the game at the time; quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers, a national celebrity, sponsored by major brands, and looking back, his actions fed into so much that has happened since: the rise of Donald Trump, the Black Lives Matter protests and a global reckoning with racism, then the backlash against what is now being called “Woke 1.0”, and the resurgence of a white nationalism that the US complacently assumed was in the past.Through all of this, Kaepernick has largely held his silence. He has rarely spoken to the media and restrained from making public statements. Why so, I ask. Surely there must have been times he’s wanted to speak out?“Oh, absolutely,” he replies. “But I go back to, like, what am I trying to accomplish by doing so?” The temptation to rebut all the lies, the bad takes, the accusations was great, he admits, but, “I realised that, coming out of the protests in 2016, there was a lot of movement and effort made to try to make it as if I was the singular voice in this space doing work, and I was the person solely leading this movement, and that’s just not the reality.”In person, Kaepernick is friendly and relaxed, speaking on a videocall from his agent’s office in New York (understandably, he doesn’t like to disclose where he lives or spends his time). Even when he’s talking about the worst moments in his life, which is most of the time in our 90-minute conversation, his face defaults to a smile and he’s quick to laugh. He’s looking as dapper as ever: black dress shirt, top button done up; neatly trimmed facial hair; his voluminous afro a work of tonsorial topiary.The reason Kaepernick is talking now is because he has a new memoir: The Perilous Fight, which details his upbringing, his illustrious sporting career, and the events leading up to and from that pivotal moment in his life. This is not Kaepernick closing off a chapter of his life, he insists, he just felt that now was the time to speak up: “It’s important for where society is, where we’re at as a country, and some of the direction that the world’s heading in, to be able to continue to move things forward.” Also, he says, “we’re coming up on the 10-year anniversary. So a lot things just naturally aligned.”double quotation markIn many respects, before 2016, Kaepernick was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the gameView image in fullscreenKaepernick takes the knee before a game against the Arizona Cardinals in October 2016.Photograph: MediaNews Group/The Mercury News/ Getty ImagesHe doesn’t need to clarify the anniversary he’s referring to. Kaepernick’s decision to protest was the culmination of “a lifetime of experiences of being Black in America,” he says. But in the moment, it was also spontaneous: “It is not something I discussed with anyone else. It was a personal belief and conviction, and originally I did it not knowing or thinking anybody would see or ask about it,” he says. He didn’t even tell his then fiance (now wife), Nessa Diab. The first three times he did it, hardly anyone noticed. At the 49ers’ preseason game in Santa Clara, California, on 14 August 2016, Kaepernick did not take the knee; he simply sat on a cool box during the pre-game Star-Spangled Banner. He was recovering from injury and not dressed for the game, so he was inconspicuous. He did the same thing for the next two games.By the third time, NFL Network reporter Steve Wyche (who is Black) had clocked it, and spoke to Kaepernick about it. Wyche had also noticed that Kaepernick had been posting all year on his social media about Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr, Muhammad Ali, Black Panther co-founder Huey P Newton and Tupac Shakur. That January, for example, he had posted aquote from Dr King: “He who accepts evil without protesting against it is really cooperating with it.”Kaepernick had certainly been on a journey in terms of his Black history education, partly thanks to Diab – who, a few years earlier, had given him a copy of Malcolm X’s autobiography and told him he’d be “for ever changed”. But his decision to act was also motivated by recent police killings of innocent Black men:Mario Woods, shot and killed by five officers in December 2015 in San Francisco, where Kaepernick was living at the time, using what was later judged “unnecessary force”;Alton Sterling, shot and killed in Louisiana in July 2016;Philando Castile, shot and killed in Minnesota the day after Sterling’s death.“You then get to a point of, if you understand the problem and you understand the reality and you understand the experience, you either look at yourself in the mirror and say, ‘I’m gonna take action and try to do something about it’, or, ‘I’m not going to, and I’m going to be complicit in this’,” he says. The reality had become clear to him: that “the United States is not a representation of my ideals and my beliefs and has not been representing myself or the Black community. And that has been true since its inception.”By the time Kaepernick took the knee for the first time, at the suggestion of his team-mate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside him, the issue had become a global news story. He, Reid and others continued to kneel through that season, often to boos and chants of “USA! USA!” Opponents accused Kaepernick of disrespecting the flag, the country, the military, and law enforcement, repeating the familiar mantra that politics should be kept out of sport. People beganselling T-shirtsoutside football stadiums showing him in the scope of a rifle or telling him to, “Shut up and stand up!” Social media posts against Kaepernick turned vicious and racist. He began to receive death threats, including letters sent to his home address. Unfamiliar cars would park outside the entrance to his and Diab’s house, within a gated community. He temporarily moved out, for their safety.Colin Kaepernick: ‘I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward’Trump, then a presidential candidate,seized on the controversy: “I think it’s a terrible thing. And maybe he should find a country that works better for him,” he told a radio interviewer. Steve King, at the time a Republican congressman, invoked Diab’s Egyptian heritage to argue that“this is activism that’s sympathetic to Isis”. PresidentObama’s responsewas different: “I think he cares about some real, legitimate issues that have to be talked about,” he told reporters.Kaepernick felt largely supported by his immediate teammates; less so by theNFLas an institution. By the end of the 2016 season, by which time dozens of other players had joined in the knee-taking, it had become clear to him they were “trying to get rid of me”, he believes. In February 2017, the 49ers’ new coach and general manager gave him a choice: he could opt out of his contract now, or they would cut him later – knowing that if he left later, his chances of signing for another team would be greatly reduced. In other words, they were pushing him out, but wanted to make it look like he was leaving of his own volition. “It was a cowardly way for them to handle it,” he says.double quotation markThere was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs layKaepernick was “both surprised and not” by the response. “History tells us that a reaction like this is likely to take place. At the same time, because I have a belief that people are fundamentally good and want to do right, I was amazed at how visceral the response was to saying we shouldn’t be killing Black people. It is almost unfathomable to me that that is something that’s a debate in this country. And on the back of that was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs lay, which then became a much more honest place to be. And there really wasn’t a whole lot of middle ground.”It must have been an alienating experience, I suggest. Were there times when it all got to him?“The same way it revealed a lot about society at large, it also revealed a lot about the people around me,” he replies. He talks of how it led to deeper relationships, new friendships, an expanded community. “So while a lot of the immediate reaction is, ‘Oh here was all of the backlash and all of the things that were difficult’, it’s also, ‘Here are all of the great things that came out of this.’ Both of those exist, but we have to put things in perspective. Maybe that’s the eternal optimist in me: I like to look at things through the lens of ‘these are opportunities to get better’.”You are relentlessly positive, aren’t you, I say to him. He laughs. “I try to be! That’s not to say that that negative thing doesn’t exist, but I don’t want to just live in that negative thing. I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward.”If there is any middle ground to occupy when it comes to race issues in the US, Kaepernick could make a pretty good claim to it. His racial identity is more complicated than it appears. He was born to a Black father and a white, teenage mother, and was adopted at five weeks old by a white family from Wisconsin (he has never met his biological parents). Rick and Teresa Kaepernick were conservative, church-going, Republican-leaning. Rick was a manager for a cheese company. They already had a son and a daughter, but had lost two sons due to heart defects and were eager to have another one, irrespective of race. So Kaepernick grew up in predominantly white communities, first in Wisconsin, then, from age four, in Turlock, California.As such, his early experiences of being Black in the US were largely as an isolated individual, often made more acute by his parents’ lack of understanding or even awareness of his racial difference. “They came in with a perspective of, ‘Hey, if we do things the same way we did with my brother and sister, everything will be OK’, and that just wasn’t the case.”Growing up Black in a white community had its advantages, he says. “You get to see and experience a lot of things that otherwise may not reveal themselves. There was a level of comfort there of like, ‘Oh well, if this Black boy is in this white family, he must have assimilated into some of the white perspectives and cultural elements. That makes it OK for us to talk freely and openly in front of him.’ You get a lot of valuable insights into people’s true perspectives, and it gives you a better understanding of how to be able to navigate that.”But he was often treated very differently when strangers did not realise he was his parents’ son. In his memoir he recounts how, aged eight, he was tied to a tree by some older white kids in his neighbourhood, who called him the N-word and told him to “go back to Niger”.Kaepernick’s youthful attempts to connect with Black culture did not always go down well with his parents, either. When he first got his hair braided in cornrows, like his hero, basketball star Allan Iverson, they told him: “You look like a thug.” They were happier when he brought home a white girlfriend than when he brought home a Black one. There were a lot of arguments, he says, over his taste in hairstyles, clothes, music. “But what I will say is, the areas that there was no question around were the idea of being a moral person and doing the right thing and treating people well … The foundational piece is, I know my parents love me as their son.”Sport was one route to connecting with his racial identity. He was outstanding from a young age – as talented at pitching a baseball as throwing a football, and a pretty good basketball player, too. As he ascended the ranks of school and college football, he came into contact with more Black peers. He also experienced the US’s racially charged law enforcement first-hand. As a teen he was pulled over and given a ticket driving his mother’s convertible with three Black friends – “driving while Black”, he jokes. Another time, at college, the cops pulled guns on his Black roommates, who were helping someone move; they had assumed it was a burglary.But Kaepernick’s discipline and commitment began to pay off: by the time he turned pro, in 2011, he was already a clear talent. The following season he led the 49ers to the Super Bowl (they lost to the Baltimore Ravens). He was one of the best “dual-threat” quarterbacks in the league – as effective running with the ball as he was passing it. In many respects, before 2016, he was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the game. He had a glamorous girlfriend (Diab was hosting a hip-hop radio show and appearing on MTV), big-name sponsors like Nike, was on the cover of magazines. “Suddenly, I was everywhere all at once,” he recalls.View image in fullscreenKaepernick with his wife Nessa Diab in New York earlier this month.Photograph: TheStewartofNY/GC ImagesAs much as he still loves the sport, Kaepernick’s protest changed his relationship to it, almost irreparably. And as much as he sought to expose racism in policing, he exposed it within football. More than 70% of NFL players are Black, but historically, team owners and coaches have been overwhelmingly white, and there have been mechanisms in place to keep it that way. In his book, Kaepernick likens the NFL’s scouting combine, where college players are assessed by NFL teams with a series of physical tests and demeaning medical assessments, to a slave market. He recounts how commodified players often are, how their injuries are often glossed over in the interests of short-term results, even how Black players’ baseline intelligence is assumed to be lower than that of white players, which makes it harder for them to claim medical benefits for brain injuries later on. “It is something that historically we will look back on as a society like, how did we ever let that fly? The same way that we ask, how did we ever allow slavery or Jim Crow to happen?”After he left the 49ers in 2017, no other team picked him up. Other players who protested had similar experiences, including Reid, even as scores more continued to take the knee. Trump, by then president,told a rallythat he’d love to see NFL owners respond by saying: “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now. Out! He’s fired.” Many of those owners were his people: white, Republican-leaning billionaires. Some werefriends and direct supporters, including New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, the Dallas Cowboys’Jerry Jones, and Miami Dolphins’Stephen Ross(who held a fundraiser for Trump in 2019).Kaepernick believes the NFL made an example of him: “By blackballing me, denying me employment because of fighting to create a better society and fighting to keep people alive, there’s very real implications about who they are as an organisation and what they believe. I think, largely, the community and society knows it and sees it,” he says.In October 2017, he sued the NFL for “collusion” in shutting him out in retaliation for his activism. The NFL settled out of court in February 2019 for an undisclosed sum. Kaepernick has signed a non-disclosure agreement so cannot go into details, he says, although he would be “very open to the NFL releasing all the documentation and letting society decide”. But he clearly regrets the way things panned out: “I was not protesting the NFL; I was protesting what was happening directly in communities and Black people being killed by police. And the NFL inserted themselves within that conversation and took a side.” (NFL Commissioner Roger Goodellhas denied Kaepernick was blackballed, saying personnel decisions are made by individual teams.)double quotation markMy lawyers got a phone call with Donald Trump asking for me to come in to a meeting. I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case thereView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianAs well as being the 10th anniversary of Kaepernick’s protest, it is also, of course, 10 years since the arrival of Trump on the political scene. Their fates seem intertwined: Trump capitalised on Kaepernick’s protest to whip up political support, then his associations with NFL owners helped shut Kaepernick out of the sport. What would Kaepernick say to Trump if they met?“Well here’s the funny part,” he says breaking into a broad grin. “My lawyers got a phone call with him asking for me to come in to a meeting, I believe it was 2017 or 2018.” There was not a lot of clarity aroundwhyTrump wanted to meet him, but it was “a very easy no”, he says. “I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a better environment and a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case there. I would be curious why there would even be a call and what the topic would be beyond trying to do a photo op.”Within a few tumultuous years, Kaepernick’s stance began to look less controversial. TheBlack Lives Matter movementhad already begun before he started kneeling, but by 2020 the catalogue of police killings of innocent and unarmed Black men, many of them captured on video, had become intolerable. The murder of George Floyd, in Minneapolis in May 2020, was a tipping point, sparking huge anti-racism protests worldwide. As a consequence, players began taking the knee across US sports – football, basketball, baseball, soccer, hockey – at every level, from high school upwards. In England, football players began to take the knee before kick-off for every game, including the national team. Sportspeople and public figures across the world joined in. Where Kaepernick had once knelt virtually alone, now he had inspired a global gesture. He takes no credit for what happened, simply observing that, when it comes to highlighting police brutality, “there are people that have been doing work on the ground directly in communities for years and decades, and a lot of this bubbled up and came to fruition and got elevated during this moment”.In terms of the so-called “racial reckoning” that ensued in the immediate aftermath of 2020, he observes that “people and organisations were pledging large sums of money to address everythingbutpolice brutality. A lot of it became about businesses using the moment to further their interests.” There was some radical reassessment of racial attitudes on all levels – societal, political, corporate – but there was also a lot of political virtue-signalling, such as house speaker Nancy Pelosi, Kamala Harris and other Democratstaking the knee in the Capitolin June 2020, scarves of kente cloth around their shoulders. The then Labour leader Keir Starmer and deputy leader Angela Rayner also performatively knelt, as did many others. Even some progressive politicians cringe at the recollection now. We are speaking shortly before Alexandrio Ocasio-Cortez gave her assessment that “Woke 1.0 was crazy” – suggesting that progressives went too far, post-BLM. This comes on top of ongoing efforts by Trump to roll back all manner of civil rights and inclusion advances: removing high-ranking Black officials from the military; allowing immigration officials to target Black and brown people; effectively operating a whites-only immigration policy. It is sometimes difficult to see what progress has been made. What does it say, for example, that Trump is still in power, a decade on?“It says we have a long way to go,” Kaepernick acknowledges. But as ever, he accentuates the positive: “I also think, within that, it has created such a clear and stark reality for so many people that they are rejecting the politics of the administration and looking for something that actually serves everyone.”double quotation markI still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do thatView image in fullscreenGrooming: Marquis Rosado. Makeup: Maricela Saucedo.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianThis is where Kaepernick’s energy is focused: building the movement. He may have been quiet but he has been busy over the past decade. HisKnow Your Rights Camptours the country teaching young people “not just how to survive but also how to thrive”. His charity funds legal assistance andindependent autopsiesfor those who need it (including the family ofNolan Wells, the Black Mississippi teenager who died in mysterious circumstances on a trip with his white friends this July). He runs a publishing company, and has donated over $1m to community projects. He’sthinking in terms ofElla Baker, the relatively unsung activist who laid the foundations for America’s civil rights movement, from the 1930s onwards. “That was centred around: yes, we need strong leaders, but we need strongpeople, and how do we elevate more people to become leaders so this truly becomes a movement?”Progressive politics is making a comeback, he says, especially within younger generations. “When we think about gen Z and gen Alpha, they’re very much coming from a perspective of, ‘Do you represent my beliefs? Do you represent who I am? And if you don’t, we’re not going to support you’ … As more and more pressure is able to be exerted from the ground up, I think those high-level conversations and positionings are going to start shifting and swinging as well.” He has a four-year-old daughter now, he adds, describing her as “relentlessly fierce”: “Being a father heightens the sense of urgency.”Given all this, isn’t Kaepernick more an activist than a sportsman now?“I look at myself as multi-faceted,” he says. “I still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready and prepared. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do that. But at the core of it, I think people should be able to live, they should be able to thrive, they should able to have dignity, have justice, and that should extend to everyone.”Kaepernick was always mindful of the roll call of Black sportspeople who took a stand for civil liberties and paid a price for it, he says. “That was something I was aware of prior to ever protesting.” Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War and was stripped of his heavyweight boxing title. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists in Black Power salutes on the podium at the 1968 Olympics, which effectively ended their sprinting careers. Curt Flood challenged the “reserve clause”, which prevented baseball players from choosing their own fates, in 1969, and forfeited his career. More recently basketball player Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, refused to stand for the national anthem throughout the 1995-96 season, for similar reasons to Kaepernick, and was suspended and fined by the NBA as a consequence.Kaepernick has had a few tryouts with interested teams, most recently in 2022 with the Las Vegas Raiders – their head coach told him, “You look bigger, faster, stronger than when I last saw you,” Kaepernick says. But the longed-for return has not happened. Is there a part of him that accepts his sporting career may be over? “We don’t have to accept that as the reality,” he replies. “There’s an opportunity to change that … so that when an athlete or when someone speaks up to try to create a better life and better future for a people, for a community, for society, they aren’t met with exile, but they’re actually embraced and people say, ‘You know what, you’re right. Let’s take the actions to actually make this better.’ When we can lay that foundation, that creates significant opportunity for change.”So he will continue to train, he says. “I will not let go of that as a discipline, as part of who I am.”If he was back on an NFL team again, would he still take the knee for the national anthem?“Absolutely,” he says. “The work still needs to be done. More people need to be brought into that work and into that conversation. And more people need to be taking action around it. And I will continue to do the work. I will continue to protest because, quite literally, people’s lives are at stake.”The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick is published by Grand Central. title: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
Content: Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg reveals the Muse ‘charm’ device during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, this week.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeta chief Mark Zuckerberg reveals the Muse ‘charm’ device during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, this week.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Fashion‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cutenessThe tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shopEllie Violet BramleySat 26 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,”the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience.View image in fullscreenThe Muse ‘charm’ device.Photograph: MetaThe “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author ofIrresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World: “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment tothe idea of personal, wearable super-intelligencethat you can chat to. As well as a broadershift towards cute technology, cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”View image in fullscreenGen Z, so attached to their Labubus, could be tempted by the charms of the Muse.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersTo try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ contentRead moreWhether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently.“That’s so AI!” is the phrasegen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.For many gen Zers who areau faitwith having acuddly toy hanging from their bags, most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.View image in fullscreenYoung girls playing with their Tamagotchis in the mid-2000s.Photograph: Charlie Stroke/AlamyPlus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [orkawaii] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”Explore more on these topicsFashionMetaAI (artificial intelligence)Wearable technologyGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: London transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express? | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question
Content: The Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyRail transportLondon transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express?With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into questionGwyn TophamTransport correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Heathrow finally builds its third runway, Londoners can expect hundreds more planes flying overhead each day. But greater congestion on the ground will be a problem too. Under Heathrow’s£33bn expansion plan, 100,000-200,000 more passengers would eventually be travelling to or from the airport each day.The most eye-catching problem has been moving part of the UK’s busiest motorway, the M25, to make space for a new 2.2-mile (3.5km) runway. A thornier one may be getting motorists out of their cars, and finding more sustainable ways for the extra passengers – and thousands of staff – to travel to and from Heathrow.Although ride-sharing, coaches and buses can play a part, scaling up rail is the clear alternative. Space on the existing line is, however, at a premium, and the Elizabeth line, built with a promise ofconnecting business travellers swiftly and directly from Heathrowto the City and Canary Wharf, only has limited paths. With everything up for negotiation, transport experts are asking: has the time come to kill off the Heathrow Express?The obvious airport train, as unwary visitors often find out too late, may not be the best one. The Heathrow Express, which charges a whopping £26 for a 15- to 21-minute one-way hop, was long one of the most expensive airport connections around (at least until it wasovertaken by the Luton Dart). It is, as advertised, technically the fastest way to central London, though passengers travelling beyond Paddington may reach their destination more quickly on the Elizabeth line or even the tube on a direct route.For those who value the speed – in addition to TV news, a toilet and a luggage rack – it may be the perfect service. But the Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers, with the number bolstered by airport staff on heavily discounted tickets.Transport for London (TfL) has signalled its belief that the service’s time is up, as the government consults on its Heathrow expansion national policy statement. MPs must approve the statement for the runway to go ahead. That no longer seems automatic: Andy Burnham’s long-term scepticism over a third runway, along with the loss of Rachel Reeves in No 11 as a champion of expansion, makes Downing Street support look ambivalent at best – even given the new chancellor’s belated assertion that the “economic case stacks up”.The Sunday Times reported this weekend that airport bosses have told ministers the third runway will not now be operational until 2039, a four year delay.However many runways the airport has, TfL said it was “worth reviewing [the Heathrow Express’s] future in the context of determining the optimal mix of services on the Great Western mainline to make the most effective use of the limited capacity available”.Map showing rail routes from Heathrow’s Terminal 5 to destinations in central LondonFor TfL, the Elizabeth line, going deeper and cheaper into the heart ofLondon, is “a more compelling service”. At the moment, only two Elizabeth line trains an hour serve Heathrow’s Terminal 5, which handles about 40% of the airport’s passengers. That means a passenger who does not carefully judge the timing may face a journey from the City or Canary Wharf to T5 of more than an hour. The frequency is due to double next year but more space into Heathrow could still be freed up.Alex Williams, the chief customer and strategy officer at TfL, told MPs at a select committee hearing this month that the Heathrow Express was “taking up valuable paths that aren’t actually well used. There’s a way of repurposing that to be more affordable, more attractive, and carry more public transport users.”Surface access, or getting people between central London and Britain’s biggest airport, underwent a step change with the Elizabeth line. Previously, the little-advertised offering Heathrow Connect joined the dots at the likes of Hayes & Harlington on a slower train to Paddington, serving many airport workers, if not international travellers. Fares were then about a third of the price of the Heathrow Express – a gap that is now less significant given that the Elizabeth line charges £15.50 to reach any of its central London stations. And for those who are able to book and plan a month ahead, the Express advance tickets can prove less expensive at £10.View image in fullscreenPeople waiting for an Elizabeth line train at Paddington.Photograph: Matthew Ashmore/AlamyTfL’s cheaper but slower alternative, the Piccadilly line (£5.90 into central London), is also due to get an upgrade of signalling and trains, increasing capacity.Two additional rail schemes have been mooted – Heathrow Southern Railway and a Western Rail link – as ways to connect into the wider national rail network, and the Elizabeth line itself could be extended to Staines – all of which would encourage many more from the suburban commuter belt to take the train rather than drive to the airport.Rebooting the railway now would coincide with the end of Heathrow Express’s operating agreement with the Department for Transport, which gives the service access rights to the national railway until June 2028. The DfT says no decision has yet been made on the future operation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s complicated: the actual operator, the FirstGroup-owned Great Western Railway, is due to be nationalised this December and become part ofGreat British Railwaysnext year. Meanwhile, Heathrow owns the stations and five miles of railway from the airport to the mainline, part of its original £1bn investment in the Express in the 1990s.The service brought in revenue of £48m for the first six months of 2026, according to a Heathrow spokesperson. They said: “It operates without taxpayer funding and helps keep airport charges down. Passengers don’t want fewer choices – Heathrow Express remains an important part of the competitive connectivity, convenience and flexibility they expect.”But many question whether enough is being done – or if there will be enough pressure on Heathrow to avoid gridlock on the roads. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, warned that the taxpayer could be left picking up the bill for public transport improvements “left undefined and unfunded in the current proposals” for expansion – estimated at up to £9bn by TfL, a figure Heathrow said it did not recognise.View image in fullscreenHeathrow has plans to increase its parking space capacity from 21,000 to 36,000.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMost passengers go to the airport by car. And while Heathrow is funding new car parks – with plans to boost its parking space capacity from 21,000 to 36,000 – and its rerouting of the M25, it has not pledged any of its £33bn expenditure on improving the trains, Williams told the select committee, adding: “If you make it easier for people to park very near the terminal, how will you encourage them to get on the train?”Without clear demands for a mode shift to public transport – as existed in the previous expansion plan, as well as in the planning permission for Gatwick’s recently approved second runway – the policy statement was “a step backwards”, Williams said, adding that in 2017 “there was a commitment or an aspiration from Heathrow to get no extra traffic. That is gone.”A DfT spokesperson said: “We are carefully considering responses to the consultation, which sets out the key requirements any future planning application for expansion would have to meet, including public transport targets.”A legal mandate could happen, a source said. But so far these are just targets: at the most stringent, 55% of airport passengers using public transport, and only when Heathrow’s third runway is fully operational.For Anthony Smith, the former passenger watchdog who now chairs the Heathrow Area Transport Forum, it seems a curious timetable. He told MPs: “If you’re trying to shift people out of cars in 20 years’ time, when you’ve got 130 million passengers, it’s just harder, harder, harder.”Explore more on these topicsRail transportHeathrow airportAir transportPublic transportTransportHeathrow third runwayRoad transportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans distance themselves from him
Author: David Smith
Headline: Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans distance themselves from him
Content: There is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesThe Saturday readDonald Trump‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanesTrump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans stray from the scriptDavid SmithSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 04.45 EDTShareDonald Trumpstood before theUnited Nationson Tuesday andthreatened to “annihilate” Iran. Yet even as the most powerful man on the planet flexed his military muscles, he was powerless to keep the gravitational pull of domestic politics at bay.Heading into the UN building inNew York, the US president wasquestioned by Kaitlan Collins, an anchor atCNN, which he had banned from the White House before a judge ruled against him. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” the 80-year-old snapped. “You should not be here covering me.”The lashing-out was a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control. Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.Federal courts are reining him in. Congressional Republicans are straying from the script. Poll numbers aretumbling to historic depths, driven by persistent inflation, rising fuel costs and an increasingly unpopular war in Iran. For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump’s aura of authority is fading.Chart of Trump’s approval rating going downRick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, prophesied: “This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter.”Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fearsRead moreTrump’s self-belief never wavers. He faced four criminal cases and two assassination attempts before winning the 2024 election. He has livedby a mantra of“it will all work out well in the end” while his supporters wear hats that state: “Trump was right about everything.”Yet he has had a rough month. TheFederal Reserve defied him on interest rates. The supreme court blocked his administration’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November’s midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Center, prompting him to threaten the national arts complex with demolition; another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering the administration to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” their access.Now even Trump’s dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November. In Florida, his home state, gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds quietlyscrubbed most Trump referencesfrom his campaign website, while the congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ran campaign advertisements openly declaring that federal immigration enforcement had gone “too far” and asserting that Latino voters “feel betrayed”.View image in fullscreenByron Donalds, the Republican candidate for Florida governor, has distanced himself from Trump.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesWilson, a co-founder ofthe Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, sees a herd mentality among congressional Republicans and compares the current mood to a wildlife documentary.“It needs aDavid Attenboroughvoiceover,” he said. “It’s like the gazelles wandering the savannah. They’re sniffing the wind now and they smell something in the wind. They know it’s a predator but they don’t know what to do about it yet. What they haven’t realised is that the predator has been among them all along. The risk factor that they face now is Trump.”For nearly a decade, elected Republicans maintained a posture of submission, fearful of drawing a primary challenger or ascathing post on Truth Social. But with the elections looming and control of Congress hanging in the balance, self-preservation is rapidly overriding loyalty to the president.Wilson said: “Now it’s reached the point where the magic doesn’t work any more.There’s no political upside from a president who is at 29% approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can’t spin away.“The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump.”View image in fullscreenGas prices on 22 September 2026 in Doral, Florida.Photograph: Lynne Sladky/APThis creates a vicious circle, Wilson argues.“The more he becomes a liability, the more he acts out. The more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it, the more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it. Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they’re paying the price, they’ve decided this has got a little too hairy.”Faced with shrinking authority and a hostile economic landscape, Trump has reverted to his trusted playbook: manufacturing spectacle, picking cultural fights and raging against the press. His recent decision toban the news outletsCNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House campus following critical coverage was viewed by critics not as a display of strength, but a symptom of deep frustration.The administration rejects such charges and insists that the president’s agenda is succeeding.Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.“The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs,” he added. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”Chart of Trump’s approval rating on important issuesBut the trend lines are only set to worsen for Trump. If Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives, they plan tolaunch investigationsinto how he has allegedly abused his office to enrich his family, grant favours to supporters, hollow out the federal government and carry out expensive construction projects. The attention economy, meanwhile, will inexorably shift to the 2028 presidential race and the question of succession.Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, said the inevitable shift of focus toward potential candidates – such as the vice-president, JD Vance,or the secretary of state, Marco Rubio – will be cause for friction.“Nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him,” said Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him. It’s his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it?”Trump is not the first president to run into trouble after winning re-election. From Richard Nixon’sWatergate downfallto Clinton’s impeachment and George W Bush’s quagmire in Iraq, second terms have historically served as the graveyard of presidential ambition.Allan Lichtman, author of a new book,Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, calls it “the second term curse”. He noted: “Second terms have been remarkably difficult for presidents.”View image in fullscreenDonald Trump arrives at the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York on 22 September 2026.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesLichtman, a history professor atAmerican Universityin Washington, believes that Trump is driven by two things: money and glory. “He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that’s dangerous,” he said. “I don’t care much about his verbal lashing-out; I don’t think that helps him at all. But who knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him? And that’s frightening.“Never underestimate the power of the president. Just becauseRepublicansare criticising him, his poll numbers are low, prospects for Republicans look dim, doesn’t mean he doesn’t have enormous power–and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained. He doesn’t care about the courts and doesn’t care about the Congress.”From this perspective, Trump’s last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicised justice department and a sweeping pardon power. With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing.Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Donald Trump fears irrelevance more than anything and he’ll rage against it as long as he can. The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive.“We’re headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable. The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets.”

title: ‘We left Ireland because there wasn’t work – and we wanted to get the hell away’: Trespasses author Louise Kennedy | Books | The Guardian
description: Her Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to write
Author: Alex Clark
Headline: Her Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to write
Content: Louise Kennedy.Photograph: Kenneth O Halloran/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLouise Kennedy.Photograph: Kenneth O Halloran/The GuardianBooksInterview‘We left Ireland because there wasn’t work – and we wanted to get the hell away’: Trespasses author Louise KennedyAlex ClarkHer Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to writeSat 26 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. You wouldn’t know it to look at her, as we chat in the sitting room of the house in Sligo that she shares with her husband, son and daughter, but this is the home that she once thought would be repossessed. The couple bought it “for stupid money” in 2007, when they also opened a restaurant, initially so successful that the only way seemed to be up. The following year, financial mayhem descended on Ireland, their customers ebbed away, and the Celtic Tiger years morphed into a country racked with job losses, bankruptcies, apparently endless debt. “I didn’t think I’d ever be able to keep the house,” she says, glancing around an elegant room dotted with beautiful objects and plants, but nonetheless relaxed and comfortable. “I’d say we only got out of negative equity about a month ago. There are probably arguments for moving now, but I’m so proud that we managed to hold on to it, I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to be carried out of here in a box.”Kennedy had been a chef for 30 years, working all over the place from Dublin to London and, for two years, Beirut, before ending up in Sligo, on Ireland’s west coast, not far from the border with her native Northern Ireland. Crucially, she had never given a thought to writing, not since a teacher had admired a poem she wrote when she was seven. Now, she is about to publish her second novel, Stations, which follows a collection of short stories, The End of the World Is a Cul-de-Sac, and her debut, Trespasses, which was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize for fiction and won other prizes in Ireland and the UK in 2022 and 2023. Last year, Trespasses gained further acclaim when it wasadapted for Channel 4in a production starring Gillian Anderson as the mother of Cushla, the young Catholic teacher who falls in love with Michael, an older, married Protestant lawyer, in 1970s Belfast.Trespasses fired readers’ imaginations because it gave an already complex love story a terrifying, high-stakes backdrop; Michael and Cushla’s relationship wasn’t simply clandestine because it was extramarital, but because they came from communities pitted against one another in an occupied country. And to recreate the detail, texture and jeopardy of Belfast at the time, Kennedy had to look no further than her own upbringing.View image in fullscreenA scene from the TV adaptation of Trespasses.Photograph: Peter Marley/Channel 4double quotation markIt was a complicated location shoot because a lot of the place was wreckedShe relates it so vividly and, at times, so humorously, that you have to remind yourself how intensely difficult it must have been. Kennedy’s Catholic family ran pubs in Belfast. One day, her grandmother was on her way to bank the takings when a bomb exploded in a building she was walking past and a chunk of glass pierced her jugular vein. “Some off-duty British soldier, a young fella who was down the town, held her neck together to stop her from bleeding to death until the ambulance came,” Kennedy recalls, before adding that her grandmother’s life was saved by the fur coat she’d been wearing. Throughout the ordeal, she wouldn’t let go of the handbag full of money, nor stop insisting she had to go and fetch her daughter from school.“There was a lot of scarring on her face because she’d been cut by glass, but already, even in 71, the plastic surgeons in the north were just brilliant at patching people up. She just had very fine lines where the scarring was. She was really lucky.” What about psychologically? “She was a complete walking trauma case. She never talked about that. She wouldn’t even have known the word trauma. But if there was a loud noise, she’d go to pieces.”double quotation markIn Northern Ireland, you just had to go on about your business, or you’d be freaking out left, right and centreMeanwhile, Kennedy’s father had experienced intimidation at work, in a factory in East Belfast where he was the only Catholic. He had been followed home, and one of their Catholic neighbours had been killed in a loyalist “romper room” – essentially, an interrogation and murder site, the slang taken from a children’s TV programme. Now, her father was training to become an accountant through evening correspondence courses, simultaneously studying and minding the children while his wife went to work in the pub. One night, Kennedy’s mother, grandmother, two uncles and a policeman found themselves standing in a tunnel opposite the building when it was blown up, an attack that found its way into Trespasses. “It was a crazy thing to happen. And I think that that was the thing about the north: you know it’s not normal, you know it’s mental, but yet it is normal because this is how you have to live. You just have to go on about your business, because otherwise you’re going to be freaking out left, right, and centre. ”Kennedy’s skill at conjuring the past without succumbing to the shorthand of nostalgia was one of the qualities that made for the success of the adaptation of Trespasses, which was written by Ailbhe Keogan, who also worked on Bad Sisters. “Ailbhe is not from the north, she’s from Kerry, and she was very open to me. I wanted the dialogue to be authentic to the north, but not just to the north. It also had to sound like 1975, and that’s quite easy for me to remember: the voice in my head is of a child in the north of Ireland in the 70s. And people don’t speak the same now as they did then. The place is really different. It was quite a complicated location shoot for that reason, because a lot of the place was wrecked and a lot of rebuilding has been done since that. It was pretty tricky to try and find a bar that hasn’t changed at all. The book is set in Holywood, County Down, where I grew up, but Holywood doesn’t look like it did in the 70s, so it was filmed in Portaferry, a village in County Down.”In 1979, life changed again. Kennedy was 12, and in her first year at grammar school, when her parents decided they’d had enough and uprooted the family to Naas, then a small town not far south of Dublin. She hated it. “From my point of view, it was really crap.” She lost her pals, it took two years to get the phone connected, and even worse, there was only one television station, “so all of my cultural references had been wiped out”. Six weeks later, they went back to Belfast for a visit, and Kennedy was shocked to find how strange a friend’s accent sounded to her. “I just thought ‘Oh my God! I don’t belong anywhere.’ I didn’t belong to either place, and I still feel that now. When you leave a place, it goes on about its business, but for me it’s frozen in time.”Back then, though, she didn’t have that perspective. “I was an atrocious adolescent. I was really angry that we’d had to leave and move to a place where there was one TV channel.” And it’s this dislocation that she’s mined for her new novel, Stations, in which two misfit teenage protagonists, Róisín and Red, cleave together to create some version of belonging. But as the story progresses from the early 1980s to this century, moving from Ireland to London, it becomes apparent that only one of them will thrive.It’s a portrait not only of teenage alienation, displacement and small-town Ireland, but of one of the waves of Irish emigration that have characterised its history. Remembering her own time in London, Kennedy says that you could walk into a pub on Sunday mornings in the 1980s and 90s and feel like you were at mass. And you could also feel that you were in flight: “We left because there wasn’t work, but we also left because it was a closed, judgmental, shithole theocracy that we were living in, and we wanted to get the hell away.” It’s that historical precision that has led Anne Enright to say of Stations that “it holds a national sorrow”, describing it as a “work of mourning and reclamation”.And in Róisín, Kennedy gave herself permission to write a “pain in the arse” character, unpopular, temperamental, self-centred, in contrast to Cushla whom, she says, readers found so likable. “I ran into a friend of mine recently who was in school with me. She was asking what the book is about and I said a character who moved from the north, and everybody in school hates her. She was like, is it a memoir?”Back to that wild pivot from cooking to writing. How did all this happen? Put simply, Kennedy was still trying to keep her ailing restaurant on its legs back in 2014 when she found herself ambushed into going along to a new creative writing group set up by the writer Una Mannion. “Why would I be doing that?” she asked the friend doing the persuading, visual artist Niamh Mac Cabe, whereupon Mac Cabe just turned up and plonked her in the car. “I thought it was the most hilarious thing I’d ever heard in my life,” Kennedy remembers. But at that first meeting of eight or so people, Kennedy found herself committing to writing a piece over the next few weeks. “From the minute that I started trying to write this mad little short story – I didn’t even know what a short story was really – I just thought: I don’t really care what happens as long as I can find a way to keep doing this.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGillian Anderson in the TV adaptation of Trespasses.Photograph: Peter Marley/Channel 4That story, which eventually found its way on to national radio, drew on a family memory, and told of a young girl in the 1920s who gets into a world of trouble when she writes Rudolph Valentino’s name in the list of that month’s deaths at church. When she read it to the group, “I fully expected everybody just to laugh or to very politely move on from having to talk about my crap story, but they were wildly enthusiastic. So I thought, ‘OK, I’m going to try to write another one.’”Partly, she was enjoying the distraction. At work, Kennedy and her husband were constantly firefighting to stave off creditors and make sure staff got paid. “We were skint. Everybody was, and I suppose the thing is that if the whole country is like that, it means that the people who in the past you might have been able to go and borrow a couple of bob from didn’t have any. They were all up the shit as well.” When the restaurant finally closed, a few months after she had joined the writing group, “I just thought, I don’t care. I could sit and fart around trying to write something for two or three hours and I wouldn’t even have thought about the business.”After that seismic change, her writing life began to blossom; she accumulated short stories, did an MA and then started a PhD at Queens University in Belfast, where she was supervised by the writer Garrett Carr, and began to publish in magazines. She acquired an agent, Eleanor Birne, who was building a list of Irish writers, and who told her that her work might be more attractive to British publishers if they thought a novel was coming. “I had lied to her and said, ‘Oh yeah, I’m kind of working on a novel’, but I wasn’t really.” She told Carr the same. But in fact, the idea for Trespasses was beginning to brew.And then, another curve ball arrived, in the form of a diagnosis of melanoma: a mole on her shoulder blade had mutated into cancer, and subsequently, the cancer had spread. First, there was the prospect of surgery and, later, immunotherapy. She didn’t, she says, want to be thinking about cancer all the time, but she knew she wouldn’t be working as she had been. “So I just rigged myself up a sling. I sat here, off my tits on really strong painkillers for a few days and watched all three series of Call My Agent. But I couldn’t really do anything, so I thought, OK, the only thing I can do is sit at the kitchen table and try to write 1,000 words a day of something that might be a novel, and see what happens. So by the time I went back to work, I had 64,000 words of something. It wasn’t really a novel. It was a pile of shite. But when I did actually go back to it, there was something on the page to fix.”Kennedy subsequently endured various complications and resurgences of her original cancer, including damage to her pituitary gland that caused sudden menopause and severe endocrine problems. She has spent several years tailoring her life around treatment – during our conversation, an alarm reminds her to take one of her many daily pills – but she’s on far more of an even keel nowadays. I ask her whether the next book will follow a chronological pattern and anchor itself in the 1990s; the answer is yes, and she’s working on it.Although she says she prefers the doing to the being when it comes to literary life – in other words, writing rather than talking about it – she’s established herself enough to rule out a return to the kitchen. At least, not professionally: before I leave, she ushers me to the table and produces, with zero fanfare, a homemade quiche, homemade bread, homemade paté and, finally, a vast homemade raspberry and lemon curd cake. Every mouthful is delicious. You can entirely imagine that, had a global financial crisis not wrecked her career as a restaurateur, she would still have been cooking up a storm: good news for diners, but a major blow to readers.Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury.To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksFictioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They accepted the money but didn’t take care of my child’: what Luna Wong’s death reveals about the treatment of international students in the UK  | Mental health | The Guardian
description: When her parents waved her off to study in England they hoped it would be a fresh start the 16-year-old needed after struggling with her mental health in Hong Kong. Instead, 10 months later, she was dead. What went so wrong?
Author: Samira Shackle
Headline: When her parents waved her off to study in England they hoped it would be a fresh start the 16-year-old needed after struggling with her mental health in Hong Kong. Instead, 10 months later, she was dead. What went so wrong?
Content: Luna Wong (centre) and her parents at the airport. Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongWhen her parents waved her off to study in England they hoped it would be a fresh start the 16-year-old needed after struggling with her mental health in Hong Kong. Instead, 10 months later, she was dead. What went so wrong?BySamira ShackleSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a young teen, one of Luna Wong’s favourite things to do was to walk to a bridge near her home in Hong Kong and sit there for a while, listening to the traffic and the water below, looking out at the lights and the activity of the city. She had a particular way of observing the world, which she expressed through photography. Her pictures were mostly landscapes, ordinary corners of Hong Kong, but she could spot an image nobody else would have seen in the same place. She was an inquisitive kid who enjoyed making people laugh, and was deeply interested in the world around her. Then in 2019, when she was 13,political unrest in Hong Kong, swiftly followed by Covid lockdowns, shrank that world to the size of her bedroom. For a prolonged period, Luna barely left her family’s flat. School became a screen; friends were only accessible virtually. She stopped sleeping properly, started having panic attacks, and was diagnosed with depression and anxiety.When the world opened up after Covid, Luna was too changed to step easily back into it. She was often so anxious she couldn’t attend school, and fell seriously behind. Her psychiatrist prescribed antidepressants, anti-anxiety medication and sleeping pills. Later, ADHD medication and an anti-psychotic drug were added to the mix. This heavy combination of prescription drugs left her lethargic in the day – though still often awake at night – and caused weight gain, which distressed her. But Luna retained her curious streak. Keen to understand her own issues better, she read about psychology, ordering textbooks to teach herself about the human mind. When her friends had problems, she offered advice, and dreamed of becoming a psychologist. But it was hard to see how this would be possible as she struggled to attend school.In 2022, two years into her mental health struggles, Luna had an idea: a move overseas. A close friend had decided to do A-levels at boarding school in the UK, and Luna wanted to go, too. Luna’s English was fluent – since infancy, her parents had read her bedtime stories in English as well as Cantonese – and she wanted to do an A-level in psychology, which wasn’t on offer in Hong Kong. But there was a bigger reason, too. This could be a fresh start, a way for Luna to decisively open up her world again.View image in fullscreenLuna, age eight, with her parents at Yuen Long wetlands Park, Hong Kong, in 2014.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongAt first, her parents, Hilda Leong and Thomas Wong, were apprehensive. Luna was still fragile. But seeing their daughter excited and motivated about this plan was enough for them to get behind it. “I hoped it would change her life, because it seemed that Hong Kong was very difficult to her at that time,” says Thomas. After consulting Luna’s psychiatrist, who said she was sufficiently recovered to travel, they decided to press ahead. In September 2022, when Luna was 16, she moved to the UK to study for her A-levels at Wrekin College, a leafy boarding school set on 100 acres of land in Shropshire. Thomas and Hilda discussed Luna’s depression and anxiety with Wrekin before she was admitted, and felt confident the school was equipped to support her needs.Nonetheless, Hilda did not sleep well while her daughter was abroad. There is an eight-hour time difference between Hong Kong and the UK, and Hilda kept her phone on the bedside table every night in case Luna rang. “I didn’t know how her life was there, and I was nervous about it,” says Hilda. But she reassured herself that this was what Luna wanted. “I told myself, she is growing up, she needs to go out into the world, she has her own life. I told myself, I will let her go.”As it turned out, they were right to worry. Luna struggled to adjust to life at boarding school. Soon after finishing year 12 at Wrekin College, Luna travelled to London for a summer school placement. It was there that, in July 2023, she took her own life.View image in fullscreenAged nine with her parents at Universal Studios Singapore, 2016.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongWhat happened to Luna reflects the mental health struggles of many young people, but it is also, in part, a story about money: a private education industry that has grown increasingly reliant on the fees international students bring, propped up by a patchwork of private companies that profit from these children while carrying almost none of the legal obligations that would normally come with caring for them. Recalling her daughter’s death, Hilda breaks down in tears. “When she left for the UK, I didn’t know she would leave us for ever.”Almost exactly three years after Luna’s death, I speak to Thomas and Hilda via a video call. They are in their apartment in Hong Kong, a framed studio portrait photo of Luna, smiling, on the wall behind them. Their grief is still raw and unresolved, and Thomas weeps as he tells me it took 14 years to conceive Luna. “We waited a long time to have this child,” he says. When their longed-for baby was born, they gave her the Cantonese name Lok Tung, which translates to “happy child”. For most of her life this was an apt description: she loved kindergarten and then school, made friends easily, and was doted on at home. “She brought happiness to the whole family,” says Thomas. It is common for people in Hong Kong to adopt an English name. Lok Tung’s first choice was Penguin, after her favourite animal, but she eventually settled on Luna, which is the name she used in the UK.Luna was close to her parents, and it was painful for them to see her retreat into herself as her mental health worsened. “Sometimes she refused to talk to us,” says Hilda. “Maybe she thought we didn’t understand her.” Thomas showed his care by cooking Luna’s favourite meals – tofu, cucumber with vinegar and sour ginger, butterfly cookies – and through his physical presence. “If she didn’t want to talk, I didn’t talk, but just stayed near her,” he says. He often sat just outside her room when she withdrew inside.double quotation markLuna’s parents chose Wrekin College for its beautiful grounds, extracurricular activities and lack of intense academic pressureView image in fullscreenWrekin College in Shropshire.Photograph: David Bagnall/AlamySending her to boarding school in the UK was a big financial decision; Thomas and Hilda do not consider themselves wealthy. Until his retirement, Thomas worked in IT customer care, and Hilda, who is younger, still works in a hospital lab. Hoping it would be the fresh start she desperately needed, they decided to cash in Thomas’s pension to cover the cost. He took the lead in researching schools, looking for ones with beautiful grounds and lots of extracurricular activities – something he felt Luna had missed out on – and where academic pressure wouldn’t be too intense. An education agent helped with the application; a service that is free for parents, because schools pay a commission of around 10% of the first-year fees for each successful applicant. Before too long, Luna was interviewed and then accepted by Wrekin College, a co-ed school founded in 1880 that describes itself as “proudly non‑academically selective”. It seemed like the perfect fit.Over the last few decades, the number of British students who board at independent schools has declined significantly, with most attending as day pupils. To fill beds and balance the books, boarding schools have become increasingly reliant on overseas students, who by definition need to board, and who sometimes pay higher termly fees. AtWrekin College, for instance, UK boarders in year 12-13 pay £15,725 a term, while international boarders pay £17,025. Today, around 40% of boarders at British boarding schools are international students, with around half of those from China and Hong Kong. A 2024 write-up of an education fair in Hong Kong in aschools industry magazinedescribed “an air of desperation” with representatives of British schools “resorting to aggressive tactics, pulling parents away from other stands”.There is a lot of money at stake throughout this process – not just for schools, but for the industries that have sprung up around them. Most schools also require that parents appoint an education guardian, someone in the UK contracted to act in loco parentis. This can be a friend or relative, but many employ professional agents, who are typically paid a few thousand pounds a year. Their main job is arranging holiday homestays with host families, who are paid a separate nightly fee, and stepping in for emergencies. Thomas and Hilda appointed someone from theWhite House Guardiansagency, discussing Luna’s mental health issues beforehand and sharing a letter from her psychiatrist. “We thought the guardian could take care of her – not just practical things like registration and holidays, but take care of her mind, help her with difficulties at school, make her feel at home,” says Hilda. “We hoped the guardian would be like a mum or dad. But, actually, it wasn’t the case.”Luna arrived in the UK in the early hours of 7 September. After her first day of lessons, teachers at the school observed that she was visibly distressed, and she contacted her parents to say she was overwhelmed. Homesickness is normal, but it soon became clear Luna was not coping. Struggling with insomnia at night, she regularly fell asleep in class, and sometimes slept through the day in the school’s wellbeing centre. On 20 September, she told a school nurse that she had previously self-harmed and experienced suicidal thoughts. This history, along with her ADHD diagnosis, had not been disclosed to the school or guardianship agency beforehand – only her depression, anxiety and panic disorder, which had been detailed in a letter from her psychiatrist. A later safeguarding review into Luna’s death attributed this to cultural differences in what her parents understood needed to be shared, rather than any attempt to conceal issues. Two days later, staff discovered that she had self-harmed. It was decided that Luna would benefit from a few days away from school – common practice at boarding schools – and staff phoned her education guardian to arrange it.Luna’s guardian was contracted to “respond appropriately to all emergency situations” on her behalf, and to visit her within two weeks of her arrival.
