However, this was Luna’s third week and she had not made contact. In a later statement for the inquest into Luna’s death, Wrekin’s safeguarding lead noted that when the school rang that evening, the guardian “did not seem to know much about Luna (not even that she went by the name Luna)”, and said she would need to contact her head office “due to White House Guardians host families not being trained to look after a pupil with mental health difficulties”. The next day, the guardian confirmed that White House would not place Luna with a host family. There is a reasonable argument that an untrained host family is no place for a child in crisis, which is the view White House Guardians took. But, according to the safeguarding review, the guardian did not offer to visit or find another solution. In a written statement, White House Guardians said that the name confusion arose because Luna had signed up to the agency under her Chinese name, Lok Tung, and that the guardian assigned to Luna had not visited because she was seriously ill with Covid. White House said it recommended Luna should be taken to A&E, although this does not appear in Wrekin’s own account of the incident. Either way, Luna never met her first guardian.View image in fullscreenLuna, age 12, at school in Hong Kong.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongEducation guardians have a heavy responsibility, and unrestricted access to the children in their care, but the law does not require them to have training in child welfare, safeguarding or mental health, nor even a basic criminal record check,though schools often require one. In 2022, the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse flagged this as a serious concern for the 26,000 international children who board in the UK each year, noting that even someone convicted of offences against children could work as an education guardian. Only last year did the government requirecriminal record checksfor holiday host families; it still requires nothing of guardians. There are some attempts to regulate the sector: White House Guardians is accredited by a charity called the Association for the Education and Guardianship of International Students (Aegis). Aegis members must hold enhanced criminal record checks and safeguarding training, but signing up is entirely voluntary, and many guardians and companies still operate with no oversight at all.School staff phoned Luna’s parents in Hong Kong to inform them about the self-harm and the plan to find her a homestay, tried repeatedly to reach her psychiatrist, and contacted the local child and adolescent mental health service. That referral lapsed when Luna – who was 16 – refused to consent. The safeguarding review found that this referral could actually have proceeded without consent. Panicked about managing Luna’s risk over the weekend, staff suggested that Thomas and Hilda appoint a different guardian, recommending a woman who was originally from Hong Kong and spoke Cantonese. She already acted for other Wrekin students from China and Hong Kong. It was a high-pressure situation, and Hilda and Thomas went ahead.The new education guardian was also Aegis-accredited but had no formal training in child mental health, self-harm or suicidal ideation. After being appointed, she came to school and spent two hours with Luna, then proposed a weekend homestay with one of her regular hosts, who was also a psychotherapist. Luna went, and returned to school somewhat calmer. What Luna’s parents did not know was that, from that weekend on, almost all communication about their daughter would run through the education guardian. Wrekin’s boarding housemistress later reflected that she spoke far more often to the education guardian than to the parents, a habit that the safeguarding review said had first become common during Covid. Although Thomas and Hilda speak warmly of the care Wrekin provided for Luna, they are frustrated they were not kept better informed. “It was absolutely not enough in my opinion,” says Hilda. “The system is that the guardian will take care of my daughter, and communicate with us. But, actually, she wasn’t doing that.”View image in fullscreenIn Japan, age 13.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongReviewing a tranche of documents – witness statements provided to police and the coroner, WhatsApp messages, therapy notes and a council-commissioned safeguarding practice review – a picture emerges of poor communication, missed opportunities to flag risk and an ever-increasing bill. The education guardian was paid a base fee of £2,700 for the year with a £1,500 top-up because of Luna’s additional mental health needs. Soon after appointing her, Luna’s parents asked the education guardian to arrange counselling. She hired Luna’s host to see her for regular counselling sessions at school – a boundary issue the host herself flagged before accepting the role. The education guardian paid her for the sessions, while billing Thomas and Hilda at a higher rate and keeping the difference. This arrangement was not illegal, but it was not disclosed to either the counsellor, or the parents, according to the safeguarding review. The education guardian told the inquest that she asked the counsellor to produce summary reports about Luna every other month, which were “sent straight to the parents”. One later homestay host overheard Luna voicing thoughts of ending her life, and told the education guardian they wanted her to leave. The safeguarding review found that the education guardian did not convey this to Thomas, Hilda or Luna, instead giving “a false reason”. On other occasions, when families did not want to take Luna back, the review said that the education guardian recorded having “pretended the host family was unwell and/or away”. Thomas and Hilda say the result was that they did not understand how acute their daughter’s crisis was.It was only after Luna’s death that her parents saw how stern the education guardian could be. In one troubling WhatsApp exchange in the middle of October 2022, Luna wrote to her to say that another pupil had hit her. It was a Saturday night and the education guardian agreed to raise it with the school on Monday, before pivoting, saying she was worried that Luna would be asked to leave Wrekin because of her mental health issues. She forwarded Luna an internal email the school had sent her, a safeguarding update saying Luna had described having “a mental breakdown”. She told Luna that the language she was using suggested she needed to “go back to Hong Kong” or be in a medical facility, concluding: “This is no joke.” When Luna protested that she was trying her best, and that she had been out of school for two years, the education guardian replied: “You are in someone else country and they are [not] going to learn chinese way to orbit around you.” And then: “You need to see a doctor or counsellor. I am only a guardian.” Shortly after 11pm, the education guardian said she was going to bed and stopped responding. Luna sent increasingly agitated messages into the silence, switching between English and Cantonese: “I trusted you. And now you’re just throwing stuff back at me … What do you want? I’m already trying to be a good student, a good daughter.” The education guardian did not reply, although she reported the hitting incident to Wrekin. “Ending the conversation this way, without any follow-up, seems very dangerous for a 16-year-old girl with depression and anxiety,” says Thomas.Luna told her parents she liked school and was making friends. But, in reality, she was struggling. Reading the counsellor’s notes, which Luna’s parents saw for the first time when they were disclosed to the coroner, a pattern emerges: flashes of intense distress – homesickness, panic attacks, despair about falling behind – followed by Luna insisting everything was fine. In early October, the counsellor reported to the school that Luna had spoken openly about self-harm and suicidal thoughts, saying “she felt comforted by the idea of death”. Elsewhere, she stressed that Luna had no plan to act on these feelings, and that in many respects she was a normal teenager. In one session she marvelled at how much pasta and potato English people ate. Teachers found her bright but under-equipped: two years out of the classroom had stripped her of the practical skills needed for academic study, and she froze in tests, sometimes writing almost nothing despite weeks of notice. Her nocturnal hours set her apart, and although she was making friends, other boarders were reluctant to share a room with her. According to the safeguarding review, the housemistress told colleagues she did not think Luna was suited to the boarding school environment. This concern does not appear to have led to any further action; instead, when her end-of-year exams went badly, Wrekin suggested she repeat the year.Luna went home three times that year, and was always happy to see her parents and catch up with friends. On her last trip back, for the May half-term, she arrived with two penguin toys – one for herself and one to comfort Hilda while they were separated. Thomas and Hilda knew Luna was finding things tough, and she stayed longer than planned. Luna was unsure about retaking the year. “We told her that it doesn’t matter, we didn’t want to put any pressure on her,” says Thomas. “We said to her she can stay in Hong Kong to study other things or go back to the UK. It is up to her.” Privately, Hilda hoped her daughter would decide to stay home – she had missed her desperately. Luna’s therapy notes record that, as she weighed whether to return, she felt a strong sense of failure, and was anxious about the cost to her parents of paying for another academic year.” They are tormented by the idea that this is why she decided to give life in the UK one more attempt.Luna’s summer had been on her education guardian’s agenda for a long time; she had recommended a summer course in psychology. Hoping it might help Luna get into university, her parents signed up. Called the Young Psychologist Summer Experience, it was a two-week residential course in London that cost £6,740. The education guardian told Thomas and Hilda via WhatsApp that it was “organise[d] by UCL”; “They will be staying inside the uni accommodation and their facilities and more. excellent program.” It was true that Luna would stay in University of London accommodation, but that was where the affiliation ended. The course was actually run by InvestIN, a private company selling what it calls “immersive career experiences” to teenagers. The education guardian was paid a commission by InvestIN for referring Luna. This arrangement was not illegal, but it was not disclosed to Thomas and Hilda, according to the safeguarding review. Residential summer programmes catering to international students are big business, and are even less regulated than guardianship. The adults who run them must be DBS-checked – but for children over the age of eight, there are no statutory minimum standards for the setting itself, and no inspection regime of the kind that governs schools.As with Luna’s therapy, the education guardian handled everything related to her stint with InvestIN. Rather than disclosing Luna’s mental health problems early so that risk could be assessed and support put in place, she waited until just before the course began and emailed a letter from Luna’s psychiatrist to a member of InvestIN’s team. An email sent by the education guardian on 5 July, the day before the course, was read out at the inquest: “She is a recover [sic] mental health patient and she worry people will reject her.” She did not mention that Luna had been flown home six weeks earlier due to her deteriorating mental health. Later, she would tell the independent reviewer that she was “worried that [Luna] would not be accepted on the programme due to the medication she had”. Hilda is bewildered by this decision. “If InvestIN couldn’t handle my daughter’s mental health problems, it didn’t matter,” she says. “She could have come back to Hong Kong.” At the inquest, the education guardian said that when she described Luna to InvestIN as “a recover mental health patient” she meant she had improved, rather than that she was fully recovered. She also said she had asked the counsellor to help Luna with the pre-enrolment form detailing her medications, but that the form had never reached InvestIN for reasons she couldn’t explain.On 6 July 2023, Luna arrived at University of London halls in King’s Cross with a large bag of psychiatric medication, and filled in the pre-enrolment form herself. At Wrekin, her medication had been looked after by the school nurse, and Luna visited twice a day to take it. InvestIN had only recently started offering residential courses and did not have processes in place for medication. Instead, they emailed Luna’s parents in Hong Kong to ask for their permission to let her handle the drugs herself. Thomas was alarmed, but as he understood it Luna would not be able to take part in the course without this consent. He agreed. Luna was taken to her room on the seventh floor, with all her medication and no provision to support her.double quotation markWe were so shocked that our daughter was not missed for two days. They accepted the money, but they didn’t take care of my childView image in fullscreenLuna on Stanley main beach in Hong Kong, 2020, age 14.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongLuna was unhappy almost immediately. She told her parents the course was useless, but they didn’t have a sense of an impending crisis. She talked excitedly about the summer ahead in Hong Kong, jokily warning her parents that various packages were arriving for her at home: a textbook; some earrings. She called Thomas to say she’d found a great second-hand bookshop, asking if there was anything he’d like, and said she’d buy him a UCL T-shirt since he’d never had the opportunity to study in the UK. But separately she was texting the counsellor. As the course progressed, she described low mood, anger, numbness and insomnia. The counsellor shared these messages with the education guardian, who told the inquest she “forwarded it immediately” to Thomas and Hilda. On the afternoon of 11 July, Luna told her counsellor she wanted to leave. Thomas and Hilda say Luna’s desire to leave was not communicated to them, though the education guardian told the inquest “I think I did tell it” to the parents. On 11 July, she replied to the counsellor saying that Luna could go home but would have to tell her parents herself. Asked at the inquest why she had not arranged for Luna to leave the course, the education guardian responded: “The student has to be the one to request that. I can’t actually tell the parents, ‘Pull her out now.’ Who is going to pay the money back?”Luna’s counsellor told the inquest that Luna did not believe her parents would be happy about her leaving the summer school early. This was painful for Thomas and Hilda to hear.When Luna didn’t turn up for her sessions the next day, it didn’t trigger alarm. InvestIN would later tell the coroner’s court that its systems were failing that week, giving inaccurate attendance data. Still, it was flagged on a staff WhatsApp group that Luna hadn’t turned up, and at lunchtime on 12 July someone knocked on her door. There was no answer, and they left it at that. It was only around 3pm the next day that another staff member went to Luna’s room with a master key. She unlocked the room and found Luna dead; it later emerged that she had taken an overdose of prescription medication. It had been more than 40 hours since she was last seen alive.It was late in the evening in Hong Kong when Thomas and Hilda got the call from InvestIN informing them that Luna was in an ambulance and “not breathing any more”. Within a few hours, they had booked flights to London and left home, arriving the next day. As they travelled, Thomas thought of his daughter’s longstanding habit of sleeping through her alarm in the mornings. Whenever she was home, he saw himself as a kind of human alarm clock, going into Luna’s room to gently shake her awake. As they travelled towards her, he prayed for a miracle, that he would be able to wake her up one last time. When they got there, it was painfully clear. “This miracle does not come,” he tells me, tears rolling down his face. “I have done it for the last time.”They were in shock, in a country neither had visited before, navigating an unimaginable situation in a second language. Information and queries were relayed to them second-hand via the education guardian. “In the UK, we lost all the connection. We didn’t know what to do or how to do it,” says Thomas. Their isolation was so profound that, astonishingly, it was not even conveyed to them that Luna had lain undiscovered for two days. They only found this out months later, when the coroner’s court sent them a full tranche of witness statements and documents ahead of the January 2024 inquest. It is difficult to overstate how distressing this discovery was. Hilda felt like the floor had opened beneath her. She remains tormented by the idea that earlier intervention might have saved Luna. “We were so shocked that our daughter was not missed for two days,” says Hilda. “They accepted the money, but they didn’t take care of my child. We cannot forgive ourselves for letting her go to this summer school.”The coroner concluded that Luna died by suicide. In her determination, she flagged that in the UK Luna had never been referred to a mental health team or been assessed by a clinician, instead continuing with medication prescribed in Hong Kong. Luna had refused to consent to one referral in September, and the adults around her treated that as the end of the matter; the safeguarding review found it should not have been, because the risk to Luna outweighed her unwillingness to engage. At the hearing, the coroner pressed the counsellor on why Luna’s overwhelming anxiety about the sacrifice her father had made to send her to the UK by cashing in his pension was not more central to their sessions. She said she didn’t have any direct contact with Luna’s parents, but assumed they knew how much she was struggling. Later, she defended her clinical approach, but under further questioning conceded: “I think if someone believed that she was going to take her own life then, yes, someone should have taken her to A&E. But I don’t think anyone believed that she was going to end her life.”double quotation mark‘We lost all our hope for the future,’ Thomas says. ‘Life has become meaningless’View image in fullscreenAge 15 with her parents at in Hong Kong in 2022, the year she moved to the UK.Photograph: Courtesy of Thomas and Hilda WongWrekin College told the Guardian that Luna was “a much-loved and valued member of our community” whose death continues to have “a profound impact” on the school. InvestIN said its “thoughts remain with Luna’s parents, family and friends”, and that it had accepted the findings of two independent reviews and the inquest, putting in place “enhanced safeguarding protocols” as a result. Neither addressed the specific findings put to them. The education guardian and Luna’s counsellor did not respond to our request for comment.For the first year after Luna’s death, Thomas cried every time he ate, thinking of his daughter and the food he cooked for her. “We lost all our hope for the future,” he tells me. “Life has become meaningless.” Still, three years later, he stays at home much of the time, not wanting to socialise or engage with the world. Luna is everywhere in their apartment. The penguin toy is still next to the bed. “It’s three years ago, but it’s like it happened yesterday,” says Hilda. “We know she has left us, but it’s hard to accept the truth.”They are angry about what happened to Luna and how the systems set up to keep her safe failed. The safeguarding review into her death recommended, among other things, statutory regulation of the guardianship sector, a multi-agency approach to vulnerable international children, and clear rules for residential summer programmes. But it was published in 2024, as the government changed, and nothing has been enacted. There have been some smaller changes: InvestIN now has a policy of keeping children’s medication in a locked cabinet, and getting staff to administer it. Aegis, the accreditation body, has tightened its criteria to insist that guardians meet students within the first fortnight regardless of their package. But there is still no statutory regulation of guardians or residential summer schools.Luna’s funeral was held at Telford crematorium on 10 August, near the school where she had spent her only year in England. It was the summer holidays, but more than 20 staff members and a handful of students came; Hilda remembers sunlight streaming in through large windows. Wrekin planted an oak tree for her, and held a memorial service during term‑time. But beyond that, Luna’s parents feel her death went painfully unseen. “She just disappeared,” says Thomas, “and nobody in the UK noticed.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMental healthDepressionSocial exclusionHealthPrivate schoolsInternational studentsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conference | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: UK prime minister says delivering fiscal stability would be ‘crucial’ to be able to fix bigger problems
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: UK prime minister says delivering fiscal stability would be ‘crucial’ to be able to fix bigger problems
Content: 1:02Andy Burnham 'prepared' to deliver radical change despite economic challenges – videoAndy Burnham‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conferenceExclusive: UK prime minister says delivering fiscal stability would be ‘crucial’ to be able to fix bigger problemsPippa CrerarPolitical editorSat 26 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite severe economic headwinds, telling the Guardian: “There’s always things you can do; it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”The prime minister acknowledged public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government limited room for manoeuvre.Andy Burnham announces new homes scheme for first-time buyersRead moreAhead of his firstLabour conferenceas prime minister, however, Burnham sought to reassure voters he was willing to make tough decisions to deliver change and show the markets he could ensure fiscal stability while preparing the groundwork for more substantial change ahead.Speaking to the Guardian on the eve of his first conference asLabourleader, he said: “The public would have more respect for us if we go and grab something difficult … and say, ‘Right, we’re going to do something here’, rather than constantly playing the political game before fixing the problems.“It’s challenging, definitely, but there are still things that you can do. Always in politics, there are things that you can do. The question is sometimes: Are you prepared to do them? Yeah, I am prepared to do them.”When asked about the need for a large fiscal buffer against shocks, he said the key thing was stability, indicating that he understood the need to reassure the markets, but that more radical transformation of the state would follow.“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances,” he said.“You have to have stability, but you have to do what you can within that. You can’t pursue a major programme of change, which is what I believe the country needs, in a chaotic situation.”After ruling out holding a snap general election before 2029, Burnham said he wanted to set out a clear path for how the country could move to a better place – and that he hadn’t been spending his time “sitting politicking and strategising” but instead was focused on fixing problems.His ambition to give people “a bit more belief that things can improve” across the country, he said, would not come from “endlessly running elections and referendums”.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham arrives with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, ahead of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, north-west England, on 26 September.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesHe denied having had discussions with his senior team about whether to call an early election. “The speculation in no way matches the internal discussion because there isn’t one,” he said, rejecting claims he did not have a mandate as the public had voted for the Labour party.However, Burnham acknowledged he was hemmed in on tax and the fiscal rules of Keir Starmer’s manifesto commitments, and suggested he would have done it differently had he been in charge at the time.“I’ve inherited those positions and, as I say, I think the main thing for me is to focus on the here and now for people, not to be self-serving about ‘oh, what would suit me?’ and playing politics. That’s not where my mind is, and possibly would have framed it different, but we are where we are, you know, and that’s the reality.”Burnham played down speculation that Labour may give more support for energy bills, with the price cap set to soar from January. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” he said, referring to VAT on electricity bills being scrapped from next week.The prime minister also reiterated that while he thought the welfare bill was too high, the will among Labour MPs was “not there for crude cuts” because they would push people into crisis, so a longer-term approach to reform was required.After warning of the risks, as well as the opportunities of artificial intelligence at the UN last week, Burnham admitted to concerns about rogue AI agents attacking state institutions in the UK, after the Australian medicare system was hit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe tricky tests awaiting Andy Burnham after Labour conferenceRead moreBurnham addressed the presence of far-right protesters on the streets of Britain, accusing Daniel Thomas, who hasled black-clad anti-migrant vigilantes on the streets of some English towns, of “creating fear” but did not go as far as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, who accused him of being an “outright racist”.Speaking of Thomas’s masked gangs, he said: “I mean that’s not Britain. That’s not what we want to see in people’s communities. There’s legitimate concerns about issues, and then there is intimidation – and that is intimidation,” he said.The prime minister also addressed political funding, which has been in the spotlight sinceReform UK received two record-breaking £36m donations from cryptocurrency billionaires, saying that – contrary to reports – he would not rule out a domestic donations cap.“You know I think we do need to continue to have a cross-party discussion about how do we uphold trust in politics? How do we not give the impression that politics can be bought and that people are, if you like, unduly influenced?”He was also open to looking at election spending limits, he said, which are now being examined by the Electoral Commission, adding that he has “real concerns” about crypto-fuelled politics.An emotional Burnham revealed that the death of his father, Roy, last week had made him more determined to deliver. “I’m in this job for what I can do for people, not for what it can do for me … to make the changes that my dad, for instance, long pushed me to make,” he said.“It’s been a hard thing, if I’m honest, coming into this position in the last three months when I also knew in my heart that I was starting this journey as my dad was ending his.From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in chartsRead more“Although that’s hard, and I’m not seeking sympathy in saying it, I say it because the coming together of those two things increases my determination to make a difference on the things that I’ve long said I want to fix.”With political courage expected to be a focus of his speech to Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he was willing to be honest with the public about what needed to happen, even if it was difficult to hear.“I think the public want to see, number one, honesty about things. So not spin or putting things a certain way that’s self-serving. They want honesty, and then they want, I think, difficult but real decisions,” said Burnham.“Not difficult decisions and making a fetish out of that, but actually grasping nettles and then moving things forward. I don’t think politics has been prepared to do that enough in recent times.”Burnham criticised previous governments for failing to tackle difficult issues such as social care, housing supply and youth unemployment, saying longer-term reform was needed because there were no “easy or quick wins”.He revealed there would be a new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” the keys to their own home. It will be funded by reallocating existing budgets, although it is unclear which ones, rather than through extra borrowing.Burnham also said he wanted to deliver significant progress on social care reform – a manifesto commitment – before the next election. “Who is going to do something to actually make it real? I’m saying to you that I am going to address this directly.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourLabour conferenceLabour conference 2026Economic policyBudgetUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
Content: People walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersMiddle East and north AfricaTrump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of HormuzUS president is said to expect renewed strikes after midtermsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS presidentDonald Trumphas said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.The US president was earlier said to be privately scepticalIranwould meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.Meanwhile, on Friday evening, hepublisheda post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.During a three-hour meeting at theUN general assemblyin New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”View image in fullscreenIran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, left, with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, at the UN general assembly in New York on Friday.Photograph: Caitlin Ochs/ReutersIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midtermsRead moreThe US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersSince then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and APExplore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaIranUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpUS foreign policyStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead after ban overturned | Northern Irish politics | The Guardian
description: Orange Order march along Garvaghy Road could take place for first time in 28 years after injunction dismissed on appeal
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Orange Order march along Garvaghy Road could take place for first time in 28 years after injunction dismissed on appeal
Content: The Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition and their legal team arrive at the high court in Belfast on Saturday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAView image in fullscreenThe Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition and their legal team arrive at the high court in Belfast on Saturday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PANorthern Irish politicsLoyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead after ban overturnedOrange Order march along Garvaghy Road could take place for first time in 28 years after injunction dismissed on appealLisa O’CarrollandHarry TaylorSat 26 Sep 2026 19.40 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA controversial loyalist parade along a nationalist street in Portadown could go ahead for the first time in nearly 30 years, after a ban was overturned late on Saturday night.The Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Road will be allowed to go ahead on Sunday morning, following a legal back-and-forth in recent days amid fears the march could unleash fresh sectarian violence.Earlier on Saturday, after a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court, Justice Smyth had issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, which was due to take place at 8am on Sunday.Smyth had urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”.But at 11.30pm on Saturday, at a sitting of the Court of Appeals, Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan said the High Court judge who granted an injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”.The march down Garvaghy Road had been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.“It is also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland,” Smyth had said earlier in the day.“Be big enough to step back from the abyss,” she had told the parties in court.Michelle O’Neill, first minister of Northern Ireland, said after the appeal decision late on Saturday: “The decision tonight to overturn the court ruling, and force an unwanted orange march through the Garvaghy Road is disgraceful.“This march is steeped in a history of hate, sectarian violence, and murder, and championed by Unionist leaders.“Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever. Sinn Féin stands fully with the Garvaghy Road community, and they have the full support of people from right across Ireland in the period ahead.”View image in fullscreenPeople gathered outside Belfast high court on Saturday 26 September awaiting the decision by Justice Smyth over the planned Garvaghy Road march.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PATheSDLP leader, Claire Hanna, said the parade plan was “provocative”. She told residents she was “so sorry” that some “bad faith actors” were “intent on reopening the hurt and the traumas of the past”.Fears of clashes increased on Saturday after a request to the commission for permission for a countermarch, a protest that, it was estimated, could be attended by up to 5,000 people, the court heard. That was later revised to 300.On Friday night, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, appealed to leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend while the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, called for “cool heads”, saying Northern Ireland had “withstood many moments of sharp disagreement over the years” and must do so again.Before her ruling, Smyth had asked the parties in court, including thePoliceService of Northern Ireland and the Parades Commission, to “consider carefully the very important issues to our society” raised in this case, and the importance that they were dealt with properly given the “importance of this case to community relations”.She also noted that the issues of judicial review were of “such fundamental importance” that it could be unwise to hold a full hearing without all the facts.Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart insisted nationalist residents on the road had “nothing to fear” from the march on Sunday, but Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the decision as “utterly reckless”.The Parades Commission placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including an 8am start and limiting the number of participants to 35 people, but did not impose any restrictions on the route.Explore more on these topicsNorthern Irish politicsNorthern IrelandProtestPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has attempted to dismiss the club’s guilty verdict as ‘noise’
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has attempted to dismiss the club’s guilty verdict as ‘noise’
Content: The Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has maintained the club’s defiant tone after they were found guilty on almost all counts of breaching the league’s financial regulations.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenThe Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has maintained the club’s defiant tone after they were found guilty on almost all counts of breaching the league’s financial regulations.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityManchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict‘We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed’Maresca quotes Socrates on social media – ‘I know nothing’Jamie JacksonSat 26 Sep 2026 10.52 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKhaldoon al-Mubarak, the Manchester City chair, has spoken for the first time since the club wasfound guilty on virtually all countsof breaching Premier League financial rules. He said “nothing has changed” and “our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began”.News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by thePremier Leaguein February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.How drawn-out saga of Manchester City’s alleged cheating came to thisRead moreThe club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when al-Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of theManchester Cityfamily. Thank you, as always, for your constant support.”View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak (right) has been Manchester City’s chair since the Abu Dhabi takeover of the club from Thaksin Shinawatra (left) in 2008.Photograph: Nigel Roddis/ReutersEarlier, City’s manager,Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”.On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence. The Guardian was sent by his representatives a screenshot of a quote attributed to Socrates, the Greek philosopher, which Maresca posted on Instagram.The quote reads: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Maresca also wrote: “Time to breathe. Time to analyse. Time to learn.”Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?Read moreElsewhere, there wwere contrasting reactions to the outcome of the Premier League investigation. Oasis’Noel Gallagher, a longtime City fan, described his shock at the news, while the club’s former chair David Bernstein believes any potential punishment should not be only financial. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, described the case as unsettling.On the Let Me Talk podcast, Gallagher said: “A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really just quite sad. Sad for the fans and for the players.”View image in fullscreenNoel Gallagher, a longtime Manchester City fan, maintains that even if the guilty verdict stands, the club’s fans will not feel any differently about their success.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesAsked if it changes the context of moments like Sergio Agüero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher said: “Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw.“Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch. Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans.“Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.”Bernstein, City’s chair from 1998-2003, told Times Radio: “I felt absolutely awful, I felt in shock yesterday. You’ve asked me on the programme because of my time as chair of City and the FA, but basically I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rightsRead more“When I was chair I think I helped get the club out of a very difficult period and started the road to better things. But to see all this tarnished in this way is very sad.“I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who’ve stayed with the club through thick and thin. It’s a pretty bad day for the fans in blue of Manchester.”As for the correct punishment, Bernstein said: “First of all, the timing is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process has to be done quickly because you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable.“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, that would be a disaster. Not just for this particular case, but for English football generally.“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”Manchester City guilty verdict ‘a historic decision’, says whistleblower Rui PintoRead moreOn BBC Radio 5 Live, Nandy said: “Most football fans will be feeling this is not a good moment for football as a whole and Manchester City fans will be feeling very anxious about what happens next. This is a really longstanding investigation, it dates all the way back to allegations that begin in 2009.“The football fans need to know the rules are applied fairly and consistently, they need to know they’re upheld and they need to know the right decision has been reached.“We do have a way to go with this, it’s very unsettling for football fans and I hope it can be resolved as swiftly as possible.”Nigel Huddleston, who was the shadow secretary of state for culture until last month, said on social media: “Whatever the next steps are, they must be conducted in an accelerated and more transparent manner or risk further damage to the reputation and integrity of English football and more unnecessary anxiety for millions of football fans.”A City spokesperson said on Friday: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.”In that statement, City said they had a ‘comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence’ of their innocence.Friday’s statement from City continued: “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaNoel GallagherPremier LeagueLisa NandynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ranulph Fiennes’ stepson appeals for funds to ‘locate and safeguard’ the explorer | Ranulph Fiennes | The Guardian
description: Alexander Millington-Cotes is concerned for welfare of the 82-year-old, who hasn’t been seen in public for two years
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Alexander Millington-Cotes is concerned for welfare of the 82-year-old, who hasn’t been seen in public for two years
Content: Ranulph Fiennes pictured in 2015: the explorer, writer and holder of several endurance records hasn’t been seen in public for more than two years.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRanulph Fiennes pictured in 2015: the explorer, writer and holder of several endurance records hasn’t been seen in public for more than two years.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianRanulph FiennesRanulph Fiennes’ stepson appeals for funds to ‘locate and safeguard’ the explorerAlexander Millington-Cotes is concerned for welfare of the 82-year-old, who hasn’t been seen in public for two yearsGeraldine McKelvieSat 26 Sep 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe stepson of SirRanulph Fienneshas launched a crowdfunder to pay for “specialist legal advice” in an attempt to locate the explorer, who hasn’t been seen in public for more than two years.Alexander Millington-Cotes, 31, has set a target of £55,000 for the fundraiser, to enable him to instruct lawyers to “locate and safeguard” Fiennes.Millington-Cotes’ mother, Louise, from whom he is estranged, has lasting power of attorney in relation to Fiennes’ care, which her son wants to see revoked.Friends and family are growing increasingly concerned for the welfare of the renowned expedition leader, who is 82 and has Parkinson’s disease.It is understood that Louise, Fiennes’ second wife, has installed him in a succession of care homes where he has not been allowed to receive visitors.According to the Telegraph, the former soldier had previously spent time in a care home in Wales under a pseudonym. It reported a watchdog had concluded his living arrangements amounted to a deprivation of his liberty because his wife had failed to ensure adequate legal safeguards were in place.The newspaper also said that Fiennes, widely considered the world’s greatest living explorer, had spent time in another care home in London, where visitors were apparently asked to sign non-disclosure agreements by Louise, 59, before being allowed to see him.Arabella McIntyre-Brown, sister of Fiennes’ late first wife, Ginny, said she was so concerned about his welfare that she checked into the London home for a week in an attempt to speak to him. She told the Telegraph that he expressed a wish to see his friends.View image in fullscreenRanulph Fiennes with his first wife, Ginny, in 1971. She died in 2004.Photograph: PAMillington-Cotes’ crowdfunder had raised almost £3,000 on Saturday afternoon. He told supporters: “Ran has spent his entire life pushing boundaries for others and representing the best of human endurance. Now, he needs us to fight for him.”He added that donations would cover “specialist legal representation and advice”, court fees and the cost of “determining [Fiennes’] exact location, to be shared with the relevant authorities”.Millington-Cotes said he had a difficult relationship with his mother, who told him he was unwelcome at the family home two years ago.About this time, Fiennes, the first person to cross Antarctica on foot, failed to appear at a gala evening organised in his honour at the Royal Geographical Society in Kensington, west London.Instead, he delivered a brief, prerecorded message from home, saying he was “not well enough” to attend in person. He has not been seen publicly since.Millington-Cotes alleged that he had been forced to visit his stepfather in secret after the breakdown of his relationship with his mother.“Since being asked to leave the family home and not come back, I can only imagine the amplification of Ran’s difficulties and isolation,” he said.“His isolation would consist of being effectively annexed in the other end of the house, with relatively minimal contact.“I remember him gleaming the occasional times I would appear unannounced with some sweet treats, which I’d had to haul with me as I climbed over the seven-foot industrial entrance gate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The last time I saw Ran was when he whisked me away while I was walking up the drive on one of my infrequent visits, sadly neither him or I realised that it may be the last time we’d see and hug one another.View image in fullscreenRanulph Fiennes in Aconcagua, Argentina, in 2017 in a still from Explorer, the documentary about him.Photograph: David Carter/©DavidCarter/FieldcraftStudios“This is the moment he told me he was proud of me, a sweet moment in my memory.”He said that, over the past two years, he had “tried multiple avenues” in an effort to locate his stepfather, whom his mother married in 2005.Ginny, to whom Fiennes was married for 34 years, had died of cancer the previous year. Louise gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, in 2006, Fiennes’ only biological child.Explorer review – compelling portrait of adventurer Ranulph FiennesRead moreWhile Millington-Cotes described his stepfather as “a man of immense heart, kindness, and selflessness who supported me for years”, he said his strained relationship with Louise had caused him “great pain and distress”.“Upon learning from other friends and family that Ran was considered missing, I put aside my own pain and immediately felt anger,” he said. “Anger that similar experiences I’d had were now being cast on to Ran. A man for as long as I could remember was completely selfless, kind and abided by an excellent moral code.”He added that he had visited various care homes hoping to find Fiennes “to have a simple conversation with him, or to be able to take him for a brief coffee”, but had so far been unsuccessful and had “left with a feeling of dismay and a slightly emptier heart”.Millington-Cotes said that any excess funds would be donated to Marie Curie and the British Heart Foundation, favoured charities of Fiennes.Explore more on these topicsRanulph FiennesSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty miss | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane missed a penalty at 2-1 to England and then Spain recovered with goals from Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal as the world champions won 3-2
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Harry Kane missed a penalty at 2-1 to England and then Spain recovered with goals from Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal as the world champions won 3-2
Content: Mikel Oyarzabal calmly chips James Trafford to make it 3-2 to Spain at Wembley.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenMikel Oyarzabal calmly chips James Trafford to make it 3-2 to Spain at Wembley.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANations LeagueOyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty missDavid Hytnerat WembleySat 26 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was another high-profile game when Thomas Tuchel’sEnglandlet a lead slip in the second half and went on to lose. But unlike the last time, it was not one for recriminations. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust. More to the point, they can accept losing to Spain who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.England were game. They were driven by Jude Bellingham, who ran on adrenaline and played to the point of maximum expression. They had positive surges either side of the interval, especially the one towards the end of the first half when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them in charge, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.Thomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdictRead moreThe biggest takeaway was Spain’s slickness. There is a reason why they won the World Cup in the summer. Why they won the European Championship before that. They are the best team in the international game by a distance. Nobody can live with them. England did well to stay within a puncher’s chance of a result in thisNations Leagueopener; Bellingham was still throwing them in stoppage time. Crucially, as Tuchel and England try to look forward after the heartbreak of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina, there was no negativity from the Wembley crowd. Even in the face of England’s defending, which was dreadfully loose.We were denied the chance to see how the fans would react to the announcement of Tuchel’s name when the teams were read out in the countdown to kick-off. Because, after going through the starting XI and the 12 substitutes, Tuchel’s name was not read out. But there were none of the dreaded boos at the full-time whistle.The match turned on a Kane penalty miss in the 54th minute. Had the captain scored rather than hitting the crossbar after his standing foot gave way in the turf, England would have been 3-1 up. Shortly afterwards, they were pegged back to 2-2 by theSpainsubstitute Álex Baena and there was a degree of inevitability about the winner from another replacement. Mikel Oyarzabal’s dinked finish was impudently brilliant. Spain had been fantastic for the opening 30 minutes and when they went again after the Kane penalty, they had too much. It was a statement of intent from them, an illustration of their remorseless desire.“Campeones” was the chant from the enclosure housing the travelling fans before kick-off and it is fair to say the visiting radio commentators were excited about seeing Spain for the first time since the second star was stitched on to their shirt. Their fervour went up a few notches in the early running when Lamine Yamal opened the scoring.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s left foot gives away as he takes the penalty. He hit the crossbar and the ball bounced out to safety.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe goal was a personal disaster for Marc Guéhi; it was almost as if the Manchester City defender had other things on his mind. It was of a piece with England’s struggles against the Spanish press. Guéhi was facing upfield as he tried to build a move from deep but his passing lanes were blocked. So he checked back and walked straight into Lamine Yamal, who robbed him and was clean through. He made the finish past James Trafford look easy.Tuchel had started Trafford ahead of Jordan Pickford, a major deviation from his stated intention for continuity from the World Cup. Pickford was erratic in the summer and was punished for some of his mistakes. Trafford has been outstanding for Leeds since joining them over the summer. Tuchel’s idea is to share the minutes between Trafford and Pickford during this window. Trafford could hear the knock of opportunity and he helped to keep England in the game as Spain pushed to add to Lamine Yamal’s goal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeet the new 55 minute England collapse, not the same as the old 55 minute England collapse | Barney RonayRead moreHow Spain pushed. They shimmered with menace. It was the movements, the speed of them – plus the breathtaking assurance on the ball. They had so many options in possession that it felt at times as if they had more men on the pitch.Ferran Torres had the ball in the net only to be pulled back for offside while Trafford stood up to make a big one-on-one block against the Spain striker after Lamine Yamal had played the through-ball. England’s backline was all over the place. Torres blew another one-on-one on 28 minutes, with Trafford making himself big while Dani Olmo rifled just wide after a sumptuous Lamine Yamal flick.England tried to throw counterpunches as they hung on. The resistance was impressive. Gordon was to the fore and so was Bellingham. They showed their personality when the chips were down. When the two combined for an equaliser that had not really been advertised, it was the prompt for a wild turnaround.It was Spain pushing only for Nico Williams to lose his footing and then the ball to Elliot Anderson. England swept forward in thrilling style, Gordon flicking to Bellingham, getting it back and surging in on goal. The low finish was nerveless.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane (on the ground) watches his header come off the thigh of Marc Cucurella to make it it 2-1 to England.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnter Kane. He was unlucky when he banged inches wide from the edge of the area after a Bukayo Saka burst. He was lucky when his header from a Nico O’Reilly cross, which Unai Simón looked to have covered, drew a panicked reaction from Marc Cucurella. The left-back jutted out his thigh to turn the ball past his goalkeeper. The fates were against Cucurella. When his mishit cross on 45 minutes sailed over Trafford, the ball came back off the far post.Bellingham appeared particularly determined to leave his imprint. The Real Madrid midfielder was in the mood for bragging rights back in La Liga. It was the power and directness of his running; the smoothness of it, the quickness of his moves. Spain could not contain him. It was his persistence after yet another surge that led to the penalty.Gordon played the pass back inside from the left and Bellingham got there before Rodri, who invited trouble when he hung out a leg. Down went Bellingham and after a review, it was decided that the contact trumped the feeling that the England player had tried to engineer it. Kane could not convert.Back came Spain. Lamine Yamal pushed a shot wide after a give and go with Baena, whose backheel was beautiful. Then Baena equalised after O’Reilly gave away the ball and Olmo quickly shifted it to the edge of the area. Baena bought himself the space for the shot with an expert drop of the shoulder.Saka curled just wide at the other end after more good work by Bellingham but the tide had turned. You could not take your eyes off Lamine Yamal while Luis de la Fuente’s attack-minded changes worked. It was Oyarzabal who made the difference from a Baena pass. England could have no complaints.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueEnglandSpainmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Content: Pope Leo waves to the crowd from his popemobile on the Champs-Élysées before celebrating mass in Paris.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo waves to the crowd from his popemobile on the Champs-Élysées before celebrating mass in Paris.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersFrancePope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in ParisCrowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 yearsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit toFrance.The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.View image in fullscreenWorshippers gather at the Place de la Concorde for Pope Leo’s open-air mass.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesBut cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promoteCatholicismand its teachings.It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.View image in fullscreenPope Leo greets crowds lining the Champs-Élysées on the second day of his visit to France.Photograph: Kiran Ridley/AFP/Getty ImagesThe security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.View image in fullscreenPope Leo delivered an outdoor mass to an estimated 700,000 people in Paris.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesAbout 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”Explore more on these topicsFrancePope Leo XIVEuropeThe papacyCatholicismChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us | Global development | The Guardian
description: Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear
Author: Tess McClure
Headline: Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear
Content: Alaa Hessi amid the rubble of her home, destroyed by an Israeli strike that also killed her three children. Since being interviewed, Alaa has given birth to a boy she named Waseem, after one of her sons who died.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlaa Hessi amid the rubble of her home, destroyed by an Israeli strike that also killed her three children. Since being interviewed, Alaa has given birth to a boy she named Waseem, after one of her sons who died.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal developmentWe followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell usBehind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hearSupported byAbout this contentTess McClureSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTShareWhat does it take to make a morning cup of tea inGaza?ForAlaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.For12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, whenaid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.View image in fullscreenRamadan on the beach at Al-Nuwairi, near Nuseirat, where he lives in a tent among the dunes.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianMost of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.Read more from the seriesThere is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, decidinghow many caloriesit will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans aplethora of ordinary objectsfrom entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.View image in fullscreenRajab al-Reefi, leader of Gaza Skate Team, helps other team-members to repair some boards.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianFrom the story ofRajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.View image in fullscreenMansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem in front of the flat-bed truck that is now her home.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianStill, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human.Prof Mahmoud Seydamwires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike.Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.You can readall five of their days here.

title: I was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in me | Australian books | The Guardian
description: As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety
Content: Australian tennis player Evonne Goolagong competes at the Queen’s Club in London, circa 1970.Photograph: Aubrey Hart/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralian tennis player Evonne Goolagong competes at the Queen’s Club in London, circa 1970.Photograph: Aubrey Hart/Getty ImagesAustralian booksI was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in meAs a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivetyEvonne Goolagong CawleySat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a regular match. Until it wasn’t. In 1969, I was 17 and had been living inSydneywith my tennis coach, Vic Edwards, and his family for several years. I had left my home town of Barellan – on Wirajudjuri country in the Riverina region of New South Wales – to pursue my tennis dreams in the big smoke.The year before, I had finished high school at Willoughby girls high – where I was the only Aboriginal student – and I was doing my secretarial course in the city. The Metropolitan Business College where I studied was conveniently located near the headquarters of the Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs.Was Wrexham’s trailblazing black footballer also the first Indigenous Australian to play overseas?Read moreThe idea for the foundation was to give city-based Aboriginal people a cultural hub where we could come together and find support. I was spending more and more time there with my friends Isabel and Bob, the latter whom I was casually dating.Isabel and Bob were young and lots of fun but they were also acutely aware of the politics of being Black. I was naive to the injustices of Australia – and the world – and I learned a lot from Isabel and the guys at the foundation.At the time, I was focused on a single goal: to become the first Aboriginal tennis champion. To achieve that goal, I had to shut myself off from everything other than tennis. That included politics.View image in fullscreenEvonne Goolagong plays against America’s Chris Evert in the 1972 women’s singles at Wimbledon.Photograph: Roger Jackson/Getty ImagesI was training for my upcoming European tour, and part of program included playing doubles with Vic Edwards’ daughter, Trisha, at the White City badge competition twice a week. Trisha and I had been playing together for years and were quite the pair. We were the “tennis twins”, in our matching dresses, at tournaments.It was during our usual doubles game at White City against two older women that something happened. Trisha and I convincingly won against our opponents, and we went to the net to shake their hands. As we reached over the net, though, one of the ladies turned to her partner and said, “That’s the first time I’ve ever been beaten by a n*****r.”The N-word. I had never been called it before. I went into shock.The word took a moment to sink in. At first, I thought I had misheard. But then Trisha responded with a cutting comment and I knew it was real. Still, the moment felt far away, as though it was happening to someone else.double quotation markSomething had irrevocably changed within me.
