My naivety had been brokenEvonne Goolagong CawleyThe older women left and I remained at the net with Trisha. Suddenly, we were crying. We both stood in the centre of the court, hugging and sobbing. The word had wounded me like a paper cut, innocuous at first, then stinging. I’m not sure why that single word had such a dramatic effect on me. It wasn’t even an Australian slander. The N-word was a cheap, American slur that reminded me of fake soap-opera trash talk. But when it was directed at me, it felt very real. Was this the way it was going to be out there in the mean streets of tennis?Still sobbing, I called the first person I thought of: Isabel at the foundation. Through tears, I told her what happened. “You jump in a taxi and get here right now,” she said.When I arrived, I was greeted by Isabel and Bob. They held me and patted my back as I cried in their arms. Isabel said she had never seen me so upset. We sat around and drank cups of coffee for hours, talking it over. “It’s OK,” Bob told me, kindly. “These things happen to us all the time. You just have to deal with it, and you can. You’re strong.”Something had irrevocably changed within me. My naivety had been broken. The protective bubble my family and the Edwardses had built around me had been smashed. I would move on but I would never be the same innocent young girl.When I got back to the house hours later, Trisha had already relayed the events to Mr Edwards. I was glad to have missed his initial fury at the incident. Mr Edwards – who was quick to anger – was remarkably matter-of-fact. He had informed the NSW LawnTennisAssociation over the phone and was in the middle of writing an official complaint. “We have to deal with this in the proper manner, through the correct channels,” he said.I don’t know what happened as a result of the call or the complaint. But I never saw the woman at White City again.View image in fullscreenAfter that, I spent more and more time at the foundation. My friends there reminded me of my people but not in a way that made me homesick; instead, they gave me a sense of feeling good about being Aboriginal. Proud – that was it! They made me feel proud to be Aboriginal.When I went on to win my first Wimbledon singles tournament two years later in 1971 – becoming the first Aboriginal woman to claim the title – the win was for all Aboriginal people.I like to think I was doing my part in my own way – by breaking new ground, taking up space and inspiring the next generation of hopeful Aboriginal athletes.I hope I have paved the way for our young ones, and that the road is a lot smoother these days.This is an edited extract fromOnly Ever Evonneby Evonne Goolagong Cawley with Alley Pascoe (Allen and Unwin), out 29 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsAustralian booksTennisRaceIndigenous AustraliansAustralia sportSydneyAutobiography and memoirextractsShareReuse this content

title: The truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’ | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implemented
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implemented
Content: An oil pumpjack at Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Venezuela.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn oil pumpjack at Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Venezuela.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersTrump administrationThe truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implementedAram Rostonin WashingtonSat 26 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has long coveted the oilfields of other nations and declared an agreement with Venezuela to be “the biggest oil deal in world history”. But the agreement, reached after the US seized Venezuelan presidentNicolás Maduro, is almost certainly doomed to collapse amid a wide array of legal and logistical issues, a Guardian investigation has found.The US president first mused about taking oil from Iran in 1987, when hetoldABC’s Barbara Walters that Iranian attacks on American shipping during the Iran-Iraq war required an extreme response. “Why couldn’t we go in and take over some of their oil, which is along the sea?” he asked. Over the ensuing years, he has returned frequently to the idea that the US should seize oil from other countries after military conflict, from Libya to Iraq.Earlier this year, Trump finally got a chance to enact his plan – at gunpoint. US forces stormedVenezuelain January and seized Maduro, who was quickly shuttled to a federal holding facility in the US and replaced by the compliant Delcy Rodríguez. Trump told the Atlantic in the days following the raid: “If [Rodríguez] doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro.”Then in August, Trump announced that the office of strategic capital (OSC) at the Pentagon, which he hasrapidly transformed, would own a third of thesecond-biggestprivate Venezuelan oil firm, North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep). Trump said the deal means he’ll soon refill the US strategic petroleum reserve, which dropped to a longtime low after the US invaded Iran.But virtually everything Trump and his cabinet have said about the deal is false and misleading, according to the experts and officials who spoke with the Guardian. The Venezuelan law governing oil development does not allow for 100-year deals, or anything longer than 25 years. The OSC isn’t authorized by US law, experts say, to own shares in companies. Moreover, they say, the deal as structured won’t bring new capital to Venezuela’s oil sector.And contrary to Trump’s claims, the Venezuelan oil will not help refill the US strategic petroleum reserve any time in the near future.There is also a curious figure at the center of the deal: Alejandro Betancourt López, the affable Venezuelan with a complex background who is becoming a partner of the US government as the owner of Nabep.Betancourt, 46, went to college in Massachusetts and has homes in Spain, the UK and New York City. He has a history in Venezuela’s energy and oil sector, owns asunglasses companyand once had Rudy Giuliani as his lawyer.Alejandro Betancourt.Photograph: Alejandro BetancourtBetancourt, who has been drawn into multiple internationalinvestigationsin connection with Venezuelan corruption allegations, was brought into the deal by a private associate of Marco Rubio, according to three people who know him. Betancourt has never been charged with or convicted of any crime.The Guardian has learned that Venezuelan government officials who are now in charge once hired investigators and hackers to dig into the source of Betancourt’s money.Experts are ultimately skeptical the oil deal can hold together.“The deal is like the big beautiful wall that Mexico will pay for,” said former US diplomat John Feeley.‘Skin in the game’It was less than a month after the January US raid that toppled Maduro that Exxon’s CEO, Darren Woods, said the country was “uninvestable” because of the “legal and commercial constructs and frameworks in place today”.Two people familiar with the process said Trump began looking for a way to make sure the US had “skin in the game” – financial ownership that would put investors at ease. The potential answer became the US stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners.Though the White House and defense department say it has 35% ownership, the Pentagon told lawmakers on the congressional armed services committee in a written briefing seen by the Guardian it has “warrants” in Nabep: rights to purchase shares, rather than the shares themselves.The state department, the administration says, will also have a right to buy 20% of all the oil Nabep pumps, at cost – meaning it should be able to buy it cheaper than the market price.“The Departments of State and War have negotiated a historic opportunity to secure US majority control of more than 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela at zero taxpayer cost,” a Pentagon spokesperson said.It’s unclear how the US would buy crude oil, or what the process would be. The state department, for its part, insists: “This is a private deal with a private company. It’s not a deal with the interim government of Venezuela and there was not a political process included in the negotiations.”View image in fullscreenOil platforms and pump jacks in Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersThat appears to be at odds with Trump’s initial announcement, which said: “The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela.” The administration says a majority of the board of Nabep, which is incorporated in Barbados, will be US citizens.The Pentagon ownership has been one of the most puzzling parts of the deal, because the idea that the Department of Defense could own more than a third of a Venezuelan oil company, or any oil company, would have been unthinkable in any previous US administration. Prior to Trump, the defense department had never operated like a private equity fund that could directly own percentages of foreign companies.But the Pentagon has been transformed. The OSC is under the authority of the deputy defense secretary, Stephen Feinberg, a powerful billionaire who wields the real financial power in the Pentagon and has surrounded himself with former employees from the private equity giant Cerberus, as the Guardian hasreported. Feinberg installed a former Cerberus employee, David Lorch, as the head of the OSC.TheTrump administrationis using a 1950s law called the Defense Production Act to allow the Pentagon to become a kind of giant investment fund. “It has turned them into a vehicle for ownership of substantial domestic and international companies,” said the former official.A former Pentagon official familiar with the project said Feinberg and Lorch structured the financial end of Trump’s Venezuela deal. “It is absolutely a Feinberg project,” said the former Pentagon official.However, the law that created the OSC actually didn’t authorize it to make equity investments, and the Pentagon’s spokespersontold Reuters: “The Office of ​Strategic Capital (OSC) ⁠does not take equity stakes in private companies” in August.View image in fullscreenStephen Feinberg testifies during a Senate confirmation hearing on 25 February 2025.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images“Congress clearly doesn’t believe that it has given the power to OSC to make equity investments,” said Ashley Deeks, the vice-dean of the University of Virginia law school, who has written about US government ownership stakes in companies for theHarvard National Security Journal.Since the OSC is not authorized to invest in shares of private companies, the Nabep ownership will be held by an entirely different Pentagon office, calledIndustrial Base Analysis and Sustainment(Ibas), according to the former Pentagon official.But the mission of Ibas has nothing to do with oil. Its job, as it says on its website, is solely to “strengthen the US Defense Industrial Base”.That incongruity is just one of the reasons major oil companies and investors privately say they are keeping clear of this deal, said Phil Gunson of the International Crisis Group, who has been briefed on the problem. “They are concerned about the irregularities. They are concerned about the terms of the deal. It’s the opacity of the agreement that has serious investors concerned,” he said.“Whether the Pentagon has the authority to act in this way is debatable,” he added.The White House directed questions about whether the OSC is authorized to own shares to the defense department. The department didn’t answer emailed questions about the matter. In a statement, a representative merely repeated some prior claims by the administration: it’s a “historic opportunity”, with control over most of Venezuela’s oil reserves.The length of the deal also doesn’t appear to be as long as the administration claims.Venezuelan legal expert Jose Ignacio Hernández says Venezuelan law is crystal clear that this is impossible, and Venezuela’s government itself has said the deal is for 25 years, not 100.“This is all just propaganda,” said Ignacio Hernández. “It cannot be implemented as announced by the administration.”The man in the middleThose who have met Alejandro Betancourt say he is remarkably pleasant and obliging. “He was a really nice guy,” says Lev Parnas, the former Giuliani associate who broke from Maga after his arrest in 2019, and who traveled with Betancourt. “I don’t like too many people but I like him, his wife, his family.”“Betancourt, he’s a good sales guy,” said another American who has known him for years. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told an interviewer in early September that Betancourt had a “track record” of producing oil.Some view him as an effective businessman who can deal with a variety of administrations and has experience both in energy and oil deals.In 2012, Betancourt bought El Alamín castle in Spain, a vast estate with its own tennis court and soccer field, according to aerial photos. The castle has become a venue to host meetings with prominent business leaders and politicians,El País reported.Betancourt has been a subject ofscandalfor well over a decade.Public scrutinyof him first emerged in the US in 2013, when a former US ambassador to Venezuela, Otto Reich, laid out a series of allegations in a civil lawsuit, including violations of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (Rico) Act, which targets organized crime, and defamation, in New York federal court. Along with his partners in a company called Derwick Associates, Betancourt made his money in building electrical plants in contracts he won by kickbacks, according to Reich’s complaint. The Rico claims were dismissed when the court found that Reich failed to establish a legal “pattern of racketeering”, and the defamation claims were rejected for lack of jurisdiction.In a letter to the Guardian, Betancourt’s lawyer Vel Freedman wrote: “Neither Derwick nor Mr Betancourt ever asked, directed, or encouraged anyone to pay a bribe.”In 2018, Betancourt’s cousin, a business partner also affiliated with Derwick, was charged in a $1.2bn money-laundering case in federal court in Miami. An affidavit submitted by an agent with Homeland Security Investigations cited an unnamed “conspirator 2”, who he said received hundreds of millions in laundered funds with the cousin, who is still a fugitive in the case.The Miami Heraldreportedit was Betancourt. In a letter to the Guardian, Betancourt’s lawyer wrote: “Mr Betancourt has never been charged with a crime in the United States. He has never been named as a defendant. The United States government has never sought his extradition, and the United States government has never publicly identified him as a target, as an unnamed co-conspirator, or as any numbered conspirator in any charging instrument.”Marco Rubio told a Venezuelan radio interviewer that Betancourt was not the subject of a US probe. “There was no investigation within our system against him.”In the height of Trump’s first term,Betancourt hired Giuliani, then Trump’s personal lawyer, as his own lawyer.His relationship with Venezuela’s government has seesawed over the years. According to two people familiar with the situation, Venezuelan authorities were so concerned over allegations about Betancourt’s finances that they hired a team of lawyers and investigators that began an intense investigation to try to track his money.Betancourt’s attorney said the businessman never misappropriated money.The investigators hired by Venezuela even used hackers to try to trace his funds. A source familiar with the hacking project said their intrusion was extensive. “His WhatsApp,” they said, “‘His accountants, his lawyers, everything.”Corporate computer hackingwas a well-known investigative tool, though usually illegal, at the time. A 2021 document obtained by the Guardian, prepared by a group of hackers, shows a list of Venezuelan targets. It lists Betancourt as a “secondary” target.View image in fullscreenThe US eased sanctions on Venezuela’s oil industry on 29 January after that country’s lawmakers passed reforms paving the way for US companies to return.Photograph: Maryorin Mendez/AFP/Getty ImagesBetancourt’s lawyer didn’t confirm the hacking, but he said that Betancourt was a major supporter of the interim opposition government backed by the US. If it happened, he said, any hacking effort “belongs in the context of Mr Betancourt’s opposition to the Maduro regime”, rather than as a legitimate financial investigation.The Venezuelan ministry of communications and information did not respond to an emailed request for comment.By 2024, Betancourt was involved in drilling again in Venezuela, with Nabep, the company he owned at the time with Harry Sargeant, an American oil executive. The company started small, at just 23,000 barrels per day, according to recent statements by Venezuela’s interim president.In September 2025, Spanish police descended on his castle in connection with a money-laundering investigation, according toSpanish press accounts.But at about that time, officials in the Trump administration were already in touch with Betancourt about the pressure on Venezuela’s government, according to a former official, as well as a businessman who was aware of it. Betancourt’s lawyer wrote that the Spanish investigation “has never resulted in any charge against Mr. Betancourt”. The Guardian was not able to confirm the status of the investigation.By 3 January, when Maduro was arrested in the US raid, a source who was involved said Betancourt played a crucial role in negotiations with Delcy Rodríguez. Betancourt’s lawyer wrote to the Guardian that Betancourt functioned as a go-between. “There was no established channel of trust between Venezuela’s interim government and the United States. Both sides spoke with Mr Betancourt, because each knew him and each was prepared to rely on him, and he facilitated communications between them.”What many people familiar with Venezuela’s recent history question is why the US government is going into business with Betancourt given his substantial baggage.“The only discernible winner in any of this is Betancourt,” said a businessman who has spent years on Venezuelan issues.For Trump, the issue is simple. “It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” he told the United Nations this week. “To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationVenezuelaOilDonald TrumpNicolás MaduroOil and gas companiesUS foreign policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: My late fiance’s favourite song was playing – and Billy said ‘Jamie’s here, isn’t that nice?’ | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: After the death of his partner, Anthony Nocera had almost given up on love. Then Billy walked through the door
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After the death of his partner, Anthony Nocera had almost given up on love. Then Billy walked through the door
Content: ‘It takes a special person, like Billy, to look at the shoes of a past lover and not try to fill them, but to leave them be and plant their shoes next to the ones left behind’: Billy (left) with AnthonyView image in fullscreen‘It takes a special person, like Billy, to look at the shoes of a past lover and not try to fill them, but to leave them be and plant their shoes next to the ones left behind’: Billy (left) with AnthonyThe moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: My late fiance’s favourite song was playing – and Billy said ‘Jamie’s here, isn’t that nice?’After the death of his partner,Anthony Nocerahad almost given up on love. Then Billy walked through the doorFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesAnthony NoceraSat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2024, about 18 months after my fiance Jamie passed away, I decided I was lonely and horny and so put myself out there on the apps. I’d placed Jamie’s ashes on the TV cabinet in the living room, so he was smack bang in the middle of his two favourite places: his spot on the couch and his coffee machine. It also meant he was in the centre of the house, which made dating hard.I had a guy over for a hook-up one night and he kept fixating on the urn. “So … He’s dead?”The moment I knew: We discussed the pill on our first date, kissed on our second. By the third, I knew he was the oneRead more“I hope so,” I said. “Otherwise the urn was a mistake.”“Wow,” he said, not getting the joke. “You’re so brave. I don’t know how you do it.”Nothing kills a boner faster than someone thinking you’re brave. When someone thinks you’re “brave”, you stop being flesh and pulsing blood and hot salty saliva and start being something coolly observed. Being a “brave widow” makes you desirable in theory. Not practice.When the urn didn’t ward off potential suitors, my cat Freyja – or Miss Freyja, as Jamie called her – did. She appointed herself my fluffy protector in Jamie’s absence. Each night, she camouflaged herself on the charcoal-grey carpet outside my bedroom and kept watch while I slept. Two emerald eyes scanning for threats.View image in fullscreen‘Maybe Freyja was secretly homophobic and only put up with me because I was the one who fed her.’Photograph: Anthony NoceraWhen Ididhave a visitor, she sprung into immediate, hostile action. She yowled and hissed when a semi-closeted doctor, who had came over for a blowjob, tried to pick her up. One guy didn’t see her flattened into the carpet and accidentally kicked her across the room. She responded by clawing his shin.After that, I figured that what I experienced with Jamie was so real and pure and true that I’d used up all the love I was allocated in my lifetime. Or that maybe Freyja was secretly homophobic and only put up with me because I was the one who fed her.I’d spent months in self-imposed celibacy, when a guy named Billy, with gorgeous green eyes and a crooked smile, messaged me. He asked about my day and I sent him a picture of a painting I’d hung up. He asked to see it in person. I said yes. When he arrived, he spotted Freyja, and before he even said hello to me, he crouched down to her level and said: “Hello Miss!”As if some muscle memory kicked in, she waddled over to Billy and flopped on her back, presenting her belly for patting while she purred. “Oh MissFreyja!” he said, when I told him her name. When he was done, he kissed me.He didn’t mention the urn until hours later – and when I told him the story of me and Jamie, he said, “Sounds like a great guy.”Freyja wove between our feet and vibrated her tail when he kissed me goodbye. As he drove away, Freyja waited by the door and let out a melancholic meow.Don’t go. I agreed.Late one night we walked past a club having a 90s party. Madonna’s Ray of Light, Jamie’s favourite song, blared out on to the street. Billy turned to me smiling, his pointy canine tooth glinting in the moonlight, and said: “Jamie’s here, isn’t that nice?” and then he squeezed my hand. I felt flutters all through my body and fell head over heels in love in a way I never thought I would again.View image in fullscreen‘[Billy is] smarter and more handsome than he realises’: Billy and AnthonyIt takes a special person, like Billy, to look at the shoes of a past lover and not try to fill them; to leave them be and plant their own next to the ones left behind. To carry something as heavy and slippery as a loss that doesn’t belong to him. To see that the pair of Jamie’s glasses I keep next to my bed are dusty, and clean them as if it’s nothing at all, even though for me it feels like the most generous thing you could do for another person.Billy is funny, patient and kind. He’s smarter and more handsome than he realises. I find it hard to think of things in terms of “forever” now, because I know how quickly things can be taken away. But I look at Billy, and think I’d be happy doing this day by day, for a long time – with Miss Freyja by our side and Jamie watching over us all.Anthony Nocera is the writer of theLog Boy, which runs from 1-10 October at Adelaide College of the Arts, Main Theatre. title: First Encounters: Julius Caesar review – so thrilling it kept a hall full of teens in pin-drop silence | Theatre | The Guardian
description: An intro to Shakespeare doesn’t get any better than the RSC’s revival of Phyllida Lloyd’s all-female prison-set production led by Harriet Walter, which is touring schools
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: An intro to Shakespeare doesn’t get any better than the RSC’s revival of Phyllida Lloyd’s all-female prison-set production led by Harriet Walter, which is touring schools
Content: Changes the air in the room … Carolina Valdés as Casca and Jackie Clune as Julius Caesar.Photograph: Helen MaybanksView image in fullscreenChanges the air in the room … Carolina Valdés as Casca and Jackie Clune as Julius Caesar.Photograph: Helen MaybanksTheatreReviewFirst Encounters: Julius Caesar review – so thrilling it kept a hall full of teens in pin-drop silenceOrmiston Bushfield Academy, PeterboroughAn intro to Shakespeare doesn’t get any better than the RSC’s revival of Phyllida Lloyd’s all-female prison-set production led by Harriet Walter, which is touring schoolsArifa AkbarSat 26 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe auditorium is stripped bare – a repurposed hall whose ascending seating resembles an amphitheatre but with plastic chairs. This show could pass for a school production, in appearance, if you didn’t know better. The Royal Shakespeare Company’s revival of Phyllida Lloyd’sall-female Julius Caesar, which originally ranat the Donmar Warehouse in 2012, is now touring secondary schools.View image in fullscreenClear-eyed … Harriet Walter as Brutus.Photograph: Helen MaybanksWe are in Peterborough, but also in Romeandin a women’s prison: Shakespeare is framed within an incarceration story, which occasionally impinges on it with interruptions from guards and prison protocols.Harriet Walter reprises her role as Brutus; Jackie Clune returns as Julius Caesar. Leah Harvey, who played the soothsayer inthe 2016 revival, now owns the role of an earnest yet calculatingly vengeful Mark Anthony.The institutional minimalism of Bunny Christie’s set design is in keeping with Lloyd’s setup of a drama society in a prison putting on the play before us, the actors dressed in similar grey, state-issue outfits. Small TV screens variously flash CCTV surveillance footage from the prison and summaries of forthcoming scenes from the play in blaring letters.The history play’s themes of justice, power, populism and violence begetting violence have plenty of resonance today. Still, it is a tall order to hold the attentions of a hall full of school pupils with Shakespearean verse and there is shuffling, giggling and nudging among them in the opening scenes. But from the moment Caesar is stabbed by Brutus’s conspirators (Clune makes this graphic, although it remains bloodless) the air in the room changes.The production holds us all captive with its propulsive action and carefully crafted lo-fi, modern elements that never simplify or reduce. There are red rubber gloves for bloodied hands, freeze-frames, fine atmospheric lighting design by Zeynep Kepekli with sudden blackouts, along with electronic music building adrenaline for the bloodlust of war (from Stormzy’s Big for Your Boots to a Fatboy Slim remix of Renegade Master and last year’s hit Partii). The violence, in this setting, could just as well be about youth gang culture, with its cycle of grudges and revenge.View image in fullscreenPlenty of resonance … First Encounters: Julius Caesar.Photograph: Helen MaybanksWalter, elegantly androgynous, again makes a clear-eyed and upstanding idealist in Brutus, motivated to preserve the city’s republican freedoms (“Not that I loved Caesar less but I loved Rome more”). Clune is fantastically strutting in leather coat.Shakespeare’s women are strong, too, key in foreseeing danger: Portia (Shalisha James-Davis) demanding husband Brutus to divulge his secrets while Calpurnia (Kosar Ali) appears as imperious as her husband, Caesar, accompanied by a childlike soothsayer (Siân Stephens) who runs creepy circles around her on a tricycle.Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaRead moreAs the blood rises, turntables are wheeled out as if part of the war machine, with soldiers pumped up for the fight. Executions are carried out with hoods and plastic guns, accompanied by the sound of real shots. It has the feel of a history play gone through a Tarantino wringer, yet still faithful to its original spirit.By the time Brutus is overcome, there is pin-drop silence among the audience, every ear pricked. It is Julius Caesar brought excitingly alive (eventhe promo videois a thrill), and as a first encounter with Shakespeare, or with theatre itself, it is hard to beat.Theschools tourruns until 23 October. Then atthe Other Place, Stratford-upon-Avon, 5-28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreJulius CaesarRoyal Shakespeare CompanyPhyllida LloydHarriet WalterPrisons and probationBunny ChristiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: I hoped my children would have epiphanies while visiting my homeland; my father suggested we go swimming instead | Malaysia holidays | The Guardian
description: I brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals do
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals do
Content: Tessa Lu with her family in Penang, Malaysia.Composite: Guardian Design/Tessa LuView image in fullscreenTessa Lu with her family in Penang, Malaysia.Composite: Guardian Design/Tessa LuMalaysia holidaysI hoped my children would have epiphanies while visiting my homeland; my father suggested we go swimming insteadI brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals doTessa LuSat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I stepped out of Penang international airport, the humidity hit me like I was peering into a just-opened rice cooker. The air carried whiffs of exhaust fumes, fried food and something earthy. It felt thrilling and familiar because I was born in Penang and lived there for six years before I moved to Australia. I looked back at my three children who were visiting for the first time. They were draped over their suitcases like wilted lettuce. “Welcome to Penang,” I said, wiping sweat off my brow.It was July 2026. It had been 13 years since I last visited Penang, when my father had hosted a lavish wedding dinner featuring a champagne fountain and swan-shaped ice sculpture for me and my new husband. For my white, Australian husband, it was a trip of firsts: his first Chinese tea ceremony; his first 10-course banquet; the first time he met my extended family. But for me, it had been the last time I’d spoken Mandarin and the last time I had seen my grandmother before she died.As my parents grew older, I worried my Chinese heritage would be lost for ever. My children spoke only English and spent their Saturdays playing sport rather than attending Mandarin lessons and calligraphy classes like I had. When Gong Gong (maternal grandfather) spoke of his childhood, the children smiled indulgently but thought he was exaggerating when he said his only toy was a discarded bicycle tyre and he’d had to share one apple with his five siblings.My ‘Chinglish’ has a cringe-inducing ocker accent – but I’m determined to pass it on to my child | Monica TanRead moreI wanted to bring my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. My father, who lives in Perth but travels there frequently, booked his flight the night I floated the idea to him.On the first morning of our trip, my father met me, my husband and our children at our hotel in central George Town. He gazed at the gleaming marble floors and wood panelling of the Eastern & Oriental Hotel and said: “When I was young, I never dared to set foot in this hotel. Only rich Europeans stayed here.” Nowwewere the rich tourists – a fact that made me feel guilty and grateful – and to the man dressed in a khaki colonial outfit and safari helmet who held a door open for us, my toddler sang a cheery: “Thank you!”We began our trip gently, letting the children luxuriate in an air-conditioned mall and paw through racks of fast fashion before we ventured outside to explore George Town on foot. “It’s not every day you get to walk through a Unesco world heritage site,” I chirped. But the heat was intense and the children’s interest in colonial architecture and street art evaporated in the afternoon sun.In the evening, my father led our search for dinner through a labyrinth of alleyways, shepherding us off the road when cars and motorbikes rumbled through. At the first restaurant, there were no free seats and the air was sulfurously pungent from a nearby durian stall. In the second place, the smoke billowing from the satay grill triggered my daughter’s asthmatic cough. Finally, we found a place that dished up barbecued pork on springy egg noodles coated in a sticky soy sauce. We fell upon our food in a frenzy. Later, we walked back to the hotel along the esplanade, marvelling at the sunset that lit up the clouds like smears of mandarin sorbet across the sky.Towards the end of our trip, we visited my father’s childhood home. We drove along a winding road that hugged the contours of the hills in the island’s north. On one side, verdant rainforest towered above; on the other side, past the guard rail, was a sharp drop, with dizzying glimpses of the houses in the valley below. When we reached Tanjung Bungah, the suburb where my father had lived, the children scowled from the backseat. My 10-year-old hissed: “When can we go shopping?” The toddler pleaded to return to the hotel’s infinity pool, which was fringed by palm trees and overlooked the Andaman Sea. Undeterred, my father stopped by a truck piled high with coconuts. A shirtless man used a machete to hack one open and stuck a plastic straw in it. My father handed it to my son, who spilled it on to his lap.We continued down a narrow dirt road and stopped at a small weatherboard house with a red tin roof. The house was empty and neglected but my father still had a key. We squeezed past two bedrooms and shuffled to the kitchen at the back. The electrical wiring was exposed and the concrete floor was gouged with holes. There were no ceilings; sunlight filtered in through the holes in the roof. The toilet was outside. The entire house was smaller than our two hotel rooms. I pictured my father, who was one of six children, living there with his family.“How did you fit all eight of you in this tiny house?” I asked.“Fourteen,” he corrected me. “With my grandparents, three uncles and one aunty.”I took my daughter on a holiday to Hong Kong to visit family. I didn’t realise how hard it would be to leave | Lucille WongRead more“Woah,” my eldest daughter said, her eyes wide. Perhaps she was thinking of her bedroom at home, which was spacious enough for two bookcases and a double bass, and had a door that she slammed for privacy. The toddler began to cry and I picked her up, wondering if she finally understood the grim poverty that her Gong Gong had endured.“I want to go back to the pool,” she sobbed.My father ushered us back into the minivan and we drove back to the hotel. I thought he might be disappointed in the children’s behaviour but, instead, he urged me to take them for a swim. I realised that I’d expected too much of them; what child could resist leaping into cool water on a muggy day or lying on a sun lounger eating ice-cream? I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege and we enjoyed our final days doing as Penang locals do: shopping and eating. On one occasion, when I ordered food in faltering Mandarin, my toddler stared at me with wonder and exclaimed: “Mum, you can speak Spanish!”Our trip did not, as I had hoped, inspire epiphanies in the children about their heritage or their grandparents’ early struggles. Perhaps these will dawn on them as they grow up. For now, it was enough that they shared some experiences that featured in my earliest memories – they’d sweltered in tropical humidity and sat on red plastic stools, slurping noodles. And their Gong Gong had hugged them goodbye in a hotel lobby where he’d once believed he did not deserve to step foot.Explore more on these topicsMalaysia holidaysAustralian lifestyleFamilyAsiaParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Raye’s I Know You’re Hurting urged me to confront a lifetime of depression | Raye | The Guardian
description: I had always ignored my anguished mental state or tried to push it aside, and CBT didn’t work for me – then one song seemed to articulate my pain
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: I had always ignored my anguished mental state or tried to push it aside, and CBT didn’t work for me – then one song seemed to articulate my pain
Content: ‘Music had made me emotional before, but only ever because of the melody’.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Music had made me emotional before, but only ever because of the melody’.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningRayeRaye’s I Know You’re Hurting urged me to confront a lifetime of depressionI had always ignored my anguished mental state or tried to push it aside, and CBT didn’t work for me – then one song seemed to articulate my painJake Jackson; as told toOlivia LadanyiSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix months ago, I was driving past John Lewis on the M40 with my wife and stepdaughter, Raye’s I Know You’re Hurting playing on the stereo, when I realised I was crying. It was the third time I’d listened to the song, but it was the first time I’d really heard it. It was as though the lyrics were speaking directly to me: “I can see you standing on the edge … You give when you have little left to give.”Music had made me emotional before, but only ever because of the melody or the arrangement or the orchestration. I have worked in music since I was 21, and as a recording and mix engineer, I’ll listen to a song all day, taking it apart to work out how to make it better. After listening to a song 200 times, it inevitably loses its meaning, and over the years, I’ve become desensitised to the power music can have. But this time, for the first time, it was the lyrics that brought me to tears.I had been struggling with my mental health for two decades – almost half a lifetime. But I hid it, scared to admit it to my family, even to myself. As Raye sings: “And you hide it so well, you do.” The last few years had been especially difficult with Covid, a divorce, becoming a stepfather to teenagers and turning 50. I’d invested so much time into my career – working 80-100-hour weeks at its peak – but I questioned what my legacy would be when I look back on my life. I’d sit in silence, a face of thunder, wallowing in self-pity. My family would ask: “What’s wrong with you?” And I’d bite my tongue, not knowing what to say, just knowing I needed to do better.I had tried cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) many times, but I found I’d just talk without acting on the steps. Still, when my wife suggested speaking to the GP about antidepressants a couple of years ago, I was reluctant, thinking it would kill my creativity. I Know You’re Hurting unlocked something in me, though. Hearing my pain articulated by Raye finally allowed me to accept that I was struggling. It gave me permission to admit it. Two months later, I made an appointment with the GP, who prescribed antidepressants. After Raye’s music spoke to me that day, I also decided to start music therapy. Exploring my thoughts through music, something I instinctively connect with, has been much more effective for me than CBT ever was.In her lyrics, Raye urges the listener to “stop trying to be so strong all alone”, and “If you need two more arms to hold these burdens, I’m here”. I realised I didn’t have to continue struggling on my own. Help was available and I had people who could support me.double quotation markI feared that antidepressants would kill my creativity but they opened up the space for me to access itA couple of weeks ago, I got a tattoo to commemorate the impact the song has had on my life. The line “close your eyes and let this music get to working” summed that up for me – the way that music can be medicine. I messaged the producer, who sent me the score, and I got the musical notes of that line tattooed on my forearm. It’s a reminder that I’m not alone, a reminder of where I am now compared with where I was. I just look at it and it makes me feel good.Around that time, my music therapist suggested I write a song. The lyrics just poured out of me – I wrote it in an hour. I’ve got an urge like never before to make music. I feared that antidepressants would kill my creativity; instead, they opened up the space for me to access it.Raye’s song told me it was going to be OK, and I still return to her perfect album This Music May Contain Hope in moments when I need to be reminded that hope can be found. One of the final tracks on the album is called Joy, which feels fitting because that’s also where I’ve ended up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFour months into taking antidepressants and starting music therapy, I argue less, I let things go more. I’m a better husband and a better father to my son and stepdaughters. My family have noticed the change in me, often saying how much happier I seem.In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. title: From Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper
Content: Austen translation … Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenAusten translation … Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Going out, staying inCultureFrom Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadDaisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caperSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaSense and SensibilityOut nowDaisy Edgar-Jones has a big bonnet to fill in the role Emma Thompson made her own in Ang Lee’s Oscar-winning version of Jane Austen’s romance. But let’s not compare: Blue Jean director Georgia Oakley’s take sees a fresh cast place new emphasis on the bond between sisters Marianne and Elinor.Her Private HellOut nowProfessional provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn returns with another slice of the outre, this time in a science fiction mode. It’s the tale of a young woman, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), who encounters a supernatural killer in diamond-encrusted gloves in a mist-shrouded city.RemakeOut nowTaking on the devastating subject of the death of his own son, revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee makes the film that no parent would want to make. Using his own home video and family archive, he creates a bereavement memoir that traces a life from infancy to adolescence to an adulthood marred by addiction.Heartofthe BeastOut nowTraining Day screenwriter David Ayer directs this thriller about one man and his dog attempting to survive in the wilderness after a plane crash. But not just any man and dog: he’s an ex-special forces officer and the dog is a retired combat dog. Curiously, it stars Brad Pitt where you might expect Jason Statham.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenFlava sensation … Honey Dijon joins the lineup at Homobloc.Photograph: Henrik NielsenJill ScottLondon,28 September; Birmingham,29 September; Manchester,1 October; London, 13 & 14 October; touring to 14 OctoberThe R&B and soul legend heads out on tour in support of To Whom This May Concern, her first album in 11 years. Expect classics, specifically from 2000’s Who Is Jill Scott?, alongside her dextrous, genre-hopping new material.Michael CraggWagner’s ParsifalRoyal Opera House, London,1to 17 OctoberIt grapples with good and evil, love and violence, life and death – so no wonder Parsifal lasts upwards of four hours. Acclaimed director Evgeny Titov makes his Royal Opera debut with this new production conducted by Jakub Hrůša. The high-wattage cast includes Stanislas de Barbeyrac, Christian Gerhaher and Ekaterina Gubanova.Flora WillsonXhosa ColeScarboroughSpa,26SeptemberContemporary and classic jazz sax maestro Xhosa Cole reworks the music of Thelonious Monk at the 23rd Scarborough jazz festival – Soft Machine, Alan Barnes and star vocalists Ian Shaw, Liane Carroll and Brigitte Beraha also enhance the event’s usual classy bill. Cole also plays London’s Vortex on 29 & 30 September.John FordhamHomoblocDepot Mayfield, Manchester,26 SeptemberBilled as a “Queer block party for all”, the late-night celebration returns to Manchester with a typically stellar lineup, including German pop star Kim Petras. Elsewhere, DJ-producer Honey Dijon goes back-to-back with underground house maverick Derrick Carter, while LSDXOXO, Erol Alkan and DJ Paulette will also be popping up.MCGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenSurreal thing …René Magritte’s La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), 1936.Photograph: Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkThis Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of MagritteGagosian Grosvenor Hill, London,to 12 DecemberIt may not be a pipe but it is an exhibition, one dedicated to the great surrealist master René Magritte and his enduring influence on art. Some major loans will hang alongside works on paper, photography and sculpture.Beverly BuchananSpike Island, Bristol,to 31 JanuaryFive decades’ worth of sculpture, painting and earthworks are packed into the first European survey for this artist who died in 2015, leaving behind a vast body of work about the US’s troubled south.Olivia BaxYorkshire Sculpture Park, nr Wakefield,to 14 MarchTwenty new, heavily textured, multicoloured and very strange sculptural assemblages by this young London-based artist, filled with salvaged materials and gloopy neon references to BMX parks.Evelyn Taocheng WangGoldsmith’s Centre for ContemporaryArt, London,to 13 DecemberExpect an outsider’s portrait of Britain in this debut UK institutional exhibition for Evelyn Taocheng Wang, taking a heavily conceptual look at what makes us so uniquely us (humour, reserve, period dramas) through sculpture, painting and installation.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenHome front economics … The Standard of Living.The Standard of LivingTheatre Royal Haymarket, London,to 12 DecemberJames Graham has an uncanny way of combining character and country. His latest play stars Rory Kinnear and is about the radical economist John Maynard Keynes, set against the backdrop of a Britain reeling from the first world war. Directed by Nicholas Hytner.Miriam GillinsonRhys James30 Septemberto 15 May; tour starts FolkestoneYet to achieve household-name status, 35-year-old James is widely considered one of UK standup’s master craftspeople. His new show Chop Logic combines a relentless stream of ingenious gags with the story of his circumcision.Rachel AroestiMurder Before EvensongWatermilltheatre, Newbury,to 14 NovemberRev Richard Coles’s cosy crime novel is adapted for the stage. It’s 1988 in the peaceful village of Champton, where life centres on the church, but a shocking murder changes everything and the rector is pulled into the investigation.MGThick & TightTuesday to 28 November; tour startsNewcastle upon TyneThe Guardian’s best dance show of 2025 goes on tour. A hilarious, subversive, offbeat treat from uncategorisable duo Thick & Tight and guests, Natural Behaviour mixes dance, text, lip-sync and silliness in surreal sketches. Subjects include the writer James Baldwin, lesbian seagulls and the dust in Quentin Crisp’s flat.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenArt attack … Kill Jackie.Photograph: Unai MateoKill JackiePrime Video,2 OctoberCatherine Zeta-Jones goes full madcap camp – and even gets to keep her native Welsh accent – in this big, bonkers crime caper about an ex-con art dealer whose past catches up with her. Daniel Ings, Raff Law and Sidse Babett Knudsen also star.WarSky Atlantic & Now,2 October, 9pmIt’s Sienna Miller v Dominic West in this deluxe new thriller from George Kay (Lupin, The Long Shadow). A film star and tech titan face “the biggest divorce trial in British legal history”, meaning their respective teams of lawyers, including Nick Mohammed, will stop at nothing in order to come out on top.East of EdenNetflix,1 OctoberZoe Kazan follows in her grandfather Elia’s footsteps with this adaptation of Steinbeck’s 1952 opus. Florence Pugh gets her teeth stuck into one of fiction’s most notorious antiheroines in Cathy Ames, whose author described her as having a “malformed soul”. Christopher Abbott plays her abandoned husband.Break ClauseChannel 4,1 October, 10pmA former couple – promising young architect Lil (comedian Lara Ricote) and directionless graduate Ben (Samuel Bottomley) – are forced to cohabit in a London flat due to a watertight rental contract in this sweet and goofy will-they-won’t-they (get back together) comedy from Jess Bray.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenBar work … Nivalis Nights.Photograph: ION LANDSNivalis NightsPC; out29 SeptemberA cyberpunk life-simulation where, instead of running around with a futuristic pistol and getting caught up in gang wars, you are just trying to make a living. Starting out with a food stand, you can eventually own the night through a network of bars, restaurants and clubs – and learn everything about the city from your loose-lipped patrons.The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – RemasteredAll platforms; out29 SeptemberOutcast monster hunter Geralt of Rivia gets caught up in the dark machinations of phantom huntsmen and warring kings in this updated and complete version of an all-time great role-player. If you have somehow yet to play this eastern European dark fantasy masterpiece, you really have run out of excuses.Keza MacDonaldStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenTop drawer … alt-rock riser Blondshell.Photograph: Reese LaytonBlondshell – ViolinsOut nowAfter Sabrina Teitelbaum’s first pop-leaning incarnation as BAUM imploded in 2020, the New Yorker morphed into alt-rocker Blondshell. While the musical backdrop is heavier and more guitar-based, that pop nous still runs through this third album, especially on the galloping Fur Elise.Julia Jacklin – The GemOut nowNamed after her local pub, the fourth album – and her first for the much-loved label 4AD – by Melbourne-based songwriter Julia Jacklin is full of lovingly crumpled rock. Exploring reinvention, longing and excavation, songs such as The Hardest Thing and I Wish are full of unforgettable melodic nuggets.Tinashe – PopstarOut nowAfter getting lost in the major-label system, US bop-maker Tinashe has thrived as an independent artist. On her eighth album she dabbles in hyperpop elasticity via the undulating Melatonin, while the low-slung Crash Out adds trap and R&B to the mix.M83 – I Wrote You a LetterOut nowThe French synth-pop outfit, led by Anthony Gonzalez, return with their 10th album, and first in three years. Worked up from demos recorded in 2024 as a way of capturing the spirit of the band’s earlier work, it opens with the blown-out alt-pop of the cinematic Blister Sunrise.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreen90 Minutes or Less Film FestPodcastHost Sam Clements programmes his dream film festival lineup in this charming series celebrating the art of well-edited cinema. Picks include Godard’s Breathless, as chosen by director Richard Linklater, and Jackass, as selected by Steve-O.DeconstructedYouTubeDetailed 3D animations dissect some of history’s most complex machines and structures on this fascinating channel. Discover the inner workings of an ancient Greek water clock and the unusual design of the Eiffel Tower elevators.Mapping India: The World’s Largest CountBBC World Service,26 September, 12.06amIndia is undertaking one of the largest counting exercises in the world: a census of its 1.5 billion inhabitants. This astounding documentary follows the logistical challenges of the process, from Delhi streets to Himalayan mountains.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content
