title: Meet the new 55 minute England collapse, not the same as the old 55 minute England collapse | England | The Guardian
description: Things started to go wrong against Spain at the same time they did against Argentina, but for very different reasons and with far more cause for optimism
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Things started to go wrong against Spain at the same time they did against Argentina, but for very different reasons and with far more cause for optimism
Content: The Spain goalkeeper, Unai Simón, celebrates Harry Kane missing a 55th-minute penalty as the England captain looks accusingly at his boot.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Spain goalkeeper, Unai Simón, celebrates Harry Kane missing a 55th-minute penalty as the England captain looks accusingly at his boot.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnglandAnalysisMeet the new 55 minute England collapse, not the same as the old 55 minute England collapseBarney Ronayat WembleyThings started to go wrong against Spain at the same time they did against Argentina, but for very different reasons and with far more cause for optimismSat 26 Sep 2026 19.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTShareYou could feel it inside the stadium, one of those moments where the air starts to shift, the birds fly backwards through the sky, and outside on Wembley Way an old man clutches his copy of the England Pathway Blueprint to his chest and cowers up at the moon. Welcome to the witching hour, 55 minutes in, when things just seem to happen to Thomas Tuchel’s England.Before this Nations League opener there was general agreement on the desirability of systems, pattern, repeatability. And you can’t say England aren’t consistent. Their last two significant matches, here andin Atlanta in July, have both involved going a goal ahead against the World Cup finalists, playing well and dominating parts of the game, right up until the 55-minute mark.Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty missRead moreAt which point a kind of voodoo descends. On both occasions the final 35 minutes have been lost 2-0. On both occasions there will, inevitably, be an attempt not just to blame the manager for decisions made in the game, but for some kind of widervibes-based DNA-relatedbetrayal.“Cowardice” is a word most often used, because football is of course war, bravery and pluck. But it is, as ever with England, technical and tactical. As it was once again here.There were 55 minutes gone against Argentina in Atlanta when Anthony Gordon putEngland1-0 up. At which point the team fell apart like an over-dunked digestive biscuit, reduced suddenly to a collection of hollow men, stuffed shirts, 12% possession merchants, the manager spooked into fielding a back five.Here the game also changed on 55 minutes. England were 2-1 up from 1-0 down at that point. For a while at the start of the second half it looked like they might be turning this game into an ordeal for their opponents, playing in surges, winning physical duels, making Spain into a team that has to run.Jarell Quansah smashed a shot into Marc Cucurella’s face, drawing huge cheers. The crowd had begun to sing the Tuchel song, to the tune of War’s Low Rider, the official notation for which is “Foot-ball’s coming home uh-gain – with Thom-as Tuch-el”. On 54 minutes a lengthy VAR check ended with a penalty awarded for a trip on Jude Bellingham that was combined also with a dive, but trip plus dive does not cancel trip. Was this an exorcism? Are we good now? Is everything going to be OK?View image in fullscreenSpain were left trailing in England’s wake by the speed of the counterattack for Anthony Gordon’s equalising goal.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersWell, no, as it turned out.Harry Kanehad already scored England’s second goal. He waited a little longer than usual, slipped on his standing leg as he planted it and pumped the kick on to the bar. 54 ticked over into 55 minutes.And at that pointSpainjust seemed to sense it, the pressure shifted and we were back in Georgia under the lights. Tuchel was up again on his touchline, arms wheeling, shiny blue gilet gleaming. The ball began to tick about between the red shirts. And suddenly Spain had regained that basking quality, easing about with that familiar sense of control, always with more angles, more space, a superior geometry, like trying to keep up with a team of 11-year-old chess prodigies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdictRead moreWithin five minutes the game was level. Fourteen minutes later Spain were 3-2 up, a lead they would hold on to. The most unfavourable interpretation of this is a pattern being established. England lost another game where they just seem to get close, to lose control, to fail to hold the midfield. Both of Spain’s decisive goals were either made or scored by Luis de la Fuente’s two attacking substitutes, neither of whom looked much like Dan Burn.But it wasn’t quite like that. For a start, England were much better here than in Atlanta, and against a better team. Wembley was its usual chilly self at kick-off, a place where even on a Saturday night the general vibe is echoey, corporate space, like a visit to the Ideal Home exhibition or a peculiarly low-throttle ABBA tribute event.And Spain scored almost immediately, the goal made by a horrible moment for Marc Guéhi and a smart finish from Yamine Lamal. For a while this was the sum of all fears, one of those games where facing this team is like trying to play football against water. Ferran Torres wasted some outrageously inviting chances. Rodri shuttled about like a man operating inside his own portable demilitarised zone. Spain will make you crawl in those moments. But England didn’t let them.There were periods of hard high pressing. Elliot Anderson was aggressive in midfield. On 36 minutes England scored a brilliant goal, one that Spain will hate, caught on the counterattack by a wonderful three-man surge from box to box, made by Anderson’s tackle, Bellingham’s surge and pass, and a lovely Gordon finish into the corner.View image in fullscreenThe simultaneous bringing-on of Pedri for Spain and James Garner for England highlighted the gap in midfield between the two teams.Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesThey kept running from there. And even after the 55-minute fade England were better. There was no long-ball stuff, no panic and some decent late chances. But really the key moment here came on 70 minutes, when both teams brought on a midfielder: Pedri for Spain, James Garner for England.Pedri immediately began to do his thing, romping about like a playful little horse, a footballer who just loves the ball, and whom the ball loves right back. At that point Spain had Pedri, Rodri and Dani Olmo, the entire Barcelona midfield, on the pitch. And for all England’s efforts, the late surge, the front-foot style, it always felt that they were being held at bay in those final moments, one hand on the forehead, arms windmilling in the space in between.But then Spain are the ultimate system team, an expression ofa deep, functioning coaching culture, not to mention the footballing nation that tortures England the most. We are all you could have had, the thing you are not. Lose again, lose better. But this was at least some kind of progress.Explore more on these topicsEnglandHarry KaneThomas TuchelSpainNations LeagueanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Republic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’ | Nations League | The Guardian
description: The Republic of Ireland’s Nations League fixtures with Israel will go ahead after a ‘significant majority’ of players voted in favour
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The Republic of Ireland’s Nations League fixtures with Israel will go ahead after a ‘significant majority’ of players voted in favour
Content: Gavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad to play Israel.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad to play Israel.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesNations LeagueRepublic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’Bolton goalkeeper issues statement after withdrawalIreland players will wear black armbands in matchPaul MacInnesin DebrecenSat 26 Sep 2026 16.18 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRepublic of Irelandwill fulfil their fixture against Israel in Hungary on Sunday night, but only after lengthy deliberations between the players resulted in a “significant majority” voting to play. The Bolton goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, however, will not be involved, after pulling out in protest.After a week in which the Irish team and officials have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott the match due to Israel’s military actions in Gaza, training was delayed by five hours on Saturday while the squad discussed whether to go ahead.“This morning, a player expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad,” said the FAI’s chief David Courell, referring to Bazunu.Israel’s match with Republic of Ireland will be an eerie occasion as political debate rages onRead more“What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive. Ultimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.”Courell said the squad had also agreed a number of measures to signal their unease with the fixture taking place. Players are to wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” he said, adding that there will be “elements of the pre-match ceremony” that will “not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland” players, namely the pre-match handshake and exchange of pennants.Bazunu, writing on Instagram, said: “Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people.“However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.View image in fullscreenThe Republic of Ireland head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson (left), and the FAI CEO, David Courell, confer during the delayed press conference.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty Images“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.“There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.”The Republic’s head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, meanwhile, said “nobody is comfortable playing these games for many reasons” as he was once again put under pressure over remarks in which hedescribed his team as “playing against genocide”earlier this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHallgrímsson said he had used a “strong” word and now regretted it. “It was a wrong word for me to use,” he said, arguing that he had meant to say that “by playing we are not accepting what is happening”. If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrímsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.”The leadership of the Israel team used their press conference to read a statement congratulating Ireland on their decision to play. “What we have seen today is that football has won,” it read. “The separation between football and politics must continue. Anything else spells chaos and creates consequences for the game we love. The Irish took the right decision in agreeing to this. Even if it took longer than it should, it was welcome.”Israeli officials said they would engage in all of the pre-match formalities with the head coach Ran Ben-Shimon confirming: “I will shake hands with Hallgrímsson.”The Israel FA will also appeal both yellow cards awarded to Saied Abu Farchi during Thursday’s defeat to Austria. Farchi was given a second yellow after he celebrated scoring an equaliser by uprooting the corner flag, an action interpreted by officials as mimicking the firing of a rifle.Israel dispute this interpretation. “Anyone familiar with him knows it was an imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty,” their spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueRepublic of IrelandIsraelUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris says Colapinto ‘shouldn’t be in F1’ after crash ends title hopes | Lando Norris | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris has issued a scathing criticism of Franco Colapinto, saying the the Alpine driver does not deserve to be in Formula One after taking the defending world champion out of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris has issued a scathing criticism of Franco Colapinto, saying the the Alpine driver does not deserve to be in Formula One after taking the defending world champion out of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Content: Franco Colapinto hits his Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly and pushes him into Lando Norris’s car.Photograph: Eric Alonso/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFranco Colapinto hits his Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly and pushes him into Lando Norris’s car.Photograph: Eric Alonso/DPPI/ShutterstockLando NorrisLando Norris says Colapinto ‘shouldn’t be in F1’ after crash ends title hopesBriton forced to retire from Azerbaijan GP when eighthColapinto given a grid drop at the next round in MalaysiaGiles RichardsSat 26 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLando Norris has issued a scathing criticism of Franco Colapinto, saying the Alpine driver does not deserve to be in Formula One and should face a ban after taking Norris’s McLaren out of the race.The Azerbaijan Grand Prix was won by Mercedes’ George Russell but Norris was forced to retire from eighth place after Colapinto caused the accident that all but ended the defending world champion’s title hopes.George Russell holds off Max Verstappen to win eventful F1 Azerbaijan GPRead moreColapinto came in toward turn one from a safety car restart far too hot and locked-up long before the corner entry. Unable to control the car, he speared into his teammate Pierre Gasly, who in turn shunted the British driver. With all three cars out of the race, Norris was left fuming.“I just got taken out. There are some drivers who shouldn’t be inFormula One,” he said.Norris is now 116 points off the championship leader Kimi Antonelli with eight meetings remaining and while mathematically he is still in the hunt the title is surely gone.McLaren had brought a swathe of new parts to the race in Baku and having sustained considerable damage, there is no guarantee they can be replaced in time for the Bahrain GP in Malaysia next weekend. That left Norris insistent Colapinto should face serious sanction.“If you cause a crash on a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban,” he said. “The FIA should be stricter by starting to hand out bans for this kind of stuff. It is just careless. It costs a lot of money, all my parts are in the bin now. It is not driving that deserves to be in Formula One.“In Formula One you would expect that drivers can anticipate that the grip will be low and tyre temperatures are low. You want to be against the best drivers and when stuff like this happens it is because they shouldn’t be there.”Colapinto apologised for causing the incident. “I can be sorry to everyone. It’s been a big mistake of course. I just locked-up and then I was very out of control,” he said.The error was hugely costly to his Alpine team as well who were on for a double points finish at the time and Gasly was similarly aggrieved at his teammate. “I don’t think I really have words and I don’t need the words now,” he said.The stewards gave Colapinto a 10-second penalty in the race but since he could not serve it having already retired, he will instead receive a grid drop at the next round.Explore more on these topicsLando NorrisMcLarenFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Laver Cup back in the balance as Team World match their captain Andre Agassi’s energy | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Alex de Minaur recovered from match point down to beat Alexander Zverev, before Carlos Alcaraz launched a comeback of his own to leave the Laver Cup level at 5-5
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Alex de Minaur recovered from match point down to beat Alexander Zverev, before Carlos Alcaraz launched a comeback of his own to leave the Laver Cup level at 5-5
Content: Andre Agassi, Team World’s captain this Laver Cup, was a constant support to Alex de Minaur in his comeback win against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndre Agassi, Team World’s captain this Laver Cup, was a constant support to Alex de Minaur in his comeback win against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTennisLaver Cup back in the balance as Team World match their captain Andre Agassi’s energyAlex de Minaur recovers from match point down to beat Alexander ZverevCarlos Alcaraz launches comeback of his own to leave event level at 5-5Tumaini Carayolat the O2 ArenaSat 26 Sep 2026 18.29 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor much of his afternoon on court againstAlexander Zverev, Alex de Minaur seemed destined to end his day with an excruciating defeat. De Minaur had rapidly found himself down a set and a break, then Zverev served for the match at 6-2, 5-4. After miraculously giving himself another lifeline, De Minaur finally faced a match point at 8-9 in the final set tie-break.No matter how grim the scoreline appeared, though, every effort he made was punctuated by roars of approval from one person in particular. There were loud screams of encouragement, pounding of chairs and stamping of feet. At one point, as doubt had crept into Zverev’s game during the second set tie-break, that unmistakable voice from the sidelines yelled out: “Check his oil! Check his oil!”Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worthRead moreThose words came fromAndre Agassiand, with such unconditional support provided by one of the greatest tennis players of all time, his Team World captain, there was no way that De Minaur could lose. De Minaur’s probing soon revealed that Zverev had indeed run out of oil, his engine failing, as the Australian recovered from match point down to close out a 2-6, 7-6 (5), 11-9 win.Agassi’s unbridled enthusiasm and support was reflected in his team as they held their own on day two of the Laver Cup against a group of higher-ranked opponents.With Team Europe leading 3-1 overnight, Learner Tien of the US opened the day with a 6-3, 2-6, 10-7 win over the Italian Flavio Cobolli before De Minaur defeated Zverev, the recent French and US Open champion.While match win were worth just one point on Friday, they were worth two on Saturday. Team Europe closed the day with a narrow 7-5 lead over Team World.Carlos Alcarazlevelled the series by saving two match points to defeat Taylor Fritz 6-3, 4-6, 13-11 before Casper Ruud and Zverev teamed up to beat Alexander Bublik and Brandon Nakashima 6-4, 7-6 (7).View image in fullscreenTeam Europe were again indebted to Carlos Alcaraz, whose comeback win over Taylor Fritz helped them take a 7-5 Laver Cup lead.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty Images for Laver CupPerhaps the most interesting aspect of this week is simply the presence of Agassi as he continues his re-emergence on to the tennis scene. For some time after his retirement, Agassi and his even more legendary wife, the 22-time grand slam champion Steffi Graf, kept a low profile at home in Las Vegas.Their lore was often only really extended through the top young players, such as Fernando Verdasco, Sorana Cirstea and Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova, who would sometimes train with them at their home. They would return from Nevada speaking of how invaluable Agassi’s counsel had been to their careers or how Graf was still in such tremendous shape that she could easily slot back in on the WTA tour. Otherwise, they minded their own business.Things have drastically changed over the past 18 months, starting with the announcement last February that Agassi would replace John McEnroe as Team World’s captain. Since then, he has been everywhere. He joined TNT Sports in the US as a commentator at Roland Garros last year, then he worked on the BBC’s commentary team for the first time in the final days of this year’s Wimbledon . His employment decisions have been received far more positively than those of his old rival Pete Sampras, who emerged back into public view at the US Open as the face of the sport prediction market Kalshi. However, Agassi is currently managed by one of the more controversial figures in the sport, Justin Gimelstob.Agassi seems comfortable talking tactics with modern players who sometimes view the sport differently to their elders. It has been enjoyable to listen to how one of the greatest tennis minds expresses those thoughts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAgassi was full of inspiration and advice for Learner Tien, who went on to beat Flavio Cobolli.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/APOne of the most memorable narratives surrounding Agassi in retirement wasthe love-hate relationshiphe famously described himself as having with the sport in his autobiography, Open. For that reason, it has been particularly satisfying to witness the unbridled joy and love he carries for the sport now, so many years removed from the stress that accompanied being a top competitor.Agassi simply cannot sit still on the Team World bench. He is constantly cheering and encouraging his players, hell bent on keeping morale up, and his boundless energy provokes positive reactions from his players. As a delirious De Minaur celebrated his victory over Zverev, his first move was to sprint to Agassi while repeatedly shouting: “You like that? You like that?” Without hesitation, Agassi responded: “I love it. I love it.” Blood was rolling down De Minaur’s knee at the end of the match after he grazed his knee on a spectacular diving forehand. In his excitement, Agassi shouted: “I wanna lick that blood off you right now.”This strong rapport between Agassi and his players was also clear in certain sentimental moments. After Tien had closed out his victory and completed all of his post-match duties on the court, he and Agassi hovered by their bench for a long, sweet debrief. Tien was clearly still frustrated by his high unforced error count, so Agassi offered him some tactical advice for future matches.Once they had finished, Tien leaned down to pick up his bag, prompting a quick intervention from the all-time great: “Dude, I’ll carry this shit for you if you want me to,” he said. “That’s how much respect I have [for you].”Explore more on these topicsTennisAndre AgassiCarlos AlcarazAlexander ZverevAlex de MinaurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nice guys finish first as Bamber and Woakes help Warwickshire seal slow-burn title | Warwickshire | The Guardian
description: Two bowlers often described as ‘the nicest guys in cricket’ played starring roles as the Bears outlasted the County Championship competition
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Two bowlers often described as ‘the nicest guys in cricket’ played starring roles as the Bears outlasted the County Championship competition
Content: Chris Woakes (left) and Ethan Bamber (right) took 96 Championship wickets between them at a combined average of 20.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris Woakes (left) and Ethan Bamber (right) took 96 Championship wickets between them at a combined average of 20.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesWarwickshireAnalysisNice guys finish first as Bamber and Woakes help Warwickshire seal slow-burn titleAli Martinat EdgbastonTwo bowlers often described as ‘the nicest guys in cricket’ played starring roles as the Bears outlasted the County Championship competitionSat 26 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.16 EDTShareEthan Bamber may be an adopted Brummie but it’s fair to say he has the city’s self-effacing nature down to a tee. After sealing Warwickshire’s ninthCounty Championshipwith one final explosion of bails, and watching captain Ed Barnard lift the trophy to cheers of “You Bears” from the stands, Bamber tried to credit anyone but himself and even claimed to be an “average cricketer”.Average? Not so fast. No bowler in Division One has sent down more than Bamber’s 445.3 overs this year, nor can top the 69 wickets that he finished on after rattling Tom Scriven’s timbers to wrap up a comprehensive innings and 79-run victory over Leicestershire. The 27-year-old ploughed through all 14 games of the campaign, with his waspish brand of wobble-seam and swing consistently undermining batting line-ups in this slow-burn triumph.Warwickshire clinch County Championship title with victory over LeicestershireRead moreAnd it was a slow burn. Nottinghamshirehad the trophy, while Somerset had the alluring narrative ofperennial runners-uppotentially breaking the curse. But Warwickshire had the clinical edge it took to claim the prize, holding firm at the start of the season andmoving into position to strikeat the back end, winning five of their last six – seven overall – and suffering just one defeat. Their reward for staying the course was a golden celebration with loved ones on a sun-drenched outfield in September.A calming influence as captain whose contributions with bat and ball have been myriad, Barnard was buzzing about a squad he took charge of in March when Alex Davies surprisingly stood down as captain. Bamber was “the nicest man in county cricket” and had gone up “four levels” since joining last year, while Sam Hain was “the most underrated” after another stellar season.Hain’s 1,048 runs at 74.85 in a summer dominated by the Dukes ball underlined his seasoned quality, with Barnard grateful – if slightly confused – that England have not stolen his services in recent times.Bamber was simply in a state of disbelief as theWarwickshiresupporters who had sung his name to the tune of La Bamba by Los Lobos queued up for selfies. There were doubts in the past, with the move from Middlesex for Edgbaston a case of looking to discover his “ceiling”.View image in fullscreenEd Barnard led Warwickshire to the title in his first season as captain.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesFor Chris Woakes, who got things moving on the third morning when he pinged Sol Budinger’s middle stump from his beloved City End, that ceiling could be higher still. “Ethan may be the nicest guy you’ll ever meet,” said Woakes, who has earned similar praise during his own career. “But he gets the bit between his teeth on the field. He really gets in the battle and demands high standards of himself. That’s off the field as well. The hard yards he puts in. I’ve never seen anyone work as hard.“He’s probably the fittest guy in our squad. He’s played all 14 games and it looks like he’d go for another 14. I feel like he deserves further honours. What that is at the minute, I don’t know. But I feel like he should definitely be in the conversation.”Woakes was another of Barnard’s standouts, his experience coming to the fore during a number of clutch moments. And not least when he and Olly Hannon-Dalby –another club stalwartand the world’s most obdurate No 11 – guided the Bears toa nerve-shredding one-wicket victoryover Sussex at the start of August and sent confidence coursing through the dressing room.View image in fullscreenChris Woakes’ three County Championship titles with Warwickshire have come over 14 years.Photograph: Jacob King/PAAt 37, Woakes could easily have called time on first-class cricket whenhis Test career endedwith thateye-watering dislocated shoulderat the Oval last summer; perhaps he could have cashed in on the franchise circuit before retirement. Instead, he chose to return to the grind and give something back to his boyhood club.“I came into the game playing county cricket and I wanted to go out of the game playing county cricket,” explained Woakes, celebrating his third title after wins in 2012 and 2021. “It’s a bit of a pinch-me moment, standing here now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After what happened last year, it was a case of ‘What’s my Everest? What’s going to get me out of bed in the morning?’ A trophy for Warwickshire was always the priority and it’s really nice to get it over the line. For the club to have won it nine times and to have three in my back pocket, that is pretty sweet.”Warwickshire clinch the title, Bairstow the hero for Yorkshire, and more: County Championship, third day – liveRead moreThere was, of course, plenty more to this triumph beyond the headliners. A move to more result-oriented pitches at home helped, as did the adhesive hands of Rob Yates at second slip by claiming a record 39 catches across the season.Two-day wins at Glamorgan and Essex during the run-in earned precious rest for the players – though plenty still came in to train – while the late-summer signing of Manav Suthar was inspired. The India Test spinner winkled out 27 wickets in just six outings, even with the quicks dominating.And while Graeme “Pop” Welch again underlined his status as one of the leading seam-bowling gurus in the country, this campaign was also masterminded by an up-and-coming English head coach: Ian Westwood. Driven, methodical and imbued with the club’s DNA, the 44-year-old has been tactically simpatico with Barnard and overseen a set-up that has ticked off all the one-percenters.They tend not to talk themselves up in this part of the world, but they really should.Explore more on these topicsWarwickshireCounty ChampionshipCounty Championship Division OneCricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: When things are going awry, Argentina will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause after Lionel Messi’s farewell against Benin
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: When things are going awry, Argentina will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause after Lionel Messi’s farewell against Benin
Content: Lionel Messi, despite his obvious limitations, was as influential as ever at the World Cup.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APView image in fullscreenLionel Messi, despite his obvious limitations, was as influential as ever at the World Cup.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APInside footballLionel MessiMessi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superheroJonathan WilsonWhen things are going awry, theAlbicelestewill no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clauseSat 26 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTShareIt isn’t quite over yet.Lionel Messiwill return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.Lionel Messi in his 30s was one of the best international players ever | Jeff RueterRead moreThen Messi retired,distraught after a missing a penaltyin the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry willArgentinabe able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.The best example came almost at the end, when Argentinatrailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.View image in fullscreenLionel Messi cries at the end of the World Cup final after Argentina’s loss to Spain.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APOther than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still canRead moreWith Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiInside footballArgentinacommentShareReuse this content

title: WSL roundup: Putellas scores first London City goal, Manchester City maintain perfect start | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Alexia Putellas scored her first WSL goal as London City Lionesses moved into second place in the WSL after beating Brighton 2-0 at home while Manchester City maintained their perfect start with a 1-0 win at Charlton

Headline: Alexia Putellas scored her first WSL goal as London City Lionesses moved into second place in the WSL after beating Brighton 2-0 at home while Manchester City maintained their perfect start with a 1-0 win at Charlton
Content: Alexia Putellas (right) takes the acclaim of her London City Lionesses teammates after scoring the opening goal against Brighton.Photograph: Andrew Redington/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas (right) takes the acclaim of her London City Lionesses teammates after scoring the opening goal against Brighton.Photograph: Andrew Redington/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueWSL roundup: Putellas scores first London City goal, Manchester City maintain perfect startTwo-time Ballon d’Or winner nets against BrightonAlex Greenwood’s free-kick sinks CharltonPress AssociationSat 26 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlexia Putellas scored her first WSL goal asLondonCityLionessesmoved second in the table after beatingBrighton2-0 at home.The two-time Ballon d’Or winner, who left Barcelona in the summer, put London City ahead in the 29th minute when she slotted a low shot into the far corner.Brighton were close to an equaliser before the break when Emily Murphy’s header struck the crossbar. title: Wakefield stun Wigan to storm into their first Super League Grand Final | Super League | The Guardian
description: Wakefield will face Warrington in the Super League Grand Final next Saturday after stunning Wigan 33-6
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Wakefield will face Warrington in the Super League Grand Final next Saturday after stunning Wigan 33-6
Content: Wakefield players and staff celebrate in front of their fans after their stunning win against Wigan.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWakefield players and staff celebrate in front of their fans after their stunning win against Wigan.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueWakefield stun Wigan to storm into their first Super League Grand FinalSemi-final: Wigan 6-33 WakefieldWakefield face Warrington at Old Trafford next SaturdayAaron Bowerat the Brick Community StadiumSat 26 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe corridors of Wakefield’s famous Belle Vue ground are lined with black and white photos of the halcyon days of the 1960s, when this grand old club were last a rugby league force. Days like these could not have seemed further away in 2023 when Daryl Powell was appointed by their new owner, Matt Ellis, with an initial remit to secure promotion back toSuper League.Irwin holds nerve to sink Leeds and send Warrington to Grand FinalRead moreBut Ellis, the local kitchen magnate who has followed Wakefield all his life, had much loftier goals for the club he had just purchased. He delivered Powell a clear message, something the Trinity coach recalled this week: “When I came, Matt said to me: ‘I want you to turn black and white into colour’.” There is only one colour on this club’s mind right now though: gold.This is one of the great sporting stories of recent times. Two years ago this weekend, Wakefield beat Doncaster 72-6 in front of just under 5,000 supporters in the Championship. Next weekend, they will walk out in the Super League Grand Final for the first time. There are rapid rises, and then there is this particular story.The club have spent the majority of the Super League era and the decades before it languishing in the lower reaches and light years away from clubs like Wigan – who they dismantled here with one of the most complete playoff performances you are ever likely to find. Now, one of rugby league’s true sleeping giants are alive, and within one win of a first league title since 1968.View image in fullscreenWakefield owner Matt Ellis (right) celebrates his club’s victory with  former commentator Chris Kamara.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockHow they did it defies description. Few gave them a chance of beating a Wigan side seemingly on an unstoppable run to an historic treble; surely not even the most optimistic of Trinity fans would have suggested a victory of this margin. The turning point was Wigan’s Adam Keighran being sent to the sin-bin early in the second half, during which time Wakefield scored 16 unanswered points.Quick GuideWigan 6-33 Wakefield: teams and scorersShowWiganField; Daniel, Keighran, Eckersley, Marshall; French, Smith; Thompson, O’Neill, Havard, Nsemba, Walters, Partington.InterchangeKerr, Ellis, Mago, Farrell.TryO’Neill.GoalSmith.WakefieldJowitt; Walmsley, Scott, Hall, Johnstone; Trueman, Sinfield; Rodwell, Smoothy, McMeeken, Vagana, Lipowicz, Tevaga.InterchangeFaatili, Hamlin-Uele, Lino, Pitts.TriesJohnstone 2, Sinfield, Hall, Rodwell.GoalsJowitt 6.Drop goalLino.RefereeL Moore.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.That turned a slender 8-6 half-time lead into a commanding 24-6 advantage. But even when Keighran returned, Wakefield were the superior team. It never really looked like Wigan could launch any sort of comeback, meaning it is Trinity who now stand on the verge of history with Warrington – the club who sacked Powell in 2023 – standing in their way.“Our mentality was always we thought we could come here and win despite what people said,” Powell said. “We were superb. This is a special group of boys and we have a great opportunity ahead of us next week.” This is a seismic moment for the game too; next week will be the first Grand Final not to feature any of Leeds, Wigan or St Helens.View image in fullscreenWakefield’s Jack Sinfield celebrates scoring a try against WiganPhotograph: Martin Rickett/PAAnd the Warriors could have no complaints, in truth. They did go ahead through Brad O’Neill’s try but that was a false dawn. By the break, Tom Johnstone’s score and two goals from Max Jowitt nudged Wakefield ahead – and they didn’t relent after half-time. Keighran’s yellow for a tip tackle on Isaiah Vagana was the semi-final’s defining moment, though.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKitchen magnate finds recipe for Wakefield joy in historic rugby league cityRead moreBy the time he returned, Corey Hall, Jack Sinfield and Johnstone had all scored tries to make it 24-6. Nobody, not even this Wigan side, can overturn a scoreline like that in a game of this magnitude. “Wakefield were outstandingly good,” Wigan’s coach, Matt Peet, conceded. “We were outplayed and out-coached: they beat us all ends up. The night belongs to them.”Peet, as magnanimous as always, is correct. This was their night, underlined by Ky Rodwell’s try after Keighran returned which just emphasised further the gap between the teams on the night. Mason Lino’s drop goal and a late Jowitt penalty were mere cherries on top: by then, the 5,000-strong travelling support – the same number that used to watch them at home - were celebrating.We often say there are incredible stories and historic moments to be written at Old Trafford. Next Saturday, that is categorically the case asWakefield Trinityfinally aim to write a new, colourful chapter in their illustrious history.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWigan WarriorsWakefield TrinityRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Gloucester’s Dewi Lake in full flow with two tries in emphatic win at Exeter | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Dewi Lake and Ben Loader scored two tries apiece in Gloucester’s 45-24 bonus-point win against Exeter, last season’s Prem runners-up
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Dewi Lake and Ben Loader scored two tries apiece in Gloucester’s 45-24 bonus-point win against Exeter, last season’s Prem runners-up
Content: Ben Loader celebrates after Dewi Lake scores Gloucester’s fifth try against Exeter.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBen Loader celebrates after Dewi Lake scores Gloucester’s fifth try against Exeter.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesPrem RugbyGloucester’s Dewi Lake in full flow with two tries in emphatic win at ExeterExeter 24-45 GloucesterBen Loader also scores two tries in bonus-point winRobert Kitsonat Sandy ParkSat 26 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloucester are determined to make significant progress up the Prem table this season and here was a hugely promising first step. The Cherry and Whites had a bonus point on the board before half-time on a breezy afternoon in Devon and had more than enough in the tank to build on a 14-point interval lead and secure a morale-boosting early away victory.Considering they claimed just one league win on the road in the whole of the 2025-26 campaign, this seven-try fusillade was a big plus, spearheaded by their new Welsh reinforcements Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan. Lake was the deserved player of the match, scoring two tries and adding significantly to Gloucester’s efforts in both the set pieces and the maul.‘I haven’t come back for a jolly’: Dan Robson on Dupont, Pau and rebuilding GloucesterRead moreThis performance was also a tribute to the summer input of Gloucester’s new forwards coach Brett Deacon, defence coach Joel Tomkins and technical director Chris Boyd, albeit helped by a distinctly off-colourExeterdisplay described as “baffling” by Rob Baxter, the Chiefs’ director of rugby. There was a touch of illness in the home camp this week but that did not wholly account for the visitors’ overall supremacy.In addition to a couple of tries for left wing Ben Loader there was considerably more cohesion and focus to Gloucester’s game, not always consistently evident on their travels in recent seasons. And crucially, they now have a central pillar around whom they will be keen to rally. In contrast to the south-west’s depleted reservoirs, this newly arrived Lake is already making a significant difference to Gloucester’s level.The visitors, in their pink change strip, certainly made the most of the wind behind them in the opening 40 minutes. There were two very similar tries from little chip kicks out to the left wing which gave the talented Loader plenty of time and space to outflank the cover but the real secret of Gloucester’s improvement was the all-round balance to their game.Rather than chucking the ball around like headless chickens there was much more solidity to their set piece and more control generally. Their defensive appetite was also impressive, forcing the Chiefs to work overtime for any tangible reward in their opponents’ 22.Quick GuideExeter 24-45 Gloucester: teams and scorersShowExeterHammersley (Haydon-Wood, 63); Feyi-Waboso, Slade, Butt (Wimbush, 60), Woodburn; Skinner, Varney; Burger (Goodrick-Clarke, 57), Yeandle (Gulley, 57), Iosefa-Scott (J Roots, 57), Jenkins (capt), Wilson (Beckerleg, 73), E Roots (Worley-Brady, 73), James, Fisilau.TriesIosefa-Scott, E Roots, Varney, Gulley.Cons:Slade 2.Gloucester:Redshaw (Denney, 73); Joseph (Barton, 78), P Cokanasiga, S Atkinson, Loader; C Atkinson, Englefield (Robson, 55); Rapava-Ruskin (Blueler, 52), Lake (capt; Innard, 55), Fasogbon (C Knight, 52), Kleyn (Ludlow, 52), Clark, Thomas, Morgan, Trenholm (Clement, 63).Tries:Loader 2, S Atkinson, Lake 2, Joseph, Denney.ConsC Atkinson 4, Barton.Yellow card:Freddie Thomas 70.Referee: Matthew Carley.Attendance8,682.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Aside from a forward rumble by Josh Iosefa-Scott and a compelling surge down the left by the forceful Ethan Roots, Chiefs were visibly lacking their usual verve and energy. The reserve forward Joe Bailey was the only player to drop out before kick-off because of illness but the extra spring in Gloucester’s step was impossible to ignore. Seb Atkinson should not have been first to Caolan Englefield’s chip in behind but, for whatever reason, Exeter’s rearguard were caught ball-watching.Lake, throwing his lineout arrows straighter than Luke Littler and galvanising everyone around him, was already a central figure even before he dived into the left corner to score his side’s fourth try just before the break. There was a certain inevitability when the former Osprey burrowed over for his second five minutes after the restart and Chiefs’ pain soon deepened further.Again, there seemed little obvious danger when Will Joseph received the ball wide on the right around the halfway line, only for the younger brother of the former England centre Jonathan to score a quite brilliant weaving solo try to help push Gloucester out to a 20-point lead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWill Joseph goes over for Gloucester’s sixth try in their comfortable win against Exeter.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesExeter now had little option but to wake up, assisted by some fresh legs off the bench, and belatedly looked more dangerous. Stephen Varney sprinted over from 30 metres out and the scrum-half would have had a second try had he not been denied by an outstanding last-ditch tackle.With Freddie Thomas sent to the sin-bin, though, Gloucester had to survive the final 10 minutes with only 14 men and Exeter’s replacement hooker, Louie Gulley, collected a try on his Prem debut to secure a try bonus point. It was swiftly trumped, though, by a last-minute try for Junior Denny, prompting a hush to descend upon the home supporters.Nor was the threadbare attendance of only 8,682 any great cause for Exeter celebration. Their new American backers will have hoped they were taking over a team pushing for a second consecutive Prem final. Suddenly their team will need to improve substantially merely to finish higher than their opponents.“I thought Gloucester were good and knew what they wanted to do today,” said Baxter. “But I don’t think I’ve seen us quite as poor in terms of some of our basics or lack of desire to counterattack into the wind in the second half. Sometimes a slap in the face like this can be good for you but it’s up to the lads how they react to it.”Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyExeterGloucesterRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Amazon’s Ring wants to replace local WhatsApp groups. It’s a recipe for curtain-twitching disaster | Imogen West-Knights | The Guardian
description: Do we really want a slick digital message board overseen by Amazon? It’s the neighbourhood nonsense we treasure, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Author: Imogen West-Knights
Headline: Do we really want a slick digital message board overseen by Amazon? It’s the neighbourhood nonsense we treasure, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Content: A mock-up of the new Ring Neighbours app.Composite: RingView image in fullscreenA mock-up of the new Ring Neighbours app.Composite: RingOpinionWhatsAppAmazon’s Ring wants to replace local WhatsApp groups. It’s a recipe for curtain-twitching disasterImogen West-KnightsDo we really want a slick digital message board overseen by Amazon? It’s the neighbourhood nonsense we treasureSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTShareRing, the Amazon subsidiary of camera-enabled doorbells fame, wants to be an even bigger part of your neighbourhood. Next month in the UK, it will belaunching Neighbours, a community app that seeks to replace the now traditional neighbourhood Facebook or WhatsApp group. It will be available inside the Ring app, free to everybody, including people without Ring products, and will include a community requests feature wherein the police can ask for footage from residents living near reported crimes, who can then choose whether or not to share it.My first thought was that this is curtain-twitching culture gone mad. If you must have a Ring doorbell (and my instinctive feeling as someone without one, a feeling I will no doubt have until I get one and decide it’s great, is that it’s narc-coded behaviour) then: OK. But doesAmazonneed to be in charge of a digital village messageboard too?The selling point, Ring thinks, is that posting will be anonymised, and posters will have to conform to strict guidelines on what they are allowed to post. It would, in other words, be very unlike the lawless badlands of a neighbourhoodWhatsApp.Maybe people really did want these groups replaced by something more centrally managed. I asked around people I knew about theWhatsApp communitiesthat they were in, and the kinds of behaviour they had witnessed. Some of it, naturally, demonstrated an ugly dislike of homeless people, fear and loathing of door-to-door salespeople, racial profiling of local youths, and the view that everyone not personally known to the residents was a criminal in waiting.Some of what people encountered on these groups was just strange: a north London WhatsApp group of more than 500 people having to disband because someone was giving away a Hewlett-Packard printer and another person said that shouldn’t be allowed because ofBDS; a woman forced to recuse herself from a neighbourhood group because she saw a toad get squashed by a car, and was inundated with local volunteers who wanted her to set up and run a toad protection squad in case there were other vulnerable toads in the area; a man with a vendetta against a local couple who were feeding the foxes that went on to rip up his garden taking to his local chat to respond with witty bons mots such as “they are as stubborn as the foxes themselves but lack their intelligence”; repeated reports about a “sick cat” that people familiar with the animal had to confirm was “just ugly”; and this is leaving out the party poopers, bin police and other assorted oddballs.But then there were the wonderful stories, too: the organisation of a funeral procession for an older woman who died on the street with no immediate family; borrowing laptop chargers and camping equipment; taking in people who had locked themselves out. And all of these led me to feel a little envious.I’ve just moved, but for four years before that I lived on a street in south London. One time, I witnessed something insane happen. My flatmate was at home one Saturday afternoon and heard an altercation on the street, and looked out the window to see what was going on. He was, in his way, curtain twitching. A neighbourhood cat, a friendly local celebrity who always greeted you as you passed, had been mauled to death by an XL bully being walked past the house where it lived.The cat’s owners were, understandably, furious and upset. The noise my flatmate heard was them trying to detain the person with the dog so they could be held accountable. Later that week, signs appeared on trees on the street inviting anybody who knew the departed cat to gather outside the family’s home for drinks. My flatmate and I looked at this sign and became anxious that nobody would go. I was moved almost to tears at the image of this grieving family, including two young children, with their trestle table of prosecco and nobody to serve it to.We needn’t have worried. Dozens of people showed up, with flowers and wine and stories of giving little pieces of chicken to the cat. At this memorial, I looked around and thought: God, it is actually quite strange and perhaps reflects poorly on all of us that most of us had never met. Our street, as far as I know, had no WhatsApp group. If it had done, I would have known these people already. Community, especially in big cities, can be hard to come by, and is precious to people when it’s found. After that cat memorial, we invited two of our newfound neighbours over for drinks. We’ve since become friends. I felt, for the first time, part of my local area.Neighbourhood WhatsApp groups can be a way to create that feeling. But. But! They are also places where people exercise their worst small-time cop impulses, demonstrate their smallmindedness, allow the little annoyances of life to induce them to send people they hardly know crazed screeds about recycling etiquette. Would you give up the latter if you had to give up the former as well, though?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere’s a comment Dave Ward, Ring’s managing director of international, gave to the Guardian about what they want to do. “We are going to coach people to make sure they’re creating the right sort of post, asking them if that’s really something they want to write or whether it really needs that descriptive term, to help stop the type of content no one wants to see and make it more community focused. That’s very different to other places [such as WhatsApp groups].”So Ring wants to streamline things, moderate, vet, polish. I have worked my way around to feeling, however, that the problem here isn’t just Ring wanting to connect us all up to the police, encouraging the darker side of local message groups, that micro-nation surveillance state tendency, or even it wanting to induct more people into local groups that can so often be irritating. It’s that the rough edges of these groups are the spice of life. You don’t have to participate in a neighbourhood WhatsApp group, but if you choose to be in one, the price for the moments of kindness and connection you can find within them is the nonsense.Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalistExplore more on these topicsWhatsAppOpinionSocial mediaAmazonAppscommentShareReuse this content

title: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: As she mulls another presidential run, the former VP is building bridges with progressive and Arab American leaders
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: As she mulls another presidential run, the former VP is building bridges with progressive and Arab American leaders
Content: ‘This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable.’Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable.’Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersThe Week in PatriarchyKamala HarrisKamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late?Arwa MahdawiAs she mulls another presidential run, the former VP is building bridges with progressive and Arab American leadersSat 26 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTShareDoes Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly actingthat way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensiveprice to pay” for the war on Iran.And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after themidterms. But by the looks of hisdismal pollingnumbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore.Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about theDemocratsreturning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results.See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – shetold votersin Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters throughmidterm campaigning.This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at aroundtablefocused on Black maternal health. Harris will also becampaigningwith the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid.Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for SenateRead moreHarris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage.The New York Timesreportedthis week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”.But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates havepublicly statedthat they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections.El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters.Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza agenocide– as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts.El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the mostlukewarmof endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axiosreportedthat Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidateshe’d endorsedwon their primaries over establishment-backed candidates.In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about.In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Insteadmanyof these votersstayed home.The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issueonce. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show arecord 60% of US adultsnow have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democratssupport an arms embargo.Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing.The murder of nine women causes a reckoning in South AfricaThebodies of nine womenhave been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months. Some were naked or partially clothed. The apparent murders, which may be connected, have reignited protests about the country’s femicide rate, which isfive times higherthan the global average. Hundreds of demonstratorsmarched throughCape Town on Thursday, demanding an end to gender-based violence.Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to train wins Asian Games silverFariba Hashimi was attacked with stones and had to train while disguised as a man when she first started cycling. Now based in Italy, Hashimi won anAsian Games silver medalon Tuesday and hopes to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles games.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Republican senator has warned that furries are infiltrating the aviation community“It’s terrifying when you think about this,” the senator Tommy Tuberville saidthis week. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.” Tuberville seems to be referencing an incident in April when pilots wereheard making“meow” sounds over an air traffic control frequency at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport. Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries?Masked lesbian infighting went ultra-viral this weekI wrote about the Last Ditch dramahere.The dangers of AI are already here“The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibsononce said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Husseinwrite in the Guardian.Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’Lian Yunzhi isreportedly“the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”.A day in the life of a pregnant woman in GazaSitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardianpublished this piece.Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium canceled due to nor’easterAhilarious developmentin the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheerantour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsKamala HarrisThe Week in PatriarchyDemocratsPalestineUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone? | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: Even Jacob Rees-Mogg pushes back on defining Englishness in exclusively ethnic terms. But the endurance of this discourse is still deeply troubling, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: Even Jacob Rees-Mogg pushes back on defining Englishness in exclusively ethnic terms. But the endurance of this discourse is still deeply troubling, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Content: A mini-roundabout painted  to represent the St George’s flag in Margate, September 2025.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA mini-roundabout painted  to represent the St George’s flag in Margate, September 2025.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionBritish identity and societyOf course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?Jason OkundayeEven Jacob Rees-Mogg pushes back on defining Englishness in exclusively ethnic terms. But the endurance of this discourse is still deeply troublingSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.09 EDTShareCan you be English and non-white? It’s a question that keeps stubbornly resurfacing in our political discourse.Last weekend, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak gave his view in a column in the Times, arguing that national identity should not be turned into a DNA test. After leaving office, Sunak,the UK’s first prime minister of colour, was subject to claims by a prominent podcasterthat he was not English because he was a“brown-skinned Hindu”. Reflecting on this, Sunak described it as a “reverseTebbit test”: the sociological concept measuring the loyalty of immigrants – and their children – in the UK depending on which cricket team they supported in international matches. “Once we say that this or that person isn’t really English or British because they are not white,” he wrote, “then we are on a very slippery slope. Some people will argue that English is an ethnic identity and British a civic identity. Though if you think those nuances are heard by most people, I fear you are being rather – perhaps even wilfully – naive.”Sunak is right that this conversation isn’t really about nuanced distinctions between ethnic and civic identities. The questioning of one’s Englishness is deeply insidious, as it is not solely articulated through supposed “legitimate concerns” about the pace of immigration, crimes committed bymigrants or ethnic minorities, or anxieties around jobs and access to public services. Instead, it is presented as a question of first principles: whether you are a “good” or “bad” minority, a citizen or non-citizen, your ancestry or skin colour means you will never truly belong. Your claim to belong in this country, and that of your descendants, will always be implicitly lesser than those who could, at least theoretically, trace their ancestry back to Oswald of Northumbria. That idea is deeply uncomfortable for many, rejected both by those who hold progressive views on immigration and community integration, and those who otherwise hold conservative views of national belonging and hardened borders.There is growing concern among sections of the British right about increasingly “ethnonationalist” impulses emerging on its fringes and entering mainstream political debate. That has particularly gathered steam with the rise of Rupert Lowe’s hard-rightRestore Britain.These beliefs belong to what the Financial Times’s Robert Shrimsley described as the right’s own “woke wing”, which fusses over “the great replacement theory and the betrayal of the west”. More moderate conservatives will want to distance themselves from these views as much as they will from theblack-clad far-right mobsthat descended on Portsmouth and Dover this summer.There are indications that some of these views are gaining greater public legitimacy. Ananalysisby the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) last year found that the percentage of those who believed “Britishness” was something you were born with had almost doubled in two years (from 19% to 36%). But there are reasons for those on the right to worry that the popularisation of these once-fringe views could alienate them from the majority, who still reject them. According to the IPPR analysis, only3%of people believe that being a “good” British citizen requires having white skin, while at least74%of English people believe that Englishness is not defined by ethnicity. The hard right’s attachment to a politics of ethnicity also threatens to upend a project that the broader conservative movement has been at pains to build over the years: a multi-ethnic coalition that can hold anti-immigration views without the Englishness or Britishness of its own members being called into question. That means maintaining a definition of national belonging that minorities can actually attain.So it may feel curious to see the Tory traditionalist Jacob Rees-Mogg,no ally of Sunak, release a series ofvideos on Xstating that “everyone who has a British passport is equally British or English” and positing that the English are“a mongrel people, not an Aryan master race”. But the desire to openly define Englishness, and Britishness, in exclusively ethnic terms remains relatively fringe, and it is not a politics that yet finds a broad coalition. Perhaps unsurprisingly, two of Sunak and Rees-Mogg’s lead opponents were minority politicians on the hard right: Reform spokespersons Suella Braverman, who insists that she cannot be English, andZia Yusuf, who recasts the argument in familiar culture war terms about those who have “betrayed” our country, and insists that “people are furious about what Rees-Mogg and Sunak are saying”.That preoccupation over ethnic nationalism isn’t purely a feature of the modern hard right; in 1701, the English writer Daniel Defoe wroteThe True-Born Englishman, a poem to defend William III, born a sovereign Prince of Orange, from xenophobic attacks disparaging his lack of ethnic “Englishness”. Defoe wrote: “Thus from a mixture of all kinds began, / That het’rogeneous thing, an Englishman”, referring to the English, as Rees-Mogg did, as a “mongrel half-bred race”. That speaks to something that is worth remembering when questions about who gets to be English recur: it has never been a property passed down intact from one generation of ethnically pure Englishmen to the next. Instead, it has continually been remade through migration, assimilation, conquering, marriage, conversion and settlement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solution | Taj AliRead moreAttempts to impose a simplified ancestry-based definition quickly become absurd, as Lowe saw when, in August,he could not answerwhether or not he would consider King Charles, whose father was born in Greece and who has German and Danish ancestry, a “white Briton”. But even a more inclusive civic-nationalist definition of Englishness raises questions with no settled answer: is it defined simply through citizenship or through language, accents, behaviours, “values”, culinary preferences or sporting affiliation? For those who believe that it is an ethnic identity based on ancestry, how many generations back must you be able to trace your lineage?Even if ethnonationalist views are stymied by more moderate voices on the contemporary right, the surfacing of these discourses is still deeply troubling for many ethnic minorities. Its traction may, for now, be limited, but it still risks contributing to a “common sense” assumption that there is something like a pure English ethnicity determined by race. Interestingly,ethnic-minority adultsthemselves are more likely to view Englishness as tied to heritage, and prefer an identification with Britishness. I can’t speculate on each individual’s reluctance, but it doesn’t displace a simple truth: there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s “English” have descended. From the Celts, the Romans, the Anglo-Saxons, the Vikings, the Normans, the Huguenots, Jewish and Irish communities – England is ancestrally mixed. That waves of arrivals over the past century have been Caribbean, African and South Asian has only made this more observable.For those who believe Englishness is threatened and marginalised by demographic change, it is precisely this process that has allowed it to endure: continued participation and attachment, not bloodlines and biological inheritance. Even if the ethnonationalist right wants to project a future based on a kind of racial nostalgia, English history itself offers very little support for it. It is a politics with nowhere to go.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: In his final UN speech, Macron may have given other leaders a valuable parting gift: the guts to stand up to Trump | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: The French president’s resolve seems to have rubbed off on the leaders of other ‘middle powers’, says Steve Bloomfield, the former international editor of the Observer
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: The French president’s resolve seems to have rubbed off on the leaders of other ‘middle powers’, says Steve Bloomfield, the former international editor of the Observer
