Content: France’s Emmanuel Macron speaks at the UN general assembly in New York City on 22 September 2026.Photograph: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrance’s Emmanuel Macron speaks at the UN general assembly in New York City on 22 September 2026.Photograph: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionEmmanuel MacronIn his final UN speech, Macron may have given other leaders a valuable parting gift: the guts to stand up to TrumpSteve BloomfieldThe French president’s resolve seems to have rubbed off on the leaders of other ‘middle powers’Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareOn the first day of the United Nations general assembly this week, two world leaders outlined competing visions for the future.Donald Trump’s speechwas disturbingly familiar to those he’s given before: a litany of false boasts and odd tangents, peppered with grim military threats against a variety of nation states. Discussing his seven-month war with Iran,he musedover whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.In Trump’s eyes, the world is there to be ruled – and ruled only by the US, whose economy is “the envy of the world” and military is “the most powerful on Earth”.A couple of hours later,Emmanuel Macrontook to the podium to offer an alternative. In a full-throated defence of international law, multilateralism and the rules-based order, the French president said we were living in a “new era of barbaric acts”. He directly criticised Russia and Israel, but much of it was clearly aimed at Trump. “They say might is right … but we will not yield,” he argued. “We cannot simply accept this new order of impunity which some are trying to erect … Do we want to live under … the law of the jungle or do we want to live in a civilised international society?”Importantly, he also acknowledged the west’s “permanent temptation to espouse double standards”. “How many times have we heard that people’s sovereignty has value inEurope, but if we look at the Middle East and Africa, it is less valuable,” he asked. “No, that is unacceptable … A life is a life. Peace and security are indivisible, and everyone has a right to them.”Over the past decade, Macron has consistently been one of the only western leaders with a morally intelligent analysis of what Europe and the world should look like. As Trump, Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu have ushered us into an age of impunity, he has defended the rules-based order and, in recent months, been at the forefront of attempts to forge new alliances to support the crumbling old ones.He has pushed the idea of European strategic autonomy more than anyone else, understanding that while Europe is an economic power, it is yet to fully realise its potential as either a military or geopolitical force. During Trump’s first term, Macron was the only major leader willing to publicly acknowledge that Nato could no longer rely on the US, leaving the alliance all but dead.And yet the big speeches have rarely led to any substantial change. His ambitious call for EU reform in 2017 went nowhere, in essencescotched by Angela Merkel, who praised his “passion” and “verve” but failed to back the substance. Likewise, in New York this week, while his analysis was sound, the solutions were slight.This isn’t necessarily all Macron’s fault. He came to power in May 2017 as the new world order was crumbling. The EU was in crisis: one of its largest members had just voted to leave, while the remaining member states were still fatally split over the fallout from the eurozone crisis earlier in the decade and the migration wave in the summer of 2015. France’s two biggest European allies have been on the slide during his time in office. He has had to work with three German chancellors, the most recent two less popular than their predecessors, and is now on his sixth British prime minister.More urgently, Trump had taken office four months earlier, signalling the start of the break up of the rules-based order that had guided the west since the end of the second world war. Had Macron had the chance to work with Barack Obama, Angela Merkel at the peak of her popularity and a British prime minister committed to the EU, things might have turned out differently.Macron’s domestic woes have increased his impotence on the world stage. He has in effect been a lame duck for the past two years, since his disastrous snap election in 2024 left him without a majority.But his speech in New York, his final UN address before he steps down as president next spring, may have a more lasting impact. It certainly set the tone for the week. Over the following days, a procession of leaders of the so-called middle powers defended the principles of the UN and offered coded criticisms of Trump. Many of those who would have been scared of speaking out last year feel more emboldened now.The Australian prime minister,Anthony Albanese, warnedthat “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone”, while Spain’s PM, Pedro Sánchez, said he sought to “defend what so many are trying to destroy” and called for countries to come together to fight “political actors and governments that want to take us back to a dark past”.The middle powers are united in their opposition. The question is whether they can agree on what they’re for. The events of the past few weeks suggest that process is under way. New alliances based on values, not geography or size, are being formed – a reinvention of multilateralism, rather than a simple defence of the old model.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo far this month, theEU and Canada have discussed the idea of “associate membership”, while the UK has formed a new coalition of middle powersto impose sanctionstargeting Israel’s unlawful occupation of the West Bank.Another new group was created at the UN this week, withFinland and Norway launching a callfor an international body to oversee the safety of AI models. It is a direct challenge to Trump, who has called concerns about AI safety a “hoax”–nonetheless, 27 world leaders signed up, including Macron, Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Albanese.What ties all this together is the idea of “values-based realism”, an argument first put forward by the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, and echoed this week by Carney, who arguably lit the “middle powers” spark in Davos earlier this year when hespoke of the “rupture”in the world order caused by Trump. The new world Carney, Macron and others are trying to build will be one of different, sometimes overlapping alliances of like-minded states.There will be an ongoing question here for Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband. Which of these groups do they join, which do they try to form themselves and which do they politely decline? Despite Burnham’s desire to lead the push for new global AI standards, the UK has so far not joined the Finnish AI group, perhaps for fear of invoking Trump’s wrath. Another issue emerged this week: how to respond toTrump’s desire to invite Putin to the G20?Each middle power will face the same conundrum: when to fight back and when to sit on the sidelines. At least now the middle powers have understood that fighting back is an option.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsEmmanuel MacronOpinionUnited NationsDonald TrumpFranceForeign policyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Look again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right success | Cas Mudde | The Guardian
description: Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right, says the political scientist Cas Mudde
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right, says the political scientist Cas Mudde
Content: Elif Eralp (front, second right), lead candidate for the Left party in the German capital, and on course for a historic win in Berlin on 20 September.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElif Eralp (front, second right), lead candidate for the Left party in the German capital, and on course for a historic win in Berlin on 20 September.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionGermanyLook again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right successCas MuddeDefeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the rightSat 26 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTShareGermany held three regional elections this month and, although each of them had a unique result, much of the media and political commentary reduced them to: “German chancellor clingsto power after latestloss to far right. Since 2016, the year of Brexit and Trump, “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” has become the overarching narrative about Europe. But while these elections were important, this reductive take both oversimplifies the complexities of contemporary European politics and drives a defeatist “end of democracy” narrative.Saxony-Anhalt’s election on 6 September wasa global news event– understandably, given Germany’s history, economy and place in Europe. The international media hadspeculated for monthsabout an outright majority for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party came close, setting arecord score with 43.8%,but it has so far failed to form a government, despite the amenable position of the “left-conservative” Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.Two weeks later, the AfD came in first again, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, with 38.2% of the vote. International media interest was much less pronounced this time, maybe because it was the second of the three ballots, but more likely because the party was not close to reaching a majority. Moreover, the far-right success was overshadowed by the dramatic defeat for the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. For the first time in the history of the Federal Republic ofGermany, the party did not make it into a state parliament. The relatively modest loss of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD), on the other hand, was barely discussed.Finally, in the Berlin state election on the same day, the Left party (Die Linke) scored a stunning victory, gaining almost twice as many new votes as the AfD, which came in only third. Berlin will most likely now be governed by a Left-Greens-SPD coalition, headed by Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish political refugees. Perhaps most striking was that a clear majority of young women (54%) voted for the “far-left” party, representing abroader leftwing trend among young womenthat continues to be ignored by most media and politics representatives.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators gather in Berlin, Germany, on 12 September 2026, to protest against the AfD.Photograph: Maria Castro/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockWhereas the Saxony-Anhalt election was oftengeneralisedas thestory of Germany, if notEurope as a whole, the Berlin election is, at best, flattened out to a story of capital cities: uniquely cosmopolitan metropoles inhabited by highly educated progressives and immigrants. No matter that Saxony-Anhalt’s population, at 2.1 million, is just slightly over half the size of Berlin’s, and is among the oldest and whitest in the country. Moreover, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a state that is much more like Saxony-Anhalt than like Berlin, will most likely also be governed by a Left-Left-Green government – a striking fact that again has gone largely undiscussed.This is not to say that the success of the far right and the defeat of the established parties in Germany are not important or alarming, but they are not the only notable features of these elections. Actually, the fact that two of the three states will have leftwing governments is in many ways more newsworthy, given that purely leftwing governments are increasingly rare in Europe. On a similar note, global media attention on Swedenwanedas soon as it was clear that the left bloc was likely to succeed in creating a new government and the far-right Sweden Democrats would not enter the government.Reducing the many complexities of contemporary politics to an “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” narrative is not only problematic because it ignores significant other developments; notably, important transformations within major cities, where multicultural electorates are moving left rather than right (seen recently in, among others,CopenhagenandNew York). But more importantly, and dangerously, it also strengthens the far-right’s populist narrative, which portrays politics as a struggle between “the elite” (that is, all the mainstream parties) and “the people” (allegedly represented by the far right).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBerlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma AydemirRead moreSimilarly, somemediahave been keen to adopt the“horseshoe” theory of politics, prominently and strategically used byMerz, in which the liberal-democratic mainstream is squeezed from both sides, by the far right and far left. This conflates two very different challenges though. While it is true that established parties are challenged by new(er) parties, particularly because younger voters vote less for the established rightandleft, this includes liberal democratic parties like the Greens, too.Moreover, while the far right does threaten liberal democracy – and the AfD even threatens democracy per se – the so-called far left rarely does. Like Die Linke, most parties that are considered “far left” are former communist parties which have become significantly more moderate over time, presenting an ideology that reflects the social democracy of the 1970s much more than the revolutionary socialism of the former communist world. In fact, few “far left” parties are still even populist these days.So, while both the far right and “far left” threaten the established parties, only the far right threatens liberal democracy. It makes political sense for established politicians such as Merz to equate liberal democracy with the established parties, but the media should not uncritically share these claims. Surveys continue to show evidence of what the US political scientist Robert Dahl termed “a democratic paradox”: where very high support for the system of democracy is combined with very high dissatisfaction with the state of real, existing democracy.By highlighting the complexities of contemporary politics, in particular the frustration of the young (women) who are looking for liberal democratic alternatives to established parties, both the far-right populist binary of “establishment versus far right” and the defeatist “end of democracy” narrative are weakened. Hopefully this will give space to liberal democratic parties, old and new, to move beyond the self-defeating strategy of catering again and again to the same stereotypical voter with“legitimate concerns”, and instead mobilise and represent different groups of dissatisfied democrats.Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author ofThe Far Right TodayExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Kyiv has become a frontline city - and winter is on the way | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Residents of Ukraine’s capital prepare for power cuts, drones and bitter cold by stocking up on generators, food and ‘dry showers’
Author: Julia Kochetova
Headline: Residents of Ukraine’s capital prepare for power cuts, drones and bitter cold by stocking up on generators, food and ‘dry showers’
Content: Maria Shuvalova and her husband have invested in an energy-storage system, in preparation for the arrival of their baby.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaria Shuvalova and her husband have invested in an energy-storage system, in preparation for the arrival of their baby.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraineKyiv has become a frontline city - and winter is on the wayResidents of Ukraine’s capital prepare for power cuts, drones and bitter cold by stocking up on generators, food and ‘dry showers’Charlotte Higginsin Kyiv. Photographs byJulia KochetovaSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt felt like the last day of summer. On a Sunday afternoon in late September, people in Kyiv strolled through the city’s botanical gardens, admiring the late-flowering dahlias. Later, the terraces in the Podil area – a neighbourhood full of bars, patisseries and bookshops – filled up with customers in search of a cocktail.The idyll was an illusion. As the day darkened, the air defence began its rumble and boom. When a projectile fell with an explosive smack on a bar table, the drinkers flinched and then laughed. It was only a conker from the chestnut tree overhead. Nursing a glass of rosé, writer Myroslav Laiuk talked about the picnic he and his wife had had the previous evening, in a park in the Obolon district – prosecco in proper glasses, cheese and charcuterie. Then a drone was shot down above their heads. Very pretty, he said, with a smile. Shooting stars. Time to make a wish.Kyiv is no longer the city it was in the summer. Since late August, the Russians have been attacking over and over again in daylight hours, rather than only at night. The crump of air-defence, whine of drones and thunder of explosions are no longer the grim music of the night, but a commonplace waking-hours symphony, disrupting schools and workplaces and threatening life. Warehouses and city petrol stations have been targeted, and at times acrid smoke blurs the clear autumn mornings. Kyiv has become a frontline city. And winter is on the way.Winter is something to dread in Kyiv. Last year the cold was terrible – temperatures into the minus 20s – and cruelly long-lasting, persisting well into February. Illustrator Sergiy Maidukov was one of many who lost heating in his flat after the Russians attacked power infrastructure, the invaders’ aim seemingly to make the capital unliveable. The indoor temperature dropped to 3C. He kept warm by layering up, but also by going for runs.View image in fullscreenDaily life in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv – the most damaged neigbourhood by the Russian attacks.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“At least for 10 minutes afterwards you felt a like normal person, and you could just wear a T-shirt”, he said. He had a steady gas supply, so he could heat up water in a saucepan for a basic wash afterwards. At intervals he’d get up from his work and dance or do push-ups – not an option for the infirm. As film-maker Iryna Tsilyk put it: “Young and strong people – they will survive every time. But how about all those invisible people that we usually don’t meet?”Tsilyk’s biggest fear was, she said, the loss of internet connectivity. Lack of water supply would be another nightmare. Maria Shuvalova, an editor in academic publishing, described the period two winters ago when, for several days, the water supply failed both in her flat and in her coworking space. She was drinking tea to keep warm while working, then needing the loo. So she would walk the 20 minutes home, pee in a bottle, then return to the coworking space; then drink more tea, and repeat the whole cycle. For bowel movements, there was a plastic bag, knotted and disposed of in the trash. Such details of life were, she joked, “shit you definitely don’t want to know”.View image in fullscreenFood supplies prepared for winter at Maria Shuvalova’s home.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianOn a stroll in the botanical gardens, Iryna Gorlach, an international cooperation expert, laughed when asked how she was preparing for the coming cold. She pulled out her phone and showed an Instagram post from a popular Kyiv account. “This winter will be super difficult, we need to prepare properly,” it said. Then three bullet points: “Buy a house in a village; go abroad; stock up on grains and cereals.” Beneath, were the words, “How I’m preparing” and a cartoon image of a panicked-looking dog holding a cross and a copy of the Bible.Leaving the city is certainly on many people’s minds – if only for a few weeks ata time if things get bad. Nastya Dyakova, chief executive of an online safety charity, has rented a seven-bedroom house in the Carpathian mountains, in far westernUkraine, where staff and their families will be able to stay rent free if the situation in Kyiv becomes practically or psychologically untenable.“It is not only a question about winter in Kyiv, but about drones,” she said. Since August, the capital has been assailed by new, faster, jet-powered, harder-to-intercept drones. “It’s become really emotionally challenging to stay in Kyiv, and we understood that it’s difficult for our team to work or to focus because they really worry about their safety. So this option in the Carpathians is available for the next six months, until the end of winter.”View image in fullscreenHalyna is selling flowers next to the burnt market in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThe Lukyanivka neighbourhood of central Kyiv has been particularly hard hit this year, with its huge shopping complex and market bombed out and burned in the early summer. Market traders have set up their stalls beside the ruins anyway: one lady, cheerfully presiding over slabs ofsalo, pork lard, proclaimed that her personal coping mechanism was going to be a plentiful supply of home distilled hooch orhorilka. Another stallholder, Halyna, cheerfully selling bouquets of lavender, dahlias and chrysanthemums, was similarly fatalistic. “It will be whatever God sends us,” she said.View image in fullscreenViktoriia Riabchenko in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianPassing the market en route to work was Viktoriia Riabchenko, an accountant. There had been a particularly good harvest this year in her dacha garden, she said, and she had a great stock of ferments: plums, sour cherries, raspberries, tomatoes, cucumbers and sweet peppers. Not that she was especially concerned about the possibility of food shortages if warehouse bombing continued, she said; Russian propaganda exaggerated the potential problem, and specific shortfalls in shops tended to be remedied fast.View image in fullscreenViktor, a delivery courier originally from Kramatorsk.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAttitudes to winter, of course, depend on one’s perspective and experience. Viktor, a delivery driver was pausing outside Lukyankivka’s branch of MacDonald’s. The plastic golden arches on the side of the building have lately been restored to crispness after the heat from the summer’s bombs and fires slid them into a Dali-like melt. He was used to the cold, outdoors all day on his moped, and, having moved from Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region, had plenty of experience with bangs and explosions. Ivan Onyshchenko, who had dropped by for a hamburger and fries from his nearby workplace, had invested in a generator that he put on his balcony on the fifth floor – a lot of fuel to carry upstairs if the electricity stayed out. Usually generators chug away at high volume; his, he promised, was “only as loud as a hairdryer”.View image in fullscreenIvan Onyshchenko at McDonald’s in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianShuvalova lives on the 14th floor of her apartment building, and joked that last year she got great thighs walking up the stairs during power outages.This year will be different though: she and her husband, who is serving in the army, are expecting a baby, and preparing for the winter has been detailed and intense. The couple have plans A, B and C – plan A is to stay in Kyiv, but leaving to stay with friends or family further from the Russian missiles is on the table.Realising they could not expect the baby to live “like moles” as they did last year – reading by candlelight and working by laptop-screen glow during days-long outages – they have invested in an energy-storage system. The unit is in effect a giant battery, about the size of a small carry-on suitcase, that can keep appliances going for a day or so, if need be. Last winter they were on sale for 160,000 UAH (about £2, 700). Cannily, the couple bought one for about half that during the summer. Shuvalova also opened a drawer to reveal an array of small power banks.View image in fullscreenDry shower packages prepared for winter at Maria’s Shuvalova home.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThe residents of their apartment block are voting on taking over the running of their own building. If they manage it, they will install a generator to power one of the lifts during power cuts, and a toilet for the bomb shelter – AKA the underground car park. Shuvalova opened cupboards to reveal stashes of water, dried grains, rice, and tinned meat. They have a camping stove and a box full of “dry shower” packs – wipes that, with 50ml of water added, can be used to wash.In her anti-natal classes, a lot of emphasis is put on breastfeeding, she said. Formula requires clean water and the ability to heat it – not to be taken for granted this winter. “Breastfeeding takes care of all that,” she said. The air-defence roared away as she spoke. People outside Ukraine may question the decision to have a baby in Kyiv under such circumstances. “We couldn’t postpone any more so we just have to adapt,” said Shuvalova. “It’s bringing a lot of meaning to our life, and joy. And pregnancy hormones are very nice. I’m so calm and not stressing at all.”View image in fullscreenThe Lukyanivka neighbourhood has been particularly hard hit this year, with its huge shopping complex and market bombed out and burned in the early summer.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianWhether fatalistic, downhearted, or meticulously prepared, the boundaries of “acceptable” or “ordinary” have been pushed outwards for Kyivans in ways unimaginable to the inhabitants of other European capitals. Only one thing is absolutely certain this unpredictable, dreaded coming winter: that it will end. According to Maidukov, the illustrator, “In the evening when you are already blue and trembling, you’re thinking, ‘OK, one day is behind me, and I need to bear maybe two or three more weeks of this, which is not such a long time’.”Last winter’s freeze, he said, was a “weird period. Each day I was on the edge, about to fall down with my morale, but I didn’t allow myself to. Because nothing will stop spring. Spring will definitely come.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeRussiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump tells female MS Now reporter to ‘be quiet’ amid questions on press pool ban | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president doubles down on criticism of CNN and MS Now as Akayla Gardner questions attempted White House ban
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: US president doubles down on criticism of CNN and MS Now as Akayla Gardner questions attempted White House ban
Content: Akayla Gardner of MS Now near the White House after being denied entry following Trump's ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico, on 20 September.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenAkayla Gardner of MS Now near the White House after being denied entry following Trump's ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico, on 20 September.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APDonald TrumpTrump tells female MS Now reporter to ‘be quiet’ amid questions on press pool banUS president doubles down on criticism of CNN and MS Now as Akayla Gardner questions attempted White House banUwa Ede-OsifoandRobert MackeySat 26 Sep 2026 19.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA day after the White House barred CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One to provide pool television coverage of the president’s trip to Tennessee,Donald Trumpdoubled down on his criticism of that broadcaster and another, MS Now, he has attempted to ban over coverage of him he calls overly negative.As he left the White House early on Saturday, Trump was asked byMS NowWhite House correspondent Akayla Gardner: “Do you only want outlets that support you to be a part of the press pool?”“No, no, no. I want real news, not fake news – like you,” Trump replied, in a moment that was not broadcast live, due to the removal of CNN as the designated pool television crew, but wasposted on social mediaby the White House.As Trump continued on, repeating past insults aboutCNNand MS Now, which he called “MS DNC”, in reference to the Democratic National Committee, Gardner pressed him harder: “Do you not want tough questions?”“Be quiet,” Trump said, before continuing to air his familiar grievance that their reporting on him is not flattering enough.Since his first presidency, Trump has labeled nonpartisan news outlets that do not openly support him “the enemy of the people”, maligning unfavorable reports as “fake news”. In his second term, he has increasingly told female reporters who ask him challenging questions to be quiet.Tensions with the press corps soared to new heights last weekend, when administration officialsrevokedthe White House credentials of MS Now, Politico and CNN afterTrump announcedwhat he himself called a “ban on the free press”.A federal judge temporarilyrestored accessfor the blacklisted outlets on Thursday, but that evening MS Now and CNN reporters and producers were prevented by Trump’s aides from covering his state dinner in honor of Chinese president Xi Jinping.On Friday, the White House removed CNN from a rotation of television networks charged with covering presidential travel. The White House Correspondents’ Association previously coordinated pool assignments, but the administration seized control of choosing which network provides pool television coverage each day during Trump’s second presidency.CNN had been scheduled to accompany Trump on Saturday, as he visited Knoxville, Tennessee, for a college football game.Real America’s Voice, a pro-Trump network that lacks the technical capability to provide live video for other broadcasters, instead accompanied the president during the brief trip. The partisan, rightwing network shared a limited number of clips of the trip on social media, including video of Trump’s image being displayed on the stadium’s big screen, which itcaptioned: “PRESIDENT TRUMP LIGHTS UP THE JUMBOTRON”.Trump returned to Washington DC on Saturday afternoon without taking questions from the print reporters who were permitted to accompany him.“He is picking a fight with the people who are telling unpleasant truths about his administration,” Brian Stelter, CNN’s chief media analyst, said on air about the network’s exclusion from Air Force One. “Today, yes, it happens to be CNN, but tomorrow it could be any other news outlet.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpMS NowUS constitution and civil libertiesUS politicsTrump administrationCNNTV newsShareReuse this content

title: Hawaii braces for powerful winds and flash flooding with Hurricane Nolo | Hawaii | The Guardian
description: Preparation begins for extreme conditions as Nolo bears down on areas still recovering from previous storms
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Preparation begins for extreme conditions as Nolo bears down on areas still recovering from previous storms
Content: Kenzielynn Kekoa of Hilo, Hawaii, helps her family fill sandbags as Hurricane Nolo approaches, on 25 September.Photograph: Eugene García/APView image in fullscreenKenzielynn Kekoa of Hilo, Hawaii, helps her family fill sandbags as Hurricane Nolo approaches, on 25 September.Photograph: Eugene García/APHawaiiHawaii braces for powerful winds and flash flooding with Hurricane NoloPreparation begins for extreme conditions as Nolo bears down on areas still recovering from previous stormsAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeavy rain and powerful winds are expected to bring flash floods and extreme surf to the Hawaiian islands over the weekend as Hurricane Nolo bears down on areas still recovering from previous storms.Nolo was churning slowly south of Hawaii’s Big Island on Saturday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (165km/h). The storm’s center was about 145 miles (235km) south of Hawaii’s southern-most point and could strengthen into a potentially life-threatening and catastrophic storm through the weekend.Forecasters warned of possible flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island expected to see rainfall totals up to 20in (51cm). Heavy rainfall also was expected on Hawaii’s other islands.“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said Friday.The humanitarian non-profit group Community Organized Relief Effort (Core) and other partners spent the week packing and shipping supplies such as camp stoves and hygiene products by air cargo from Oahu to the Big Island for a community relief hub that has been active since August’s Hurricane Lala.Residents are still recovering from Lala, which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.Donald Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for the state of Hawaii, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate assistance from across the federal government and provide funding support for emergency measures.Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits, and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating hundreds of Hawaii national guard members.View image in fullscreenA closed ticket counter for Southwest Airlines at Hilo international airport on 25 September.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APHawaii county officials on the Big Island were urging residents in flood-prone areas to consider taking refuge at shelters being set up or other locations.Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the storm.Meanwhile,Mexicois under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it heads toward the Baja California peninsula after bringing storm conditions to the south-western coast. Polo was producing maximum sustained winds of 155 miles per hour (249km/h) Saturday but is expected to gradually weaken before making landfall Monday.View image in fullscreenLouie Taasan hauls sandbags from his truck to place along his driveway in Hilo on 25 September.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APOne of the towns in Polo’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast where access to basic needs is already fickle.“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel there. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”The town has only had full-time electricity for a couple of years, and it still experiences frequent outages. Without power, residents can’t refrigerate food or pump water. The closest gas station is so far away that fuel is stored and sold from tanks in the town and frequently runs out if there is high demand.Robles Meza said the community feels left to brace itself for the storm without the help of authorities.“We must prepare on our own, each of us protecting our homes and belongings,” she said, adding that she wished officials would pre-position heavy machinery for clearing roads, along with emergency generators.For now, she said, the only plan is to convert the local elementary school into a shelter.“While this is important, we also have other impacts to consider,” she said, like what the town will do if it is cut off from help.San Juanico has experienced late summer storms, but Polo feels different, said Jeffrey Westman, an American who was first drawn to the town’s world-class surf break 40 years ago and owns a property there.“During the last couple of years, the storms have felt big and strong and scary,” said Westman, 63, who is in Europe right now but concerned for the locals in San Juanico, particularly about their ability to receive food deliveries or reach larger grocery stores if road access is cut off.Washed-out roads could also block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitución.Westman said he is hopeful Polo behaves the way some past storms have, losing intensity before reaching the Baja coastline.“A lot of times they do start petering out” as they approach, he said. “I’m hoping that’s the case.”Explore more on these topicsHawaiiHurricanesExtreme weatherUS weatherMexicoAmericasShareReuse this content

title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering | Ecuador | The Guardian
description: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’
Content: US forces intercepted the Ecuadorian vessel Manta on 5 September before the vessel was destroyed.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, SouthView image in fullscreenUS forces intercepted the Ecuadorian vessel Manta on 5 September before the vessel was destroyed.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, SouthEcuadorUS strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not waveringAttorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’Tiago RogeroSouth America correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.View image in fullscreenEcuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September.Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/APOn 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters nearEcuador.“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.View image in fullscreenA US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.Photograph: US Southern Command/X“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.View image in fullscreenTen crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy.Photograph: Ecuadorian NavyUS Southern Commandpostedan edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the lateston 16 September– to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.‘We were terrified they were going to kill us’: fishers who survived US boat strike speak outRead moreView image in fullscreenA still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: US Southern Command @SouthcomAlso, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.Donald Trumphas compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.View image in fullscreenMarines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.Noboa has responded with acontroversial “iron-fist”approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.View image in fullscreenRelatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025.Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty ImagesThis crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has erodedhuman rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorisingjoint operationsand granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troopstaking part in raidslast Thursday.“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador forthe New Yorkermagazine.View image in fullscreenPeople look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged.Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province.Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created calledShield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is aserious contenderin October’s election.So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.View image in fullscreenFishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersIsacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four peoplewere killedin the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the USwould “stillblow up ships if need be”.Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes asextrajudicial killings,and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.Despite Trump’s claims,available datashow they have hadno impacton the volume of cocaine entering the country.Journalists and human rights groups have managed toidentify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.View image in fullscreenRelatives wait for 32 crew members to be released under precautionary measures in Manta, Ecuador, on 8 September 2026. The 24 crew members of the Maria Candelaria and eight from the Conquista II face judicial proceedings on suspicion of illicit association and fuel trafficking after their vessels were intercepted and destroyed by US forces in the Pacific Ocean.Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPAIn Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishershave been subjected to“violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted forlack of evidence.“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this yearremain unclaimed.The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vesselFiorella disappearedwith eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.Human rights organisations and journalists identifiedtwo more caseswith similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Postreportedthat the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.View image in fullscreenMaria Mero and her mother, Maria Cueva, speak during an interview after Mero’s husband Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado and brother Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva disappeared from the boat Fiorella after a strike in June 2026.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersView image in fullscreenMaria Cueva holding a picture of her son Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersBoth the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.Explore more on these topicsEcuadorMarco RubioAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Greek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosion | Greece | The Guardian
description: Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’
Content: Emergency personnel search for survivors in the rubble of a building that partially collapsed following an explosion in the Plaka neighbourhood.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersView image in fullscreenEmergency personnel search for survivors in the rubble of a building that partially collapsed following an explosion in the Plaka neighbourhood.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersGreeceGreek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosionEmergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’Helena Smithin AthensSat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a two-storey apartment block in the heart of ancient Athens to collapse “in a matter of seconds”, killing six people.Emergency teams found the victims, including four American tourists, on Saturday, more than 24 hours after the early morning explosion in the historic Plaka district.The fire service said the bodies of three women and three men had been found, but stopped short of identifying them. A Briton and his Greek wife, 77 and 78, who lived in a flat on the building’s upper floor, were among those killed, the Guardian was told.“The bodies have been taken to the morgue where postmortems will be conducted,” the city’s vice-mayor, Paris Charlaftis, said in a telephone interview from the blast scene. “Our focus now is on the explosion’s cause. What could have happened to bring the building down in a matter of seconds?”Rescuers had deployed thermal cameras and geophones, used to detect deep subsonic frequencies, in the hope of finding survivors. Earth-moving machines and specially trained search dogs were brought in to move and comb mounds of rubble through the night.Before the bodies were pulled from the ruins on Saturday, police put the missing at six, saying four were Americans staying in a short-term rental on the building’s first floor. Two brothers and their wives, all four were due to fly to the US on Friday, just hours after the explosion.View image in fullscreenA rescuer searches the remains of the building.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty Images“When they failed to turn up for the flight they had checked into only a day earlier, that gave us a further lead,” a source said. “It became clearer that they must have been there when the blast occurred.”The Briton, a talented artist, who lived with his wife on the second floor, was described by Charlaftis as being partially disabled. “He had kinetic issues, and it was thought likely they, too, were in the building [at the time of the blast].”Nestled around the foot of the fifth-century BC Acropolis, Plaka is especially popular with tourists. The picturesque district draws thousands of visitors daily, with many staying overnight in the hotels and short-term rentals in neoclassical houses and small apartment blocks along its alleyways and narrow streets.The mayor of Athens, Haris Doukas, who rushed to 15 Lysikratous, where the mid-20th-century building had once stood, was quick to describe the incident as an “unprecedented disaster”.At least three people were known to have been injured when the explosion occurred at 7.30am, shattering the windows of nearby buildings and scattering debris far and wide. A motorist driving down Lysikratous described how his car was lifted into the air by the sheer force of a blast that some in the neighbourhood likened to an earthquake, others to a bomb. Emergency workers could be seen hastily removing two women on stretchers from a building next door who had been wounded by flying debris.Speculation is rife that a gas leak triggered the collapse but officials said there were many “cogent theories” at play. Fears of the leak emanating from the first-floor short-term rental was among them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs part of efforts to address a burgeoning housing crisis,Greece’s centre-right government has sought to ban short-term rentals in Plaka – clamping down on permits and tightening regulations.On Saturday, as speculation mounted over the cause of the blast, criticism grew over the ability to “properly control” establishments that were often unregulated.“This awful incident will fuel further debate over who inspects short-term rentals that no one who lives in Plaka wants anyway,” said Giorgos Zafeiriou, an architect who heads the local residents’ committee. “Hotels have chambers that regulate them but who inspects and controls Airbnb and serviced apartments that often may not be up to par?”Civil protection crews and emergency disaster management teams have been ordered to remain on site until the cause of the explosion is found, officials said.“It was a huge explosion, so getting to the bottom of it must now be the priority,” added Zafeiriou. “Six people have lost their lives.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: What is El Niño, what causes it and can we reduce the risks?  | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: This year’s ‘godzilla’ climate phenomenon has already broken temperature records. We ask a climate scientist what is happening
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: This year’s ‘godzilla’ climate phenomenon has already broken temperature records. We ask a climate scientist what is happening
Content: Cracked ground at the dried-up Guarne Lagoon in Arví Park amid drought conditions linked to the El Niño phenomenon in Medellin, Colombia, 3 September 2026.Photograph: Juan David Duque/ReutersView image in fullscreenCracked ground at the dried-up Guarne Lagoon in Arví Park amid drought conditions linked to the El Niño phenomenon in Medellin, Colombia, 3 September 2026.Photograph: Juan David Duque/ReutersEl Niño southern oscillationExplainerWhat is El Niño, what causes it and can we reduce the risks?This year’s ‘godzilla’ climate phenomenon has already broken temperature records. We ask a climate scientist what is happeningJonathan WattsSat 26 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’s huge El Niño, which comes less than two years since the last one, has alreadybroken temperature records. To understand what is happening, and why, the Guardian interviewed ProfMat Collins, a climate scientist at the University of Exeter, the author of some of the world’s most important climate reports and an expert on the dynamics of the El Niño southern oscillation.View image in fullscreenMat Collins.Photograph: suppliedWhat is El Niño?It is a natural climate pattern that affects large parts of the world, often bringing higher temperatures, more droughts and floods. This occurs when the normally cool, dry east Pacific becomes warmer and wetter, shifting rainfall patterns in the tropical Pacific and with other impacts far beyond that. It usually occurs every three to seven years, but is very erratic. The last one was in 2023-24.What’s the best way to describe the relationship between El Niños and human-caused global heating?The easiest way to think about this is that they are two separate things that layer on top of each other. So if you’ve already got drought conditions as a result of global warming, then an El Niño is going to exacerbate that. The harder question is how they interact with each other. With our models, we can use hundreds of years of simulations to work that out but we lack the data to do that from the observational record, although some palaeoclimate reconstructions suggest the present day frequency of El Niño is quite unusual.How strong is this year’s El Niño? Some are calling it a ‘godzilla’ or ‘super El Niño’It has already broken records and could be on course to be the strongest in a thousand years. The sea surface temperature of the El Niño region of the Pacific has already reached the previous 2015 high of 3C above average, which is almost unthinkable. And it still hasn’t peaked so we won’t know how much higher it will get until the end of the year.But measuring the size in comparison with previous El Niños is difficult because the baseline of sea surface temperatures in the eastern tropical Pacific is steadily rising due to global warming.So there are two things happening – human-driven climate change and the natural variability of El Niño – and it is not easy to say how much each is contributing to the record high ocean temperatures. But together, they make extremes more likely.Currently temperatures in the eastern Pacific are on course to be 4C above the average, which is far beyond anything seen before. If that trend continues, we could see an incredible El Niño event.Which areas of the world will be most affected?Around the peak of the El Niño, there are likely to be more wildfires in Indonesia and drought in the Amazon rainforest. The Indian monsoon has already been weakened because of El Niño. Temperatures are likely to be higher around the Pacific Rim and as far away as the UK. Meteorologists suggest the UK will see a wetterwinter and autumn and possibly a drier, colder spring. I’m not certain about that because weather in the UK is just so variable.View image in fullscreenBurnt trees after a wildfire in Sungai Putri, in West Kalimantan province, Indonesia.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersWere the recent high temperatures in the UK and the wildfires in Europe, Canada and the US also worsened by El Niño?I don’t think so because they came so soon after the onset of the El Niño and there is normally a lag. Those conditions are more likely to be a signal of global warming, combined with persistent anticyclonic circulation patterns that cause weather systems to be settled (or stuck) for long periods. On top of climate change that makes record heat more likely.Several scientific papers, including by you, suggest there is a possibility that human-caused climate change is making El Niños more frequent and intense. Isn’t it frustrating that there is still no smoking gun that can prove that with 100% certainty?That’s just science. One paper we published suggested the signal will emerge first in terms of rainfall patterns. So I think that we may have a clearer picture in the next decade.James Hansen, arguably the world’s most influential climate scientist of the past 50 years, argues that human-driven climate change is likely behind the abnormal strength of this El Niño. What’s your take on that?It’s a plausible hypothesis but hard to prove.Will warmer Pacific ocean surface temperatures guarantee fiercer El Niños?Climate change makes it more likely El Niños will be fiercer, but that is still not certain. That’s because the impact of an El Niño depends on the temperature difference with other oceans, such as the Atlantic and the Indian. The rainfall goes where the warmest water is found. If that warmth is distributed, then so will be the rainfall. If that warmth is concentrated in one ocean, then the rainfall will shift around so it is more intense in that basin.View image in fullscreenAerial view of the German Channel off the coast of Koror, the capital of Palau, in the western Pacific Ocean.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesMay this year’s huge El Niño be a sign that the world’s oceans are – to use a non-scientific term – vomiting heat into the atmosphere because they are reaching the limit of their ability to absorb excess energy?Well, that’s kind of what happens during an El Niño, which is a transfer of heat from the ocean to the atmosphere. But it’s just part of a cycle. It’s not as if the ocean has reached some limit and then can’t hold any more. I guess there’s still plenty of cold water in the world that we can heat up so I don’t know if there’s a physical limit.What would be your hunch about whether El Niños are going to get more powerful in the future?I certainly think the impacts are going to be greater and if we are to believe our models, then the rainfall response is also going to be bigger. There will be bigger and more impactful El Niños over the coming decades.How can we reduce the risks?Knowledge can help. If we go back to the 1982-83 El Niño, people really did not know what was happening. Back then, one of my colleagues got a message from someone on a ship in the east Pacific saying the temperature of the water was off the scale. He had never seen anything like that before. Nobody understood then. But now we’ve got a forecast system which can confidently predict these things six to nine months ahead. So you can prepare. You can tell farmers in Latin America to plant different crops. You can warn governments in south-east Asia to think about their infrastructure and to strengthen defences against wildfires.Ultimately, the main response should be to reduce greenhouse gases, but perhaps there are also options to do weird and wonderful geoengineering – for example to change the properties of clouds in the eastern Pacific which may influence the scale and timing of El Niño events. One paper suggests you could terminate a big event by creating lots of clouds, which would cool the surface of the ocean in the east Pacific.Would such geoengineering help or could it make things worse?It is not yet clear because the heat comes from the deep ocean. So even if you manage to prevent an event in one year, it may come back the next.On an emotional level, how do you feel at the prospect of even more impactful El Niños in the future?It’s worrying. El Niño causes huge disruptions to agriculture and the global economy. This is very bad for people, particularly in poorer countries who are already suffering the consequences of climate change and now they get an El Niño event on top of that. Luckily, we have good predictions now and it is important to maintain that capability, for example collecting real-time data from the Pacific Ocean. Then we can be forewarned.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisClimate scienceExtreme weatherDroughtWildfiresexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: I’m virtually living in the woods now. Wildlife is everywhere | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Owls, bats, badgers and countless birds are my new neighbours, but I’ve been particularly taken by a mystery tree – and its resident treecreeper
Author: Kate Bradbury
Headline: Owls, bats, badgers and countless birds are my new neighbours, but I’ve been particularly taken by a mystery tree – and its resident treecreeper
Content: ‘Moving around the tree as if climbing an imaginary curved staircase.’ A treecreeper.Photograph: Alan Williams/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Moving around the tree as if climbing an imaginary curved staircase.’ A treecreeper.Photograph: Alan Williams/AlamyCountry diaryTrees and forestsCountry diary: I’m virtually living in the woods now. Wildlife is everywhereLewes, East Sussex:Owls, bats, badgers and countless birds are my new neighbours, but I’ve been particularly taken by a mystery tree – and its resident treecreeperKate BradburySat 26 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave made the woods my home, moving from Brighton to the outskirts of Lewes, where the garden backs on to the remains of an old oak wood. Here there’s a riot of wildlife: a badger that makes snuffle holes in the lawn, a family of tawny owls in the trees and a cauldron of bats in the chimney.View image in fullscreenThe mystery tree in Kate’s garden.Photograph: Kate BradburyI have plans to let the wood expand into the garden, but in the meantime there’s a mystery tree whose branches almost reach my bedroom window. It’s nearly dead, stressed from too many droughts, perhaps, or coming to a natural end. Some have suggested it’s a willow, but I suspect it’s a cultivated species I’m not familiar with.Without leaves, flowers or fruit there’s not much to help with identification, but there’s fresh growth in the canopy that might make the job easier soon. The exposed branches lay bare a world of birds that I wouldn’t otherwise see – tits, robins, blackbirds, thrushes, woodpeckers and nuthatches.My favourite, though, isthe treecreeper. It stops by in the morning, moving around the tree as if climbing an imaginary curved staircase. It will be searching for insects and spiders, using its long bill to probe beneath the bark, its curved toes to cling to the trunk and its stiff tail feathers for balance.Country diary: The nuthatch takes a toxin that can paralyse our heartsRead moreI spot its white bib first, then reach for my binoculars and admire its intricate brown and gold plumage, which helps it blend in with the bark.Resident in Britain, treecreepers leave their breeding territories in autumn and move to a winter habitat in a nearby woodland or park, sometimes joining a roving group of tits. So my morning visitor may soon be gone. But I hope it returns in spring to build a nest of spiders’ webs, grass, moss and feathers, and to scale my mystery tree once more.Standing dead wood is a rare garden habitat, and I admit to worrying about winter storms and the tree’s proximity to my house. But dead wood is full of life, as the treecreeper and its friends attest. I am watering the roots, hoping a moist soil will yield more growth, and that there’s life in the old tree yet.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsTrees and forestsCountry diaryRural affairsBirdsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Work intensifying on UK laws to stamp out concert ticket touts, say sources | Music industry | The Guardian
description: Artists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resales
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Artists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resales
Content: Tinie Tempah performs at the 2026 Boardmasters festival. The rapper said fans and artists deserved better than to see tickets “siphoned away”.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTinie Tempah performs at the 2026 Boardmasters festival. The rapper said fans and artists deserved better than to see tickets “siphoned away”.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesMusic industryWork intensifying on UK laws to stamp out concert ticket touts, say sourcesArtists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resalesRob DaviesSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has stepped up work on new laws to stopticket touts fleecing fans, as the prime minister came under pressure from artists including the drummer from the Smiths, one of his favourite bands.Keir Starmer said last year that the government would “stop fans from being ripped off” byoutlawing the for-profit resale of tickets on sites such as Viagogoand StubHub, a pledge Labour first made in its 2024 election manifesto.Despite support from a host of globally renowned artists, including Radiohead, Dua Lipa and Coldplay, the measure wasnot included in this year’s king’s speech, prompting concern among music industry figures that the proposal had been shelved.But multiple sources told the Guardian that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has assembled a sizeable “bill team”, a group of civil servants who are drafting the policy and will help shepherd it through parliament.They are understood to be considering ways to mitigate the risk that touts and resale platforms simply base themselves offshore to bypass any new legislation.View image in fullscreenDua Lipa performs in Hamburg. The singer has been vocal on the need to tackle the for-profit resale of concert tickets.Photograph: Gregor Fischer/Redferns for ABAThe culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, told the House of Commons this month that Andy Burnham “feels particularly passionate” about the issue and the government would treat it as a priority. Nandy is due to give a speech at Labour conference on Wednesday, at which she could provide further detail.On Friday, industry figures and artists including the rapperTinie Tempahand the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce called on the prime minister to act fast, citing new evidence of touts targeting small venues in Greater Manchester.Research examined 300 events across 13 venues where tickets were being touted onViagogo, including Band On The Wall, Gorilla, YES, Rebellion, New Century and the White Hotel.All were advertised at significantly over cost price, while some did not feature information about the seller, an apparent breach of competition rules. Under government plans, companies would face much tougher penalties for failing to enforce these rules.Other tickets appeared to be “speculative”, meaning that they had been fraudulently listed by touts who do not have them but hope to procure some once they have agreed a sale.The most expensive was £5,899 for Mica Millar’s show at New Century – a 19,728% mark-up.Tickets to a 40th anniversary celebration of the Smiths’ The Queen Is Dead, featuring a conversation between Joyce and the producer Stephen Street, were being touted for £549 each.Joyce said it was “time to stop this for good”, while Tempah said fans and artists deserved better than to see tickets “siphoned away by people who contribute nothing to live music but are happy to profit from it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTickets for Mica Millar’s Manchester show were advertised at a 19,728% mark-up.Photograph: prJust three touts – based in Latvia, North America and Germany – were responsible for more than 75% of the listings, research by the music industry group FanFair Alliance found. Viagogo dispute the claim, saying the proportion held by the trio was significantly lower.Viagogo also listed tickets for tiny, obscure events, including an evening with the “world’s greatest psychic” in Inverness, a rum tasting in Devizes, and stargazing in Tavistock.The company said actual sale prices were much lower than the high-priced listings identified by FanFair Alliance.“Viagogo takes its obligations under the law seriously and is fully compliant in the UK. Our policies prohibit speculative listings,” it added.If the government does go ahead with a ban on ticket touting, it would bring the UK in line with Ireland, which outlawed touting in 2021.At present, the unauthorised resale of football tickets is illegal across the UK.Resale of concert or theatre tickets without authorisation is permitted, although individual touts have been prosecuted andjailed in rare instanceswhere they have been judged to have committed fraud.Fans lost £60m to touts between Labour’s announcement of the policy and April this year, the telecoms company and venue sponsor O2 has estimated, with fans of acts including Olivia Dean, Bad Bunny and Ariana Grande “fleeced” by markups of up to 1,000%.The Guardian has repeatedly exposed exploitative tactics in secondary ticketing, including speculative selling and theuse by touts of specialist softwareto hoover up tickets and flip them for profit, often via sites such as StubHub and Viagogo.A DCMS spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good. For too long, fans have been ripped off and we’re determined to right that wrong.“That’s why we are bringing forward draft legislation in this parliamentary session to ensure that our measures are truly effective, enforceable and future-proof and fans get the protection and security they have always deserved.”Explore more on these topicsMusic industryTicket pricesViagogoTinie TempahnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jill Dando murder: technological advances allow police to review CCTV 27 years later | Jill Dando murder | The Guardian
description: BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved
Content: Jill Dando was killed outside her home in Fulham, west London.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenJill Dando was killed outside her home in Fulham, west London.Photograph: NetflixJill Dando murderJill Dando murder: technological advances allow police to review CCTV 27 years laterBBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solvedKevin Rawlinsonand agencySat 26 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTechnological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC broadcaster Jill Dando, Scotland Yard has revealed.Advances in CCTV enhancement technology have allowed detectives to return to 27-year-old footage of Putney Bridge Underground station, Scotland Yard said. But detectives stressed that the review was part of existing inquiries – not a new investigation.The former Crimewatch presenter was 37 years old when she was shot and killed outside her home in Fulham, west London, on 26 April 1999. An unidentified person, referred to as “Man X”, was captured on camera near Putney Bridge station – about a mile from Dando’s home – shortly after the attack.A driver had seen a man “running for his life” on Fulham Palace Road around the time of the shooting, the Mirror reported. She later picked out Man X in the station CCTV as the person who had been sprinting.A Met spokesperson said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando’s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.“The review of CCTV footage forms part of ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter.”Outside her work on Crimewatch, Dando was also seen during the 1980s and 1990s on BBC shows including travel show Holiday and The Antiques Inspectors.She began as a reporter at her local paper The Weston Mercury in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, before moving to the morning programme Breakfast Time, which later became BBC Breakfast.In 2019, the detective who led the inquiry into Dando’s murder expresseddoubt the case would ever be solved. Speaking in a BBC documentary to mark 20 years since the television presenter’s shooting, Hamish Campbell said he did not think any new suspects would ever be brought to court.“Do I think somebody will come back to court? Probably not, no. Sometimes, I felt we were a day away from solving it and other times, I thought: ‘No, we’re a long way away’. Senior officers were asking: ‘What are the likelihoods of this case being resolved?’“We had over 2,000 people named as potential suspects or responsible. Some actions to trace and eliminate one person might take a day. One action might take two weeks. But there’s thousands of them and that’s the issue of managing stranger homicides.”Explore more on these topicsJill Dando murderCrimePoliceForensic sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargers | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: Only 26% of PHEVs sold across top 20 models can use chargers with power of 50kW or more, analysis finds
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Only 26% of PHEVs sold across top 20 models can use chargers with power of 50kW or more, analysis finds
Content: The cars, which are able to run on electric batteries as well as combustion engines, have been promoted as a way to cover long distances while still reducing emissions.Photograph: Xiu Bao/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe cars, which are able to run on electric batteries as well as combustion engines, have been promoted as a way to cover long distances while still reducing emissions.Photograph: Xiu Bao/AlamyElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsThree-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargersOnly 26% of PHEVs sold across top 20 models can use chargers with power of 50kW or more, analysis findsAlex DanielSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree-quarters of the 20 top-selling plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) in the UK cannot use rapid chargers, research has found, amid concerns that many are essentially “petrol cars pulling round a heavy battery”.The cars, which can run on electric batteries as well as combustion engines, have been promoted by carmakers as a way to cover long distances in a single drive – unlike fully electric cars – while still reducing emissions.But only 26% of the vehicles sold across the top 20 models, which include the Jaecoo 7, the Ford Kuga and Hyundai Tucson, are able to use rapid chargers with powers of 50kW or more, according to analysis by the industry body, ChargeUK.High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study findsRead moreThese chargers can quickly top up a car battery – for example at a motorway service station – adding a significant amount of range in 20 to 30 minutes. Cars that cannot use them are limited to much slower charging speeds, meaning drivers wanting to recharge mid-trip may face a wait of several hours.
