Hybrid owners may instead choose to rely on their petrol engines.Shane Brennan, the chief executive of ChargeUK, said: “A plug-in hybrid electric vehicle that is never plugged in is a costly petrol car pulling round a heavy battery. PHEV drivers unable to charge on the public charging network quickly fall into patterns of being petrol reliant.“Government must not be hoodwinked into promoting the idea that boosting PHEV sales is a meaningful step towards electrification. It is a spectacular own goal to be seduced by a mythical ‘PHEV compromise’.”Repeated studies have found PHEVs pump outsignificantly more planet-heating pollutionthan official figures show. Despite this, the government last year allowed manufacturers tosell more of them towards their EV targets.PHEVs were the fastest-growing type of car sold in the UK last year, with 227,000 registered – up almost 35% on 2024 – according to official data. A further 180,000 have been sold so far this year.The top 20 models sold also include the BYD Seal, the MG HS and the BMW 3 Series, none of which can use rapid chargers.In a recentconsultationon the zero emission vehicle mandate, the government said PHEVs were driven on electric power far less than official figures suggested. The report said the method used to calculate emissions savings “significantly overestimates electric driving, as in real life many drivers charge infrequently, meaning real world CO2 emissions are higher than official figures”.However, it is expected to weaken targets for pure EV sales even further when a consultation on changing the mandate closes in October, after a period of intense lobbying from the car industry. Last week, Nissan suggested it couldwithhold a £170m investment in its factoryin Sunderland if the UK does not weaken the rules.None of the top 20 models can use ultra-rapid chargers, the fastest tier on the network, capable of adding significant range in a matter of minutes. Rapid charging is defined as 50kW and above and ultra-rapid as from 150kW.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRapid and ultra-rapid chargers make up about a quarter of the UK’s public charging points, according to government figures, but deliver the majority of the network’s total charging capacity because they are so much faster.By contrast, every one of the top 20 models of pure electric vehicles sold last year could use rapid chargers, and 64% could use ultra-rapid ones.It comes after carmakers raised discounts on combustion engine cars last month, including hybrids, and weakened them on electric, as they neared their annual EV sales targets.Autotrader said average discounts for petrol cars listed on its platform jumped sharply to 11.9% in September from 11.3% in August. Meanwhile EV discounts fell to 10.7% from 11.1%, which the group said was mainly down to companies such as Mercedes-Benz and MG “scaling back their incentives as they close in on their required ZEV mandate levels for the year”.A government spokesperson said it was taking a practical approach by letting drivers choose plug-in hybrids, adding that the vehicles’ real-word carbon emissions were still 40% lower than the average petrol or diesel car.Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryMotoringAutomotive emissionsGreenhouse gas emissionsEthical and green livingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Severely disabled young people should get fast-track access to benefits, Milburn says | Benefits | The Guardian
description: Alan Milburn said 16- to 24-year-olds with most complex needs should not have to keep proving they cannot work
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Alan Milburn said 16- to 24-year-olds with most complex needs should not have to keep proving they cannot work
Content: The former Labour MP Alan Milburn led a review into youth unemployment amid a crisis in the UK where nearly 1 million are not in education, employment or training.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenThe former Labour MP Alan Milburn led a review into youth unemployment amid a crisis in the UK where nearly 1 million are not in education, employment or training.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PABenefitsSeverely disabled young people should get fast-track access to benefits, Milburn saysAlan Milburn said 16- to 24-year-olds with most complex needs should not have to keep proving they cannot workPatrick ButlerandWill ParmanSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung people whose complex disabilities mean they have little prospect of getting a paid job should get fast-track access to disability benefits, an official review of youth employment will say.The review, by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, will say 16- to 24-year-olds with the most severe lifelong needs should be guaranteed swift and unconditional benefit support rather than having to prove they cannot work.Currently, many disabled youngsters and their families have to endure repeated lengthy, adversarial and often distressing assessments to access personal independence payment (Pip) and universal credit health benefits.The guarantee could include young people with profound and multiple learning disabilities, severe neurological conditions, and those with severe and complex needs who qualify for NHS continuing healthcare support.The review, expected in October, will say there is no need for repeated disability benefits assessments for this group, and young adults should not have to constantly demonstrate proof of lifelong conditions and impairments diagnosed at birth or in early childhood that mean they cannot work.“I’ve heard too many stories of young people with the most severe disabilities left waiting, worrying and fighting for the support they’re entitled to,” Milburn told the Guardian. “Too often they’re having to battle through dehumanising tick-box assessments designed to catch people out, not care for them.”He added: “A different approach is needed for disabled people whose condition is so severe that they could never work. By right they should get faster support rather than having to prove it over and over again to get the help they deserve.”The separate government-commissioned Timms review into Pip concluded in an interim reportearlier this yearthat the Pip assessment process was justifiably regarded by many claimants as “soul-destroying” and degrading.The disability charity Sense, which supports disabled people with complex needs, welcomed the principle of fast-track guarantees but said it was important young people who were able and willing to work were not written off.Harriet Edwards, the director of influencing at Sense, said: “It would be a significant step forward for young disabled people with the most complex needs and their families, and for those who have long campaigned to end the exhausting and humiliating process of multiple assessments.“But we must not write young disabled people off. Those who want to and are able to work need specialist employment support and genuine opportunities, alongside the financial protection they need to live their lives.“Government must now take this recommendation forward. The detail will be crucial, including who is eligible, whether exemptions go far enough, and how this will work across different disability benefits so people aren’t left navigating different rules and assessments.”Tara Harris, 57, from the West Midlands, described obtaining disability benefits for her son Ollie, 25, who has complex disabilities, as a “bureaucratic nightmare”. She said the system involved “constant battles of chasing things and not having things. It’s ‘computer says no.’” It was also stressful. “I feel like I’ve had to be a tiger mum,” she said.Harris said her son could not do paid work but had been supported to volunteer at a cafe two days a week. The Pip assessment required her to describe his progress in a routinely negative way. She fears that if she were to “put things in a positive language, then you don’t get Pip”.She said: “It’s really hard to have these sorts of conversations in front of Oliver. Because it sort of demeans him, and he’s absolutely wonderful, amazing person and deserves to have money to be able to be an adult.”The government commissioned Milburn to address a growing youth jobs crisis in the UK in which nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training).Hisinterim report, published in June, made it clear young people diagnosed with lifelong complex needs who are never be able to work must be protected by the benefit system. But it also hinted that young people with less severe conditions who could be supported to work may see reductions in benefitsMilburn, a minister in Tony Blair’s government, last month called forinvestment in specialist internshipsdesigned to secure work for young people with special educational needs to address “devastating” joblessness rates for those with learning disability, autism and mental illness.Explore more on these topicsBenefitsWelfareDisabilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Major storm in US north-east knocks out power for 100,000 and floods roads | US weather | The Guardian
description: Residents across New Jersey, Massachusetts, Delaware and New York without electricity as storm hits
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Residents across New Jersey, Massachusetts, Delaware and New York without electricity as storm hits
Content: People secure lawn furniture as a nor'easter advances on the north-east US on 25 September 2026, in Gloucester, MassachusettsPhotograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenPeople secure lawn furniture as a nor'easter advances on the north-east US on 25 September 2026, in Gloucester, MassachusettsPhotograph: Robert F Bukaty/APUS weatherMajor storm in US north-east knocks out power for 100,000 and floods roadsResidents across New Jersey, Massachusetts, Delaware and New York without electricity as storm hitsAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 16.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA slow-moving, powerful storm known as anor’eastercrept along the coast of the US north-east on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to thousands of people while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.Tens of millions of people were in the path of the storm, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. About 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.Hurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of MexicoRead moreThe forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There would potentially be “a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain … over the next few days for the north-eastern US”, said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service (NWS) in College Park, Maryland.On Long Island,New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets.In the coastalNew Jerseyborough of Surf City, Kenny Formica sat at his home watching surveillance cameras showing water rising inside the marina he owns. Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4m in damage to his business.Before the storm, Formica said, workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm’s way and parked the marina’s trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. One customer sent him a video at about 4am of his 25ft (7.6-meter) boat after it had blown off its lift.“This is like an 8,000lb boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat – just gone,” Formica said.In Ocean City, Maryland, heavy surf caused beach erosion, washed out fencing by the dunes and was leading to flooding.“In all the canals, the water is up really high and coming into people’s backyards,” Jay Boyd said by telephone.Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard inMassachusettson Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some east coast flights through the weekend.Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tinyNew Jerseybeach community of Sea Bright, said the borough was bracing for winds up to 50mph (80km/h) and flooding that could reach up to 6ft (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start on Saturday and worsen by midday.“It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the north-east. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.”Kelly added that he hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.Peak wind gusts were expected to approach 60-65mph (97-105km/h) on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, and about 50-55mph (80-89km/h) around Boston and 35-40mph (56-64km/h) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with the NWS in Norton,Massachusetts.“It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said.Belk said nor’easters were not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season was that leaves still remain on trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn could cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey andDelaware, wind gusts could reach 60mph (96.6km/h), according to the NWS. In south-eastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, gusts could be almost as powerful, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard andNew Yorkhad been canceled on Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday-afternoon game to Friday to create a split double-header. Separately,Ed Sheeranannounced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.Explore more on these topicsUS weatherNew JerseyBostonMassachusettsNew YorkDelawarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Broken promises, confiscated land: the hyperscale AI datacentre being built in a tiny Indian village | Datacentres | The Guardian
description: Locals say Google’s $15bn project in Andhra Pradesh has resulted in smallholdings being taken back off them by the government
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Locals say Google’s $15bn project in Andhra Pradesh has resulted in smallholdings being taken back off them by the government
Content: The farmers of Tarluvada, who have protested against Google’s mega-scale AI datacentre coming to their small rural village in south-east India. Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The GuardianLocals say Google’s $15bn project in Andhra Pradesh has resulted in smallholdings being taken back off them by the governmentByHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin TarluvadaSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.View image in fullscreenA traditional house in Tarluvada.Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The GuardianFew in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.Just as protests haveerupted globallyover AI datacentres – fromCaliforniaand Texas to Scotland andAustralia– communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”View image in fullscreenBRB Naidu, Tarluvada village head.Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The GuardianPointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.Publicly itwas announcedas a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.View image in fullscreenAcres of forests being cleared for Google’s AI datacentre around Tarluvada.Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The GuardianActivists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’sEconomic Survey2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.World’s first wind-powered underwater datacentre starts operating in ChinaRead moreBut locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.A map situating Tarluvada on the eastern coast of India, near the Bay of Bengal.Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with adeliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres –documented emitters of heat– could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenP Venkat Rao, a Dalit farmer, pumps water in the village. He was forced to give up his land for the Google datacentre and now has no livelihood.Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The GuardianThe strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought whilepolluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.View image in fullscreenApplaraju, one of the villagers who lost his land for grazing his cows to the Google’s AI datacentre being built in Tarluvada.Photograph: Hannah Ellis-Petersen/The Guardian“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.Datacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report saysRead more“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentresIndiaSouth and central AsiaGoogleLand rightsDeforestationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heads of OpenAI and Anthropic called to face Senate inquiry after rogue agent incidents | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have been invited to appear before the Greens-led inquiry into AI and datacentres
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have been invited to appear before the Greens-led inquiry into AI and datacentres
Content: Sam Altman (left) and Dario Amodei have been called to face a Senate inquiry into AI by the Australian government.Photograph: Jason Redmond,ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSam Altman (left) and Dario Amodei have been called to face a Senate inquiry into AI by the Australian government.Photograph: Jason Redmond,ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralian politicsHeads of OpenAI and Anthropic called to face Senate inquiry after rogue agent incidentsSam Altman and Dario Amodei have been invited to appear before the Greens-led inquiry into AI and datacentresFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniSat 26 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief executives of OpenAI andAnthropichave been called to face a Senate inquiry after rogue OpenAI agents hacked Australian and US government websites.Sam Altman andDario Amodeiwere requested to appear at the Greens-led inquiry into AI and datacentres as their companies negotiate with the Labor government for greater access to Australian content in exchange for a greater local presence.A separate joint committee, led by Labor members, has not made a similar request.Anthony Albanese returned to Sydney on Saturday, where he challenged OpenAI to explain why there had been multiple breaches involving its agents, including thehack of Australian government sites.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestThe prime minister said OpenAI’s confirmation its agents had alsomeddled with US government websitesshowed there were “dozens” of cases of AI agents accessing information without authorisation.“What this does is confirm … [is] that there needs to be [an] appropriate national response, as well as an international response, to make sure that humans stay in charge,” he told reporters.Albanese spoke to Altman on Wednesday (US time) before revealing the hack and said the CEO had offered “further discussions” on security.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, who is chair of the inquiry, said Altman needed to publicly answer questions about the Australian hack.“This can’t all be done behind closed doors,” Hanson-Young said. “The public has a right to know what went on here.”An inquiry grilling would risk embarrassment for the companies and the government after months of private negotiations to allow AI training on millions of global texts in Australia.Albanese did not directly answer when asked earlier this week whether the incident had changed the government’s view on whether to partner withOpenAI.Murray Watt, the environment minister, said on Saturday OpenAI’s behaviour was “completely unacceptable”.“I think OpenAI has some work to do to ensure that Australians can trust its technology,” Watt told reporters in Melbourne.“If OpenAI or other AI companies want to have the trust of the Australian people, they need to act a lot more transparently and provide information a lot more quickly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemmaRead moreThe Greens have called for global regulation to slow the development of AI and a local moratorium on datacentre development.The party’s spokesperson for AI, David Shoebridge, was blocked from taking a seat on the government-led committee. The party has used its own inquiry to listen to community groups opposing datacentre construction and interrogate executives behind the developments.Altman and Amodei have grown increasingly vocal about the risks of rapid AI development. Hanson-Young said the two CEOs’ public warnings were at odds with their companies’ calls for urgent reform to enable AI training.“If they truly believe their own warnings they must front up … and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like,” Hanson-Young said.“Australians deserve to know what these big AI companies are doing with our data, how much water and electricity their data mining activities will consume and what the impact will be on our communities and our culture.”Hearings will resume in Canberra on 1 October.OpenAI and Anthropic have been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseSam AltmanAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicAustralian GreensShareReuse this content

title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections | Brazil | The Guardian
description: President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday described fixed-odds betting as being ‘like a cancer’.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday described fixed-odds betting as being ‘like a cancer’.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesBrazilLula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian electionsPresident’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggestAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 03.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazilian president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the UN general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the coming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.Explore more on these topicsBrazilGamblingTravel & leisureAmericasFixed-odds betting terminalsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvanewsShareReuse this content

title: Amelia Bullmore: ‘I met my husband doing Romeo and Juliet. We weren’t the leads – it wasn’t that tidy’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The actor on getting caught gossiping, the footballer she has a crush on, and having both her best and worst kiss in one night
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The actor on getting caught gossiping, the footballer she has a crush on, and having both her best and worst kiss in one night
Content: Amelia Bullmore: ‘More sex, money or fame? I wouldn’t adjust any of the above.’Photograph: Kate Green/BAFTA/Getty Images for BAFTAView image in fullscreenAmelia Bullmore: ‘More sex, money or fame? I wouldn’t adjust any of the above.’Photograph: Kate Green/BAFTA/Getty Images for BAFTAThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewAmelia Bullmore: ‘I met my husband doing Romeo and Juliet. We weren’t the leads – it wasn’t that tidy’Rosanna GreenstreetThe actor on getting caught gossiping, the footballer she has a crush on, and having both her best and worst kiss in one nightSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in London, Amelia Bullmore, 62, studied drama at Manchester University. In 1990, she became a regular on Coronation Street and her later TV credits include I’m Alan Partridge, Ashes to Ashes, Twenty Twelve, Happy Valley and Riot Women. She appeared in and wrote episodes of the long-running series Scott & Bailey and also wrote for This Life. In 2005, her first play, Mammals, co-won the Susan Smith Blackburn award. From 10 to 31 October she stars in Margaret Atwood’s playThe Penelopiad at York Theatre Royal. She is married to actor Paul Higgins, has two daughters and lives in London.When were you happiest?I’m often very happy when I’m in – or just out of – the sea.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Chipping in, overtalking.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Not being direct.What was your most embarrassing moment?Gossiping about someone and it getting back to them.Aside fromproperty, what’s the most expensive thing you’vebought?Holidays. We had an amazing splash-out in Venice at Christmas. It was the first year without both my mum and dad and it seemed a good idea not to attempt to do the old version without key players.What is your most treasured possession?A necklace my mum gave me when I was 14.What would your superpower be?To be able to split in two to, for example, make a pot of soup while finishing off a bit of work.What do you most dislike about your appearance?I’ve mostly got the hang of it but, if it’s no trouble, could I please have longer legs and a staggering mane?double quotation markWho would play you in the film of your life?It would never get greenlit, so we don’t need to worry about castingIf you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?Several postal deliveries a day.What does love feel like?All that’s required.Who would play you in the film of your life?It would never get greenlit, so we don’t need to worry about casting.What is your most unappealing habit?Attacking my cuticles.Who is your celebrity crush?Alan Shearer. My husband calls me when he’s on TV, which is kind but needless, as I can identify Alan’s voice from anywhere in the house.What did you want to be when you were growing up?A ballet dancer, an actress in the RSC doing wall-to-wall Chekhov, a writer.What was the last lie that you told?“I’m ready.”What is your guiltiest pleasure?Clothes shopping.What or who is the greatest love of your life?In the romance category, Paul Higgins must get a special mention for staying power and jokes. I adore our kids. I absolutely love my family. I couldn’t get by without my friends. I think love of colleagues (there’s probably a Greek word for it) is under-recognised.What was the best kiss of your life?It was shortly after the worst kiss, with Paul in 1992, a very awkward wooden kiss, and then, later that same night, take two was much better. We met doing Romeo and Juliet. We weren’t Romeo and Juliet – it wasn’t that tidy.What has been your biggest disappointment?The London Eye. I thought the cabs were going to be open and that it was going to travel at speed.If not yourself, who would you most like to be?Sarah Lamb (the American ballet dancer) for a day.When did you last cryand why?Today, rehearsing.What would you like to leave your children?A bolthole. An actual one, and an inner one.Luke Evans: ‘As a child I was in love with Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones’Read moreWhat do you consider your greatest achievement?Making the babies and pushing them out.What has been your closest brush with the law?I was pulled over as a young driver. I’d had some cider, the tyres were bald and I hadn’t approached the roundabout sensibly. They let me off.What keeps you awake at night?Doing things like this; thinking I might have got up someone’s nose; menu planning.Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?I wouldn’t adjust any of the above.What happens when we die?I can’t wait to find out. I can actually.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&ACelebrityAmelia BullmoreActingDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Break Clause: two lovers flatshare during a breakup – and it makes for totally refreshing TV | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: They sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’t
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: They sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’t
Content: Will-they-won’t-they … Lara Ricote as Lil and Samuel Bottomley as Ben in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/Kerry SpicerView image in fullscreenWill-they-won’t-they … Lara Ricote as Lil and Samuel Bottomley as Ben in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/Kerry SpicerThe watcherTelevision & radioBreak Clause: two lovers flatshare during a breakup – and it makes for totally refreshing TVThey sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’tRhik SamadderSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been at more than one party where a stranger has told me they are still living with their ex, even sharing a bed. I don’t judge. I’ve experienced this myself. I remember a sad, uncanny time at the end of a relationship. Untangling our lives but not our bodies, supporting the other through their worst pain while trying to ignore the fact that the worst pain is you. But sometimes these strangers tell me they have been living this way for months, perhaps years, and my empathy flips to horror. “What the hell is going on in your house?” I think.I found answers in Break Clause (Thursday, 10pm), a new Channel 4 dramedy. It’s the story of sweethearts Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote), Leeds University graduates who decide to transplant their lives to London. On the eve of moving, there’s an incident that leads to a terrible confession in the hallway of their new flat. Ben and Lil break up – in the presence of their estate agent, who tells them the paperwork is irrevocable. They will have to live together for six months until the contract break clause. That’s awkward! But can tenancy rights correct a relationship wrong?Break Clause mines territory other shows ignore: the biting economic pressure of being young in a housing crisis. There’s no suspension of disbelief here, no twentysomethings living in loft apartments the size of a Virgin Atlantic business lounge. The couple live in south London, in an ex-council flat with grotty underpasses. Ben has a meet-cringe with a neighbour who spots him bin-diving for food. He’s copying videos posted by foraging influencers. “I think they mean the bins outside M&S, not the big ones under flats,” she replies.View image in fullscreenAll together now … Break Clause.Photograph: Channel 4Lil is an architect, Ben is a writer. It’s hard for any household to survive income inequality, by which I mean only one of them has one. Lil gets a job, at a firm, on a promotion track, while Ben volunteers to be injected with viruses for £800. Honestly, I’m not sure he is a good writer. Partly because he thought that a medical trial was a job interview, partly because he attempts to steal a YA novel idea from a teenager he tutors. Also, he’s too nice.Then there’s dating, which takes place under each other’s noses. Ben and Lil are trying to be friends. What choice do they have, forced cheek by jowl? They could illegally sublet, I suppose, but it probably wouldn’t give them both the means to live elsewhere. Perhaps their relationship isn’t over, the series teases. But should it be?‘I’m not even an actor – I was just grieving!’ Rising star Lara Ricote on the heartache behind her new breakup comedyRead moreIf a 22-year-old were to confess to me they weren’t sure their current partner was “the one”, I would tell them baldly that obviously they weren’t, and that their relationship with relationships had barely begun. There’ll be more of this pain, I’d say, harder lessons, plus a healthy whack of bad timing and cosmic injustice. It’s probably a good thing I don’t have young people who look up to me.Break Clause’s will-they-won’t-they can feel thin, and John Thomson is underused as Ben’s father. But it’s funny, there’s verve to the dialogue and direction, plus a winning performance from Mexican-American comedian Ricote, an effervescent mix of Megan Stalter and Jenny Slate. She lands the best gags – such as when Lil, seized by the romance of a moment, will jump into a game of double dutch with teenagers, or lean her head on a stranger’s shoulder as they sit on a bench by the Thames. Repulsed and confused, they all give her a dirty look. “Bad call on my part,” Lil acknowledges.Mostly, it’s refreshing to watch a show that isn’t wholly convinced love conquers all. In this economy? I’m convinced that twentysomething couples who live together now do so primarily to split rent. Certainly, no one in London is in love. They can’t access the upper tiers of the self-actualisation pyramid required, because they’re too stressed about not having a pension. Most comedies exist in a fantasy realm, where all housing is affordable. But escapism isn’t everything. Maybe rental regulation is the romance this generation needs.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe watcherTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A couple of times people walked out’: how an Anne Frank musical became the hottest theater ticket of the year | Off-Broadway | The Guardian
description: The creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapper
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapper
Content: ‘Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.’Photograph: Shawn SalleyView image in fullscreen‘Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.’Photograph: Shawn SalleyOff-Broadway‘A couple of times people walked out’: how an Anne Frank musical became the hottest theater ticket of the yearThe creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapperJuan A RamírezSat 26 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s difficult to not invoke the term “woke” when discussingSlam Frank, the 2025 musical that reimaginesAnne Frankas a pansexual Latina. Controversial even before its first performance, it giddily satirizes identity politics through its show-within-a-show structure, in which a progressive theatre company attempts to modernize the Holocaust victim’s story by paralleling it to the struggles faced by marginalized people today. Here, the mother of “Anita” is Black, her father is neurodivergent and, while hiding in Amsterdam, they are very much immigrants.Creator Andrew Fox recognizes “a temptation to categorize it as anti-woke art”, but points readily at the show’s fans and detractors, who fall across every conceivable party line, and cautions against one-note interpretations. “I think the piece is just trying to grapple with the last 15 years of cultural and intellectual upheaval and get some comedy out of it.”Following last year’s sold-out run at the Asylum NYC comedy club (now retroactively referred to as a workshop), it will premiere off-Broadway proper at the Orpheum theatre on 4 October.The idea started online, if you can believe it, when Fox stumbled across a2022 tweetdissecting Frank’s alleged white privilege. The composer-lyricist got to work on a hip-hop musical inspired by that absurd debate, and reconnected with an old school friend, writer Joel Sinensky, who suggested they implement the backstage concept. (Before then, Fox says, “it was closer toOleannathan to Waiting for Guffman.”)“We have many things that we disagree on, but the thing that we were always very united on is this feeling that we were tired of didactic theater,” Sinensky says. “A lot of the work that’s been made commercially in the last decade has been very direct about what you’re supposed to take away from it, and we wanted to write something that was a reaction to that – that was about that.”So while the current sociopolitical moment (post-#MeToo, post-Covid, post-“Woke 1.0”) is certainly a target in the musical’s line of fire, its form lampoons the art that has resulted from that zeitgeist.Hamiltonis a major inspiration – if that’s the word – with Slam Frank’s logo riffing on the blockbuster bio-musical’s own, and its musical sensibility imitates its verbose, sloganeering rap.Pre-Existing Condition review – Lupita Nyong’o is phenomenal in domestic abuse dramaRead moreWhat it doesn’t borrow from Hamilton, purposefully, is a clear ideology. The production’s social media, managed by Fox, has been a masterclass in subterfuge and trolling. (“Fasting is Fatphobic,” reads an Instagram post shared on Yom Kippur.) Fox, who is Jewish, says one of their guiding intentions was to never convey “a specific viewpoint or message”.“We committed pretty early to making something that, anytime we feel like we’re making one point and it’s starting to feel like a lecture, we swing in another direction,” he says. “It lets us focus on making the piece as effective as possible at getting reactions, getting laughs, getting shock.”Sinensky says he revels in Reddit reviews of the show, which alternately label him and Fox as pro-Zionist, antisemitic, extremist right- and leftwing: “That, to me, is one of the best indicators that we succeeded – that people can see it and love it or get angry for different reasons.”Online chatter aside, reviews have been largely positive. The show’s publicist (understandably) makes the most out of anX postby Ben Brantley, the former New York Times theater critic, arguing that it “may be the most important new show around”. Its director, Sam LaFrage, recalls avisit from Patti LuPone, who he says came backstage at Asylum NYC to mention how moved she’d been.View image in fullscreenAusten Horne, Amelia Louise Barr and Olivia Bernábe in Slam Frank.Photograph: Shawn Salley“I get really excited by something that makes me feel like art is back,” says LaFrage. “Like, wecando plays that make people uncomfortable, and say the things that have been left unsaid because we’ve been worried about getting canceled, you know? The play within the play is a great container to exercise that right, to be artists. Slam Frank is about what’s happened to art.”Like Fox and Sinensky, LaFrage feels the musical is a way to poke fun at his own “woke” past, something he thinks also legitimizes the honesty of its satirical intent. “I used to do drag queen family theater downtown,” he says with a mix of pride and chagrin.Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Read more“When Trump got elected, obviously that was awful, but I let woke get the best of me,” says Walker Stovall, who plays a character modeled after the camera operators in big-budgetJamie Lloydproductions. Like LaFrage, he speaks with an earnest tongue-in-cheek. “You should be critical about the way you think and about what you’re taught, but I think when I was letting it get in the way of connecting with other people is when it all went bad.”Fox echoes the sentiment that respectability politics have served an opposite effect. Many of the characters in Slam Frank often get bogged down in well-meaning, barely intelligible jargon. (At one point, someone wonders “through what assemblage of counter-hegemonic labor shall the scaffolding of our interlocking systems of oppression be rendered obsolete?”)“It’s a very strange way of speaking and writing that kind of detaches people from their own thoughts,” he says. “Part of what our show tries to do is represent that experience of being part of a culture that is becoming less human and more abstract, and how funny or horrifying that can be.”Ironically, the musical was previously ejected from a highbrow workshop hosted by BMI, the music licensing organization, for that un-abstracted bravado. According to Fox, “what got it kicked out was the non-binary coming out song, and as far as I know, there wasn’t a single non-binary person in that room. Then the next year, a bunch of new non-binary people joined the workshop and that was their favorite song in the show.”Olivia Bernábe, the non-binary actor who plays Anita, says they find the number “hysterical”. They first learned of the show through Fox’s TikTok videos, and thought it was “just an intense commit-to-the-bit, but with really good music”.“I know that there are people who do get offended,” says Bernábe. “There have been a couple of times where people have walked out; I don’t know if they forget that it’s satire, or it could be that everyone has a different threshold for it. Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.”View image in fullscreenThe cast of Slam Frank.Photograph: Shawn SalleyThere’s plenty of button-pushing atop that righteous jestering: the entrance to the Orpheum’s auditorium, for example, has been made to look like the bookcase which led to the Frank family’s hideout, with a neon sign welcoming visitors to “The Attic”. But Fox thinks “the culture was ready to move in this direction” of irreverence, paraphrasing a quote fromRick Rubin, the famous record producer, “that ideas are in the air and that somebody’s gonna get them. If you don’t go forward with it, that idea doesn’t die with you.”“There are many things in the culture reflective of things that Slam Frank is doing, so it’s clearly something in the air,” he says. “There’s certainly questions about the manipulation of the sanctity of the Holocaust in the popular imagination. I’ve gotten some emails that are like, ‘People don’t take this topic seriously anymore because of you,’ and I’m like, ‘I’ve been talking to people for the last three years; they were ready to not take it seriously anymore.’”Slam Frank’s final 20 minutes, set off by a truly audacious plot twist, are its most controversial, widening its scope from historical satire to contemporary excoriation. It was the only aspect to give Stovall any misgivings, before he recognized its value.“My gut instinct was, ‘Don’t do this to my girls,’” he says, half joking. “I had to think about it and be like, ‘Why do I have a problem with this? I don’t actually have a problem with this. This is hilarious.’ And the reason I had a problem with it is why I think it’s important to put it onstage, right?”Slam Frank is at the Orpheum theatre,New York, until 30 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOff-BroadwayUS theaterTheatreAnne FrankComedyNew YorkMusicalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #262: Why laughing at the movies isn’t always funny | Culture | The Guardian
description: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?
Content: Exorcist II: The Heretic … left to right, Max von Sydow, Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher on set, directed by John Boorman.Photograph: PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenExorcist II: The Heretic … left to right, Max von Sydow, Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher on set, directed by John Boorman.Photograph: PR IMAGEThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #262: Why laughing at the movies isn’t always funnyIn this week’s newsletter: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?Gwilym MumfordSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore every screening at the West End’s Prince Charles Cinema, a public service message is played. It’s usually oneread by John Waters, welcoming cinemagoers to the “most depraved and beautiful movie theatre in London”, before imploring them to “turn off your cellphone, asshole”. More recently, though, a new message has been played, read by none other than Timothée Chalamet, who made a guest appearance at the cinema last year. Along with the usual requests for phones to be switched off, Timmy makes an unusual plea: for audience members not tolaugh “like Max Cady”at moments in the film that aren’t supposed to be laughed at. Because the Prince Charles mostly plays older movies, there can be what Chalamet calls a “disconnect” between the time that the film was made and today: ropey scenes of sex or violence, outdated language or technology, or anything else that jars with modern sensibilities and causes people to hoot derisively.It’s a surprisingly real problem, not just at the Prince Charles but at any repertory cinema. On Reddit there are plenty of threads bemoaning people guffawing at everything fromA Space Odysseyto the films ofDavid Lynch, a phenomenon one film writer on Substack has christened ‘performative laughter’. For anyone caught in a cinema when this unwelcome cackling occurs, it can be a killer. There’s little more guaranteed to break the spell of a non-comedy film than laughter: scary movies are instantly made about 75% less scary, thrillers become less white-knuckle, dramas lose their weight.If uninvited laughter is bad enough for audiences, think about the people making the films. Surely nothing is worse for a director – aside from an absence of laughter in a film that you intended to be funny, perhaps – than people laughing at something you’ve poured your passion, creativity and hard work into. For a sense of how devastating it can be, watchBoorman and the Devil, a terrific documentary in cinemas this week about John Boorman’s Exorcist sequel, Exorcist II: The Heretic (pictured above), one of the most maligned films in movie history.Boorman wasn’t a fan of William Friedkin’s original Exorcist film, considering it sadistic and exploitative. So he sought to make a radically different follow-up, swapping out the first film’s creeping, low-lit dread for something grand, fantastical and even a little bit hopeful – an ambition that surely should have served as a massive flashing warning sign to Warner Bros execs, which bankrolled the film to the sum of a then unprecedented $14m. Boorman’s sequel hardly lacked for ambition: its sprawling plot included detours to Africa and Latin America, a device called a synchronizer that merged people’s brainwaves, and original Exorcist star Linda Blair (pictured below) tapdancing, for some reason.View image in fullscreenTap dancing extraordinaire … Linda Blair in Boorman and the Devil.Photograph: PR IMAGEWhat it didn’t have – arguably by design – was scares, precisely what those who flocked to see the film in huge numbers after the first film’s success were expecting. When they didn’t get them, they responded with confusion, boredom and finally laughter. The press soon picked up on audiences rolling in the aisles across America and the intense negative buzz around the film caused it to plummet at the box office after its first week.Things got so bad that Boorman set about frantically re-editing a film that was already in cinemas, giving it a more unhappy ending and removing some of its more guffawed-at moments. His changes came too late for the US – Warner Bros determined it would be too pricey to replace the prints of a film they already regarded as a sunk cost, though international audiences did get the new version – and too late to save its reputation: it still regularly appears on worst-of-all-time lists.Boorman and the Devil gently attempts to salvage Exorcist II’s standing, spotlighting its pioneering use of Steadicam, occasionally beautiful cinematography, and general sense of vaulting ambition. It’s notable though, that even many of the documentary’s more sympathetic talking heads – directors, film critics, industry professionals – still consider it a bad movie. It does have a very prominent defender in Boorman himself, now 93, who is interviewed at length in the film. He believes he did good work on Exorcist II, but still feels “the old wound” of its disastrous reputation, and of that mocking laughter.His reaction is understandable, but there are positive ways to respond to such a setback. Another film that regularly appears alongside Exorcist II in those damning lists isThe Room, Tommy Wiseau’s genuinely abysmal 2003 drama. It’s a film that is so bad that it achieved firm cult-classic status with a certain type of film fan. In fact the Prince Charles cinema does a roaring trade in screenings of the film, where audiences ignore Chalamet’s pre-film message to snigger en masse at its terrible dialogue, bizarre plotting and horrible wooden acting. Wiseau himself regularly turns up to introduce the film and do Q&As, and is treated with the same adulation as any A-lister. He’s turned mass mockery into cult-hero status – a presumably profitable little sideline. Proof, perhaps, that laughter can sometimes be the best medicine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: I’ve been replaced by a younger model … it’s a relief | Family | The Guardian
description: My wife has summarily relieved me of gardening duties, in favour of ‘Gardening Steve’. Inevitably, there’s a catch
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: My wife has summarily relieved me of gardening duties, in favour of ‘Gardening Steve’. Inevitably, there’s a catch
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: I’ve been replaced by a younger model … it’s a reliefMy wife has summarily dismissed me from outdoor duties, in favour of ‘Gardening Steve’. Inevitably, there’s a catchTim DowlingSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife wants to hire someone to put the garden in order. She knows I’ll object, because it’s really something I should be doing, but she also knows I won’t do it. In truth, I’ve lost heart. Two scorching months without rain wreaked havoc on the garden: the lawn turned the colour of a winter sky; seedlings vaporised; established shrubs died. When the rains finally came, the garden bounced back – but by then I didn’t care any more.As part of her campaign my wife has let it be known that paying someone to fix the garden is no reflection on me, because I’m a businessman with little time to devote to things of the soil.“If you’re promising this will never be held against me at any point in the future,” I say.“I am,” she says.“Then I simply don’t believe you,” I say.“Anyway, I’ve already found someone,” she says. “He’s coming Monday.”“I figured,” I say.“And with all your free time, you can finally do the kitchen table,” she says. I think: oh no.double quotation markThe problem is: while he’s working, I have to work. I can’t just sit in my office shed, staring out of the windowWe bought our kitchen table 30 years ago from a workshop that was throwing it away. It’s made of four old roof rafters knocked together, and the top needs sanding down and refinishing about every five years. I do it, on average, once every 10.“I bought everything you said you needed for the job three years ago,” my wife says.“I still need sandpaper,” I say. “Specific sandpaper.”My wife keeps referring to the person she hired as “Gardening Steve”, rather than “Steve the Gardener”. I don’t know whether she is making assumptions about his qualifications – like, maybe he doesn’t know the Latin names of plants – but she is insistent.On Sunday afternoon I’m comparing the sandpaper I just bought with the footprint of my electric sander when my wife walks into the kitchen.“Ready to start?” my wife says.“No,” I say. “These sanding sheets say ‘Universal Fit’, but it turns out there are three sorts of universal.”“Will you be here at 11 tomorrow?” she asks. “For Gardening Steve?”“It makes him sound as if he has his own podcast,” I say. “Gardening Leave, with Gardening Steve.”“Can you remember to charge up the hedge trimmer?” she says.“He doesn’t bring his own hedge trimmer?” I say.“No, he doesn’t,” she says.The middle one helps me move the table out on to the lawn. I spend the afternoon trying to sand off the grubby, gummy top layer, with the ill-fitting sanding sheets flying off the sander sporadically. It begins to rain, and I call the middle one to help me carry the half-sanded table back inside.“I forgot how much I hate this job,” I say.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Maybe you can do the rest when Gardening Steve is here,” my wife says.“Are you kidding?” I say. “In front of him?”The next day Gardening Steve arrives and, after a brief tour of the garden and its failings, begins work. It turns out it’s not shaming to have a much younger man stand on top of my ladder and hack away at a dead clematis. It’s actually a relief. And for as long as he’s here, I can avoid the kitchen table.double quotation markYou’re a businessman, I tell myself. Look at your screen, and type. Steve, meanwhile, barely takes a breakThe only problem is: while he’s working, I have to work. I can’t just sit in my office shed, staring out of the window, because there’s a man out there cutting back a wisteria which has wound its tendrils around the handle of a spade I left leaning against the wall six months ago.You’re a businessman, I tell myself. Look at your screen, and type. Steve, meanwhile, barely takes a break. Under these circumstances I put in a relentless six-hour writing day. I get a lot done, but by 5pm my concentration is shot. I find myself, slouched and glassy-eyed, watching Gardening Steve pull up thick-rooted weeds on the other side of the open door. Before I can stop myself, I speak.Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guideRead more“Don’t feel, you know, that you have to …” I say.“Sorry?” says Steve.“I mean it’s not necessary to eradicate them,” I say. “As long as you can’t see them.” For some reason, this feels like life advice.“Yeah, OK,” he says.“The tortoise likes those,” I say. “So I just let them grow back.”“Got it,” he says, resuming his work. With some reluctance, I resume mine.I’m a million miles away when Steve knocks on the glass an hour later.“I’m off,” he says. “I’ll be back probably Wednesday.”“OK, great, thanks,” I say, thinking: I have Tuesday off! Then I remember the table.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was mesmerised by how the fog turned the tower into a monolith’: Derek Zhao’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: Zhao was out jogging around Treasure Island, near San Francisco, when he spotted a lonely tower stabbing through the clouds
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: Zhao was out jogging around Treasure Island, near San Francisco, when he spotted a lonely tower stabbing through the clouds
Content: Arrival, 2026, shot on iPhone 16 Pro Max.Photograph: Derek ZhaoView image in fullscreenArrival, 2026, shot on iPhone 16 Pro Max.Photograph: Derek ZhaoSmart shotPhotography‘I was mesmerised by how the fog turned the tower into a monolith’: Derek Zhao’s best phone pictureZhao was out jogging around Treasure Island, near San Francisco, when he spotted a lonely tower stabbing through the cloudsGrace HollidaySat 26 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery morning, Derek Zhao jogs the perimeter of Treasure Island, his home, situated an eight-minute ferry ride from San Francisco. “It’s an endless source of frustration for me that I can’t bring my cameras with me,” he says. “When the island gifts me its beautiful scenes, I should be grateful that phones have pretty decent cameras, too.”‘The balloons made me smile but his expression made me stop’: Harivansh Verma’s best phone pictureRead moreZhao works as a machine-learning engineer at Disney California. He relocated from Texas last year to take up the role, finding the 400-acre human-made island to be the perfect location, “close enough to the office and all the culture the city has to offer, but far enough that I’m waking up to the sound of seagulls instead of car horns”.He took this image earlier this year, stopping mid-jog to capture the top of San Francisco’s Salesforce Tower. “I was mesmerised by how the fog, caused by what’s known as a marine layer, completely covered the rest of the skyline, leaving only the tower looking like a monolith,” he says. “It’s ironic that something that obscures, like fog, can make a scene more clear.”It’s only recently that Zhao has come to realise that his favourite photos don’t come from travels with his professional cameras, but “improbable scenes near home that somehow only reveal themselves when I’m not expecting them. It brings me considerable peace that despite living in such close proximity to the centre of things I feel ambivalent about – tech, AI, urban density, hustle culture – the universe can still grant such awe-inspiring moments of quiet.Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wonderful, full-fat indulgence’: the best (and worst) supermarket lemon cheesecake, tasted and rated | Dessert | The Guardian
description: We sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: We sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?
Content: Best of the zest: our taster took into account the lemon content – and the additives – as he put cheesecake to the test.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenBest of the zest: our taster took into account the lemon content – and the additives – as he put cheesecake to the test.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterDessertReview‘Wonderful, full-fat indulgence’: the best (and worst) supermarket lemon cheesecake, tasted and ratedWe sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?The best supermarket party cakesTom HuntSat 26 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLemon cheesecake is traditionally made by whipping cream, cream cheese, sugar and lemon, then pouring that on to a base made from melted butter and crushed biscuits (butter, flour, oats, sugar), before putting it in the fridge to set. That’s eight ingredients max, yet the average for today’s store-bought versions is 24.Every cake in today’s test falls firmly into the ultra-processed food category and typically contains at least five ingredients that aren’t found in domestic kitchens. Although real lemon juice or concentrate features in every one, lemon oil and acidity regulators are used to ensure that tart, lemony flavour.Although every cheesecake is edible and delicious in some way, and made so by that ultimate trio of salt, sugar and fat, the quality of taste and texture differs greatly. The best ones have a wonderful fattiness, a tart, lemony complexity and a good ratio of biscuit to topping; the worst tasted of stale biscuits, acidity regulators and plastic packaging.The best supermarket lemon cheesecakesBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Sicilian lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£7.50 for 580g at Waitrose (£1.29/100g)★★★★☆A pale lemon cheesecake topped with a spoon of lemon marmalade and a thick, sweet and firm but still crumbly base. Dangerously moreish. Not too sweet (19.2% sugar), full-fat indulgence and a wonderful, bitter lemon edge. No emulsifiers, preservatives, acidity regulators, colours or flavourings, but does contain seven additives, including certified sustainable palm oil, palm kernel oil, palm fat and invert sugar syrup.Best bargain:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5.50 for 500g at Sainsbury’s (£1.10/100g)★★★★☆A very deep mascarpone cheesecake with a layer of set curd on top, a spoon of lemon rind marmalade in the centre, a thick base and a 60:40 cheese-to-biscuit ratio.Verysweet (25.3% total sugars), plus the lemon curd in the cheese mix gives it a dense texture. Four additives – palm oil and potassium citrates, carotenes, invert sugar syrup – though no emulsifiers, preservatives, stabilisers or thickeners.And the rest …Tesco Finest lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5.50 for 500g at Tesco (£1.10/100g)★★★★☆A pale cheesecake with candied lemon peel garnish and blobs of lemon curd throughout. A light, moussey texture, quite sweet (21% sugar) with a strong lemon flavour, a nice, compact base and a 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. No emulsifiers, preservatives or acidity regulators, but six additives nonetheless, including palm oil, amidated pectin, algal carotenes and invert sugar syrup.Morrisons the Best Sicilian lemon cheesecakesView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 192g at Morrisons (£1.82/100g)★★★☆☆Two small individual cheesecakes topped with a zesty lemon curd, a dash of white chocolate and a good ratio of moist biscuit base to topping. Made with British milk and Sicilian lemons, this is super-sweet (27.7% sugar), but there are no preservatives, colours or stabilisers, and only four additives (palm oil, invert sugar syrup, soya lecithins, flavouring).M&S Sicilian lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5 for 585g at Ocado (86p/100g)★★★☆☆A light, moussey and quite sweet (20.5% sugar) deep-dish cheesecake with bitter lemon curd on top. A 65:35 cheese-to-biscuit ratio, but the base tastes a bit stale. Emulsifier- and preservative-free, but still nine additives including palm oil, palm kernel oil, sodium citrates and invert sugar syrup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnglish Cheesecake Company lemon & mascarpone cheesecake slicesView image in fullscreen£4 for 180g at Ocado (£2.22/100g)£4 for 180g at Tesco (£2.22/100g)★★☆☆☆Two large slices with a nice, firm base and a 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. An odd synthetic acidic aroma (probably from the citric acid and potassium sorbate), but a good, strong lemon flavour and moussey texture. The least sweet cake in the test (17.7% sugars), but eight additives including palm oil, modified starch, soya lecithins and flavouring. A Great Taste one-star winner in 2024.Gü Spanish lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£3.95 for 170g at Ocado (£2.32/100g)£3.95 for 170g at Sainsbury’s (£2.32/100g)★★☆☆☆Moussey and saucy with a crumbly, moist base (thanks to the ramekin format). Super-sweet (26% sugars), and less lemony than most, with a synthetic, sour flavour. Emulsifier-free, but six additives including RSPO-certified palm oil, invert sugar syrup and modified starch.The Bakery at Asda zingy lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£4.78 for 500g at Asda (96p/100g)★★☆☆☆Super-rich, cheesy, creamy and not too sweet (19% sugars), with lemon coulis swirled into the top and a good 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. Low actual lemon content (2%) with a distinct lemon oil flavour. Seven additives, including palm oil, polyglycerol esters of fatty acids, mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids and potassium metabisulphite.Co-op Irresistible lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£4 for 160g at Co-op (£2.50/100g)★★☆☆☆Noticeably rich and creamy, with a lemon curd layer on top and a moist base. Very sweet (23% sugars), tart and lemony, with a distinctive lemon oil intensity. No preservatives or stabilisers beyond modified starch, but there are seven additives including palm oil, glucose syrup, invert sugar syrup and citric acid.Aldi Specially Selected lemon & white chocolate cheesecake slicesView image in fullscreen£2.09 for 180g at Aldi (£1.16/100g), in store only★☆☆☆☆A very sweet (20.8% sugars), fluffy cheesecake with a powerful, bitter lemon flavour, a soft digestive biscuit base and extra sweetness from the white chocolate topping. Eight additives, including palm oil, modified starch, soya lecithins and potassium sorbate.For more, read thebest (and worst) supermarket dark chocolateExplore more on these topicsDessertThe FilterFoodCakeFruitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cooking with Tom Kerridge, the Michelin ‘meatfluencer’ | Tom Kerridge | The Guardian
