description: The star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilli
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilli
Content: ‘Practically orchestral’: Tom Kerridge at work on a venison chilli.Photograph: Jenny Zarins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Practically orchestral’: Tom Kerridge at work on a venison chilli.Photograph: Jenny Zarins/The GuardianCooking with...Tom KerridgeInterviewCooking with Tom Kerridge, the Michelin ‘meatfluencer’Zoe WilliamsThe star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilliSat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Kerridge is the king of meat: first as a chef, transforming pub classics like pork belly into Michelin-starred fare atThe Hand and Flowersin Marlow 20 years ago, and later openingThe Butcher’s Tap and Grillin the same village; then as a cookery writer: hisOutdoor Cooking– The Ultimate Modern Barbecue Bibleof 2021 is well named, being both as comprehensive and as worshipful as a holy book; and recently as a “meat-fluencer”, making gorgeous skills videos on Instagram andYouTube.That was just destiny, he says (more or less). “When you’re cooking in a classic brigade system, the sections are like a larder: you’ve got starters, you’ve got garnish, you’ve got meat and fish, you’ve got pastry. The meat is the lead section, where the most experienced chef is, because that’s where you land when you’ve learned to treat vegetables with love and respect. If you fuck up cabbage, it doesn’t cost a lot.” It’s true, it doesn’t, but if you saw the care Kerridge puts into dicing an onion – peeling its layers apart like he’s making a mosaic, assiduous even about half an inch of waste – of anonion– you’d know that love and respect aren’t really about money.View image in fullscreenTreated with respect: the veggie ingredients for venison chilli.Kerridge is in his hideaway, also in Marlow, making a venison chilli, which flies off his menu for reasons I am shortly to discover. Even though itisSeptember, he is passionate that people should stop thinking of venison as an autumn-only meat – it’s available all year round. You could definitely become a connoisseur by knowing the difference in flavour profile between a red deer and a muntjac, but not by consigning it to some perfect season. You have to “drive flavour into it,” he says: “it sits there with beef but it’s much leaner, so it’s harder in some ways, because there’s no fat content.” The flipside is that it takes on spice really well, and by the time this dish is done – slow-roasted loin, a ragu made separately, everything cooked for hours, combined at the end with some fat chunks of salami – there’s a lot going on, and it is practically orchestral.Part of that experimentation and complexity is driven by necessity. When Kerridge started in his first kitchen, it was at theCalcot Manorin Tetbury, a classic posh hotel restaurant – one Michelin star, many layers of tablecloth, a food sensibility that was all about fine dining and being somewhat French: “the best ingredients, all racks of lamb and fillets of beef.” That was 1991, and he was 18 – it became quite a racy and experimental decade, in food as well as everything else, and tastes changed to incorporate the rest of the animal. In 2001, Kerridge became head chef ofBellamy’sin London, but that wasn’t as formative asAdlards: “amazing restaurant, small space, really busy, right in the middle of Norwich. That was the first time that I thought: ‘Maybe I could do this’.”View image in fullscreen‘If you saw the care Kerridge puts into dicing an onion ...’At The Hand and Flowers, Kerridge could stamp the place with his ambition: Michelin-starred food for people who didn’t want to dress like they were going to the opera. It’s hard even to remember the atmosphere of the hushed formality Kerridge ushered away. It’s no accident that his was the first ever pub to get its second Michelin star; helovespubs. “Wintertime walks across the Lake District, ending up in a pub with an open fire, that smell of crackling wood, beer and steamed puddings; summertime beer gardens; city-centre pubs; London pubs, where loads of city workers are all stood outside, packed together like fish: all of them are amazing, and the one thing they all have in common is a sense that it doesn’t matter where you come from – irrespective of your educational background, financial background, they’re warm. Everybody understands how a pub works, and everyone’s welcome.”The financial crash took a bit of weathering for Kerridge, and he didn’t start expanding his slate of restaurants until 2015. But by that time, after two series ofGreat British Menu,the BBC had started to hang whole concepts off his name –Proper Pub Food,Spring Kitchen,Best Ever Dishes– and he had name recognition, but never as a panto personality; he always came across on screen exactly as he does off it: a decent, practical-minded, funny bloke who would follow a flavour to the ends of the earth but never make a soliloquy about it. By 2020, he had three restaurants in Marlow, two in London including at theCorinthia Hotel,and one in Manchester. “Then, when Covid came, it was terrifying. We lost an awful lot of money: an event company we had closed, and the restaurant in Manchester ended up closing too – but everybody was in the same boat.”‘I’ve never known fear like it’: Tom Kerridge on booze, bad-boy chefs and the crisis for pubs and restaurantsRead moreThe financial pressures facing the industry at the moment are of a different order of magnitude, Kerridge says. “Six or seven years ago, a good restaurant might make 10% profit – not big numbers but you could make that work. Now, a lot of great places are making a fraction of that, and some aren’t breaking even.”Foodand energy costs have gone up massively, business rates are high, and the minimum wage and national insurance changes hit this industry particularly hard because it’s quite staff-intensive. “The cost of employing a young person over the last four years has gone up by a third. There’s no way you can put those costs on to the punter – they just won’t go out, or they’ll go to other places that aren’t putting them on. Then it becomes a race to the bottom; a competition to see who can lose the least money.”Kerridge is very active in the campaign to cut VAT on the sector from 20 to 10%, which seemed to be falling on deaf ears, but then the prime minister changed and the mood changed, and before long a business rate cut was announced, but just for pubs. Restaurants may yet see a slice of government largesse, but at the moment it feels to Kerridge like “there’s no help, there’s no cavalry coming over the hill”, and this is corroding creativity everywhere, because chefs don’t have the headroom to take risks and mess about: 21 hospitality venues are closing every week in the UK.View image in fullscreenTom Kerridge making venison chilli: ‘roast the hell out of the mince before you do anything else.’But back to that chilli. The venison haunch, which has been braising for three hours already, has gone into the ragu and the whole thing is a rich and sheeny mahogany, which is the daunting bit for the home cook – how to avoid a grey mess without the cheap win of a can of tomatoes? And Kerridge is anti chucking-in-a-can of tomatoes.There are cheffy touches at the end. Coriander oil actually couldn’t be simpler – you just whizz coriander with olive oil – but it looks so chic against a splodge of sour cream it’s unreal. A bit of grated chocolate, a bit of lime; I guess we would once have called this fusion – French and Mexican – but now it feels like the satisfyingly inevitable result of anyone blessed with a deer. “I was a kid who grew up in the 1980s,” Kerridge says. “It was crispy pancakes and potato waffles, in a single-parent family on an estate in Gloucester. We weren’t cooking tea every night. But my mum would do Sunday lunch, and she’d do it for everyone we brought back from the rugby club. She didn’t have any money – we never really had a joint; she just used to roast sausage meat and then do all the vegetables. There was always enough, and it was always delicious.” It’s not the obvious origin story for Kerridge, but in a way, it is.View image in fullscreenTipping point: venison ‘takes on spice really well’.A tip that will change your cookingWhen making chilli or bolognese, roast the hell out of the mince before you do anything else. Do this on the hob: put the meat in a pan with a bit of oil, high heat, and roast it for much longer than you would ever have dreamt. Take it way past the point of just having a bit of colour. When it starts to leave its charred remnants on the bottom of the pan, don’t worry – the onions going in afterwards will deglaze all that with their natural juices. When it starts to look very dark – pretty nubbly and dry – again, don’t fret; it will rehydrate later when you add the stock. Don’t trouble yourself over whether it’s lean mince or not: you can sieve off the rendered fat after this first stage, then you get all the benefits of fattier meat with none of the grease. “When you think of the flavour profile you get from a barbecue, or the outside bits of roast beef – that’s the bit everyone likes. And that’s what you’ll get from this ragu.” I tried this myself when I got home, and it was hands down the best bolognese I’ve ever made.Tom’s favourite utensil: the cast-iron panView image in fullscreenTom Kerridge – ‘This is absolutely chef-proof,” he says, “indestructible.”The famous lacquered versions – Le Creuset and whatnot – are the ones that look good in the interiors magazines, but matte black and unvarnished as the day it was born is Tom’s preference (Kerridge has developed a range for M&S, which I wouldn’t normally mention except it’s very good value). “This is absolutely chef-proof,” he says, “indestructible.” If you think of all pans as quite hard to destroy, that’s because you only use yours once or twice a week. A pan that can survive life in a restaurant, 10 uses a service, with outrageous heat (both direct and indirect), rambunctious cheffy fireworks, and still last a lifetime is a higher-order pan.Venison chilliView image in fullscreenVenison chilli as made by Tom Kerridge, with some soured cream and coriander oil on the side..I love a regular beef chilli, but this venison version is something else! Using a combination of diced haunch and venison mince gives the dish a real depth of flavour and a great texture. Although it takes a bit more time, it’s pretty straightforward, and the result is well worth it. Finishing the rich dish with dark chocolate, red wine and a zing of lime perks it up beautifully.Serves6-8For the venison haunchVegetable oil,for cooking1kg venison haunch,diced2 carrots,halved4 celery sticks,trimmed and cut in half1 onion,peeled and quartered1bouquet garni(sprig each of thyme and rosemary and a bay leaf, tied together with kitchen string)2 garlic cloves,peeled and sliced1 litredark rich beef or venison stockFor the chilli2 tbsp cumin seeds2 tbsp coriander seeds2 tsp chilli powder2 tsp cracked black pepper400g minced venisonVegetable oil,for cooking2 onions,peeled and diced4 garlic cloves,peeled and finely grated150g Milano salami or chorizo,diced400g tin kidney beans,drained and rinsed150ml red wineFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lime75g dark chocolate(70% cocoa solids),grated, plus extra to serveSalt and freshly ground black pepperCreme fraiche, to serveHeat the oven to 140C (120C fan)/275F/gas 1. Heat a glug of oil in a large, heavy-based, flameproof casserole over a high heat. Sear the diced venison, in batches to avoid overcrowding the pan, for a few minutes until well coloured on all sides. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside in a bowl.Lower the heat, add the carrots to the pan and saute until they have taken on plenty of colour. Now add the celery, onion and bouquet garni and fry for a few minutes, then add the garlic and cook for another minute or two.Return the meat to the pan, pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Put the lid on and transfer to the oven to braise for three hours, until the meat is succulent and deliciously tender.Remove the meat from the oven and cool slightly. Put a colander over a bowl, and tip the venison braise into the colander to strain off the stock. Reserve the stock and separate the meat from the vegetables. Transfer the meat to a bowl and set aside;discardthe vegetables and bouquet garni.For the chilli, put a small frying pan over a medium heat and add the cumin and coriander seeds. Toast for two to three minutes, rattling the pan, until fragrant. Let it all cool slightly, then grind to a powder using an electric spice grinder or pestle and mortar. Tip into a bowl and mix in the chilli powder and black pepper.Heat a large, nonstick frying pan over a medium heat. Add the minced venison and dry-fry, stirring frequently, for 20–25 minutes, until it is nicely browned and has a tasty, nutty flavour. It should be very crisp. Drain the mince in a colander to remove any excess fat and set aside.While the mince is cooking, heat a dash of oil in a large, deep, nonstick saute pan over a medium heat and fry the onions and garlic for eight to 10 minutes, until softened. Stir in the ground spices and cook for two to three minutes to release their flavour.Stir in the cooked mince and salami or chorizo, cook for two to three minutes, then pour in the reserved stock from the braised haunch. Add the kidney beans, give it a stir and bring to a boil. Lower the heat to a simmer and reduce the sauce until it’s thick and stew-like – about 20 minutes.Stir in the venison haunch and heat through for five minutes. Pour in the red wine, bring to a boil and add the lime zest, then lower the heat, season to taste and warm for a few minutes.Remove from the heat and stir in the chocolate. Serve the venison chilli on warmed plates, with a dollop of creme fraiche and a little more chocolate grated over the top.This is an edited extract from Tom’s Table, published by Bloomsbury at £25. title: Athens on a plate – a food-lover’s guide to the Greek capital | Athens holidays | The Guardian
description: Top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the city
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the city
Content: Highlight: Tucking in at Epta Martyres wine bar, Athens.Photograph: Angelos GiotopoulosView image in fullscreenHighlight: Tucking in at Epta Martyres wine bar, Athens.Photograph: Angelos GiotopoulosEat your way around...Athens holidaysAthens on a plate – a food-lover’s guide to the Greek capitalAthens-born chef Nick Molyviatis and Greek restaurant supremo David Carter share their top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the cityDavid Carter and Nick Molyviatis, as told to Joanna TaylorSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoffeeNormally we stay around Plaka, soAnanais the coffee shop I go to most often. There’s alsoBehold The Manin Exarchia, which is one of the coolest coffee shops I’ve been to. Exarchia has a really rebellious, anti-establishment feel and this place completely fits that – it has great music, great coffee and it’s just very cool. I don’t think there’s a coffee shop in London that’s quite like it. DCView image in fullscreen‘Casual and low-key’: Anäna Cafe, Plaka, Athens.My favourite is also Anana; It’s casual and low-key, with somewhere to sit down and relax. I’ll have a freddo espresso (espresso shaken over ice), which is basically the Greek national coffee now. NMAthens: a new, confident Greek cuisineBakeriesFor pastries,Akrais one of the best places in Athens. The food itself is rustic, simple and delicious, and the pastries are unbelievably technical. There’s something almost incongruous about it – you eat very simple savoury food and then a dessert arrives that’s incredibly elaborate. It shouldn’t necessarily work, but it does. DCView image in fullscreenRoll up! No Crumbs bakery.No Crumbsopened this year and I’ve already been a few times. It’s a little outside the centre, but it’s where I’d go for breakfast or something to eat on the move. In central Athens, I also likeFillo, which specialises in traditional pies from around Greece. Last time I went, they had three differentspanakopitas from three different regions. NMBreakfastI don’t really do breakfast in Athens. We’ll normally get coffee, then at about 11am go toDiporto, which is usually our first proper stop. It’s this incredible, old, rundown restaurant near the market: cash only, orders taken with a pen, massive wine barrels in the room, no choice of wine. They just put wine and water on the table. The food is incredibly simple: chickpeas, beans, vegetables cooked down slowly, sometimes grilled sardines or fish from the market. You could recreate a Greek taverna in London, but you could never recreate Diporto. There’s such magic in it. DCView image in fullscreen‘Such magic’: Diporto restaurant, Athens.Photograph: Hector Christiaen/AlamyIf I want to start the day properly, I go to Ipiros inside the meat market, at about 10.30am. It’s not really breakfast; it’s a proper meal. They serve slow-cooked dishes in huge pots and we usually get the tripe soup, which is good for a hangover, with loads of bread. Then we walk around the corner to Diporto and have the opposite: braised beans, chickpeas, salad and, whatever time it is, wine. NMTraditional tavernasWhenever we fly into Athens, we try to go straight toTaverna To Trigonoin Kalyvia, out by the airport. It’s as magic as a taverna gets. One side of the menu is salads, tzatziki, cheeses and breads; the other is grilled meat such as sausage, spit-roast lamb, offal, lamb chops, sheep chops. Everything is cooked to order and served with incredible abundance and generosity. It’s very simple: good produce, salt, oregano and lemon; nothing is over-embellished. I wouldn’t go to Athens without going there. DCView image in fullscreenChop-chop! Manári restaurant, Athens.Manáriis a proper meat chop house in central Athens. It’s relatively new, but it feels as traditional as possible, and you don’t need to travel into the mountains outside the city to find meat that good. I order the lamb chops, pasta with meat juices and tomato salad. The lamb chops are as good as – if not better than – a good dry-aged steak. Another favourite isTavern Spanosin Kato Patisia, for lamb chops and meats cooked slowly on the spit. Once they run out, they run out. NMNew-wave restaurantsLinou Soumpasis & Siais probably the most forward-thinking restaurant in Athens right now, and probably one of the best in Greece. It takes quite humble, seafood-led food and gives it a fine edge without losing its simplicity. The room is incredibly simple and every detail is really considered. Last time I went, they served a version ofkakavia, the traditional fish soup, which was essentially a beautiful fish and vegetable broth with olive oil. Something that simple, done that well, is incredible. DCView image in fullscreen‘Restrained and modern’: Linou Soumpasis and Sia restaurant, Athens.Linou is one of my go-tos, too. It reminds me a bit ofLyle’smeetsBrat. It has a restrained approach to food that still feels very modern. I’d also go toPharaoh, particularly for the vegetables and whatever they’re doing with fermented wheat, andAteno, which we went to twice in two days on my last trip. Get the Greek salad, stuffed vegetables and fries with mushrooms and eggs. I also really likeEx Machina: their saganaki is fried cheese but served cold, and I always want to see what [the chef] Adam Kodovas is doing with the seafood broth because the dish changes every few months, while the formula remains the same. I go toAkrafor lunch because they serve smaller portions and I can order as many dishes as possible. NMSeafoodTravoltais banging; it’s old-school and a bit likeBentley’sin London. You get huge plates of crudo and whole fish, and they have an amazing prawn and squid skewer with squid ink and olive oil that they mix at the table. It can get expensive (fish is incredibly expensive in Greece), but if you’re really into seafood it’s very cool.Phitais another good seafood place, a little further out. DCView image in fullscreen‘Old school’: Travolta restaurant, Athens.Photograph: Monika KritikouTravolta would be my choice for more classic seafood, too. If you want something more elevated, I’d go toIodionear Kolonaki. There’s one dish I’ll always remember, which is raw fish served cold with a crisp sheet of rice paper on top and a warm avgolemono sauce – a classic Greek sauce made with egg and lemon. You grab everything together in one bite and it’s great. NMCheap eatsFor souvlaki, the best is often at little roadside or market stalls. Last time we were in Exarchia, we found a tiny souvlaki stall mainly serving the market vendors. Forsouvla, the bigger rotisserie-style meats, we go toPsitopoleio Peloponnhsos. They serve huge pieces of meat, lamb heads; all sorts of pretty gnarly stuff cooking on the rotisserie. DCGyros are a dangerous subject for Greeks because everyone has their favourite.Achilleasin Neos Kosmos is one of the few places that still makes their own [meat rotisserie] (rather than buying it ready-made). In the centre, I really likeHoocut. They aren’t technically gyros because they slice the meat raw, cook it and then chop it again into small strips, but the mentality is similar. For a late-night version, go toMandrakiin Kaisariani. They’re open until about 2am and cook meat on spits late into the night. Their gyros are huge and often sell out. It’s cheap, traditional and the sort of thing people actually eat every day. NMWine and cocktailsWine is Fineis really good for a pre-dinner drink, and I also loveEpta Martyres, from the people behindLoggia[on Sifnos]; I’d been to both loads of times before I even realised they were connected. In Greece, I tend to want wines that are light and bright.Assyrtikois the obvious one; in that climate you want something really zippy. DCView image in fullscreenBaba Au Rum, Athens.Pharaohhas a great wine list, andTanini Agapi Mouis an amazing wine bar. A Greek grape I discovered this year is Vidiano. Vidiano can lean quite dry but still feels really pleasant and crisp; depending on where it’s grown, the fruit and minerality change a lot. It’s easygoing but complex at the same time. NMLine Athensis quite molecular and it’s the kind of place you stay for the night. The cocktails are some of the best I’ve ever had in my life, let alone Athens.Baba au Rumis right in the mix, too. There’s alsoRumble in the Junglebehind The Bar in Front of the Bar. The first is a bar where you walk in and think, “This is cool,” then go through another door into the second, even cooler bar hidden behind it. It’s very Athens. DCYou have to mention Line and The Bar in Front of the Bar. At Bar in Front, they’re trying to be as zero waste as possible, and you basically order through a window in a wall and sit drinking in the street. I choose what to drink according to the weather – last time I had a frozen martini that was almost like a slushie. At Line, the Paloma is usually my go-to, although on my last two visits I had one of their punches, which changes regularly. NMMarkets and food shoppingWe always go to Athens’ central fish and meat markets. I particularly recommend being in Athens on a Saturday because that’s when you find all these farmers’ markets around the city. Some of my best times in Athens have been wandering around those. DCView image in fullscreenPreparing fish ahead of a busy day at the central fish market.Photograph: Image Professionals GmbH/AlamyNear Diporto there’sMiran, a charcuterie shop with a huge range of cheeses and cured meats that they make themselves. Buy something there, pick up some bread and take it home. There’s also a huge farmers’ market every Saturday around Exarchia with outstanding produce. NMOut of townI really likeVouliagmeni, down on the coast where the Four Seasons is. We used to drive down there in the morning for sunrise, or chase the sunset if we were filming. Lake Vouliagmeni is there, too. It’s much more suburban, with huge houses and tree-lined boulevards, and it’s absolutely beautiful. You probably need a car. I don’t have one particular restaurant to send you to; for me it’s the area itself. DCView image in fullscreenLake Vouliagmeni, near Athens.Photograph: Nito/ShutterstockFor meat, go out towards the airport to Kalyvia. There are two enormous tavernas,Christoforosand To Trigono. During the week they can be completely empty, but at the weekend you’ll struggle to get a table. People tend to swear allegiance to one or the other; I don’t have a favourite. It normally depends on who’s driving me and where they want to go. Although the last few times I’ve been to Christoforos. NMDavid Carter is the founder of London hospitality groupDCCO, whose restaurants includeOmaandAgora, and Nick Molyviatis is co-founder ofZylia, also in London.Explore more on these topicsAthens holidaysEat your way around...FoodGreek food and drinkGreece holidaysRestaurants (Food)Restaurants (Travel)ShareReuse this content

title: How Athens discovered a new, confident Greek cuisine | Greek food and drink | The Guardian
description: Athens is now a food capital where you can enjoy bustling bars, traditional taverna fare or unearth a new-wave gem in its many restaurants – but it wasn’t always this way
Author: Sofka Zinovieff
Headline: Athens is now a food capital where you can enjoy bustling bars, traditional taverna fare or unearth a new-wave gem in its many restaurants – but it wasn’t always this way
Content: Photograph: neirfy/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: neirfy/Getty Images/iStockphotoEat your way around...Greek food and drinkHow Athens discovered a new, confident Greek cuisineAthens is now a food capital where you can enjoy bustling bars, traditional taverna fare or unearth a new-wave gem in its many restaurants – but it wasn’t always this waySee our recommendations for eating and drinking around AthensSofka ZinovieffSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVisiting Athens for its food might have sounded like a joke to previous generations. Unlike many other Mediterranean countries, including Italy, Spain and Turkey, Greece had no renaissance and no aristocracy to fund chefs and develop sophisticated cuisines. Simple village dishes didn’t always translate well: in the past, tourists would suffer a summer scorching and some desiccated moussaka so they could puff up the Acropolis in August before skedaddling to an island. However, recently the Greek capital has undergone a gastronomic renaissance.Athens always offered the joys of eating outdoors – by the sea in summer, or winter sunshine on the city’s streets – but these days chefs are rethinking the uses of Greece’s unrivalled ingredients, such as scented, sun-ripened tomatoes, barrel-aged feta, and the best olive oil in the world. Enlightened visitors are also re-thinking their trips, arriving at more temperate times of year, and taking advantage of how culinary traditions are moving in exciting directions. They’re exploring beyond the tourist traps and over-Airbnb-d areas around the Acropolis, finding treasures in humbler neighbourhoods such as Petralona, Keramikos, or hipster Kypseli. A bonus is the growing number of restaurants serving food from Asia, Africa, the Balkans and the Middle East.View image in fullscreenA bustling outdoor farmers’ market in central Athens.Photograph: Dimitris Asproloupos/AlamyIn the 1980s, Athenians were leaving behind a history of rural poverty,fasoládabean stew, and a largely vegetarian diet. They discovered fast food and began eating too much meat. The 1990s saw new levels of wealth; brunch, sushi and lobster spaghetti were aspirational goals for the upwardly mobile. By the time of the 2004 Athens Olympics, a cohort of Athenians existed who had never known hunger, war or dictatorship. Consequently, the economic crisis that began in 2009 was a devastating shock and the next decade saw severe unemployment and deprivation, accompanied by an influx of traumatised refugees and migrants.Athenians who didn’t depart during the brain drain took stock. Unable to pay the rent, some moved back in with parents and grandparents, and others relocated to ancestral villages; rare is the person who has no toehold on an island or mountainside. Family olive groves beckoned, vineyards were tended, organic farming debated. Alongside the unlikely flourishing of the arts in Athens during the crisis (actors, musicians and artists often worked unpaid), there was a flowering of Greek foodies. They examined things previously taken for granted by most Athenians: eating seasonally, shopping at farmers’ markets, sourcing locally. Covid provided a final push.View image in fullscreenA mix of modern and traditional: Travolta restaurant in Athens.Boosted by foreign appreciation of the Mediterranean diet and its delicious, healthy basic ingredients, Athenians returned to their grandmothers’ kitchens – literally in the case of Anastasia Miari, who wrote the celebratedYiayia: Time-perfected Recipes from Greek Grandmothers. This trend “isn’t just nostalgia or a return to tradition”, chef and writerCarolina Dorititold me. “It’s a new confidence in Greek cuisine, where tradition has become something alive that we can build on, rather than something fixed in the past.” Doriti celebrated this trend for “honest and rooted cooking” in her wonderful books Salt of the Earth andThe Greek Islands Cookbook. For this sort of excellent but unpretentious food, she loves the restaurantsLesvionin theGalatsineighbourhood of Athens andAthosinVotanikos.Alongside simple and enlightened Athenian tavernas are Michelin-starred restaurants, where local ingredients are metamorphosed in exquisite concoctions for tasting menus. There are riffs on grandma’s chickpeas and wild greens as she never imagined, and Yiayia might be even more astonished at how her descendants dine on Japanese-Greek hybrids, such as soba noodles with tahini, Ethiopiandorowat, Georgian khachapuri and Lebanese fattoush. Eating in Athens has changed.Sofka Zinovieff has lived in Athens for 25 years. Her latest novel is Stealing Dad. title: Henry Harris’ vegetarian recipe for French onion and parsley soup | Food | The Guardian
description: A thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbs
Content: Henry Harris’ French onion and parsley soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ French onion and parsley soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFoodHenry Harris’ vegetarian recipe for French onion and parsley soupA thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbsHenry HarrisSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was a child, my mother often made onions in white sauce to serve with roast lamb. I loved their thick, velvety texture and how they brought richness, sweetness and even more savouriness to a good Sunday lunch. A similarly thick tangle of onions features in the classicsoupe à l’oignon gratinée,which can’t really be mimicked without a deep, dark, beefy stock, so rather than even try, it’s best to introduce another layer of flavour entirely. The parsley here yields a very different end result that also proves to be rather comforting.Onion and parsley soupPrep15 minCook1 hr 15 minServes4-6125g unsalted butter6 large onions, peeled and finely slicedSalt and black pepper2 bay leaves1 litre vegetable stock250ml double cream1 large bunchflat-leaf parsley, picked75gemmental(suitable for vegeatarians), finely grated4 tbsp croutonsMelt the butter in a large, heavy pan on a medium heat, then add the sliced onions. Season generously with pepper and a little salt, add the bay leaves, then cover and leave to cook gently for 45 minutes to an hour, stirring regularly, until the onions have sweated down to the softest vegetable mass – you want to take them to the point when, were you to squeeze them in your hands, they would turn to a pulp.Add the stock, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir in the cream and cook for another five minutes. Taste and add more salt and pepper if needed.At the very last minute, finely chop the parsley, stir it into the soup and ladle immediately into warmed bowls. Serve topped with the grated cheese and a few croutons.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. title: Blind date: ‘I do wish I hadn’t stepped on that dog – but she assured me it was OK’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Miklos, 25, a PhD student, meets Minnie, 23, who works in film production
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Miklos, 25, a PhD student, meets Minnie, 23, who works in film production
Content:
Composite: David Levene & Alicia CanterView image in fullscreenComposite: David Levene & Alicia CanterBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘I do wish I hadn’t stepped on that dog – but she assured me it was OK’Miklos, 25, a PhD student, meets Minnie, 23, who works in film productionSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenMiklos on MinnieWhat were you hoping for?To take a step outside my comfort zone. To meet the love of my life.First impressions?Confident, and just as confused as I was about how to start off a blind date.What did you talk about?The optimal time horizon to plan your life ahead – we oscillated between one and 10 years. After that, I’m embarrassed to admit, loads of K-pop.Most awkward moment?On my way to the loo I stepped on a dog by accident. I felt horrible, but Minnie assured me it was OK.Good table manners?The food was so intimidatingly tasty it forced the best table manners out of us. Hers were almost too good, I’d say.Best thing about Minnie?She is from the best part of town (in my opinion) and it shows. She is unabashedly herself.Would you introduce Minnie to your friends?They love a bottle of wine. She loves a bottle of wine. There is nothing more to say.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Minnie in three wordsTalkative. Fuzzy. Edgy.What do you think Minnie made of you?I think she saw me quite accurately: nerdy, but willing to push boundaries and have some fun.Did you go on somewhere?We did not.And ... did you kiss?No kissing was had.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I wish I had not stepped on that dog – that’s it really.Marks out of 10?9.Would you meet again?By the end of the date, it was clear to both of us that we were missing a romantic spark … That’s life!View image in fullscreenMiklos and Minnie on their dateView image in fullscreenMinnie on MiklosWhat were you hoping for?A fun evening.First impressions?Very lovely guy, good vibes. I was a tad late and he was super understanding. He also noted that he often goes by Mickey, which is pretty funny.What did you talk about?Travel. Studies. Controversial opinions on music concerts. Katseye (sorry, Miklos).Most awkward moment?Neither of us could figure out the menu.Good table manners?Yes, very polite.Best thing about Miklos?He is super different from me. It was nice chatting with someone who has lived such a different life.Would you introduce Miklos to your friends?Hypothetically yes, but only as a friend.Blind date: ‘Bizarrely, she suddenly realised she knew my daughter’Read moreDescribe Miklos in three wordsIntelligent, chatty, inquisitive.What do you think Miklos made of you?That I was easy to talk to.Did you go on somewhere?Nope, just headed home.And ... did you kiss?Couple of hugs, not the vibe for a kiss.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?We both said we would have liked to have been in a different part of town by the canal (the restaurant was lovely though).Marks out of 10?7.Would you meet again?Probably not, but no hard feelings.Miklos and Minnie ate attheBull and Last,LondonNW5. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Happy birthday! What deals and discounts does your age unlock?  | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: From a getting part-time job at 14 to receiving a letter from the king at 100, some milestone ages hold advantages in Britain
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: From a getting part-time job at 14 to receiving a letter from the king at 100, some milestone ages hold advantages in Britain
Content: On your birthday, you can have your cake and eat it … plus there the milestone gifts unlocked when you reach certain ages.Photograph: Oleksandr Latkun/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenOn your birthday, you can have your cake and eat it … plus there the milestone gifts unlocked when you reach certain ages.Photograph: Oleksandr Latkun/Getty Images/iStockphotoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Consumer affairsHappy birthday! What deals and discounts does your age unlock?From a getting part-time job at 14 to receiving a letter from the king at 100, some milestone ages hold advantages in BritainHilary OsborneandRupert JonesSat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 06.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you just unwrapped some presents? Been sitting in a soft play centre and watched a toddler blow out some candles? Double-checked what time the party starts later?With 26 September beingstatistically the most common day to have a birthdayin England and Wales, according to the Office for National Statistics, it is quite possible that you or someone close to you is marking another trip around the sun.Even if you no longer celebrate the big day with a party or family outing, there are still reasons why it is worth noting because some milestones bring gifts of their own.Age 12You canlegally buy Christmas crackers. At this stage, the jokes will be much older than you are.View image in fullscreenCrackers can now be added to the Christmas shopping list.Photograph: stuartbur/Getty Images/iStockphotoAge 14You can get a part-time job. There are some professions – acting and modelling, for example – where you can work from a younger age. There are some local councils that allow you to work from the age of 13 for a very limited number of hours a week.Age 16You are entitled to earn £8 an hour under the UK’sminimum wagelaws. You may also have to pay national insurance (NI). This tax is collected by your employer if you earn more than £242 a week from one job. You will be issued with a NI number and card before your birthday. You should receive a letter – make sure you read it and amend any mistakes.You can also take charge of yourchild trust fund(if you have one) although you cannot withdraw the money yet. You and your parents should get a letter from the provider about this.Age 17View image in fullscreenYou can start motoring.Photograph: Benjamin John/AlamyThis is the legal driving age for most people in the UK. You can apply for your provisional licence much earlier in Great Britain – from the age of 15 years and nine months, or two months before you turn 17 if you live in Northern Ireland. It costs £34 to apply online and £43 to do so by post in Great Britain, or £62.50 in Northern Ireland.Age 18You can withdraw your child trust fund orjunior Isa– but you do not have to. If it is a child trust fund, you can transfer it to an Isa; if it is a junior Isa, it will automatically become an adult one. Lots of people areunaware they have a child trust fund: you can check for yourself or your child on thegovernment website.At this age you can open an Isa – either cash or stocks and shares. You could choose a lifetime Isa, which is designed to help you raise a deposit for a home and is not an account you can dip into, or a standard Isa, which will be more flexible.Benefits such asuniversal creditcan be claimed once you turn 18 if you are not in education and are on a low income or out of work. Payments are lower for under-25s than older claimants.The minimum wage you are entitled to also goes up to £10.85 an hour (currently – the rates change in April each year).Age 21You are entitled to the full adult minimum wage, which is now £12.71 an hour.Age 26View image in fullscreenThere are discount travel options on the railways after outgrowing what was once called a Young Persons Railcard.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianYou have outgrown what used to be called the Young Persons Railcard but have no fear: you can still get one-third off train travel, only nowwith a 26-30 Railcard. It costs £35 for a year and is available online, so you can buy it and use it on the same day.Age 28You are no longer a young person in the eyes of car rental companies. They typically charge a young driver’s fee: a surcharge that is usually about £35 a day and is paid on top of the regular hiring cost. The age up to which this is charged varies by company. At Budget, for example, it is up to the age of 25, while at Europcar, it is 26. At Sixt the surcharge applies to bookings by those under 28.Age 39View image in fullscreenLast call for lifetime Isas.Photograph: 57stock/AlamyThis year is your last chance to open alifetime Isa. This is the tax-free account that offers a government bonus on your savings every year to help you save a deposit for a property or towards your retirement. The account is available to 18- to 39-year-olds who can pay in up to £4,000 a year each. This is boosted by a payment worth 25% of what you paid in each month. Between the ages of 40 and 50 you can keep paying into the account. At 50 you will not be able to add any more; you can withdraw the money to buy a home or when you turn 60.Age 40People inEngland, Wales and Northern Irelandwho have a close relative with a glaucoma diagnosis can get free eye tests from the age of 40. Ask your optician if you think this applies to you.Age 50View image in fullscreenSaga is well known for providing holidays.Photograph: SaGa/Alamy“Welcome to the Saga club!” is the sort of thing people say when you hit your half century. Saga is the company well known for offering products and services, including insurance and holidays, exclusively to the over-50s.This is also the age when you may be targeted by over-50s life insurance providers. With this type of cover, typically aimed at those aged 50 to 85, you pay a fixed monthly premium and are guaranteed a fixed payout when you die –but there are downsides.There are some train discounts available to those who are 50 and older. ScotRail hasClub 50, which gives you a 20% discount on most tickets when bought online, plus other benefits (it costs £15 a year). In England, for Greater Anglia and Stansted Express services, there is theClub 50 Railcard(£25 for a year), which works in a similar way.Age 55This is usually the earliest age at which you cantake money from your private or workplace pension– it is rising to 57 from 6 April 2028. You may be able to take your pension before 55 if, for example, you need to retire early because of poor health. However, a private pension is normally designed to pay out from about the age of 65, so you will usually get less money than you expect if you access it early.View image in fullscreenThe age of 55 is typically the earliest age at which you can take money from your private or workplace pension.Photograph: Warren Bourne/AlamyThat’s because the headline estimate of your future retirement income that will be in the documents usually assumes you will continue paying in until the scheme’s normal pension age.Some cinemas offer cheap tickets to those aged 55-plus (but for most, 60 is the important age). The upmarket Everyman chain runsSilver Screen: weekly matinee screenings with a reduced ticket price for those 55 or older. Tickets include a complimentary hot drink and a slice of cake.Age 60In England,NHS prescriptions become free, saving you £9.90 an item. They are already free for everyone in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.Some good travel schemes kick in at this age. The over-60s can get a third off rail travel with aSenior Railcardcosting £35 for a year or £80 for three years. The average saving that holders enjoy is said to be £114 a year.If you live in London, you can get a60+ London Oyster photocard, which gives you free travel on buses, the tube and other transport within the capital, but is subject to some restrictions. You have this until you reach state pension age and are eligible for aFreedom Pass. If you are in Wales, you can travel for free on most bus services in Wales and the borders and get discounted or free travel on many rail services by getting aConcessionary Travel Card.View image in fullscreenNHS prescriptions become free in England at 60.Photograph: Julien Behal/PAOn the shopping front, the retailer Iceland offers 10% off for all customers aged 60 or over every Tuesday. You need an Iceland Bonus Card (this is free) and to show valid proof of age at the till – for example, a senior bus pass, driving licence or senior railcard. This in-store-only deal applies to all UK Iceland and The Food Warehouse stores but excludes Iceland Local and The Range stores.​The bakery chain Patisserie Valerie offers the over-60s with a valid passport or driving licence 10% off. To access this, you need to verify your age via a service run by a separate company.In England and Wales, you become entitled to a free NHS eye test. In Northern Ireland, you can get a free Health and Social Care (HSC) sight test. In Scotland, NHS eye tests are free for everyone.Many local authority leisure centres offer free swimming for over-60s at specified times, and some theatres – including theNational Theatre in Londonandsome ATG venues– give discounts on selected shows.Age 65A few companies offer discounts – for example, at some Hilton hotels in the UK, guests who are 65-plus can enjoy savings of up to 6%. This is also the age that some theatre discounts for older people kick in (for example, atBirmingham Hippodromeand theRSCin Stratford-upon-Avon).View image in fullscreenA ballet at the Birmingham Hippodrome.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianYou should also be able to get thefree NHS flu jab. This is typically offered from September or October (in regions such as England and Wales, this includes those who will turn 65 by 31 March 2027).Age 66+If you were born on or before 5 April 1960, your state pension age is 66. As of now it is rising gradually each month, and by one month at a time, until it reaches 67 in April 2028. It will eventually rise to 68, affecting those born after April 1977.The new state pension (as opposed to the old basic state pension) is up to £241.30 a week, and entitlement can unlock other benefits and help. TheMoneyHelper websitehas more information.Age 75You can apply fora free TV licence, provided you (or your partner living at the same address) receivepension credit.Age 80View image in fullscreenMore help is available for energy bills.Photograph: Mark Sykes Energy And Power/AlamyTo get the winter fuel payment for 2026-27, you have to be 66-plus (born on or before 27 June 1960) – however, those aged 80-plus (born before 28 September 1946) can get more: a total of £300. It is available to those in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland has its own scheme), andthe rules are complicated.Some people who receive little or no basic state pension are able to apply for the “over 80 pension”. This can now give you £110.75 a week.Age 100You can geta free birthday messagefrom King Charles when you hit 100 – and then every year from age 105 onwards.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsOffice for National StatisticsChristmasWork & careersNational insuranceChild trust fundsMotoringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dolce & Gabbana mixes it up as pressure mounts for turnaround | Milan fashion week | The Guardian
description: With Jennifer Lopez providing some star power, the Italian house’s Milan show came at a crucial time for the brand
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: With Jennifer Lopez providing some star power, the Italian house’s Milan show came at a crucial time for the brand
Content: Jennifer Lopez walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026 at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II on Tuesday.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images for VogueView image in fullscreenJennifer Lopez walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026 at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II on Tuesday.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images for VogueMilan fashion weekDolce & Gabbana mixes it up as pressure mounts for turnaroundWith Jennifer Lopez providing some star power, the Italian house’s Milan show came at a crucial time for the brandChloe Mac DonnellSat 26 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this weekJennifer Lopezwalked down the Vogue World catwalk in Milan wearing a black beaded A-line bustier dress from Dolce & Gabbana. On Saturday, she sat in the front row at the Italian house’s womenswear show in a three-piece velvet suit from the same brand, her look topped off with a baker-boy cap.The reminder ofDolce & Gabbana’s inimitable celebrity connection is no coincidence. In a turbulent luxury market, the brand has found itself trying to navigate anearly £400m debt pile.View image in fullscreenJennifer Lopez arrives for Dolce & Gabbana’s ‘Stravaganza Siciliana’ on Saturday.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageIn August, the company, embroiled in controversy over the years, reached an agreement with its banks that gave it until March 2028 to settle its debt.In exchange for the waiver, the brand must carry out a series of “extraordinary corporate transactions”, which reportedly include the sale of some of its properties.It is one of the few fashion houses that remains independent. Gucci and Bottega Veneta are owned by the French conglomerate Kering while Fendi has been absorbed by LVMH.With pressure mounting for a turnaround, especially if the company wants to remain in control, Saturday’s “Stravaganza Siciliana” show offered the brand two opportunities.The first was to remind its existing fans of its legacy rooted in Italian identity. The second was to outline its vision of the new gen Z customer it needs to attract to remain relevant and jump-start sales.A voiceover spoke of women rooting through the wardrobes of their mothers and grandmothers. “Women today do not look at it as though it were a museum,” read the script. “They try things on, layer and mix. Grandmother dresses granddaughter.”On the catwalk this translated into antique-inspired lace and crochet dresses and skirts styled with cropped tweed jackets and masses of jewellery. Less Sicilian widow, more upbeatragazza,denim was a particular focus, with low-slung jeans teamed with everything from baby D&G-emblazoned T-shirts to sheer pussybow blouses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe brand’s signature molto maximalist mood was also in full swing with beading and embellishment galore. One pair of jeans was smothered in dangling crucifixes and devotional medals. In place of buttons, jackets were fastened with euro-sized sparkling jewels.Elsewhere, leopard print appeared across both croc leather coats and miniskirts that the design duo described as rising “against decorum”. Stefano Gabbana, whostepped down as chairat the beginning of the year, took his bow in a leopard print shirt, next to his design partner of 41 years, Domenico Dolce, who wore all black. According to reports, Gabbana is weighing options for his share of the company, which amounts to almost 40%.Explore more on these topicsMilan fashion weekJennifer LopezDolce & GabbananewsShareReuse this content

title: 15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UK | Hotels | The Guardian
description: From a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxes
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: From a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxes
Content: The Copley Arms in Hessenford in Cornwall.Photograph: Mike DaveyView image in fullscreenThe Copley Arms in Hessenford in Cornwall.Photograph: Mike DaveyHotels15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UKFrom a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxesRhiannon BattenSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTShareThe TempusDoxford, NorthumberlandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zac+ZacFrom the chequerboard restaurant chairs to the disco ball-glittered bar and leopard print-cushioned bedrooms, this 41-bedroom hotel has more than a hint of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland about it. The 2026 winner of Visit England’s gold award for best small hotel, the Tempus recently opened eight wooden cabins overlooking the estate’s lake, and runsstargazing breaksin partnership with nearby Kielder Observatory. This month sees the launch of wellness experiences, combining gentle yoga and sound baths, while foraging workshops celebrate the estate’s wild bounty. Alnwick, Bamburgh and kipper-smoking Craster are close by.Doubles from £121B&B,thetempus.co.ukThe Old Bridge InnAviemore, the CairngormsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rupert ShanksYou can walk, cycle, swim or kayak straight from the door of this pub and bunkhouse on the banks of the River Spey in outdoorsy Aviemore. This mellow gastropub serves smoked haddock chowder and Caribbean lamb curry pies along with Cairngorm Brewery’s ales – and you’re likely to catch some live folk music too. Fresh from a recent revamp, its seven vintage-inspired bedrooms are decorated in autumnal shades of gold, green, rust and teal. Ranging from simple dorms to en suite doubles and family rooms, they come with access to a shared kitchen and dining room for DIY dinners and breakfasts.Family rooms forup to fivefrom £80room-only,oldbridgeinn.co.ukThe Black HorseAmberley, SussexView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsFood is the big draw at this new pub with rooms in the South Downs. Run by farm-to-fork restaurateurs the Gladwin brothers, the 12-bedroom inn is their first venture outside London, and their first with accommodation. One thing they are deeply familiar with is local producers – not least their own family. Beef comes from their farm, wines from their vineyard, Nutbourne, and some of the pub’s artwork has been painted by family matriarch Bridget. Stay over and you can wake to breakfasts of homemade brioche with just-laid eggs, farmhouse sausages or trout gravadlax. Stroll around the village, with itscastle hotelandpottery, orhikeover to Arundel then catch a train back to Amberley.Doubles from £125B&B,blackhorse-pub.comThe AbergwaunFishguard, PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPembrokeshire is home to spectacular beaches, but if an autumn storm blows in, it’s great to have galleries, cafes, pubs and cinemas where you can take cover. That’s where Fishguard comes in. This small harbour town has quietly blossomed over the last couple of years. The latest opening is the Abergwaun, a bistro with rooms launched in July by the folk behind the nearbyRed Onion cafe. Feast on locally line-caught seabass with kelp beurre blanc, then drift off to sleep in one of five smart, latte-coloured bedrooms. The next day, take in a pottery workshop atTŷ Clai, hike along thePembrokeshire coast pathfor a Sunday roast at theSailor’s Safety,or catch a gig atFfwrn.Doubles from £140B&B,theabergwaun.co.ukThe Lister ArmsMalham, Yorkshire DalesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jo Ritchie/The GuardianMalham is one of the Yorkshire Dales’ great hiking hubs, withMalham Tarn, the amphitheatrical cliffs ofMalham Cove, andJanet’s FossandGordale Scarwaterfalls within easy reach – and staying in the village became a little easier this summer with the opening of Lister Farmhouse. Its 13 bedrooms pair smart taupe, olive and blueberry fabrics with warm wood and leather. Part of the expanded Lister Arms, which includes rooms at theinn itselfand at a nearbybarn conversion, the new farmhouse bedrooms are two minutes’ walk away, beside sister pub theBuck Inn. For breakfast, stroll across a packhorse bridge to the pub.Doubles from £135B&B,listerarms.co.ukThe Great DecoyHurstbourne Tarrant, HampshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsFormerly the George & Dragon, when this Test valley pub with rooms opened in June, its name was changed to the Great Decoy in a nod to the area’s second world war history, when the surrounding countryside was used as part of a network of decoy sites to draw enemy bombers away from strategic targets. These days, a tempting mix of pub bangers (venisonsteak frites, wood-fired pizzas), plump-pillowed bedrooms and affordable rates is luring a more peaceful crowd. The pub is a low-beamed, candlelit haven and its eight bedrooms mix antiques with bright modern art and jauntily striped, scalloped headboards.Doubles from £90B&B,thegreatdecoy.co.ukThe Riverside InnRoss-on-Wye, HerefordshireView image in fullscreenIt was in Ross-on-Wye in the late 18th century that the artist and writer Rev William Gilpin set the blueprint for British tourism. Popularising the picturesque, he encouraged travellers to explore the local landscape for pleasure, helping to establish the idea of the British scenic escape (albeit infamously suggesting that “a mallet judiciously used” might improve the ruined charm of Tintern Abbey). More than two centuries later, five elegant new bedrooms have just opened at the Riverside Inn, giving modern-day visitors a suitably comfortable base from which to explore the area’s antiques and salvage shops, and stroll the leafy riverside pathways aroundSymonds Yat. Named afterCharlie Mackesycharacters, the rooms are decorated with finds fromBaileys Home Storeand other local businesses.Doubles from £180B&B,riversideinn-wyestreet.comThe William CecilStamford, LincolnshireView image in fullscreenOn the edge of the Burghley estate, along one of Stamford’s cute-as-a-bonnet Georgian streets, this treasured hotel underwent a major renovation two years ago. Named after Lord William Cecil, chief advisor to Elizabeth I, the 18th-century building is home to 26 bedrooms decorated in Bridgerton-meets-Babington chic, all chalky pink and sage green stripes, ginghams, velvets and chintz. The latest addition is Wild Floral, a botanical-inspired room launched this summer in collaboration with Lincolnshire designerSophie Allport. Head out to explore the copper-flecked parkland ofBurghley House, then return for pheasant kiev and blackberry tart at Milly’s, the in-house bistro.Doubles from £155B&B,thewilliamcecil.co.ukCorsham HouseCorsham, WiltshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsIt was no surprise that Corsham was chosen as a backdrop for the recent TV dramatisation of Jilly Cooper’s Rivals – the market town is a primetime destination. Wild peacocks roam its Georgian streets, a “secret” garden unwinds behind statelyCorsham Court– home to one of Wiltshire’s finest private art collections – and independent shops and cafes rule. In the centre of it all is Corsham House, a new brasserie and bottle shop with rooms that opened in July. Once a bank, it’s now profiting from the town’s “Bath in miniature” credentials, serving its signature Corsham chips with chicken salt alongside fat rump cap steaks, and putting guests up in 11 small but daintily designed bedrooms painted in shades of rose, damson and beech.Doubles from£111 room-only,corshamhouse.comThe Copley ArmsHessenford, CornwallView image in fullscreenJust off the A387, between Plymouth and Looe, this riverside pub with rooms is worth detouring off the beaten Cornish track for. Recently taken over by the couple behind Lydford’s award-winningCastle Inn, its 17th-century core has been elegantly refurbished. Fill up on fish tacos or the catch of the day, then head upstairs, or into the cottage just behind the inn, to slumber in one of eight earthily coloured, softly lit bedrooms (the cottage rooms are the quietest). The following morning, wake to a full Cornish before hiking a loop through the woods of theSeaton Valleyor strolling a section of theSouth West coast pathover to Looe.Doubles from £100B&B(two nights for £160from Sept-April),copleyarms.co.ukThe Swallow Falls InnBetws-y-Coed, Eryri (Snowdonia)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tinman PhotographyJust across the road from its namesake waterfall, this former coaching inn reopened last year after a major overhaul, offering visitors a comfortable and affordable base for exploringEryri national park. Its 38 bedrooms are painted in warm, muted shades and bookended by floral wallpapers, tongue-and-groove panelling and bright, metro-tiled bathrooms. Family rooms come with sturdy wooden bunk beds and, downstairs, you can order lasagne or sausage and mash in a space framed by fringed lampshades, floral curtains and mossy green paintwork. From the inn, you can follow a riverside trail into the village of Betws-y-Coed or soak up the autumn colours on one of the waymarked paths in the nearbyGwydir forest park.Doubles from £76B&B,inncollectiongroup.comThe CrownBildeston, SuffolkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lucy TomsEstate-to-plate dining is the cornerstone of this sunshine-hued Tudor inn between Bury St Edmunds and Ipswich. One of several Suffolk pubs and hotels owned by the Nedging Hall estate, who completed a sympathetic makeover this spring, it has 13 smartly understated new bedrooms. It’s fully plugged into the estate’s homegrown supply chain; the owners also operate a butchery, kitchen garden and East Anglia’s oldest brewery, Mauldons (for which they grow malt barley). Head out on a gentlethree-mile loop walk to neighbouring Chelsworth, then take a seat by the dining room’s open fire to feast on treacle-cured pork ribeye with garlic croquettes, and deliciously wibbly Basque cheesecake.Doubles from £195B&B,thebildestoncrown.comThe Customs HouseBowling, West DunbartonshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyA hop, skip and jump (or 30-minute train ride) north-west of Glasgow, this stylish new hotel sits at the western end of the Forth and Clyde canal. Well-placed for towpath walks and cycles, it’s a grand reimagining of what was built in 1790 as the customs house for Bowling harbour. There are seven tweed-hued bedrooms in the main building, each with a view of the water and each named after a different cargo, and a floating lodge suite was added this summer, along with a sauna and cold plunge. When the restaurant opens in a neighbouring building next year, it will operate as a full-service hotel but, for now, staff are only on site during the day; evening arrivals are self check-in and continental breakfasts self-serve.Doubles from £120B&B,thecustomshousebowling.co.ukLe Strange ArmsOld Hunstanton, NorfolkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Matt Keal PhotographyClose to theRSPB reserve at Snettishamand the nature reserve atHolme Dunes, this stretch of north Norfolk coastline is a prime destination for spotting waders and waterfowl as they stop to rest on their way south, and is similarly restorative for humans. Follow a day of beach walks and sky-gazing with dinner at newly renovated gastropub theAncient Mariner– menu highlights include Barsham’s beer-battered fish and chips, and cheeseboards ripe with local favourites Norfolk Dapple and Binham Blue – before walking across to sister hotel Le Strange Arms to sleep. Its more affordable standard rooms have yet to be updated, but recently renovated self-catering lodges and apartments put a modish mustard and navy spin on seaside chic.Doubles from £91room-only,lestrangearms.co.ukWild DuckEwen, the CotswoldsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Chris TerryOpen fires? A scene-stealing, carved wood bar? Plates of buttery chicken and chips? Double Diamond ale on tap? If you were Pinterest-boarding the fantasy Cotswolds pub after a yomp through the fields (or along the river – the Thames Path starts 10 minutes’ drive away), it would be something like the Wild Duck. Just south of Cirencester, this 16th-century gardeners’ cottage turned coaching inn has been stylishly overhauled by local hospitality luminaries Sam and Georgie Pearman. Reopened in March, it now has five bedrooms above the pub and 14 others in a new wing, each decorated with heritage wallpapers, Edward Bulmer paints, antique finds and custom-designed rugs.Doubles from £150B&B,countrycreatures.comPrices are for October-November and were correct at time ofpublication

title: Why do you close your eyes when you sneeze? The kids’ quiz | Family | The Guardian
description: Five multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes ​
Author: Molly Oldfield
Headline: Five multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes ​
Content: Illustration: Hennie Haworth/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Hennie Haworth/The GuardianThe kids' quizFamilyWhy do you close your eyes when you sneeze? The kids’ quizFive multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes​Submit a questionMolly OldfieldSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.Elsa, 9, asks: why do you close your eyes when you sneeze?It’s to stop germs getting into your eyesBecause your eyes will fall out if they’re openIt’s part of the motor responseWhen your nostrils open, then your eyes have to closeReveal2.Clementine, 11, asks: can spiders hear?No, they don’t have ears!Yes, despite not having ears, they can still hearThey can only hear very high-pitched soundsThey can only hear very low-pitched soundsReveal3.Lara, 8, asks: what is the most popular pasta shape in the UK?PenneMacaroniSpaghettiFusilliReveal4.Rei, 9, asks: why are flea markets called “flea” markets?It’s suspected to come from the Spanish: “mercado de pulgas”They were originally called “free” markets, because all the items were freeThe markets originally sold fleasIt’s suspected to come from the French: “marché aux puces”Reveal5.Orla, 11, asks: why do humans close their eyes to sleep?To keep our eyeballs safe from debrisTo stop our eyes from drying outTo block lightAll of the aboveRevealMolly OldfieldhostsEverything Under the Sun, a podcast answering children’s questions. title: Green shoots? Burnham cultivates rural links in attempt to ‘build back trust’ with farmers | Farming | The Guardian
description: Ministers have been speaking to farming activists to try to build bridges after tax changes introduced under Starmer soured relations
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Ministers have been speaking to farming activists to try to build bridges after tax changes introduced under Starmer soured relations
Content: Arable farmer Olly Harrison, who was contacted by Andy Burnham during the Makerfield byelection campaign.Photograph: Sent by himView image in fullscreenArable farmer Olly Harrison, who was contacted by Andy Burnham during the Makerfield byelection campaign.Photograph: Sent by himFarmingGreen shoots? Burnham cultivates rural links in attempt to ‘build back trust’ with farmersMinisters have been speaking to farming activists to try to build bridges after tax changes introduced under Starmer soured relationsHelena HortonSat 26 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an arable farmer, Olly Harrison’s WhatsApp messages are normally concerned with the more mundane matters of working the land: logistics, supplies and the occasional chat about the weather.So when a recent message came through fromAndy Burnham, it was more than a little unexpected.The personal touch wasn’t just the act of a politician on the campaign trail – Burnham was fighting the Makerfield byelection at the time – Harrison said it showed a change of approach to farmers.“He’s trying to meet farmers, he wants to meet up,” said Harrison, who farms near Liverpool.Under the Starmer administration farmers had been hit with new taxes, including a loathed inheritance tax. Harrison said the dialogue between the government and agricultural workers had been nonexistent.Now Burnham appears to have sown the seeds for a better relationship, telling farmers on a visit this summer that government had a “long way to go to build back trust” with farmers, and the UK needed to “guarantee our own food production”. Green shoots, perhaps.Harrison was one of a group of activist farmers who took umbrage at the 2024 budget. His fellow protesters, who included Jeremy Clarkson, rolled furiously into Westminster on tractors after the chancellor’s announcement to yell and beep at No 10 and the Treasury.View image in fullscreenJeremy Clarkson joins the farmers’ protest in central London over the changes to inheritance tax rules in the 2024 budget.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PATheir protests garnered crowds of tens of thousands, arguing the new taxes would lead to the closure of farms as the tax bill would significantly outstrip revenue.Since then the group become a thorn in the government’s side, following former environment secretary Steve Reed when he spoke at farming events in order to beep their tractor horns loud enough to drown him out.Burnham’s team appears to have weighed the benefits of keeping this noisy, tractor-driving community of dissenters on side and is actively working to repair the fractured relationship.It may already be yielding results, as there is no planned protest by farmers at this year’s budget. A bridge may have been built, but is by no means guaranteed to last.Last year, a record 6,300 forestry, fishing and farming businesses closed, according to the Office for National Statistics. This has been linked by some to the tax changes, though extreme weather and rising inflation have undoubtedly played a part.Former Labour cabinet minister Lord Blunkett recently said at a Countryside Alliance event: “It’s very strange because we’ve never won so many rural seats since 1945 – around 135 Labour MPs are either rural or semi-rural – and their voices need to be heard much more clearly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLord Blunkett speaking at a countryside campaigning event in central London earlier this month.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIt seems Burnham is trying to do this. The Mail on Sunday recently reported that a U-turn on the inheritance tax is on the table for the next budget. Government sources have confirmed to the Guardian that it is a possibility and that ministers are looking for a sweetener for farmers. This could be a reduction in inheritance tax, or more money for nature-friendly farming.One rural Labour MP said: “There are other things you could do for farmers that could be significantly better than changing inheritance tax again – new money for farming would be great and also meaningful progress on procuring public food from British farmers.”The farming budget that replaced EU subsidies has been a shambles. Earlier this week,thousands of farmers were left empty-handedwith the government’s £253m annual budget spent in just six hours.“I have had some very upset emails from farmers,” the MP said. “The current system creates an exclusionary aspect, for those who can afford a land agent to get the email in. We need a new system.”They added that Starmer froze out rural MPs who questioned his decision on inheritance tax: “Under Keir it wasn’t just farmers who felt shut out, it was rural MPs too. There has been a step-change since Andy came in with the relationship with backbenchers.”The new environment secretary,Angela Eagle, appointed by Burnham, has been on the road in recent weeks to visit farms and strike up a rapport with farmers.Martin Williams, one of Harrison’s fellow activists, farms arable crops on the banks of the River Wye in Herefordshire. Eagle came to visit him in recent weeks: “It is surprising what you can achieve if people actually speak to each other,” said Williams. Of Burnham, he added: “He is a savvy politician, he knows that you can’t throw away a whole contingency of voters. It was very difficult to get any meaningful dialogue with government but under the new regime it has changed quite markedly.”View image in fullscreenAngela Eagle arrives in Downing Street after being appointed as environment secretary by Andy Burnham in July.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesHarrison also had a visit from Eagle: “When Angela turned up it was just like I knew her. The Defra team said ‘she wants to know what’s going on and hear your opinion’, she brought policy advisers.”It helped that the Defra secretary is a nearby MP: “Angela only lives over the river from me, we didn’t disagree on anything.”Though Burnham and his team seem to have avoided a protest, they may have an uphill battle winning back the farming vote. A recentpoll from the Country Land and Business Associationfound that 0% of farmers would vote Labour again.Harrison said: “I’ve had a few comments saying don’t trust them, they haven’t got a vote left in the countryside, that is totally understandable. There are some farmers who are so angry still.”The government may have something left to fear from Jeremy Clarkson, who was recently spotted filming an episode of his popular Amazon show, Clarkson’s Farm, with David Cameron. The former prime minister issued a rare rebuke against the government, callingthe inheritance tax on farm assets “stupid”. Clarkson declined to comment when the Guardian asked if, like Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham would be banned from his Cotswolds pub.Explore more on these topicsFarmingAndy BurnhamAngela EagleRural affairsInheritance taxBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: France gave the Statue of Liberty. China sends pandas. What do diplomatic gifts mean – and how do you choose one? | World news | The Guardian
description: France’s offer to the American people was a point made on a colossal scale, and world leaders’ exchange of tokens remains a complex art
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: France’s offer to the American people was a point made on a colossal scale, and world leaders’ exchange of tokens remains a complex art
Content: The head of the Statue of Liberty on display in a park in Paris.Photograph: Hum Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe head of the Statue of Liberty on display in a park in Paris.Photograph: Hum Images/AlamyWorld newsFrance gave the Statue of Liberty. China sends pandas. What do diplomatic gifts mean – and how do you choose one?France’s offer to the American people was a point made on a colossal scale, and world leaders’ exchange of tokens remains a complex artKim WillsherSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was one of the most potent political gifts of modern times: the Statue of Liberty, a colossal neoclassical sculpture made inFranceand offered to the American people in the late 19th century.The size and symbolism of Liberty Enlightening the World (the statue’s original name) was intended as a mark of friendship to commemorate the centenary of the 1776 US declaration of independence. Delivered a decade late, it was also a reminder – perhaps a pointed one – of France’s critical role in helping the US break free from Britain.The Statue of Liberty is now one of the world’s most recognised monuments, its creator, Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, less so – a state of affairs Paris’s Musée d’Orsay is seeking to remedy with an exhibition highlighting the sculptor’s life and career.As with most diplomatic offerings, there was an element of self-interest behind the idea of making such a spectacular gift to the US at such a specific time. Over a chic dinner at Versailles in 1865, the liberal politician Édouard Laboulaye suggested the gesture celebrating American liberty might prompt France’s authoritarian ruler Napoleon III, whom he and Bartholdi opposed, to introduce greater liberté at home.Bartholdi agreed. The artist and sculptor, from Colmar in eastern France, was looking for a monumental project. In his 20s he had drawn up plans for a lighthouse in the form of a robed Egyptian woman bearing a torch to be placed at the entry to the Suez Canal, but it was deemed too expensive by Egypt’s ruler.Work, however, could not start until after Napoleon III was deposed in 1870.
