In 1884 residents around rue de Chazelles, in the north-west 17th arrondissement of Paris, would have been amazed to see the statue rise gradually from the workshop to tower above the area, before it was taken to pieces, put on a train to Rouen and then shipped to New York.View image in fullscreenThe Statue of Liberty, clad in scaffolding, rises above the streets of Paris in 1885.Photograph: Keystone-France/Gamma-Keystone/Getty ImagesThe Musée d’Orsay exhibition, which runs until 31 January 2027, features 100 works by Bartholdi and includes an immersive virtual reality journey showing the statue’s conception and construction to mark the 140th anniversary of its inauguration and the 250th anniversary of American independence.The exhibition curators, François Blanchetière and Juliette Chevée, stress that Bartholdi’s concept of liberty was not that of the French revolutionaries. “It is a freedom based on the law, not on violence. The venture is artistic but also political, media related, technical and above all international and diplomatic,” they said.Bartholdi and Laboulaye, who did not live to see the statue installed, hoped the Statue of Liberty would strengthen Franco-American friendship and ties. Bartholdi has been largely forgotten and the statue’s French connection often overlooked as it became a global symbol of freedom.In his 2022 book Diplomatic Gifts: A History in Fifty Presents, the career diplomat Paul Brummell, now Britain’s high commissioner to Mauritius, traced how offerings from the Trojan horse to the Statue of Liberty had been used as political, propaganda and diplomatic tools since ancient times.“Gifts these days are low-key,” he told theWashington Diplomat newspaper. “But looking back into history, diplomatic gifts went right to the heart of the thinking of the great kings. They didn’t hold back.”View image in fullscreenThe giant panda Hsing-Hsing (left) nuzzles Ling-Ling in their US enclosure.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveBut does gift diplomacy work?Chinafamously gave the US two giant pandas, Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing, after President Richard Nixon visited Beijing in 1972, leading to the phrase “panda diplomacy”. In return the US sent Beijing two musk oxen named Milton and Matilda. The arrival of the pandas at Washington’s Smithsonian National zoo attracted more than a million visitors in their first month, helping soften American public perceptions of China.It is a move Xi Jinping repeated this week, sending two pandas he called an “envoy of friendship” to Atlanta zoo. Trump gave Xi a sculpture of a bald eagle, the US national symbol.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump presents a statue of a bald eagle at a White House state dinner for Xi Jinping.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAIn totalitarianNorth Korea, the windowless International Friendship Exhibition, 90 miles north-east of the capital, Pyongyang, has 150 rooms of presents given to the former leaders Kim Il-sung, who died in 1994, and Kim Jong-il, who died in 2011.The eclectic collection includes an alligator holding a wooden tray of cocktail glasses with a matching ashtray from the Sandinistas of Nicaragua, a ZIS-110 armoured car from the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin, a basketball signed by Michael Jordan from the former US secretary of state Madeleine Albright, and a copy of Björk’s 2007 album Volta.It is a collection intended to convince North Koreans isolated from the outside world that their leaders have international support.Some diplomatic gifts have been hits, others misses. When the the then British prime minister, Gordon Brown, visited Washington in 2009, he gave Barack Obama an elaborate pen holder carved from the timbers of a Royal Navy anti-slavery ship. Obama’s gift to Brown was aDVD collection of the president’s favourite films.More problematically, a symbolic button given to Russia by the US secretary of state Hillary Clinton in 2009 to signal improved relations and stamped with the word “reset” in Russian instead read “overcharge” due to a translation error.Peter Ricketts, who spent 40 years in the diplomatic service and is a former British ambassador to France, said gifts between ministers were “a complete pain”.“Anything above a few pounds has to be declared and either handed in or bought out of your own pockets, so for politicians they can be a bit of an embarrassment,” Lord Ricketts said. “At state visit level it can be a little different. [But] it has to be clever and really stand out as something special to make any difference.”He said British royals had mastered the art of the carefully chosen gift and mentioned two that stood out as “really successful”.The first wasKing Charles presenting Donald Trump with the original brass bellfrom the second world war British submarine HMS Trump. “It was personal, historic, a lovely object and it was gold coloured – President Trump loved it,” said Ricketts.The second was Queen Elizabeth’s gift of a black labrador puppy to the French president Valéry Giscard d’Estaing during his 1976 state visit. “Giscard d’Estaing loved it and insisted on speaking to it in English all its life,” he added.Royals regularly receive gifts. Elizabeth II received a giant grasshopper-shaped wine cooler that turned into an occasional table from the French president Georges Pompidou in 1972. A tribe on Tanna, a remote island in the South Pacific, who revered Prince Philip as a living god – until his death in 2021 – sent the royal a grass penis sheath as worn by their rulers.In 1826, Muhammad Ali, the pasha of Egypt, sent the French king Charles X a female Masai giraffe called Zarafa, who lived in the Jardin des Plants for 18 years until her death in 1845. But a camel presented to the French president François Hollande during a 2013 visit to Mali was less fortunate; the animal was left for safekeeping with a family in Timbuktu but was promptly slaughtered and used in a tagine. Mali promised to replace it with a “bigger and better-looking camel”.View image in fullscreenCherry trees given by Japan still bloom in Washington DC.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockA few so-called soft-power presents have left a lasting legacy. In 1912, the Japanese capital Tokyo donated 3,020 cherry trees to the city of Washington DC. They still flower to this day. Since 1947, Oslo has sent London a tall Christmas tree every year in recognition of the city welcoming its exiled government when the country fell to the Nazis, and the Netherlands sends 20,000 tulip bulbs to Canada every year in gratitude for Ottawa sheltering its royal family during the second world war.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsDonald TrumpChinaFranceJapanNorwayKing Charles IIIfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering | Ecuador | The Guardian
description: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’
Content: US forces intercepted the Ecuadorian vessel Manta on 5 September before the vessel was destroyed.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, SouthView image in fullscreenUS forces intercepted the Ecuadorian vessel Manta on 5 September before the vessel was destroyed.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, SouthEcuadorUS strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not waveringAttorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’Tiago RogeroSouth America correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.View image in fullscreenEcuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September.Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/APOn 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters nearEcuador.“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.View image in fullscreenA US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.Photograph: US Southern Command/X“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.View image in fullscreenTen crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy.Photograph: Ecuadorian NavyUS Southern Commandpostedan edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the lateston 16 September– to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.‘We were terrified they were going to kill us’: fishers who survived US boat strike speak outRead moreView image in fullscreenA still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: US Southern Command @SouthcomAlso, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.Donald Trumphas compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.View image in fullscreenMarines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September.Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.Noboa has responded with acontroversial “iron-fist”approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.View image in fullscreenRelatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025.Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty ImagesThis crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has erodedhuman rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorisingjoint operationsand granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troopstaking part in raidslast Thursday.“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador forthe New Yorkermagazine.View image in fullscreenPeople look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged.Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province.Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created calledShield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is aserious contenderin October’s election.So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.View image in fullscreenFishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersIsacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four peoplewere killedin the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the USwould “stillblow up ships if need be”.Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes asextrajudicial killings,and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.Despite Trump’s claims,available datashow they have hadno impacton the volume of cocaine entering the country.Journalists and human rights groups have managed toidentify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.View image in fullscreenRelatives wait for 32 crew members to be released under precautionary measures in Manta, Ecuador, on 8 September 2026. The 24 crew members of the Maria Candelaria and eight from the Conquista II face judicial proceedings on suspicion of illicit association and fuel trafficking after their vessels were intercepted and destroyed by US forces in the Pacific Ocean.Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPAIn Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishershave been subjected to“violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted forlack of evidence.“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this yearremain unclaimed.The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vesselFiorella disappearedwith eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.Human rights organisations and journalists identifiedtwo more caseswith similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Postreportedthat the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.View image in fullscreenMaria Mero and her mother, Maria Cueva, speak during an interview after Mero’s husband Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado and brother Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva disappeared from the boat Fiorella after a strike in June 2026.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersView image in fullscreenMaria Cueva holding a picture of her son Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva.Photograph: Karen Toro/ReutersBoth the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.Explore more on these topicsEcuadorMarco RubioAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections | Brazil | The Guardian
description: President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday described fixed-odds betting as being ‘like a cancer’.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday described fixed-odds betting as being ‘like a cancer’.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesBrazilLula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian electionsPresident’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggestAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 03.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazilian president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the UN general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the coming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.Explore more on these topicsBrazilGamblingTravel & leisureAmericasFixed-odds betting terminalsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvanewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’ | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US
Content: Protesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenProtesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPAustralia newsAustralian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in USJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSat 26 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 18.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.View image in fullscreenProtest signs as Donald Trump speaks at the General Motors proving ground testing facility in Milford, Michigan, on 27 July.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.View image in fullscreenProtesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPThe pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns includinga 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a2 gigawatt gas-powered centrein the Northern Territory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power –has planned to override statesand ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsDatacentresProtestAI (artificial intelligence)Protest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Private colleges around Australia offering last-minute discounts for diploma allegedly ‘misused by shonks’ | Australian education | The Guardian
description: Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in country
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in country
Content: Ads posted to social media and shared among immigration education agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the graduate diploma of management (learning) or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenAds posted to social media and shared among immigration education agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the graduate diploma of management (learning) or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAAustralian educationPrivate colleges around Australia offering last-minute discounts for diploma allegedly ‘misused by shonks’Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in countryGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiSat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrivate colleges are offering discounts to rush students into a diploma the federal government is cancelling over concerns it is being “misused by shonks”.The government announced in early September it would deregister the graduate diploma of management (learning) which it suspected was being used by “non-genuine” students to remain in Australia. The course is taught by close to 450 institutions, has over 15,000 students studying currently and more than 40,000 students registered for future enrolment following completion of a different vocational course.Ads posted to social media and shared among agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the course or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October. Any students already enrolled and studying by that date are allowed to complete it.Australia unveils new rules to trim immigration, targeting backpackers, students’ families and visa overstayersRead moreSome immigration education agents have offered promotions for the month of September, including in WhatsApp messages and texts, encouraging students to join the course or those who have a future enrolment to study now. Several ads promote discounted course fees or a free certificate of enrolment to join immediately.One private college has sent immigration agents a promotion offering “attractive” commissions with same-day offer letters and confirmation of enrolment for students, with two “special intakes” on 21 September and 2 October – just three days before the course is cancelled.Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), supported the decision to cancel the course and said it could put some private providers trying to loophole the system into financial trouble.“The government for all the right reasons moved to stop non-genuine international students from using this course to stay in the country,” Honeywood said.“High-quality providers will always have a place in the international education ecosystem … they would rather have these factory-type private providers out of the system for all the right reasons.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailSome education migration providers are encouraging the more than 40,000 international students with a future enrolment to start the course now before it is cancelled. Some of those students would need to do so, or choose a different course such as a bachelor’s or master’s with a high qualification level to maintain their visa conditions. That could mean completing two courses at the same time.Students who have “packaged” a lower-level vocational course with the graduate diploma to be completed after, will need to enrol into a higher-level course to maintain their visa requirements.One student who spoke to Guardian Australia on the condition of anonymity said they had initially come to Australia to study a bachelor’s degree but unenrolled after one semester on the advice of a migration agent to do a VET course in carpentry, followed by the graduate diploma in management. The graduate diploma and the VET course would fulfil the qualification level required to maintain a valid international student visa.They said they were being told to commence the graduate diploma now.“I talked to the agent, and they told me the new rules. They want me to study concurrently, [so] I can study both courses at the same time. I don’t know if I can take this much study load,” the international student said.They said other friends doing the same course pathway were also given the same advice, and were also stressed by the potential workload.A migration agent, who asked not to be named, said they had heard of other agents and institutions pushing students to expedite their enrolment, but they warned the government would view this suspiciously. They said they were concerned that this behaviour would damage the reputation and credibility of the rest of the sector.They also said private institutions might look at setting up other courses such as the graduate diploma of strategic leadership that just over 34 colleges currently teach or the graduate diploma of portfolio management that is taught by just a few, that have the same visa requirement level.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJulian Hill, the assistant minister responsible for cancelling the course, said the department and education regulator would be “closely watching student and provider behaviour”.View image in fullscreenAssistant minister for citizenship andmulticultural affairs, Julian Hill.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP“Students and providers are on notice that curious patterns of early commencement or new enrolments will be investigated and action taken against those doing the wrong thing,” Hill told Guardian Australia.At the time of the announcement in September that the course would be deregistered, Hill said in a statement: “The Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks.”Melanie McFarlane, New South Wales president of theMigrationInstitute of Australia, said some education agents were helping their students into master’s courses to maintain their visas.“Those students needing to find an alternate course, they’re being placed by, I would say, reputable agents, into a master’s degree within the same institution where that graduate diploma was otherwise available,” she said.“But then you’ve got the other side where there are migration agents who are potentially going out of business because of all the changes to the industry … and might be rushing students into that course in the time that they can.”It is part of a wider crackdown by the government to curb visa-hopping and overstayers in Australia.The government has now banned international students from starting one qualification and then transferring to a lower-value qualification which would allow them to remain in the country and work more hours instead of studying. This would help prevent a student enrolled in a bachelor’s degree from downgrading to a vocational course.Hill said the government had also banned commissions for agents transferring students between courses in Australia.“This has helped but the quantum and pattern of transfers remains concerning, so from next year international students looking to change providers will have to apply for [a] new visa.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian educationAustralian immigration and asylumBusinessAustralian politicsMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly told to stop wearing keffiyeh at Sydney school sues for racial discrimination | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’
Content: Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School, is suing NSW for racial discrimination after allegedly being ordered to stop wearing a keffiyeh at the school.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenWasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School, is suing NSW for racial discrimination after allegedly being ordered to stop wearing a keffiyeh at the school.Photograph: The GuardianNew South WalesPalestinian careers adviser who was allegedly told to stop wearing keffiyeh at Sydney school sues for racial discriminationWasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdeshola OreCommunity affairs reporterSat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly directed to stop wearing a keffiyeh at a Sydney government school because it was a symbol that “may cause discord” has lodged a racial discrimination case in the federal court against the state ofNew South Wales.Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School – an inner-city selective government school – alleges the then acting principal told him in 2024 that the keffiyeh was seen as a symbol of conflict. He alleges the state’s conduct is unlawful for breaching the Racial Discrimination Act.El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh – a traditional scarflinked to the struggle for a Palestinian state for decades– at school in January 2024, three months after Hamas’ 7 October attacks and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza.His statement of claim, filed in the federal court last month, alleges Geoffrey Denyer, the then acting school principal, met with him on 15 May 2024 and said words to the effect of “I have been directed to direct you to remove this item of clothing”, indicating to El-Haj’skeffiyeh.View image in fullscreenWasim El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh to Sydney Girls High School in January 2024.Photograph: The GuardianDenyer also said words to the effect of the direction had come “from above, possibly from the minister” and that action would be taken if El-Haj did not comply, the statement of claim alleges.In an email sent the same day, after El-Haj requested the issue be laid out in writing, Denyer outlined the terms of the direction he had received.“Consistent with the Department’s Controversial Issues and Code of Conduct policies, the staff member in question should be given clear advice, from you, that this item of clothing should not be worn at school, nor in the performance of any duties in connection with his employment. That advice should be complied with immediately,” the email said.“It is understandable that, in such times as these, feelings and emotions are strong. However, our schools need to remain free of symbols which stir these emotions, and which may cause discord.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEl-Haj alleges that in a further conversation with Denyer he said words to the effect of “any symbol ofPalestineis seen as a symbol of conflict”.In August 2024, El-Haj met with Maria Serafim, a NSW Department of Education official, who detailed six anonymous concerns, including that he had worn a symbol of “partisan conflict” by wearing the keffiyeh, the statement of claim alleges.An internal complaint El-Haj made about the direction did not lead to its withdrawal. The careers advisor appealed the decision about the complaint to the secretary of the NSW Department of Education, Murat Dizdar.Responding to this, Dizdar upheld the school’s decision. In a letter to El-Haj in February 2025, he recognised the keffiyeh “is a garment of cultural significance for the Palestinian community” but said the department did not want to compromise the “safety, wellbeing and security in all our school communities”.View image in fullscreenWasim El-Haj says he was told words to the effect of ‘any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict’.Photograph: The Guardian“Unfortunately, our schools are not immune to external events, such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the tragic loss of innocent lives,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Regrettably, within our school communities, some individuals and groups may seek to politicise global conflicts or others may form that perception, and as such we always remain politically neutral in public schools when such events can impact on operations.“It is with this context that the senior officers and the school advised you to not wear the keffiyeh to school.”El-Haj took periods of leave from his employment during 2024 and resigned from Sydney Girls High School in March 2025.El-Haj alleges the state of NSW has engaged in unlawful conductunder section 9(1)of the Racial Discrimination Act.The state of NSW is yet to file its defence in the federal court.The matter is due to be next heard for a case management hearing on 3 November, federal court records show.A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education said it was “committed to maintaining neutral and apolitical school environments, in line with its policies.”Guardian Australia understands the department is not able to make further comments while the matter is before court.This story was amended on 27 September 2026. An earlier version stated El-Haj was on leave for seven months – he worked intermittently through those months.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesAustralian educationPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosion | Greece | The Guardian
description: Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’
Content: Emergency personnel search for survivors in the rubble of a building that partially collapsed following an explosion in the Plaka neighbourhood.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersView image in fullscreenEmergency personnel search for survivors in the rubble of a building that partially collapsed following an explosion in the Plaka neighbourhood.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersGreeceGreek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosionEmergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’Helena Smithin AthensSat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a two-storey apartment block in the heart of ancient Athens to collapse “in a matter of seconds”, killing six people.Emergency teams found the victims, including four American tourists, on Saturday, more than 24 hours after the early morning explosion in the historic Plaka district.The fire service said the bodies of three women and three men had been found, but stopped short of identifying them. A Briton and his Greek wife, 77 and 78, who lived in a flat on the building’s upper floor, were among those killed, the Guardian was told.“The bodies have been taken to the morgue where postmortems will be conducted,” the city’s vice-mayor, Paris Charlaftis, said in a telephone interview from the blast scene. “Our focus now is on the explosion’s cause. What could have happened to bring the building down in a matter of seconds?”Rescuers had deployed thermal cameras and geophones, used to detect deep subsonic frequencies, in the hope of finding survivors. Earth-moving machines and specially trained search dogs were brought in to move and comb mounds of rubble through the night.Before the bodies were pulled from the ruins on Saturday, police put the missing at six, saying four were Americans staying in a short-term rental on the building’s first floor. Two brothers and their wives, all four were due to fly to the US on Friday, just hours after the explosion.View image in fullscreenA rescuer searches the remains of the building.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty Images“When they failed to turn up for the flight they had checked into only a day earlier, that gave us a further lead,” a source said. “It became clearer that they must have been there when the blast occurred.”The Briton, a talented artist, who lived with his wife on the second floor, was described by Charlaftis as being partially disabled. “He had kinetic issues, and it was thought likely they, too, were in the building [at the time of the blast].”Nestled around the foot of the fifth-century BC Acropolis, Plaka is especially popular with tourists. The picturesque district draws thousands of visitors daily, with many staying overnight in the hotels and short-term rentals in neoclassical houses and small apartment blocks along its alleyways and narrow streets.The mayor of Athens, Haris Doukas, who rushed to 15 Lysikratous, where the mid-20th-century building had once stood, was quick to describe the incident as an “unprecedented disaster”.At least three people were known to have been injured when the explosion occurred at 7.30am, shattering the windows of nearby buildings and scattering debris far and wide. A motorist driving down Lysikratous described how his car was lifted into the air by the sheer force of a blast that some in the neighbourhood likened to an earthquake, others to a bomb. Emergency workers could be seen hastily removing two women on stretchers from a building next door who had been wounded by flying debris.Speculation is rife that a gas leak triggered the collapse but officials said there were many “cogent theories” at play. Fears of the leak emanating from the first-floor short-term rental was among them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs part of efforts to address a burgeoning housing crisis,Greece’s centre-right government has sought to ban short-term rentals in Plaka – clamping down on permits and tightening regulations.On Saturday, as speculation mounted over the cause of the blast, criticism grew over the ability to “properly control” establishments that were often unregulated.“This awful incident will fuel further debate over who inspects short-term rentals that no one who lives in Plaka wants anyway,” said Giorgos Zafeiriou, an architect who heads the local residents’ committee. “Hotels have chambers that regulate them but who inspects and controls Airbnb and serviced apartments that often may not be up to par?”Civil protection crews and emergency disaster management teams have been ordered to remain on site until the cause of the explosion is found, officials said.“It was a huge explosion, so getting to the bottom of it must now be the priority,” added Zafeiriou. “Six people have lost their lives.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Content: Pope Leo waves to the crowd from his popemobile on the Champs-Élysées before celebrating mass in Paris.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo waves to the crowd from his popemobile on the Champs-Élysées before celebrating mass in Paris.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersFrancePope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in ParisCrowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 yearsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit toFrance.The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.View image in fullscreenWorshippers gather at the Place de la Concorde for Pope Leo’s open-air mass.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesBut cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promoteCatholicismand its teachings.It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.View image in fullscreenPope Leo greets crowds lining the Champs-Élysées on the second day of his visit to France.Photograph: Kiran Ridley/AFP/Getty ImagesThe security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.View image in fullscreenPope Leo delivered an outdoor mass to an estimated 700,000 people in Paris.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesAbout 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”Explore more on these topicsFrancePope Leo XIVEuropeThe papacyCatholicismChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests | Heart attack | The Guardian
description: New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices
Content: Every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of surviving a cardiac event by 10%.Photograph: Photographer, Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEvery minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of surviving a cardiac event by 10%.Photograph: Photographer, Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty ImagesHeart attackDrones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggestsNew research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devicesNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment –every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil,France.Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion ofAEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes.The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Swedenand has saved lives.In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.More than 16m at risk of death by cardiac arrest in England and Wales due to ‘defibrillator deserts’Read more“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsHeart attackHealthHospitalsDrones (non-military)FranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: British climber, 28, dies in fall in northern Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Mountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa range
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa range
Content: The Picos de Europa mountain range in northern Spain is popular with walkers and climbers.Photograph: Iñigo Fdz de Pinedo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Picos de Europa mountain range in northern Spain is popular with walkers and climbers.Photograph: Iñigo Fdz de Pinedo/Getty ImagesSpainBritish climber, 28, dies in fall in northern SpainMountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa rangePress AssociationFri 25 Sep 2026 22.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British man has died after falling about 61 metres (200ft) while descending from the summit of a mountain in northernSpain, according to local law enforcement.The 28-year-old mountaineer fell down a vertical gully on the east side of the Torrecerredo – the highest peak of the Cantabrian mountains – on Thursday afternoon, the Spanish Civil Guard for the Asturias region said.The mountaineer’s remains were located after a rescue team aboard a helicopter flew over the area, the Civil Guard said.Two specialists were lowered to retrieve the man’s body and his belongings which had been scattered during the fall.The incident occurred during the descent, about 20 metres below the Torrecerredo peak, the Civil Guard said.The mountaineer’s body was transported to La Morgal, a regional sports and aviation facility in Llanera near the Asturian city of Gijon.A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said it had contacted local authorities about the death.Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,649 metres, is the highest peak of the Picos de Europa mountain range, which is part of the larger Cantabrian Mountains range.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
Content: People walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersMiddle East and north AfricaTrump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of HormuzUS president is said to expect renewed strikes after midtermsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS presidentDonald Trumphas said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.The US president was earlier said to be privately scepticalIranwould meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.Meanwhile, on Friday evening, hepublisheda post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.During a three-hour meeting at theUN general assemblyin New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”View image in fullscreenIran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, left, with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, at the UN general assembly in New York on Friday.Photograph: Caitlin Ochs/ReutersIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midtermsRead moreThe US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersSince then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and APExplore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaIranUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpUS foreign policyStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing
Content: The Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankUN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against PalestiniansIsrael ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoingAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 07.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupiedWest Bank.The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update.The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements.It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially.“This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement.Israelsaid it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.”The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply.The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny.Earlier this month,Britain banned trade with Israeli settlementsin the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action.Explore more on these topicsWest BankUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaHuman rightsPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us | Global development | The Guardian
description: Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear
Author: Tess McClure
Headline: Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear
Content: Alaa Hessi amid the rubble of her home, destroyed by an Israeli strike that also killed her three children. Since being interviewed, Alaa has given birth to a boy she named Waseem, after one of her sons who died.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlaa Hessi amid the rubble of her home, destroyed by an Israeli strike that also killed her three children. Since being interviewed, Alaa has given birth to a boy she named Waseem, after one of her sons who died.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal developmentWe followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell usBehind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hearSupported byAbout this contentTess McClureSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTShareWhat does it take to make a morning cup of tea inGaza?ForAlaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.For12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, whenaid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.View image in fullscreenRamadan on the beach at Al-Nuwairi, near Nuseirat, where he lives in a tent among the dunes.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianMost of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.Read more from the seriesThere is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, decidinghow many caloriesit will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans aplethora of ordinary objectsfrom entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.View image in fullscreenRajab al-Reefi, leader of Gaza Skate Team, helps other team-members to repair some boards.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianFrom the story ofRajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food.
