He has attended national championship games and regular season contests in the SEC and Army v Navy.He alsoattended Game 3 of the NBA finalsbetween the New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs in June, went to the 2025 Daytona 500 car race, and presented the World Cup trophy to Spain at the final in July. And last year, he was the first president to attend a Super Bowl. He left the Super Bowl after half-time.Headset communications emerged as the latest subplot surrounding this presidential visit. Coaches communicate with each other on their headsets throughout the game and also call in plays to the quarterback. Disruptions to those communications, from a deafening crowd, technical glitch or presidential security measure, can present problems for coaches and teams.Coaches involved in last season’s College Football Playoff championship between Miami and Indiana in New Orleans cited that game as an example of how Trump’s movements affected them.View image in fullscreenUS president Donald Trump looks at a laptop held by his executive assistant Natalie Harp alongside Tennessee senator Bill Hagerty during the Tennessee-Texas game at Neyland Stadium.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersTrump left in the fourth quarter of a tense Indiana 27-21 victory. Sarkisian said Miami coach Mario Cristobal told him Trump’s leaving at that point disrupted communications on the Hurricanes’ final possession, which ended with a game-clinching interception.Indiana coach Curt Cignetti disputed Sarkisian’s version of events around the final drive. But Cignetti noted communications briefly cut off in a key moment of the fourth quarter as Indiana was trying to protect their lead.In his weekly radio show on Thursday, Cignetti recalled that when Trump left the game “around the seven-minute mark ... there were two or three plays we couldn’t hear at all.”That included a misdirection touchdown run by Miami’s Malachi Toney.“Communication device came back right after the [Toney’s] touchdown,” Cignetti said. “And we had no problem the rest of the game.”According to the media pool report of Trump’s movements at the game, the president left the stadium with “with just under 8 minutes left in the 4th quarter”.View image in fullscreenFans pack Neyland Stadium during Tennessee’s game against Texas as US president Donald Trump attends the SEC matchup in Knoxville.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APThe White House on Friday insisted Trump’s departure caused no problems for the teams.“No, President Trump’s departure from the CFP championship in January did not cause headset or comms issues for the teams,” the White House posted on X.It’s unclear if Trump’s presence at other games like the Super Bowl have created issues. An NFL spokesman declined comment Friday when asked if league officials work with the Secret Service when a president attends a game like the Super Bowl to minimize any impact on team communications.University of Tennessee officials sent a midweek advisory encouraging fans to arrive “significantly earlier” than for a typical game. Neyland Stadium has an official capacity of 101,915 with this game the 30th consecutive sellout.Fans were warned of the Secret Service conducting enhanced screening at the stadium gates and to “expect increased wait times as kickoff approaches”.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballDonald TrumpCollege sportsUS sportsTennesseeShareReuse this content

title: Japan schoolboy, 11, wins gold while empty seats blight Asian Games | esports | The Guardian
description: Japan’s Yuki Kurihara becomes one of the Asian Games’ youngest champions as organisers lament empty seats in Aichi-Nagoya
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Japan’s Yuki Kurihara becomes one of the Asian Games’ youngest champions as organisers lament empty seats in Aichi-Nagoya
Content: Japan’s Yuki Kurihara celebrates with his gold medal after winning the Puyo Puyo Champions esports final at the Asian Games in Nagoya.Photograph: Dita Alangkara/APView image in fullscreenJapan’s Yuki Kurihara celebrates with his gold medal after winning the Puyo Puyo Champions esports final at the Asian Games in Nagoya.Photograph: Dita Alangkara/APesportsJapan schoolboy, 11, wins gold while empty seats blight Asian GamesYuki Kurihara storms to Puyo Puyo title aged 11Organizers ‘not satisfied’ with sluggish ticket salesWeightlifting world records continue to tumbleAgenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEel-loving schoolboy Yuki Kurihara, 11, won an Asian Games gold medal in Japan on Saturday, more weightlifting world records were set and organizers admitted they were “not satisfied” with ticket sales after swaths of empty seats were seen at the athletics.Kurihara, believed to be the youngest competitor at the Games in Aichi-Nagoya, romped to a 10-2 victory in theesportsgame Puyo Puyo Champions after going 1-0 down in the final.Thirteen-year-old swim sensation sets women’s 200m butterfly record at Asian GamesRead more“To be completely honest, I felt a bit embarrassed, so I couldn’t really show my expressions or change my face much,” Kurihara said after blowing away a series of opponents, some three times his age.Kurihara, who says he eats eel to prepare for contests, bowed slightly as he received his gold medal and gave a small wave.“I’m really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy,” he said.Asian Games organizers admitted ticket sales for some sports had been slow after the main athletics stadium saw a sparse crowd for the second night running.The Games said fewer than 60% of tickets had been snapped up for eight sports, including football, as well as the showpiece closing ceremony.“We are not satisfied,” Satoshi Murate, secretary-general of the Games organizing committee, said in response to a question from AFP about spectator numbers.Some tickets given to sponsors and other stakeholders had not been used, he said.View image in fullscreenJapan’s Yuki Kurihara competes against South Korea’s Kang Dong-shin during the Puyo Puyo Champions esports final at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday.Photograph: Dita Alangkara/AP“Seats have been allocated but some people can’t come. As a result, some competitions do have noticeable empty seats, and we find that regrettable.”The Games also apologized for transport and accommodation mix-ups that left some athletes stranded for hours.“Whatever the cause, [the organizing committee] is responsible for providing the service and I sincerely apologize for the mistakes,” Murate said.Six more world records were set in weightlifting, taking the Games total to 15 in four days, as North Korea’s Ri Won Ju won the men’s 70kg for his country’s fifth gold in eight events so far.Japan’s Masanori Miyamoto set a new snatch mark of 154kg but had to settle for silver when Ri lifted a world-record 198kg in the clean and jerk for a 349kg total, also a new record.In the men’s 75kg, Indonesia’s Rahmat Erawan Abdullah won a second consecutive Asian Games gold after setting world records in the clean and jerk (206kg) and total (366kg).Abdullah won Olympic bronze in Tokyo and Asian Games gold in Hangzhou three years ago, both at 73kg.North Korea’s Ri Chong Song also won gold in Hangzhou, but at the heavier 81kg bodyweight, and he began Saturday by setting a world record in the snatch of 162kg.But he failed with his final two lifts in the clean and jerk and was relegated to bronze with a 357kg total, behind Thailand’s Olympic silver medalist Weeraphon Wichuma, who finished on 365kg.View image in fullscreenMedalists Kang Dong-shin of South Korea, silver, Yuki Kurihara of Japan, gold, and bronze medalists Kuo Tzu-ang of Taiwan and Tanarak Wongkitikun of Thailand celebrate after the Puyo Puyo Champions esports final at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday.Photograph: Dita Alangkara/APBahrain’s Salwa Naser set an Asian Games record on a rain-sodden athletics track as she won the women’s 400m gold by a wide margin.Naser clocked 49.20sec, more than three seconds clear of Iran’s Zahra Zarei Manoujan (53.38). India’s Prachi Choudary completed the podium.In the men’s 400m, Thailand’s Joshua Atkinson’s late dip gave him gold in a thrilling finish as he edged the UAE’s Sulaiman Abdulrahman.Atkinson clocked 44.90sec, nine-hundredths of a second ahead of Abdulrahman, with Japan’s Joseph Nakajima taking bronze.Bahrain’s Nelly Korir broke the Asian Games record to win the women’s 1,500m in 4:04.50.In the women’s marathon, Bahrain’s Shitaye Habte finally won an Asian Games gold, 16 years after taking silver in the 10,000m at the Guangzhou Games.The mother of three held off Ciren Cuomu of China and Japan’s Mikuni Yada to cross the line in 2:27.31.“Maybe it is the time to stop,” Habte said.“I am 36 years old. But my target for my last competition is the [2027] world championships.“I have three babies and my second, he said, ‘Mama, don’t run.’ He wants me at home. But now he will be very happy.”Japan were beaten 75-70 in the women’s basketball, breaking the hearts of the home fans packed into the 17,000-capacity Aichi International Arena in Nagoya.A second Games competitor also failed a doping test, the International Testing Agency said.Dayanch Keletliyev of Turkmenistan returned a positive test for the prohibited substance meldonium in an out-of-competition test on September 20.He lost in the karate kumite round of 32 the next day.Explore more on these topicsesportsShareReuse this content

title: WNBA 2026 playoff predictions: can the dynastic Aces – or anybody – deny the dominant Lynx? | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Our writers pick the champion, key players and dark horses as the WNBA postseason tips off on Sunday
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: Our writers pick the champion, key players and dark horses as the WNBA postseason tips off on Sunday
Content: Minnesota Lynx players Dorka Juhasz, Maya Caldwell, Napheesa Collier and Olivia Miles look on during an August game against the Golden State Valkyries at Chase Center in San Francisco.Photograph: Noah Graham/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMinnesota Lynx players Dorka Juhasz, Maya Caldwell, Napheesa Collier and Olivia Miles look on during an August game against the Golden State Valkyries at Chase Center in San Francisco.Photograph: Noah Graham/NBAE/Getty ImagesWNBAWNBA 2026 playoff predictions: can the dynastic Aces – or anybody – deny the dominant Lynx?Our writers pick the champion, key players and dark horses as the WNBA postseason tips off on SundayElla Brockway,Bryan Armen Graham,Stephanie KaloiandAndrew LawrenceSat 26 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow will we remember the WNBA’s 30th season?At least big-picture, asthe end of one era of the league and the beginning of another, in part because of Cathy Engelbert’sannouncementearlier this month that she will step down as commissioner at the end of this year. It’s fair to say this season has been a microcosm of her up-and-down seven-year tenure: more growth than ever, excellent basketball, breakthroughs for a new generation of stars, and high highs, but also low lows – refereeing controversies and manufactured culture-war hysterics chief among them.EBUnfortunately, for thetransgender panicthatswallowed much of the conversationaround it. Never mind there has never been a trans woman – a person assigned male at birth who transitions to align with their gender identity – on a WNBA roster. The hypothetical eligibility question became a months-long culture-war spectacle, diverting attention from what should have been a celebration of the league’s expansion and extraordinary competitive depth.BAGThere’s been plenty of talk about the WNBA’s growth in recent years, usually measured in viewers and dollars. This season brought the growing pains that come with greater visibility, asoutside narrativeschallenged the league’s progressive, player-first identity. But amid those tensions, theWNBAalso welcomed two new teams, brought thousands of new fans into the fold and, most importantly, produced perhaps the deepest and best basketball the league has seen.SKAs the year offair play, culture wars and expansionthat preceded the genuine mainstream breakout. It also becomes notable, in retrospect, for how muchA’ja Wilson’s greatnesswas overlooked amid the Sturm und Drang.ALTeam that will be missed the most in the playoffsI’ll go with theToronto Tempo,mainly because I wanted to see Playoff Marina Mabrey. She was one of the league’s most exciting players through the first half of the year, and her record-tying53-point gameon 25 June will go down as one of the season’s highlights. Unfortunately, it was also Toronto’s peak: they were hampered by injuries, including to Mabrey, and they went 2-23 from that game onward, so they were never a realistic contender.EBA year after reaching the WNBA finals, thePhoenix Mercurycollapsed to 16-28 and missed the playoffs entirely. That means no Alyssa Thomas, one of the league’s dynamic talents and the engine of last year’s runners-up.BAGI may be biased because I live there and cover them often, but it would have been really fun for thePortland Fireto have the chance to inject their signature relentlessness into the playoffs. It’s also pretty startling to realize the postseason will be played without the Phoenix Mercury on the floor.SKAt a glance, theSeattle Stormhaving their worst season since their first season after making the playoffs in seven of the last eight years, with a pair of championships, would seem like reason to hit the panic button. But Sonia Raman and her young team – not least Flau’jae Johnson and Awa Fam, two of their top contributors as rookies – just need time to mature.ALView image in fullscreenA’ja Wilson and the Las Vegas Aces have won three of the past four WNBA championships.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesHigh seed at risk of going out earlyLas Vegas Aces.Indiana’s Aliyah Boston knows how to play against A’ja Wilson. (If she’s healthy - Boston had a flare-up of a leg injury in the Fever’s regular-season finale.) The Aces are just 11-10 against playoff teams this season and haven’t beaten a playoff team without NaLyssa Smith, who is out with a season-ending leg injury. This matchup of the league’s top two scoring offenses could go either way.EBLas Vegas Aces.A strange pick for a dynasty thathas won three of the past four titles, but Indiana may be the most dangerous No 6 seed imaginable. The Fever boast the WNBA’s highest-scoring offense behind Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark, while the Aces enter without injured starting forward NaLyssa Smith.BAG‘It’s payback time’: the WNBA-leading Lynx are on the hunt for title redemptionRead moreLas Vegas Aces.I am pretty sure I am going against my own standing rule (never count the Aces out), but the Fever are going to come out of the gate hungry and hoping to avenge last year’s second-round loss. It is difficult to imagine Las Vegas losing in the first round, but stranger things have certainly happened.SKMinnesota Lynx.I mean, they enter the playoffs on their patchiest streak, having lost four of their last six games – including three straight (although they did intentionally rest their starters down the stretch while jockeying for a more favorable first-round matchup). That said, it would still be a genuine surprise if Minnesota wound up one-and-done after the stunning season they’ve had.ALLong shot to winWashington Mystics.In ourpreseason predictions, I picked the Mystics as my surprise contender and wisely said they would “keep the league’s heavy hitters on their toes”. They followed through! The Young Hos – a nickname coined by top-five draft pick Lauren Betts, properly cheeky for the league’s youngest roster – enter these playoffs having won seven of their final eight regular season games, including four in a row to close out things this month. Their matchup with the Atlanta Dream could be the best of the first round.EBNew York Liberty.An eighth seed with Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu and Jonquel Jones is a spicy meatball. The Liberty went 13-6 down the stretch and boast one of the league’s best offenses since the All-Star break. A first-round date with the Lynx is a brutal draw, but in a best-of-three series one bad day at the office could leave mighty Minnesota immediately facing a road elimination game.BAGWashington Mystics.If we’re talking about an unexpected win – say, crashing the second round – why not Washington? They’ve been one of my favorite stories of the season, brushing aside everyone’s low expectations and having a hell of a time while winning. The Mystics have played the Dream tough all season, and I can absolutely see them springing a first-round upset. If we’re talking a true long shot to win the whole thing, though, give me the Fever – although that obviously hinges on the above.SKDallas Wings.What a difference a year and a coaching change makes for the Wings. There’s a lot to like about Paige Bueckers and Arike Ogunbowale in the clutch. If they really get rolling, watch out.ALskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost important player this postseasonOlivia Miles, Minnesota.With her, the Lynx are the obvious front-runners for their first WNBA title since 2017. Without her, the road gets tougher. Before she sat out the final two games of the regular season with a calf injury, Minnesota had played just two games without her. They won one and lost the other. They made it through much of the season without a 100%-Napheesa Collier, but surviving without a 100%-or-close-to-it Miles would be a much more difficult task.EBKelsey Mitchell, Indiana.Clark draws most of the attention (for better or worse), but Mitchell enters the playoffs as Indiana’s most important player. She averaged 25 points and put together a WNBA-record run of 27 consecutive 20-point games. Against a Las Vegas team forged from championship steel, Indiana may need Mitchell’s shot-making to keep the league’s most prolific offense humming when the stakes rise.BAGOlivia Miles, Minnesota.If she’s healthy and ready to go – or even if she isn’t – I’m saying Miles. Without her, the Lynx will be forced to figure out scenarios they haven’t really had to face most of the season; with her, they will be very difficult to stop.SKOlivia Miles, Minnesota.Every defense Minnesota face will be stepping up its efforts to shut her down. But if she can keep the Lynx offense firing and Napheesa Collier, Natasha Howard and Kayla McBride involved, the sky’s the limit – and I’m not talking about that miserable outfit in Chicago.ALView image in fullscreenThe sixth-seeded Indiana Fever could give defending champions Las Vegas all they can handle in the first round.Photograph: Jess Rapfogel/Getty ImagesPlayoff semi-finalistsLynx v Mystics, Valkyries v AcesEBLynx v Mystics, Wings v AcesBAGLynx v Dream, Valkyries v AcesSKLynx v Dream, Valkyries v AcesALThe champions will be ...Golden State Valkyries.I’m going to be contrarian and pick the second-year Valkyries. They’re not entering the playoffs on the strongest run of form, but Gabby Williams looked stronger in the season finale and they still have the league’s best defense. If they can round back into the kind of form they were showing this summer - they won 10 of their 12 games in August before sputtering after the Fiba break - they could pull off a run. If my preseason prediction of WNBA All-Star Veronica Burton couldn’t come true, then I will settle for WNBA champion Veronica Burton.EBMinnesota Lynx.They were the league’s pace-setters for basically the entire regular season and rank in the top four at both ends despite Collier missing half the year. Olivia Miles has transformed the backcourt, while Kayla McBride, Courtney Williams and Natasha Howard supply ample playoff experience. It’s high time for four-time WNBA champion Cheryl Reeve, one of basketball’s finest coaches, to get one for the thumb.BAGMinnesota Lynx.It’s their year. The Lynx haven’t won a championship since 2016 and are, frankly, overdue – but they’re also more ready than they’ve been the last few years to win it all. Cheryl Reeve is so good at her job it’s almost easy to overlook what how extraordinary this season has been for the team, while Olivia Miles is clearly on the path to greatness. A championship in her rookie season? Pretty great.SKMinnesota Lynx.They always had the defense. But Miles’s offense and general unstoppability puts Minnesota back on top after Maya Moore’s sudden retirement hastened the end of their 2010s reign. Now the only question is whether they can keep this crew together, Collier specifically, to start another dynastic run.ALExplore more on these topicsWNBABasketballLas Vegas AcesIndiana FeverGolden State ValkyriesMinnesota LynxAtlanta DreamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has attempted to dismiss the club’s guilty verdict as ‘noise’
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has attempted to dismiss the club’s guilty verdict as ‘noise’
Content: The Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has maintained the club’s defiant tone after they were found guilty on almost all counts of breaching the league’s financial regulations.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenThe Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has maintained the club’s defiant tone after they were found guilty on almost all counts of breaching the league’s financial regulations.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityManchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict‘We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed’Maresca quotes Socrates on social media – ‘I know nothing’Jamie JacksonSat 26 Sep 2026 10.52 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKhaldoon al-Mubarak, the Manchester City chair, has spoken for the first time since the club wasfound guilty on virtually all countsof breaching Premier League financial rules. He said “nothing has changed” and “our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began”.News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by thePremier Leaguein February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.How drawn-out saga of Manchester City’s alleged cheating came to thisRead moreThe club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when al-Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of theManchester Cityfamily. Thank you, as always, for your constant support.”View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak (right) has been Manchester City’s chair since the Abu Dhabi takeover of the club from Thaksin Shinawatra (left) in 2008.Photograph: Nigel Roddis/ReutersEarlier, City’s manager,Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”.On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence. The Guardian was sent by his representatives a screenshot of a quote attributed to Socrates, the Greek philosopher, which Maresca posted on Instagram.The quote reads: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Maresca also wrote: “Time to breathe. Time to analyse. Time to learn.”Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?Read moreElsewhere, there wwere contrasting reactions to the outcome of the Premier League investigation. Oasis’Noel Gallagher, a longtime City fan, described his shock at the news, while the club’s former chair David Bernstein believes any potential punishment should not be only financial. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, described the case as unsettling.On the Let Me Talk podcast, Gallagher said: “A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really just quite sad. Sad for the fans and for the players.”View image in fullscreenNoel Gallagher, a longtime Manchester City fan, maintains that even if the guilty verdict stands, the club’s fans will not feel any differently about their success.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesAsked if it changes the context of moments like Sergio Agüero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher said: “Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw.“Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch. Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans.“Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.”Bernstein, City’s chair from 1998-2003, told Times Radio: “I felt absolutely awful, I felt in shock yesterday. You’ve asked me on the programme because of my time as chair of City and the FA, but basically I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rightsRead more“When I was chair I think I helped get the club out of a very difficult period and started the road to better things. But to see all this tarnished in this way is very sad.“I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who’ve stayed with the club through thick and thin. It’s a pretty bad day for the fans in blue of Manchester.”As for the correct punishment, Bernstein said: “First of all, the timing is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process has to be done quickly because you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable.“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, that would be a disaster. Not just for this particular case, but for English football generally.“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”Manchester City guilty verdict ‘a historic decision’, says whistleblower Rui PintoRead moreOn BBC Radio 5 Live, Nandy said: “Most football fans will be feeling this is not a good moment for football as a whole and Manchester City fans will be feeling very anxious about what happens next. This is a really longstanding investigation, it dates all the way back to allegations that begin in 2009.“The football fans need to know the rules are applied fairly and consistently, they need to know they’re upheld and they need to know the right decision has been reached.“We do have a way to go with this, it’s very unsettling for football fans and I hope it can be resolved as swiftly as possible.”Nigel Huddleston, who was the shadow secretary of state for culture until last month, said on social media: “Whatever the next steps are, they must be conducted in an accelerated and more transparent manner or risk further damage to the reputation and integrity of English football and more unnecessary anxiety for millions of football fans.”A City spokesperson said on Friday: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.”In that statement, City said they had a ‘comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence’ of their innocence.Friday’s statement from City continued: “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaNoel GallagherPremier LeagueLisa NandynewsShareReuse this content

title: George Russell holds off Max Verstappen to win eventful F1 Azerbaijan GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: George Russell held off Max Verstappen by one-tenth of a second to win a crash-filled Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku and cut into Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: George Russell held off Max Verstappen by one-tenth of a second to win a crash-filled Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku and cut into Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead
Content: George Russell’s first win since Austria in June has kept him in the hunt for the Formula One driver’s championship.Photograph: Peter Fox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell’s first win since Austria in June has kept him in the hunt for the Formula One driver’s championship.Photograph: Peter Fox/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026George Russell holds off Max Verstappen to win eventful F1 Azerbaijan GPBriton leads from pole to claim third win of the seasonRussell closes gap on leader Kimi Antonelli, who rose from 16th to fifthGiles RichardsSat 26 Sep 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJaw set resolute on the podium,George Russellgave notice he is not quite ready to go gentle into that good night thanks to a commanding victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Saturday. With a lot of ground to make up, and not many races left to do it, the win was something of the shot in the arm he required to at least stay within touching distance of the Formula One title.Russell’s win from pole to flag in Baku ensured he took advantage of a meeting where his Mercedes teammate and the title leader,Kimi Antonelli, endured his worst weekend of the season.Norris says some drivers ‘shouldn’t be in F1’ after Colapinto shunt dents title hopesRead moreThat Antonelli made a strong comeback to claim fifth from 16th was impressive, but also indicative that the 20-year-old Italian had approached his task with one eye on the crown. Nonetheless, Russell could not be faulted in doing all he needed to, ensuring he clawed back 15 points and reducing the deficit to 66 points with eight races remaining.It was the culmination of a meeting where Russell had been on top throughout and virtually untouchable. From pole on Friday, then leading from the front of the field, he produced a drive that was all but flawless, including managing two tense safety car restarts and holding off being hounded to the line by a very quick Max Verstappen, his lead at the flag just one-tenth of a second.Put under pressure by the Dutchman climbing all over his gearbox in a tense final 10 laps after the second safety car, Russell held his nerve, a salutary reminder that his sketchy form this year belies his talent.He had not conceded the lead throughout, but very much earned the win by beating the charging Verstappen, who also produced a fine drive to take second from eighth on the gridHis Red Bull teammate, Isack Hadjar,was third in his first race after being out for six weeks with an injury.View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell crosses the line with Max Verstappen looming in his rear-view mirrors.Photograph: Andrej Isaković/Reuters. This was Russell’s first win at the Azerbaijan GP, his third of the year, and is exactly what he needed. It appears to vindicatehis intent to come backfrom the summer break and, as he noted, drive “instinctively” after difficulties with the car in the first half of the season. Certainly the confidence he showed in it in Baku paid off, his sense of calm vindication and pleasure at once more proving himself palpable afterwards.He has suffered poor luck this season, but has also struggled to adjust as well as Antonelli tothe new regulationsand the new cars, yet when he is on it he is implacable and almost untouchable. A repeat of this form and he may yet believe the gap to his teammate does not quite seem such a chasm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAzerbaijan Grand Prix: George Russell holds off Max Verstappen to win – as it happenedRead more“After the summer break I feel like I have gone from strength-to-strength and I feel more like myself and that’s a good thing,” he said. “Win every race, that’s the gameplan. My teammate has had an incredible season and now we’ve got to crunch time. I’ve got to focus on myself.”The result must also be considered a good return for Antonelli.Having made an error in qualifying, clipping the barrier early in the session, to come back to fifth was an impressive feat of damage limitation. It again demonstrated his impressive racecraft: this is the second time he has been tasked with coming back in a dominant car, having drivenfrom 19th to the win at Monza. With a longer lap and the field more spread out than in Italy, fifth here might be as high as he could have hoped for.View image in fullscreenLando Norris emerged unscathed, if angry, after being wiped out by Franco Colapinto.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APIt was also the considered and calculated drive of a campaigner with one eye on the championship. He kept out of trouble admirably, including showing lighting reactions when diving out of the way of the pile-up on the first safety car restart after Alpine’s Franco Colapinto hurtled into his teammate, Pierre Gasly, and in turn collected McLaren’s Lando Norris.That left the world champion furiousand his lingering hopes of a title defence in tatters.Antonelli had been somewhat out of sorts after losing track time to a mechanical problem in practice and making his mistake in qualifying, so he had, notably, tempered his usual hard-charging approach.“George had an incredible weekend, he had a lot of confidence. [But] this weekend was my worst of the year by far in terms of performance,” he said. “I wasn’t there, really present, especially with what happed so early on. Didn’t take the same risks especially after qualifying. Today was more damage-save mode instead of full-on attack.”He expects to come back stronger next weekend at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia, while Russell knows he has to take a new engine for which there will be a grid penalty to serve. For now, on the streets of Baku, he has reasserted himself with as comprehensive display of his skill as might be considered possible and given his teammate a timely reminder that he remains determined to take this title fight as deep as possible.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneGeorge RussellMotor sportMercedes GPKimi AntonellinewsShareReuse this content

title: I was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in me | Australian books | The Guardian
description: As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety
Content: Australian tennis player Evonne Goolagong competes at the Queen’s Club in London, circa 1970.Photograph: Aubrey Hart/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralian tennis player Evonne Goolagong competes at the Queen’s Club in London, circa 1970.Photograph: Aubrey Hart/Getty ImagesAustralian booksI was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in meAs a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivetyEvonne Goolagong CawleySat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a regular match. Until it wasn’t. In 1969, I was 17 and had been living inSydneywith my tennis coach, Vic Edwards, and his family for several years. I had left my home town of Barellan – on Wirajudjuri country in the Riverina region of New South Wales – to pursue my tennis dreams in the big smoke.The year before, I had finished high school at Willoughby girls high – where I was the only Aboriginal student – and I was doing my secretarial course in the city. The Metropolitan Business College where I studied was conveniently located near the headquarters of the Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs.Was Wrexham’s trailblazing black footballer also the first Indigenous Australian to play overseas?Read moreThe idea for the foundation was to give city-based Aboriginal people a cultural hub where we could come together and find support. I was spending more and more time there with my friends Isabel and Bob, the latter whom I was casually dating.Isabel and Bob were young and lots of fun but they were also acutely aware of the politics of being Black. I was naive to the injustices of Australia – and the world – and I learned a lot from Isabel and the guys at the foundation.At the time, I was focused on a single goal: to become the first Aboriginal tennis champion. To achieve that goal, I had to shut myself off from everything other than tennis. That included politics.View image in fullscreenEvonne Goolagong plays against America’s Chris Evert in the 1972 women’s singles at Wimbledon.Photograph: Roger Jackson/Getty ImagesI was training for my upcoming European tour, and part of program included playing doubles with Vic Edwards’ daughter, Trisha, at the White City badge competition twice a week. Trisha and I had been playing together for years and were quite the pair. We were the “tennis twins”, in our matching dresses, at tournaments.It was during our usual doubles game at White City against two older women that something happened. Trisha and I convincingly won against our opponents, and we went to the net to shake their hands. As we reached over the net, though, one of the ladies turned to her partner and said, “That’s the first time I’ve ever been beaten by a n*****r.”The N-word. I had never been called it before. I went into shock.The word took a moment to sink in. At first, I thought I had misheard. But then Trisha responded with a cutting comment and I knew it was real. Still, the moment felt far away, as though it was happening to someone else.double quotation markSomething had irrevocably changed within me. My naivety had been brokenEvonne Goolagong CawleyThe older women left and I remained at the net with Trisha. Suddenly, we were crying. We both stood in the centre of the court, hugging and sobbing. The word had wounded me like a paper cut, innocuous at first, then stinging. I’m not sure why that single word had such a dramatic effect on me. It wasn’t even an Australian slander. The N-word was a cheap, American slur that reminded me of fake soap-opera trash talk. But when it was directed at me, it felt very real. Was this the way it was going to be out there in the mean streets of tennis?Still sobbing, I called the first person I thought of: Isabel at the foundation. Through tears, I told her what happened. “You jump in a taxi and get here right now,” she said.When I arrived, I was greeted by Isabel and Bob. They held me and patted my back as I cried in their arms. Isabel said she had never seen me so upset. We sat around and drank cups of coffee for hours, talking it over. “It’s OK,” Bob told me, kindly. “These things happen to us all the time. You just have to deal with it, and you can. You’re strong.”Something had irrevocably changed within me. My naivety had been broken. The protective bubble my family and the Edwardses had built around me had been smashed. I would move on but I would never be the same innocent young girl.When I got back to the house hours later, Trisha had already relayed the events to Mr Edwards. I was glad to have missed his initial fury at the incident. Mr Edwards – who was quick to anger – was remarkably matter-of-fact. He had informed the NSW LawnTennisAssociation over the phone and was in the middle of writing an official complaint. “We have to deal with this in the proper manner, through the correct channels,” he said.I don’t know what happened as a result of the call or the complaint. But I never saw the woman at White City again.View image in fullscreenAfter that, I spent more and more time at the foundation. My friends there reminded me of my people but not in a way that made me homesick; instead, they gave me a sense of feeling good about being Aboriginal. Proud – that was it! They made me feel proud to be Aboriginal.When I went on to win my first Wimbledon singles tournament two years later in 1971 – becoming the first Aboriginal woman to claim the title – the win was for all Aboriginal people.I like to think I was doing my part in my own way – by breaking new ground, taking up space and inspiring the next generation of hopeful Aboriginal athletes.I hope I have paved the way for our young ones, and that the road is a lot smoother these days.This is an edited extract fromOnly Ever Evonneby Evonne Goolagong Cawley with Alley Pascoe (Allen and Unwin), out 29 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsAustralian booksTennisRaceIndigenous AustraliansAustralia sportSydneyAutobiography and memoirextractsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Tebow pauses ties with Christian wealth group amid predatory sales allegations | Tim Tebow | The Guardian
description: Former Heisman Trophy winner says he was ‘caught off guard’ by investigation into Christian group accused of pressuring followers into costly financial courses
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Former Heisman Trophy winner says he was ‘caught off guard’ by investigation into Christian group accused of pressuring followers into costly financial courses
Content: Former NFL quarterback Tim Tebow attends the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field At Mile High last Sunday.Photograph: Justin Edmonds/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFormer NFL quarterback Tim Tebow attends the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field At Mile High last Sunday.Photograph: Justin Edmonds/Getty ImagesTim TebowTim Tebow pauses ties with Christian wealth group amid predatory sales allegationsFormer Heisman winner pauses ties with Life SurgeTebow calls allegations ‘extremely serious’Group accused of pushing courses costing $40,000AgenciesSat 26 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTim Tebow said Friday he is “pausing his relationship” with Life Surge, a Christian organization that’sbeen accused of using predatory sales tacticsto exploit its followers’ faith and financial insecurity.Tebow, the 2007 Heisman Trophy winner who is currently a college football analyst with ESPN’s SEC Nation, said his team is conducting an internal investigation. He spoke on campus in advance of the Mississippi-Florida game at Florida Field on Saturday.“The allegations are extremely, extremely serious, and it’s something that we take very serious,” Tebow said. “So, for us, we’re having our team do an investigation, but also pausing our relationship ‘til we can learn more about the facts to be able to understand more.”Why are members of the Super Bowl champion Eagles promoting a right-wing Christian wealth scheme?Read moreTebow said he was “caught off guard” by the Pablo Torre Finds Out podcast that focused partly on Tebow’s speaking engagements with Life Surge.“I was at an anti-human trafficking conference [Thursday], and my team shared [it] with me when we were leaving as we were flying to Alabama for the event, and kind of caught off guard with some of it,” Tebow said. “I think that’s why I’m really trying to understand more of the facts to really learn it.”His message to his loyal followers amid the allegations:“It’s really important to get answers to understand every bit of that,” he said. “My heart ... was to be able to share something that I love to share, which is the love of Christ and the good news of the gospel. And so I think it’s really important that we can really understand all the facts and details of it.”The podcast’s investigation raised questions about Tebow’s knowledge of the organization’s practices.Life Surge, which hosts around 30 events annually, typically brings in Christian celebrities like Tebow to headline events. At Life Surge’s one-day events, attendees are urged to sign up for impact classes that pitch packages ranging from $10,000 to $40,000, according to the podcast.If attendees can’t afford the price tag, Life Surge reportedly connects them with third-party lenders who encourage them to apply for credit cards or take out home-equity loans, according to the podcast.Life Surge has denied any wrongdoing, according to the podcast.Explore more on these topicsTim TebowCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty miss | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane missed a penalty at 2-1 to England and then Spain recovered with goals from Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal as the world champions won 3-2
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Harry Kane missed a penalty at 2-1 to England and then Spain recovered with goals from Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal as the world champions won 3-2
Content: Mikel Oyarzabal calmly chips James Trafford to make it 3-2 to Spain at Wembley.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenMikel Oyarzabal calmly chips James Trafford to make it 3-2 to Spain at Wembley.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANations LeagueOyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty missDavid Hytnerat WembleySat 26 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was another high-profile game when Thomas Tuchel’sEnglandlet a lead slip in the second half and went on to lose. But unlike the last time, it was not one for recriminations. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust. More to the point, they can accept losing to Spain who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.England were game. They were driven by Jude Bellingham, who ran on adrenaline and played to the point of maximum expression. They had positive surges either side of the interval, especially the one towards the end of the first half when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them in charge, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.Thomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdictRead moreThe biggest takeaway was Spain’s slickness. There is a reason why they won the World Cup in the summer. Why they won the European Championship before that. They are the best team in the international game by a distance. Nobody can live with them. England did well to stay within a puncher’s chance of a result in thisNations Leagueopener; Bellingham was still throwing them in stoppage time. Crucially, as Tuchel and England try to look forward after the heartbreak of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina, there was no negativity from the Wembley crowd. Even in the face of England’s defending, which was dreadfully loose.We were denied the chance to see how the fans would react to the announcement of Tuchel’s name when the teams were read out in the countdown to kick-off. Because, after going through the starting XI and the 12 substitutes, Tuchel’s name was not read out. But there were none of the dreaded boos at the full-time whistle.The match turned on a Kane penalty miss in the 54th minute. Had the captain scored rather than hitting the crossbar after his standing foot gave way in the turf, England would have been 3-1 up. Shortly afterwards, they were pegged back to 2-2 by theSpainsubstitute Álex Baena and there was a degree of inevitability about the winner from another replacement. Mikel Oyarzabal’s dinked finish was impudently brilliant. Spain had been fantastic for the opening 30 minutes and when they went again after the Kane penalty, they had too much. It was a statement of intent from them, an illustration of their remorseless desire.“Campeones” was the chant from the enclosure housing the travelling fans before kick-off and it is fair to say the visiting radio commentators were excited about seeing Spain for the first time since the second star was stitched on to their shirt. Their fervour went up a few notches in the early running when Lamine Yamal opened the scoring.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s left foot gives away as he takes the penalty. He hit the crossbar and the ball bounced out to safety.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe goal was a personal disaster for Marc Guéhi; it was almost as if the Manchester City defender had other things on his mind. It was of a piece with England’s struggles against the Spanish press. Guéhi was facing upfield as he tried to build a move from deep but his passing lanes were blocked. So he checked back and walked straight into Lamine Yamal, who robbed him and was clean through. He made the finish past James Trafford look easy.Tuchel had started Trafford ahead of Jordan Pickford, a major deviation from his stated intention for continuity from the World Cup. Pickford was erratic in the summer and was punished for some of his mistakes. Trafford has been outstanding for Leeds since joining them over the summer. Tuchel’s idea is to share the minutes between Trafford and Pickford during this window. Trafford could hear the knock of opportunity and he helped to keep England in the game as Spain pushed to add to Lamine Yamal’s goal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeet the new 55 minute England collapse, not the same as the old 55 minute England collapse | Barney RonayRead moreHow Spain pushed. They shimmered with menace. It was the movements, the speed of them – plus the breathtaking assurance on the ball. They had so many options in possession that it felt at times as if they had more men on the pitch.Ferran Torres had the ball in the net only to be pulled back for offside while Trafford stood up to make a big one-on-one block against the Spain striker after Lamine Yamal had played the through-ball. England’s backline was all over the place. Torres blew another one-on-one on 28 minutes, with Trafford making himself big while Dani Olmo rifled just wide after a sumptuous Lamine Yamal flick.England tried to throw counterpunches as they hung on. The resistance was impressive. Gordon was to the fore and so was Bellingham. They showed their personality when the chips were down. When the two combined for an equaliser that had not really been advertised, it was the prompt for a wild turnaround.It was Spain pushing only for Nico Williams to lose his footing and then the ball to Elliot Anderson. England swept forward in thrilling style, Gordon flicking to Bellingham, getting it back and surging in on goal. The low finish was nerveless.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane (on the ground) watches his header come off the thigh of Marc Cucurella to make it it 2-1 to England.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnter Kane. He was unlucky when he banged inches wide from the edge of the area after a Bukayo Saka burst. He was lucky when his header from a Nico O’Reilly cross, which Unai Simón looked to have covered, drew a panicked reaction from Marc Cucurella. The left-back jutted out his thigh to turn the ball past his goalkeeper. The fates were against Cucurella. When his mishit cross on 45 minutes sailed over Trafford, the ball came back off the far post.Bellingham appeared particularly determined to leave his imprint. The Real Madrid midfielder was in the mood for bragging rights back in La Liga. It was the power and directness of his running; the smoothness of it, the quickness of his moves. Spain could not contain him. It was his persistence after yet another surge that led to the penalty.Gordon played the pass back inside from the left and Bellingham got there before Rodri, who invited trouble when he hung out a leg. Down went Bellingham and after a review, it was decided that the contact trumped the feeling that the England player had tried to engineer it. Kane could not convert.Back came Spain. Lamine Yamal pushed a shot wide after a give and go with Baena, whose backheel was beautiful. Then Baena equalised after O’Reilly gave away the ball and Olmo quickly shifted it to the edge of the area. Baena bought himself the space for the shot with an expert drop of the shoulder.Saka curled just wide at the other end after more good work by Bellingham but the tide had turned. You could not take your eyes off Lamine Yamal while Luis de la Fuente’s attack-minded changes worked. It was Oyarzabal who made the difference from a Baena pass. England could have no complaints.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueEnglandSpainmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Republic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’ | Nations League | The Guardian
description: The Republic of Ireland’s Nations League fixtures with Israel will go ahead after a ‘significant majority’ of players voted in favour
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The Republic of Ireland’s Nations League fixtures with Israel will go ahead after a ‘significant majority’ of players voted in favour
Content: Gavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad to play Israel.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad to play Israel.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesNations LeagueRepublic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’Bolton goalkeeper issues statement after withdrawalIreland players will wear black armbands in matchPaul MacInnesin DebrecenSat 26 Sep 2026 16.18 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRepublic of Irelandwill fulfil their fixture against Israel in Hungary on Sunday night, but only after lengthy deliberations between the players resulted in a “significant majority” voting to play. The Bolton goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, however, will not be involved, after pulling out in protest.After a week in which the Irish team and officials have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott the match due to Israel’s military actions in Gaza, training was delayed by five hours on Saturday while the squad discussed whether to go ahead.“This morning, a player expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad,” said the FAI’s chief David Courell, referring to Bazunu.Israel’s match with Republic of Ireland will be an eerie occasion as political debate rages onRead more“What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive. Ultimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.”Courell said the squad had also agreed a number of measures to signal their unease with the fixture taking place. Players are to wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” he said, adding that there will be “elements of the pre-match ceremony” that will “not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland” players, namely the pre-match handshake and exchange of pennants.Bazunu, writing on Instagram, said: “Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people.“However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.View image in fullscreenThe Republic of Ireland head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson (left), and the FAI CEO, David Courell, confer during the delayed press conference.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty Images“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.“There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.”The Republic’s head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, meanwhile, said “nobody is comfortable playing these games for many reasons” as he was once again put under pressure over remarks in which hedescribed his team as “playing against genocide”earlier this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHallgrímsson said he had used a “strong” word and now regretted it. “It was a wrong word for me to use,” he said, arguing that he had meant to say that “by playing we are not accepting what is happening”. If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrímsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.”The leadership of the Israel team used their press conference to read a statement congratulating Ireland on their decision to play. “What we have seen today is that football has won,” it read. “The separation between football and politics must continue. Anything else spells chaos and creates consequences for the game we love. The Irish took the right decision in agreeing to this. Even if it took longer than it should, it was welcome.”Israeli officials said they would engage in all of the pre-match formalities with the head coach Ran Ben-Shimon confirming: “I will shake hands with Hallgrímsson.”The Israel FA will also appeal both yellow cards awarded to Saied Abu Farchi during Thursday’s defeat to Austria. Farchi was given a second yellow after he celebrated scoring an equaliser by uprooting the corner flag, an action interpreted by officials as mimicking the firing of a rifle.Israel dispute this interpretation. “Anyone familiar with him knows it was an imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty,” their spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueRepublic of IrelandIsraelUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in Slovenia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Scotland were held to a goalless Nations League draw by Slovenia in Sébastien Pocognoli’s first match since taking over from Steve Clarke
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Scotland were held to a goalless Nations League draw by Slovenia in Sébastien Pocognoli’s first match since taking over from Steve Clarke
Content: Oli McBurnie (second left) goes close for Scotland.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenOli McBurnie (second left) goes close for Scotland.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PANations LeaguePocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in SloveniaEwan Murrayat the Stadion StoziceSat 26 Sep 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSébastien Pocognoli grimaced on Friday when recalling his debut as an international player for Belgium. Alessandro del Piero and Italy discovered favourable opposition when preparing for the 2006 World Cup. Pocognoli will also look back, in time, at his first game as the manager ofScotland.Blue skies, a dainty stadium in Ljubljana and a second-half display that provided glimpses of optimism in respect of Scotland’s world, post-Steve Clarke. The best-forgotten first 45 minutes can be explained away by a squad operating under a new regime. By full time,Sloveniawere grateful for their point. Scotland’s players took deserved applause.Slovenia 0-0 Scotland: Nations League – liveRead moreScotland’s failing here was a familiar one.A lack of goals haunted Clarke. Nonetheless, this version of Scotland did at least create a series of openings. Scott McTominay, a key attacking threat, was missing. Instilling ruthlessness in a team is no easy task; it is one, however, Pocognoli has the coaching credentials to meet. Slovenia, on this evidence, have the more significant challenges.“The feeling in the dressing room is positive because of the second half,” said Pocognoli. “We should have scored but I am very happy with the general performance of the strikers. It was only the last details we missed.” His demeanour was upbeat.Ninety-four days had passed sinceScotland’s loss to Brazilall but confirmed World Cup elimination. When that meek exit was certain,Clarke announced his resignation. Players and supporters alike seem caught between being highly grateful to Clarke for materially altering Scotland’s fortunes and heralding regime change.In Slovenia, Pocognoli sampled international management for the first time at the age of 39. Slovenia failed to reach the World Cup, with the rows of empty seats telling the story of a country that is not at all convinced by its footballing outlook. The absence of Benjamin Sesko did nothing to help a shot-shy side.Ireland players vote to go ahead with Israel matches despite ‘different views’Read moreScotland could hardly bemoan poor preparation. Pocognoli had whipped his squad and mini-army of backroom staff to La Manga in the buildup to thisNations Leaguegame. With a sense of revolution in the air, the head coach unleashed a hitherto unseen front two: Robbie Ure was making his international debut while Oli McBurnie returned after years in the wilderness. The opening half only proved there is little point deploying multiple strikers if there is no adequate means of supplying them.Scotland were awful in that first period. The football was passive and directionless. Players looked well-enough drilled off the ball, but descended into a state of panic when in possession. Slovenia, who were little better than ordinary, should have seized upon these shortcomings. To his credit, whatever message Pocognoli forcefully pressed home during the break had an effect.View image in fullscreenSébastien Pocognoli barks instructions during his first game in charge of Scotland.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAAndraz Sporar had the ball in the net for the hosts in the eighth minute only for an offside flag to go up. Sporar subsequently missed a golden opportunity from six yards after fine work from Danijel Sturm. As Aljosa Matko shanked wide of Angus Gunn’s goal, the Tartan Army’s groans were audible.Save a Ure shot from 20 yards that clipped the outside of a post, Scotland were nonexistent as an attacking force. An overhit Billy Gilmour pass that flew out of play when intended for the marauding Andy Robertson rather summed things up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcBurnie should have marked his Scotland return with a goal within five minutes of the restart. He opted to try to jink around Jan Oblak rather than slam a shot past the goalkeeper. Oblak morphed into Inspector Gadget, stretching out his arms while grounded to pinch the ball from McBurnie’s feet.This triggered Scottish improvement; Gilmour forced a save after a one-two with McBurnie. Aaron Hickey could not quite divert a John McGinn corner on target. Oblak had to be sharp to deny the Scotland substitute Kieron Bowie before doing likewise to McBurnie from the resultant corner.Second-half Scotland involved a huge upturn. McBurnie said he would not be able to sleep due to his profligacy. Seventeen Scotland caps are yet to yield a goal.Bowie’s miss, 12 minutes from time, was in the category of howler. Gilmour, increasingly influential as Scotland dominated, had fed his teammate. Pocognoli was emboldened, sending on Ben Gannon-Doak to replace Hickey. In old money, that represented a winger for a full-back.Scotland huffed, puffed, pushed and wheezed. Slovenia stood firm. Pocognoli nodded with approval as the whistle blew. Next up, a Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueSloveniaScotlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content
