title: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: When things are going awry, Argentina will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause after Lionel Messi’s farewell against Benin
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: When things are going awry, Argentina will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause after Lionel Messi’s farewell against Benin
Content: Lionel Messi, despite his obvious limitations, was as influential as ever at the World Cup.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APView image in fullscreenLionel Messi, despite his obvious limitations, was as influential as ever at the World Cup.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/APInside footballLionel MessiMessi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superheroJonathan WilsonWhen things are going awry, theAlbicelestewill no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clauseSat 26 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTShareIt isn’t quite over yet.Lionel Messiwill return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.Lionel Messi in his 30s was one of the best international players ever | Jeff RueterRead moreThen Messi retired,distraught after a missing a penaltyin the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry willArgentinabe able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.The best example came almost at the end, when Argentinatrailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.View image in fullscreenLionel Messi cries at the end of the World Cup final after Argentina’s loss to Spain.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APOther than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still canRead moreWith Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiInside footballArgentinacommentShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated? | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: We analyse what City must do to appeal, why even that might not be the end of the legal wrangling, and the potential penalties if the verdict is upheld
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: We analyse what City must do to appeal, why even that might not be the end of the legal wrangling, and the potential penalties if the verdict is upheld
Content: There could be a long way to go before we know if the sun truly has set on Manchester City’s era of Premier League dominance.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThere could be a long way to go before we know if the sun truly has set on Manchester City’s era of Premier League dominance.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianManchester CityAnalysisManchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?Paul MacInnesWe analyse what City must do to appeal, why even that might not be the end of the legal wrangling, and the potential penalties if the verdict is upheldSat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTShareWhat happens next?Manchester Cityhave been found guiltyof the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League.In keeping with the history of this case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for thePremier Leagueare correct.Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 chargesRead moreIf these assumptions are accurate, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for isnews of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown.If City do appeal, what happens?The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined. In hoping to make the case that the judicial panel were wrong in their observations, City would be allowed to submit new evidence, providing it had not been previously available to them, and make new oral presentations. Once the hearing is concluded, a verdict would be expected in 30 days.If an appeal fails, what then?According toPremier League rule W.97, “the decision of an Appeal Board shall be final”, but even this is subject to one final route, that of arbitration. This would mean appearing in front of another panel of eminent legal figures, but the criteria for any hearing would be a lot stricter and successful arbitration only possible in the main if the judicial panel or appeal board was found to have abused the legal process. City have recently been through the arbitration process with the Premier League over its rules related to associated party transactions and, after an initial verdict challenged two applications of the rules but otherwise found them to be sound,City and the Premier League reached a settlementwhich stopped the case from going to court.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen and how would City be punished?If City managed to overturn the verdict, there would of course be no sanction. If City’s appeals failed, there are a number of measures available to the panel. They start at fines and end at complete expulsion from the league, with a variety of sporting sanctions including point deductions falling in between. Given the magnitude of the verdict, City can expect to receive a punishmentat the sharper endof the scale should any appeal not prove successful.Could relegation be the end of it?It seems unlikely. Premier League clubs and those who have been relegated from the division are understood to have been assessing any financial losses they may have incurred during the period City were winning and, appeal pending, breaking the rules. A wave of lawsuits is likely to follow, with Manchester United, for example, having finished second behind City in 2017-18 and potentially denied a record-breaking 21st league title in the process. It is possible that clubs who were relegated could argue that they were sent down because of points denied them by a City side subsequently found to have cheated. Premier League clubs reportedly lost their appetite for legal action after an estimated £50m cost to the competition last season, but if the verdict against City revealed this week is ultimately upheld, a new wave of lawsuits will surely follow.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancesFinancial fair playFootball politicsBusinessanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdict   | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel denied that Manchester City being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules was a distraction for the club’s England representatives during their defeat to Spain
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Thomas Tuchel denied that Manchester City being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules was a distraction for the club’s England representatives during their defeat to Spain
Content: England’s Marc Guehi reacts after his mistake gave Spain an early lead at Wembley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEngland’s Marc Guehi reacts after his mistake gave Spain an early lead at Wembley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnglandThomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdictTuchel says England ‘will learn’ from 3-2 loss to SpainCity’s Nico O’Reilly and Marc Guehi at fault in defeatJacob Steinbergat WembleySat 26 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel denied that Manchester City beingfound guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rulesis a distraction for the club’s England representatives after Nico O’Reilly and Marc Guéhi made costly errors during the3-2 defeat by Spain.News that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges against them broke on Friday afternoon, dragging the attention away from England’s preparations for theirNations Leaguegame against the world champions at Wembley a day later. It did not stop Tuchel from starting Guéhi, O’Reilly and Elliot Anderson against Spain but the topic was on the agenda after England’s first game since the World Cup ended in disappointment.Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty missRead moreAlthoughEnglandmet demands to play on the front foot after collapsing in their World Cup semi-final against Argentina they lived to regret Harry Kane missing a penalty when they led Spain 2-1 in the second half. But while defensive errors proved costly – Guéhi and O’Reilly gifted Spain two goals – Tuchel is confident that the storm encircling City is not an issue.“I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case,” England’s manager said. “I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking aboutSpain, and the team and meetings. Not for me. The players have more time than me so for sure I can imagine that they talk about it. It’s good that they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”Tuchel was not booed by the Wembley crowd and took the positives from a bright England display, but he was disappointed his team could not end Spain’s 39-match unbeaten run. “If we learn from it there are some positives to take from it,” the German said. “We will try to do a review tomorrow. We will highlight the positives. There is stuff we can do better.View image in fullscreenNico O’Reilly challenges Lamine Yamal during England’s defeat by Spain.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images“There is no sense in showing individual mistakes or saying please don’t do mistakes. There are things we can do better. We wanted to be the team to beat them. We think we had them. We think we had them at half-time. It is something to build on.”England went behind when Lamine Yamal punished an error from Guéhi. They led at half-time thanks to goals from Anthony Gordon and Kane, only for the captain’s missed penalty to prove a turning point. Spain displayed their technical class and showed their strength in depth by bringing on Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal to turn the game with two clinical strikes.“It was a bit of a missed chance,” Gordon said. “I thought it was a great game to watch and to play in, some of the attacking play was at the highest level. But I think in a game like that mistakes cost you. You always feel like it’s you’re giving it away rather than them winning it. They were as good as us and we were as good as them. I’m just gutted about the mistakes.“I don’t think there is a gap [to Spain] I feel like we’re right there. We can win that game so easily. If the penalty goes in we can go on and win the game.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel gives instructions to Jude Bellingham at Wembley.Photograph: Robin Jones/Getty ImagesTuchel felt it was a missed opportunity and he explained that his decision to leave Trent Alexander-Arnold on the bench was because of Jarell Quansah’s defensive prowess at right-back. “There was a lot of defending to do on the side,” he said. “We need to close the gap. We needed Jarell’s speed. Jarell did excellent in the week. Jarell did excellent in the World Cup. It’s not his shirt, he has to fight for it, but he came into this camp with a little advantage.”England are away at Czechia on Tuesday, visit Croatia next Saturday and host Czechia on 6 October before this camp ends. Tuchel picked James Trafford over Jordan Pickford and will give the Leeds goalkeeper another chance against Czechia.Explore more on these topicsEnglandSpainThomas TuchelNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Laver Cup back in the balance as Team World match their captain Andre Agassi’s energy | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Alex de Minaur recovered from match point down to beat Alexander Zverev, before Carlos Alcaraz launched a comeback of his own to leave the Laver Cup level at 5-5
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Alex de Minaur recovered from match point down to beat Alexander Zverev, before Carlos Alcaraz launched a comeback of his own to leave the Laver Cup level at 5-5
Content: Andre Agassi, Team World’s captain this Laver Cup, was a constant support to Alex de Minaur in his comeback win against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndre Agassi, Team World’s captain this Laver Cup, was a constant support to Alex de Minaur in his comeback win against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTennisLaver Cup back in the balance as Team World match their captain Andre Agassi’s energyAlex de Minaur recovers from match point down to beat Alexander ZverevCarlos Alcaraz launches comeback of his own to leave event level at 5-5Tumaini Carayolat the O2 ArenaSat 26 Sep 2026 18.29 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor much of his afternoon on court againstAlexander Zverev, Alex de Minaur seemed destined to end his day with an excruciating defeat. De Minaur had rapidly found himself down a set and a break, then Zverev served for the match at 6-2, 5-4. After miraculously giving himself another lifeline, De Minaur finally faced a match point at 8-9 in the final set tie-break.No matter how grim the scoreline appeared, though, every effort he made was punctuated by roars of approval from one person in particular. There were loud screams of encouragement, pounding of chairs and stamping of feet. At one point, as doubt had crept into Zverev’s game during the second set tie-break, that unmistakable voice from the sidelines yelled out: “Check his oil! Check his oil!”Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worthRead moreThose words came fromAndre Agassiand, with such unconditional support provided by one of the greatest tennis players of all time, his Team World captain, there was no way that De Minaur could lose. De Minaur’s probing soon revealed that Zverev had indeed run out of oil, his engine failing, as the Australian recovered from match point down to close out a 2-6, 7-6 (5), 11-9 win.Agassi’s unbridled enthusiasm and support was reflected in his team as they held their own on day two of the Laver Cup against a group of higher-ranked opponents.With Team Europe leading 3-1 overnight, Learner Tien of the US opened the day with a 6-3, 2-6, 10-7 win over the Italian Flavio Cobolli before De Minaur defeated Zverev, the recent French and US Open champion.While match win were worth just one point on Friday, they were worth two on Saturday. Team Europe closed the day with a narrow 7-5 lead over Team World.Carlos Alcarazlevelled the series by saving two match points to defeat Taylor Fritz 6-3, 4-6, 13-11 before Casper Ruud and Zverev teamed up to beat Alexander Bublik and Brandon Nakashima 6-4, 7-6 (7).View image in fullscreenTeam Europe were again indebted to Carlos Alcaraz, whose comeback win over Taylor Fritz helped them take a 7-5 Laver Cup lead.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty Images for Laver CupPerhaps the most interesting aspect of this week is simply the presence of Agassi as he continues his re-emergence on to the tennis scene. For some time after his retirement, Agassi and his even more legendary wife, the 22-time grand slam champion Steffi Graf, kept a low profile at home in Las Vegas.Their lore was often only really extended through the top young players, such as Fernando Verdasco, Sorana Cirstea and Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova, who would sometimes train with them at their home. They would return from Nevada speaking of how invaluable Agassi’s counsel had been to their careers or how Graf was still in such tremendous shape that she could easily slot back in on the WTA tour. Otherwise, they minded their own business.Things have drastically changed over the past 18 months, starting with the announcement last February that Agassi would replace John McEnroe as Team World’s captain. Since then, he has been everywhere. He joined TNT Sports in the US as a commentator at Roland Garros last year, then he worked on the BBC’s commentary team for the first time in the final days of this year’s Wimbledon . His employment decisions have been received far more positively than those of his old rival Pete Sampras, who emerged back into public view at the US Open as the face of the sport prediction market Kalshi. However, Agassi is currently managed by one of the more controversial figures in the sport, Justin Gimelstob.Agassi seems comfortable talking tactics with modern players who sometimes view the sport differently to their elders. It has been enjoyable to listen to how one of the greatest tennis minds expresses those thoughts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAgassi was full of inspiration and advice for Learner Tien, who went on to beat Flavio Cobolli.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/APOne of the most memorable narratives surrounding Agassi in retirement wasthe love-hate relationshiphe famously described himself as having with the sport in his autobiography, Open. For that reason, it has been particularly satisfying to witness the unbridled joy and love he carries for the sport now, so many years removed from the stress that accompanied being a top competitor.Agassi simply cannot sit still on the Team World bench. He is constantly cheering and encouraging his players, hell bent on keeping morale up, and his boundless energy provokes positive reactions from his players. As a delirious De Minaur celebrated his victory over Zverev, his first move was to sprint to Agassi while repeatedly shouting: “You like that? You like that?” Without hesitation, Agassi responded: “I love it. I love it.” Blood was rolling down De Minaur’s knee at the end of the match after he grazed his knee on a spectacular diving forehand. In his excitement, Agassi shouted: “I wanna lick that blood off you right now.”This strong rapport between Agassi and his players was also clear in certain sentimental moments. After Tien had closed out his victory and completed all of his post-match duties on the court, he and Agassi hovered by their bench for a long, sweet debrief. Tien was clearly still frustrated by his high unforced error count, so Agassi offered him some tactical advice for future matches.Once they had finished, Tien leaned down to pick up his bag, prompting a quick intervention from the all-time great: “Dude, I’ll carry this shit for you if you want me to,” he said. “That’s how much respect I have [for you].”Explore more on these topicsTennisAndre AgassiCarlos AlcarazAlexander ZverevAlex de MinaurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool rehire Julian Ward as sporting director to replace Richard Hughes | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as their sporting director for a second time after the departure of Richard Hughes to Al-Hilal
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as their sporting director for a second time after the departure of Richard Hughes to Al-Hilal
Content: Julian Ward, who was Liverpool’s sporting director for one season in 2022-23, has returned to the role after two years as technical director for owners FSG.Photograph: Liverpool FCView image in fullscreenJulian Ward, who was Liverpool’s sporting director for one season in 2022-23, has returned to the role after two years as technical director for owners FSG.Photograph: Liverpool FCLiverpoolLiverpool rehire Julian Ward as sporting director to replace Richard HughesClub’s owners FSG move swiftly to fill key postMove comes amid upheaval in Anfield hierarchyAndy HunterSat 26 Sep 2026 18.08 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 04.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool have appointed Julian Ward as their sporting director for a second time after thedeparture of Richard Hughesto Al-Hilal. Ward, who was Liverpool’s sporting director for the 2022-23 season, has spent the past two years as technical director for Fenway Sports Group, the club’s owners.The process of finding a successor to Hughes, who left for the Saudi Pro League after two and a half years at Anfield when the summer transfer window ended, was led by the FSG president, Mike Gordon.Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo reflects on ‘tough summer … in football and life’Read moreWard has worked in various capacities forLiverpoolover the past 14 years, including European scouting manager, assistant sporting director and sporting director.His appointment offers continuity at a time of upheaval in the Liverpool hierarchy with Hughes and Michael Edwards, the former chief executive of football at FSG, leaving this year and the owners in the process of sellinga 38% stake in the club to 1892 Holdingsfor £2bn. The consortium, fronted by Amit Bhatia and including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, has an option for a full takeover should FSG decide to sell up.View image in fullscreenJürgen Klopp signs a contract extension in April 2022 with FSG’s Michael Gordon (left) and Ward, then Liverpool’s assistant sporting director.Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesThe 45-year-old Ward replaced Edwards as sporting director in 2022, but told FSG he wished to step away for personal reasons a few months into the role. Luis Díaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Núñez were signed during his first spell although the manager at the time, Jürgen Klopp, had a greater say on transfers after Edwards left.Ward remained highly regarded by FSG, however, and Gordon, who had resumed the day-to-day running of Liverpool after Hughes’s departure, considers his extensive knowledge of the club and of squad planning as invaluable. As FSG’s technical director, Ward had oversight of the global talent strategy that has led Liverpool to sign several highly rated young prospects this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLiverpool’s new sporting director will lead the club’s football operation alongside the assistant sporting director, David Woodfine, the chief scout, Barry Hunter, FSG’s director of football development, Pedro Marques, and Andoni Iraola’s senior leadership team.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolFenway Sports GroupnewsShareReuse this content

title: England 2-3 Spain: Nations League football – as it happened | Nations League | The Guardian
description: England were 2-1 up when Harry Kane’s penalty hit the bar; the world champions made them pay
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: England were 2-1 up when Harry Kane’s penalty hit the bar; the world champions made them pay
Content: 4h ago17.12 EDTDavid HytnerIt was another high-profile game when Thomas Tuchel’sEnglandlet a lead slip in the second half and went on to lose.But unlike the last time, it was not one for recriminations. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust. More to the point, they can accept losing to Spain who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.England were game. They were driven by Jude Bellingham, who ran on adrenaline and played to the point of maximum expression. They had positive surges either side of the interval, especially the one towards the end of the first half when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them in charge, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty missRead moreThomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdictRead moreShareUpdated at18.55 EDT

title: Vollering pips Niewiadoma to seal dramatic road race world title | Cycling Road World Championships | The Guardian
description: The Tour de France Femmes champion, Demi Vollering, won the longest-ever edition of the women’s world road race championship in a brutal and compelling finale in Montreal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The Tour de France Femmes champion, Demi Vollering, won the longest-ever edition of the women’s world road race championship in a brutal and compelling finale in Montreal
Content: Demi Vollering sealed world road race glory in a brutal finale in Montreal.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering sealed world road race glory in a brutal finale in Montreal.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockCycling Road World ChampionshipsVollering pips Niewiadoma to seal dramatic road race world titleDemi Vollering powers to victory in brutal Montreal raceTour de France Femmes champion wins sprint finishJeremy WhittleSat 26 Sep 2026 14.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemi Vollering won the longest edition of the women’s world road race championship in a brutal and compelling sprint finale in Montreal.The 29-year-old’s success capped a remarkable season in which she has also won a second Tour de France title, the Giro women, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Tour of Flanders.Evenepoel targets historic sweep as opportunity knocks without PogacarRead moreIn what proved to be an enthralling race, the biggest names in the women’s peloton duelled their way over the multiple climbs on the Canadian circuit, before the Dutch rider applied the coup de grace in the closing metres.“It was an amazing race and I was very proud to be part of it,” Vollering said. “I worked so hard towards this goal and it takes guts to truly believe. I’m so proud of everybody from the team. They rode the whole race from the front.”Eight laps of a 13.4km circuit, which included the steep gradients of the Voie Camillien-Houde, took their toll on a diminished peloton, which lost favourite Paula Blasi when the Spaniard abandoned after crashing for a second time.Defending champion and home favourite, Magdeleine Vallieres was another of a group of 15 riders to crash while speeding downhill, with 95km to race, along with Great Britain’s Flora Perkins and Tour of Britain winner, Kim Le Court.A battered and bruised Vallieres finally abandoned with a little over 60km to race. Her departure opened the door to a volatile and intriguing race that showcased the drama and unpredictability of women’s racing.The resulting ebb and flow saw numerous changes in the lead until the three leading riders in this year’s Tour de France Femmes – Vollering, Kasia Niewiadoma, of Poland, and Italian national champion, Elisa Longo Borghini – traded blows on the final lap en route to the uphill sprint finish.With less than 200m to go, Vollering and Niewiadoma were side by side, but the Dutch rider’s acceleration proved too much for her rival, who crossed the line apparently suffering from cramp.Vollering’s initial attack, which came with 40km of racing remaining on the steepest section of road had almost backfired when she was recaptured with less than 20km to go.View image in fullscreenDemi Vollering is held aloft by teammates on the podium.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty Images“There were so many moments when I thought I’d taken off too early,” she said. “It was so close. When they came back (to me) I was like ‘Oh shit — this is still not over.’ But never give up until the finish line.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen her initial attack came, the race looked likely to follow a familiar script of Vollering soloing to success.The Dutch rider was chased by a select group of eight that included Niewiadoma, Marlen Reusser and Longo Borghini. With 20km remaining the group fractured, under the impetus of 2024 Tour de France winner Niewiadoma and Longo Borghini, with Vollering wilting after 20km spent alone in the lead.But in a finale that encapsulated the compelling nature of the race, the favourites regrouped at the start of the final lap, and Longo Borghini launched her own attack.Vollering, however, mustered the energy to attack again, this time decisively, to repay the efforts of her expertly drilled Netherlands team.Longo Borghini clung on to hold off the pursuing Reusser and claim the bronze medal, while Pfeiffer Georgi was the best British finisher, in 11th place.Explore more on these topicsCycling Road World ChampionshipsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wallaroos storm back in second half to blow away Scotland in WXV series | Women's rugby union | The Guardian
description: Australia came from behind to beat Scotland 30-10 in their WXV Global Series clash after a dominant second-half display in Edinburgh
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australia came from behind to beat Scotland 30-10 in their WXV Global Series clash after a dominant second-half display in Edinburgh
Content: Australia’s Kaitlan Leaney takes the game to Scotland.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Kaitlan Leaney takes the game to Scotland.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesWomen's rugby unionWallaroos storm back in second half to blow away Scotland in WXV seriesScotland 10-30 AustraliaVisitors trail 10-5 in Edinburgh but battle backAAPSat 26 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia delivered the most accomplished display of their European campaign, roaring back from a half-time deficit to blow away Scotland 30-10 and end a six-match losing streak.After defeats to world champions England and France in successive weekends, the Wallaroos marked Michaela Leonard’s historic 50th Test with a second-half display of power and precision in Edinburgh.Down 10-5 at the break, Australia, who hadn’t won a Test all season, conjured up their best form, scoring three well-worked tries in the space of eight minutes and going on to rack up 25 unanswered points to dominate their WXV Global Series clash at Hive Stadium, next door to Murrayfield.Zoe Harrison rescues Red Roses with thrilling last-gasp try against New ZealandRead moreIt proved a landmark day for two standouts, with the 31-year-old lock Leonard becoming the first Wallaroo ever to win a half-century of caps and Desiree Miller scoring their opening try six minutes before the break to rack up 100 Test points.The 24-year-old Sydney speedster’s try still wasn’t enough to drag Australia back on to level terms as the No 8 Evie Gallagher’s 15th minute score, plus a conversion and penalty from Helen Nelson, gave the hosts the interval advantage. The Wallaroos’ post-break resurgence was then stimulated by the captain, Siokapesi Palu, and an inspiring rallying cry to her team at half-time.“The atmosphere was crazy. Going into half-time, the girls knew we had to take it up a notch just to compete with Scotland,” said Australia’s player-of-the-match, Faitala Moleka.“They’re a physical team and they were just pumping us at the rucks, but there was a massive mindset shift from the girls, and after a speech from our captain, we came out determined and got that win.”View image in fullscreenBrianna Hoy roars in delight after scoring Australia’s third try.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesThe comeback started in the 50th minute when a powerful rolling maul from the visitors was cynically brought down just before the line by Gallagher. Sam Wood snapped up the ball to burrow over for the score, while Scotland suffered the double whammy of their star forward then being sent to the sin-bin for 10 minutes.Australia had failed dismally to capitalise on a plethora of French yellow and red cards the previous week but this time they were ruthless as tries from Brianna Hoy and Moleka quickly followed.The loosehead prop Hoy even offered a delightful hint of a dummy before she ploughed over while Miller was electric from the restart, setting up a counterattack from their own 22 before Moleka provided the robust finish.Wood sealed the victory with a couple of penalties, courtesy of Australia’s scrum domination in worsening conditions, as the visitors maintained their 100% record against Scotland, who’ll face the Wallaroos in return fixtures in Sydney and Canberra next month.“The girls have certainly been progressing in our performance week to week, so it’s a really pleasing way to finish,” said the assistant coach Mike Ruthven.Explore more on these topicsWomen's rugby unionAustralia women's rugby union teamScotland women's rugby union teamRugby unionAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

description: How will the USA and Peru fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: How will the USA and Peru fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT will play their first game since the World Cup on Saturday against Peru.Photograph: Christopher Torres/EPAView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino’s USMNT will play their first game since the World Cup on Saturday against Peru.Photograph: Christopher Torres/EPASoccerUSMNT v Peru: How to watch, TV channels & live stream Saturday 26 SeptemberHow will the USA and Peru fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsGraham RuthvenSat 26 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2026 World Cup and the abrupt exit to Belgium in the last 16 is behind the US men’s national team, with Mauricio Pochettinonamingseveral uncapped youngsters on his roster as a new cycle begins.Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie, Folarin Balogun and a few other established figures have been left off the roster. The USMNT will use matches againstPeru, Chile, Mexico and Canada to set a new direction for the future.Peru are entering a rebuilding phase after failing to qualify for this year’s World Cup and are similarly aiming to use this friendly in Orlando to set the tone for a successful next cycle.Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s international friendly, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options.USA v PeruTime:9.30pm BST/4.30pm ETStadium:Inter.co Stadium (Orlando)How to watchUnited States:TNT (Stream on Fubo)Canada:Stream on FuboWhat to watch forThelack of experiencein Pochettino’s squad is particularly stark in the attacking ranks, where Damion Downs is the only forward with a cap to his name. Cole Campbell, Justin Ellis, Julian Hall and Cavan Sullivan are all uncapped.Other youngsters such as Mathis Albert, Zavier Gozo, Neil Pierre, Brooklyn Raines and Frankie Westfield could be in line for debuts. With so many uncapped players in the squad, it’s difficult to predict what sort of performance theUSAwill produce.Pochettino established a platform by reaching the last 16 of the World Cup. Nobody knew if the Argentinian would remain as USMNT head coach after the end of the tournament, but he has since embraced the challenge of developing the next generation of American talent.Player to watch:Cavan Sullivan, USA – The 16-year-old Sullivan is justifying the hype, earning his first USMNT call-up on the back of a run of six goals in six games for the Philadelphia Union.
