title: ‘I’m pretty sure I didn’t imagine it’: the little-known trio of high schoolers who made USMNT history | USA | The Guardian
description: The idea of 16-year-olds like Cavan Sullivan playing for the US senior team was once unfathomable – until three teenagers appeared in a 1991 friendly
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The idea of 16-year-olds like Cavan Sullivan playing for the US senior team was once unfathomable – until three teenagers appeared in a 1991 friendly
Content: During his time in charge of the USMNT, Bora Milutinovic had a reputation for calling up youngsters to the senior level.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDuring his time in charge of the USMNT, Bora Milutinovic had a reputation for calling up youngsters to the senior level.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesUSA‘I’m pretty sure I didn’t imagine it’: the little-known trio of high schoolers who made USMNT historyThe idea of 16-year-olds like Cavan Sullivan playing for the USMNT was once unfathomable – until Mike Slivinski, Mark Jonas and Nelson Vargas appeared in a 1991 friendlyPablo Iglesias MaurerSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf 16-year-oldCavan Sullivantakes the field for the US men’s national team in the coming days, he will join a list of youngest-ever US players that has no shortage of recognizable names.At the top is onetime phenom (turned cautionary tale) Freddy Adu, still the youngest player to ever appear for the US men. Names in the top 20 like Eddie Gaven and Bobby Convey will feel familiar to longtime US fans; Christian Pulisic, Yunus Musah and Gio Reyna are all still very much in the picture and may well prove to be Sullivan’s future partners in attack.Just below Adu’s name and above those five mentioned is a trio of names unknown to the vast majority of US fans: Mike Slivinski, Mark Jonas and Nelson Vargas. All three players made their debut in a 1991 friendly against Jamaica, with Slivinski and Jonas both younger than Sullivan will be should he appear for the US this window. Only Vargas featured for the US again, capped an additional three times between 1991 and 1994.Meet the USMNT’s next generation: a cheat sheet for 12 new players in campRead moreThe idea of a 16-year-old representing the US at the senior level has been mainstreamed by now, but it was unheard of in the early 1990s, long before the US Soccer Federation pumped millions into youth development and talent identification. So much so that when Sullivanreceivedhis call-up last week, nobody seemed to even remember the three players who, more than three decades ago, carved their names into the record books.“A buddy of mine sent me an article about [Cavan’s call-up], and it said he’d be the second-youngest player in US history,” says Slivinski, breaking into laughter. “What am I, a fucking ghost? I don’t think it was a dream, I’m pretty sure I didn’t imagine the one game I played.”When Bora Milutinovic took the reins as US head coach in 1991, he inherited a program approaching the most pivotal moment in its history. A year earlier, the US had appeared in their first World Cup in four decades. In three years, the country would host the tournament for the first time. It was imperative, then, that the USMNT put in a decent showing on home soil.Milutinovic took a long, wandering path to the USMNT, with stops as a player or coach in a dozen or so different countries. He led Mexico at the 1986 World Cup and Costa Rica in 1990, guiding both sides to their then-best-ever finishes. His reputation as a bit of a miracle worker – a specialist extracting results out of underperforming teams – was a perfect fit for a US side who lacked little in the way of grit but still missed the quality to compete with the world’s best.In short order, Milutinovic set out on a talent identification journey that was unprecedented at the time, calling hundreds of players into varying camps and handing nearly 50 of them their first caps in his three years at the helm.In August 1991, that scouting journey took Milutinovic to the U-17 World Cup in Italy. There, an unheralded group of US youngsters bossed an Italy squad featuring Alessandro Del Piero and an Argentina team led by Marcelo Gallardo and Juan Sebastián Verón. The US would be undone by Qatar in the quarter-finals, but several players had managed to leave their mark on Milutinovic and his staff.Among them was Slivinski, who’d grown up in a trailer park in St Charles, Missouri, across the river from St Louis. Long before the era of MLS Next Pro or elite youth travel teams that sometimes resemble professional clubs, Slivinski honed his skills at his local high school, eventually earning a look from US Soccer.“Those Italy players from that U-17 World Cup left and went back to training with Fiorentina,” Slivinski says, laughing. “I left that tournament and went right back to training with Francis Howell North [high school].”Slivinski’s partner in midfield, Vargas, also caught Milutinovic’s eye. Vargas’s footballing journey in some ways mirrors that of US legend Clint Dempsey, whose skillset and mentality was tempered playing in the Mexican men’s leagues of his home town. Raised by a Colombian father, Vargas was featuring in Miami’s highly-competitive Sunday leagues at age 13, often lining up against ex-professional players twice his age and size.“If you’re good enough,” Vargas says now, “you’re old enough.”Like Slivinski, Jonas was 16 at the time and also played for his high school team. His profile, though, was greatly boosted by his presence on an elite club side in Maryland, a hotbed that had produced several members of the 1990 World Cup squad. Jonas was a participant in the federation’s Olympic Developmental Program, at the time the only true pathway for a youth player to stay on the radar of the senior national team.View image in fullscreenA news clipping from Nelson Vargas’s time at the U-17 World Cup.Photograph: Nelson VargasThe three arrived in North Carolina three days before the USMNT’s 14 September friendly against Jamaica and joined a mix of other newcomers and regulars. The three high schoolers joined up with US staples such as Paul Caligiuri, Fernando Clavijo and Hugo Pérez.“Just being around some of the guys from the full team, it was incredible,” Jonas says. “Chris Henderson was there. I remember Clavijo left a huge impression on me, he was a very hard-nosed player. It was crazy to see how everything translated; I was a kid and that was the first time I had ever played against full-grown men, the speed of everything.”“Time and space,” Vargas says, “becomes a lot harder to manage with grown men, if you’re not used to it. Everything happens a lot faster.”There is no video of the match – there never was, as most US friendlies weren’t widely broadcast. When asked, none of the three even had a photo of their time with the senior team. But by most accounts Slivinski, who had been handed a surprise start, acquitted himself well. The US took a first-half lead on a goal by indoor and outdoor soccer journeyman Sadri Gjonbalaj. Not long after, Slivinski made his mark, drawing a foul about 25 yards from goal and coming very close to converting it on the ensuing free kick. Then came a breakaway and a shot across the face of goal which once again challenged Jamaica’s keeper.“This experience is indescribable,” Slivinski told the local paper after the match. “It’s just a massive honor. I am thrilled, nervous and a little speechless, honestly.”Vargas and Jonas entered the match in the second half, doing enough to draw praise from Caligiuri and Milutinovic. The occasion, though, seemed entirely lost on the press; soccer-specific publications likeSoccer Americanoted the fact that Slivinski had become the youngest-ever US men’s player (Mia Hamm debuted for the women at age 15 in 1987), but newspapers never made mention of the fact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“If it would have happened today, it would have been a big deal,” says Vargas. “But soccer in the US just wasn’t what it is now, at all, there was no social media or coverage back then. But that is what it is.”Mauricio Pochettino regrets not being ‘more involved’ with Balogun decisionRead moreThe attention isn’t the only thing that eluded the trio of youngsters after their debut, which for Jonas and Slivinski served as their lone appearances with the US.“I kept my jersey on after the match, I wore it back to the hotel soaking wet,” says Slivinski. “Thinking maybe they’d let me keep it. But that shows you how different a time it was – [US Soccer] probably didn’t have the money to do that.”All three US debutants had dreams of future call-ups, of maybe even making the 1994 World Cup squad. For Slivinski and Jonas, those dreams proved fruitless; injuries derailed Slivinski’s national team ambitions, though he’d go on to win an NCAA championship at the University of Virginia and MLS Cup with DC United before hanging up his cleats in 2000. He never played with the national team again.“Injuries, I guess, did me in,” Slivinski says. “But I also didn’t try hard enough, I don’t think. Mentally, I just wasn’t there.”Jonas, too, faced his own frustrations. In 1992, he departed for North Carolina State, where he’d earned an athletic scholarship. It seemed a decent move at the time, but he quickly found himself with a college coach hesitant to release him to attend youth national team camps. Quickly, Jonas disappeared from Milutinovic’s radar and disappeared into the wild world of late-’90s US minor league soccer, featuring for the likes of the Cleveland Crunch, Philadelphia KiXX and Virginia Beach Mariners.“It was frustrating,” Jonas says. “A total grind. There were guys that were younger than me in college that I was definitely better than – they got more opportunities than I did just because of their age and the way the landscape changed. After the national team, if you weren’t getting called up any more then you were essentially on your own. I remember cold-calling coaches trying to get tryouts, teams were folding every year. It was just night and day to what it is now.”Vargas would go three years before pulling on the US shirt again, eventually featuring in a trio of late-1994 friendlies just before Milutinovic was forced out as US boss. Vargas remembers incoming head coach Steve Sampson warmly, but Sampson never gave him a look. He’d get one more chance, though, to represent the US, featuring for the Olympic team at the 1996 Games in Atlanta. Vargas did manage a decent run in MLS, featuring for the Miami Fusion and Tampa Bay Mutiny, both of whom folded not long after Vargas retired in 2000.Vargas did hit the pitch once more, though: he played former USMNT player John Souza in The Game of Their Lives, the film dramatization of the US’s shock victory over England at the 1950 World Cup.View image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan, who turns 17 next week, could put his name on the list of youngest players to debut for the USMNT during this window.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesAll three have since transitioned into youth coaching, perhaps offering them some unique insight into the potential fate of Sullivan and the other teenagers on Mauricio Pochettino’s roster for this international window. Comparing the environment those kids came up in with the one they navigated, though, proves difficult.“When I was Cavan’s age, that was 35 years ago,” Jonas says. “It’s good to see things changing. I am coaching in MLS Next right now; these teams are treated like national teams, practically. There’s residency, all of their expenses are taken care of, they travel in buses and planes and they’re flying together, wearing the same stuff. It’s insane, it is nothing like what we came up in. There was just no real support back then.”“It is great that these kids get these opportunities,” Vargas adds. “This kid Cavan, he has all the tools. Why not let him test himself against the best players, the older players? The only way you learn how to deal with the fire sometimes is to get thrown into it.”Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to play | Activism | The Guardian
description: Ten years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rights
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Ten years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rights
Content: Colin Kaepernick, photographed in August this year.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick, photographed in August this year.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianActivism‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to playTen years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rightsSteve RoseSat 26 Sep 2026 06.59 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTShareColin Kaepernick still gets up at 4.30am every morning to train. “Strength training, speed training, position training – still do all of the same type of workouts I did while I was playing,” he says cheerily. “And then go about the rest of my day.” It is almost 10 years since Kaepernick last played a game of top-flight football. His career was abruptly and cruelly cut short just as it was peaking, after the National Football League (NFL) effectively closed ranks and shut him out for being too political. Now, at 38 years old, he is well aware that his chances of a return are dwindling by the day, but he remains as game-ready as ever. “I stay relentless at it,” he continues in his easy drawl. “I look at it from the perspective of, ‘What are the things that I can control?’ And what I know I can control is being prepared for when opportunity knocks, and to also continue knocking, on my end, looking for ways and opportunities … just staying resilient and focused and disciplined – that is what’s gotten me to this point in my life.”Kaepernick’s story is defined by the events of late 2016, when he repeatedly refused to stand for the pre-game national anthem – resulting in a chorus of booing on the pitch, insults and outrage off it, and exclusion from the sport he still loves. He was one of the biggest names in the game at the time; quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers, a national celebrity, sponsored by major brands, and looking back, his actions fed into so much that has happened since: the rise of Donald Trump, the Black Lives Matter protests and a global reckoning with racism, then the backlash against what is now being called “Woke 1.0”, and the resurgence of a white nationalism that the US complacently assumed was in the past.Through all of this, Kaepernick has largely held his silence. He has rarely spoken to the media and restrained from making public statements. Why so, I ask. Surely there must have been times he’s wanted to speak out?“Oh, absolutely,” he replies. “But I go back to, like, what am I trying to accomplish by doing so?” The temptation to rebut all the lies, the bad takes, the accusations was great, he admits, but, “I realised that, coming out of the protests in 2016, there was a lot of movement and effort made to try to make it as if I was the singular voice in this space doing work, and I was the person solely leading this movement, and that’s just not the reality.”In person, Kaepernick is friendly and relaxed, speaking on a videocall from his agent’s office in New York (understandably, he doesn’t like to disclose where he lives or spends his time). Even when he’s talking about the worst moments in his life, which is most of the time in our 90-minute conversation, his face defaults to a smile and he’s quick to laugh. He’s looking as dapper as ever: black dress shirt, top button done up; neatly trimmed facial hair; his voluminous afro a work of tonsorial topiary.The reason Kaepernick is talking now is because he has a new memoir: The Perilous Fight, which details his upbringing, his illustrious sporting career, and the events leading up to and from that pivotal moment in his life. This is not Kaepernick closing off a chapter of his life, he insists, he just felt that now was the time to speak up: “It’s important for where society is, where we’re at as a country, and some of the direction that the world’s heading in, to be able to continue to move things forward.” Also, he says, “we’re coming up on the 10-year anniversary. So a lot things just naturally aligned.”double quotation markIn many respects, before 2016, Kaepernick was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the gameView image in fullscreenKaepernick takes the knee before a game against the Arizona Cardinals in October 2016.Photograph: MediaNews Group/The Mercury News/ Getty ImagesHe doesn’t need to clarify the anniversary he’s referring to. Kaepernick’s decision to protest was the culmination of “a lifetime of experiences of being Black in America,” he says. But in the moment, it was also spontaneous: “It is not something I discussed with anyone else. It was a personal belief and conviction, and originally I did it not knowing or thinking anybody would see or ask about it,” he says. He didn’t even tell his then fiance (now wife), Nessa Diab. The first three times he did it, hardly anyone noticed. At the 49ers’ preseason game in Santa Clara, California, on 14 August 2016, Kaepernick did not take the knee; he simply sat on a cool box during the pre-game Star-Spangled Banner. He was recovering from injury and not dressed for the game, so he was inconspicuous. He did the same thing for the next two games.By the third time, NFL Network reporter Steve Wyche (who is Black) had clocked it, and spoke to Kaepernick about it. Wyche had also noticed that Kaepernick had been posting all year on his social media about Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr, Muhammad Ali, Black Panther co-founder Huey P Newton and Tupac Shakur. That January, for example, he had posted aquote from Dr King: “He who accepts evil without protesting against it is really cooperating with it.”Kaepernick had certainly been on a journey in terms of his Black history education, partly thanks to Diab – who, a few years earlier, had given him a copy of Malcolm X’s autobiography and told him he’d be “for ever changed”. But his decision to act was also motivated by recent police killings of innocent Black men:Mario Woods, shot and killed by five officers in December 2015 in San Francisco, where Kaepernick was living at the time, using what was later judged “unnecessary force”;Alton Sterling, shot and killed in Louisiana in July 2016;Philando Castile, shot and killed in Minnesota the day after Sterling’s death.“You then get to a point of, if you understand the problem and you understand the reality and you understand the experience, you either look at yourself in the mirror and say, ‘I’m gonna take action and try to do something about it’, or, ‘I’m not going to, and I’m going to be complicit in this’,” he says. The reality had become clear to him: that “the United States is not a representation of my ideals and my beliefs and has not been representing myself or the Black community. And that has been true since its inception.”By the time Kaepernick took the knee for the first time, at the suggestion of his team-mate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside him, the issue had become a global news story. He, Reid and others continued to kneel through that season, often to boos and chants of “USA! USA!” Opponents accused Kaepernick of disrespecting the flag, the country, the military, and law enforcement, repeating the familiar mantra that politics should be kept out of sport. People beganselling T-shirtsoutside football stadiums showing him in the scope of a rifle or telling him to, “Shut up and stand up!” Social media posts against Kaepernick turned vicious and racist. He began to receive death threats, including letters sent to his home address. Unfamiliar cars would park outside the entrance to his and Diab’s house, within a gated community. He temporarily moved out, for their safety.Colin Kaepernick: ‘I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward’Trump, then a presidential candidate,seized on the controversy: “I think it’s a terrible thing. And maybe he should find a country that works better for him,” he told a radio interviewer. Steve King, at the time a Republican congressman, invoked Diab’s Egyptian heritage to argue that“this is activism that’s sympathetic to Isis”. PresidentObama’s responsewas different: “I think he cares about some real, legitimate issues that have to be talked about,” he told reporters.Kaepernick felt largely supported by his immediate teammates; less so by theNFLas an institution. By the end of the 2016 season, by which time dozens of other players had joined in the knee-taking, it had become clear to him they were “trying to get rid of me”, he believes. In February 2017, the 49ers’ new coach and general manager gave him a choice: he could opt out of his contract now, or they would cut him later – knowing that if he left later, his chances of signing for another team would be greatly reduced. In other words, they were pushing him out, but wanted to make it look like he was leaving of his own volition. “It was a cowardly way for them to handle it,” he says.double quotation markThere was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs layKaepernick was “both surprised and not” by the response. “History tells us that a reaction like this is likely to take place. At the same time, because I have a belief that people are fundamentally good and want to do right, I was amazed at how visceral the response was to saying we shouldn’t be killing Black people. It is almost unfathomable to me that that is something that’s a debate in this country. And on the back of that was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs lay, which then became a much more honest place to be. And there really wasn’t a whole lot of middle ground.”It must have been an alienating experience, I suggest. Were there times when it all got to him?“The same way it revealed a lot about society at large, it also revealed a lot about the people around me,” he replies. He talks of how it led to deeper relationships, new friendships, an expanded community. “So while a lot of the immediate reaction is, ‘Oh here was all of the backlash and all of the things that were difficult’, it’s also, ‘Here are all of the great things that came out of this.’ Both of those exist, but we have to put things in perspective. Maybe that’s the eternal optimist in me: I like to look at things through the lens of ‘these are opportunities to get better’.”You are relentlessly positive, aren’t you, I say to him. He laughs. “I try to be! That’s not to say that that negative thing doesn’t exist, but I don’t want to just live in that negative thing. I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward.”If there is any middle ground to occupy when it comes to race issues in the US, Kaepernick could make a pretty good claim to it. His racial identity is more complicated than it appears. He was born to a Black father and a white, teenage mother, and was adopted at five weeks old by a white family from Wisconsin (he has never met his biological parents). Rick and Teresa Kaepernick were conservative, church-going, Republican-leaning. Rick was a manager for a cheese company. They already had a son and a daughter, but had lost two sons due to heart defects and were eager to have another one, irrespective of race. So Kaepernick grew up in predominantly white communities, first in Wisconsin, then, from age four, in Turlock, California.As such, his early experiences of being Black in the US were largely as an isolated individual, often made more acute by his parents’ lack of understanding or even awareness of his racial difference. “They came in with a perspective of, ‘Hey, if we do things the same way we did with my brother and sister, everything will be OK’, and that just wasn’t the case.”Growing up Black in a white community had its advantages, he says. “You get to see and experience a lot of things that otherwise may not reveal themselves. There was a level of comfort there of like, ‘Oh well, if this Black boy is in this white family, he must have assimilated into some of the white perspectives and cultural elements. That makes it OK for us to talk freely and openly in front of him.’ You get a lot of valuable insights into people’s true perspectives, and it gives you a better understanding of how to be able to navigate that.”But he was often treated very differently when strangers did not realise he was his parents’ son. In his memoir he recounts how, aged eight, he was tied to a tree by some older white kids in his neighbourhood, who called him the N-word and told him to “go back to Niger”.Kaepernick’s youthful attempts to connect with Black culture did not always go down well with his parents, either. When he first got his hair braided in cornrows, like his hero, basketball star Allan Iverson, they told him: “You look like a thug.” They were happier when he brought home a white girlfriend than when he brought home a Black one. There were a lot of arguments, he says, over his taste in hairstyles, clothes, music. “But what I will say is, the areas that there was no question around were the idea of being a moral person and doing the right thing and treating people well … The foundational piece is, I know my parents love me as their son.”Sport was one route to connecting with his racial identity. He was outstanding from a young age – as talented at pitching a baseball as throwing a football, and a pretty good basketball player, too. As he ascended the ranks of school and college football, he came into contact with more Black peers. He also experienced the US’s racially charged law enforcement first-hand. As a teen he was pulled over and given a ticket driving his mother’s convertible with three Black friends – “driving while Black”, he jokes. Another time, at college, the cops pulled guns on his Black roommates, who were helping someone move; they had assumed it was a burglary.But Kaepernick’s discipline and commitment began to pay off: by the time he turned pro, in 2011, he was already a clear talent. The following season he led the 49ers to the Super Bowl (they lost to the Baltimore Ravens). He was one of the best “dual-threat” quarterbacks in the league – as effective running with the ball as he was passing it. In many respects, before 2016, he was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the game. He had a glamorous girlfriend (Diab was hosting a hip-hop radio show and appearing on MTV), big-name sponsors like Nike, was on the cover of magazines. “Suddenly, I was everywhere all at once,” he recalls.View image in fullscreenKaepernick with his wife Nessa Diab in New York earlier this month.Photograph: TheStewartofNY/GC ImagesAs much as he still loves the sport, Kaepernick’s protest changed his relationship to it, almost irreparably. And as much as he sought to expose racism in policing, he exposed it within football. More than 70% of NFL players are Black, but historically, team owners and coaches have been overwhelmingly white, and there have been mechanisms in place to keep it that way. In his book, Kaepernick likens the NFL’s scouting combine, where college players are assessed by NFL teams with a series of physical tests and demeaning medical assessments, to a slave market. He recounts how commodified players often are, how their injuries are often glossed over in the interests of short-term results, even how Black players’ baseline intelligence is assumed to be lower than that of white players, which makes it harder for them to claim medical benefits for brain injuries later on. “It is something that historically we will look back on as a society like, how did we ever let that fly? The same way that we ask, how did we ever allow slavery or Jim Crow to happen?”After he left the 49ers in 2017, no other team picked him up. Other players who protested had similar experiences, including Reid, even as scores more continued to take the knee. Trump, by then president,told a rallythat he’d love to see NFL owners respond by saying: “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now. Out! He’s fired.” Many of those owners were his people: white, Republican-leaning billionaires. Some werefriends and direct supporters, including New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, the Dallas Cowboys’Jerry Jones, and Miami Dolphins’Stephen Ross(who held a fundraiser for Trump in 2019).Kaepernick believes the NFL made an example of him: “By blackballing me, denying me employment because of fighting to create a better society and fighting to keep people alive, there’s very real implications about who they are as an organisation and what they believe. I think, largely, the community and society knows it and sees it,” he says.In October 2017, he sued the NFL for “collusion” in shutting him out in retaliation for his activism. The NFL settled out of court in February 2019 for an undisclosed sum. Kaepernick has signed a non-disclosure agreement so cannot go into details, he says, although he would be “very open to the NFL releasing all the documentation and letting society decide”. But he clearly regrets the way things panned out: “I was not protesting the NFL; I was protesting what was happening directly in communities and Black people being killed by police. And the NFL inserted themselves within that conversation and took a side.” (NFL Commissioner Roger Goodellhas denied Kaepernick was blackballed, saying personnel decisions are made by individual teams.)double quotation markMy lawyers got a phone call with Donald Trump asking for me to come in to a meeting. I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case thereView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianAs well as being the 10th anniversary of Kaepernick’s protest, it is also, of course, 10 years since the arrival of Trump on the political scene. Their fates seem intertwined: Trump capitalised on Kaepernick’s protest to whip up political support, then his associations with NFL owners helped shut Kaepernick out of the sport. What would Kaepernick say to Trump if they met?“Well here’s the funny part,” he says breaking into a broad grin. “My lawyers got a phone call with him asking for me to come in to a meeting, I believe it was 2017 or 2018.” There was not a lot of clarity aroundwhyTrump wanted to meet him, but it was “a very easy no”, he says. “I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a better environment and a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case there. I would be curious why there would even be a call and what the topic would be beyond trying to do a photo op.”Within a few tumultuous years, Kaepernick’s stance began to look less controversial. TheBlack Lives Matter movementhad already begun before he started kneeling, but by 2020 the catalogue of police killings of innocent and unarmed Black men, many of them captured on video, had become intolerable. The murder of George Floyd, in Minneapolis in May 2020, was a tipping point, sparking huge anti-racism protests worldwide. As a consequence, players began taking the knee across US sports – football, basketball, baseball, soccer, hockey – at every level, from high school upwards. In England, football players began to take the knee before kick-off for every game, including the national team. Sportspeople and public figures across the world joined in. Where Kaepernick had once knelt virtually alone, now he had inspired a global gesture. He takes no credit for what happened, simply observing that, when it comes to highlighting police brutality, “there are people that have been doing work on the ground directly in communities for years and decades, and a lot of this bubbled up and came to fruition and got elevated during this moment”.In terms of the so-called “racial reckoning” that ensued in the immediate aftermath of 2020, he observes that “people and organisations were pledging large sums of money to address everythingbutpolice brutality. A lot of it became about businesses using the moment to further their interests.” There was some radical reassessment of racial attitudes on all levels – societal, political, corporate – but there was also a lot of political virtue-signalling, such as house speaker Nancy Pelosi, Kamala Harris and other Democratstaking the knee in the Capitolin June 2020, scarves of kente cloth around their shoulders. The then Labour leader Keir Starmer and deputy leader Angela Rayner also performatively knelt, as did many others. Even some progressive politicians cringe at the recollection now. We are speaking shortly before Alexandrio Ocasio-Cortez gave her assessment that “Woke 1.0 was crazy” – suggesting that progressives went too far, post-BLM. This comes on top of ongoing efforts by Trump to roll back all manner of civil rights and inclusion advances: removing high-ranking Black officials from the military; allowing immigration officials to target Black and brown people; effectively operating a whites-only immigration policy. It is sometimes difficult to see what progress has been made. What does it say, for example, that Trump is still in power, a decade on?“It says we have a long way to go,” Kaepernick acknowledges. But as ever, he accentuates the positive: “I also think, within that, it has created such a clear and stark reality for so many people that they are rejecting the politics of the administration and looking for something that actually serves everyone.”double quotation markI still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do thatView image in fullscreenGrooming: Marquis Rosado. Makeup: Maricela Saucedo.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianThis is where Kaepernick’s energy is focused: building the movement. He may have been quiet but he has been busy over the past decade. HisKnow Your Rights Camptours the country teaching young people “not just how to survive but also how to thrive”. His charity funds legal assistance andindependent autopsiesfor those who need it (including the family ofNolan Wells, the Black Mississippi teenager who died in mysterious circumstances on a trip with his white friends this July). He runs a publishing company, and has donated over $1m to community projects. He’sthinking in terms ofElla Baker, the relatively unsung activist who laid the foundations for America’s civil rights movement, from the 1930s onwards. “That was centred around: yes, we need strong leaders, but we need strongpeople, and how do we elevate more people to become leaders so this truly becomes a movement?”Progressive politics is making a comeback, he says, especially within younger generations. “When we think about gen Z and gen Alpha, they’re very much coming from a perspective of, ‘Do you represent my beliefs? Do you represent who I am? And if you don’t, we’re not going to support you’ … As more and more pressure is able to be exerted from the ground up, I think those high-level conversations and positionings are going to start shifting and swinging as well.” He has a four-year-old daughter now, he adds, describing her as “relentlessly fierce”: “Being a father heightens the sense of urgency.”Given all this, isn’t Kaepernick more an activist than a sportsman now?“I look at myself as multi-faceted,” he says. “I still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready and prepared. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do that. But at the core of it, I think people should be able to live, they should be able to thrive, they should able to have dignity, have justice, and that should extend to everyone.”Kaepernick was always mindful of the roll call of Black sportspeople who took a stand for civil liberties and paid a price for it, he says. “That was something I was aware of prior to ever protesting.” Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War and was stripped of his heavyweight boxing title. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists in Black Power salutes on the podium at the 1968 Olympics, which effectively ended their sprinting careers. Curt Flood challenged the “reserve clause”, which prevented baseball players from choosing their own fates, in 1969, and forfeited his career. More recently basketball player Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, refused to stand for the national anthem throughout the 1995-96 season, for similar reasons to Kaepernick, and was suspended and fined by the NBA as a consequence.Kaepernick has had a few tryouts with interested teams, most recently in 2022 with the Las Vegas Raiders – their head coach told him, “You look bigger, faster, stronger than when I last saw you,” Kaepernick says. But the longed-for return has not happened. Is there a part of him that accepts his sporting career may be over? “We don’t have to accept that as the reality,” he replies. “There’s an opportunity to change that … so that when an athlete or when someone speaks up to try to create a better life and better future for a people, for a community, for society, they aren’t met with exile, but they’re actually embraced and people say, ‘You know what, you’re right. Let’s take the actions to actually make this better.’ When we can lay that foundation, that creates significant opportunity for change.”So he will continue to train, he says. “I will not let go of that as a discipline, as part of who I am.”If he was back on an NFL team again, would he still take the knee for the national anthem?“Absolutely,” he says. “The work still needs to be done. More people need to be brought into that work and into that conversation. And more people need to be taking action around it. And I will continue to do the work. I will continue to protest because, quite literally, people’s lives are at stake.”The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick is published by Grand Central. title: OpenAI says agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users in latest example of rogue activity | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Disclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agents
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Disclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agents
Content: An OpenAI booth during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn OpenAI booth during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI says agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users in latest example of rogue activityDisclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agentsReuters andLuca IttimaniFri 25 Sep 2026 20.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo ⁠months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, theChatGPTmaker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.The latest example came on Friday whenOpenAIsaid its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to ⁠say when the images were posted.Also on Friday, OpenAIconfirmedits agents had accessed US government websites, including those of the Security and Exchange Commission and the commerce department, accessing US Census data from the latter. The company was also investigating an attempted breach of the education department’s website, as reported by the New York Times.OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemmaRead moreThe disclosures reveal a ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated ⁠that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activity and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.OpenAI said its review would take “months” to complete given the scale of the work, and said it had notified “dozens” of third parties about improper activity.Most of the leaked images have been ⁠taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for ​training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.Before user posts are ‌used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out ‌metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might ‌leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or – just on Wednesday – by Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister, at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.Albanese said Australia had not been told that OpenAI agents had also breached US government sites, but the news was “not surprising” in the wake of the Australian incident.After Donald Trump downplayed warnings of AI threats as a “hoax” and ruled out US regulation, Albanese reiterated calls for global coordination to regulate AI development.“What this does is confirm … that there needs to be [an] appropriate national response, as well as an international response, to make sure that humans stay in charge,” Albanese told reporters in Sydney on Saturday.“The key risk is humans not being in charge of the rollout of this technology.”The 21 July announcement that OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by ​their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On 16 September, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain”.Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers.Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to ⁠include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that ​went unnoticed by the company for months.Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives”.In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement”. Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)HackingChatGPTPrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests | Heart attack | The Guardian
description: New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices
Content: Every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of surviving a cardiac event by 10%.Photograph: Photographer, Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEvery minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of surviving a cardiac event by 10%.Photograph: Photographer, Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty ImagesHeart attackDrones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggestsNew research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devicesNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment –every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil,France.Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion ofAEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes.The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Swedenand has saved lives.In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.More than 16m at risk of death by cardiac arrest in England and Wales due to ‘defibrillator deserts’Read more“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsHeart attackHealthHospitalsDrones (non-military)FranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’ | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US
Content: Protesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenProtesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPAustralia newsAustralian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in USJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSat 26 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 18.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.View image in fullscreenProtest signs as Donald Trump speaks at the General Motors proving ground testing facility in Milford, Michigan, on 27 July.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.View image in fullscreenProtesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September.Photograph: James Ross/AAPThe pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns includinga 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a2 gigawatt gas-powered centrein the Northern Territory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power –has planned to override statesand ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsDatacentresProtestAI (artificial intelligence)Protest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Oxford lets OpenAI train its AI models on Bodleian Library | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: University staff voice concerns over reputational risk of partnering with company behind ChatGPT
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: University staff voice concerns over reputational risk of partnering with company behind ChatGPT
Content: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has been digitising material from Oxford’s Bodleian Library to populate its training set.Photograph: Michael Dwyer/APView image in fullscreenOpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has been digitising material from Oxford’s Bodleian Library to populate its training set.Photograph: Michael Dwyer/APOpenAIOxford lets OpenAI train its AI models on Bodleian LibraryUniversity staff voice concerns over reputational risk of partnering with company behind ChatGPTEthan Penny andDan MilmoSat 26 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Oxfordhas allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data.The Bodleian material digitised byOpenAIhas been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents.Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers.However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data.An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was “proud” to ensure “the AI models of today preserve the world’s historical knowledge for the future”.“With more than a billion people using this technology in everyday life, it’s important it reflects different cultures, histories and perspectives,” they added.Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology.Booksellers have also reported aspate of ordersfor obscure titles such as a guide to agricultural implements in 18th-century Africa or biographies of 1950s car drivers. Secondhand bookshop owners have speculated that because the titles are unlikely to exist online in digitised form,they represent fresh datathat can beconsumed by the next generation of AI models.Scraped websites are increasingly saturated with AI-generated material, making them less useful for training models, and developers have turned to physical, often historical, book collections.OpenAI has struck similar agreements with US research libraries such as Boston Public Library, Caltech, MIT, and the University of Michigan under a project called NextGenAI. Oxford is the only UK member of the project.By June 2025, 125,000 images scanned from historical dissertations had been shared with OpenAI from the Bodleian collection, including PhD theses from European and American universities written in the 19th and 20th centuries. Other texts scanned include a rare collection of 10,000 16th-century “broadside ballads” containing song lyrics and musical notes that were once circulated on Tudor street corners. Staff have also discussed digitising of 18th-century Irish state papers, the private letters of Irish novelist Marie Edgeworth, and Dorothy Hodgkin’s penicillin notebooks.The OpenAI contract with Oxford also raises the prospect of the mass digitisation of the Bodleian’s collection consisting of 23m items. The minutes also discussed the creation of an “Ask the Bod” chatbot.A spokesperson for the University of Oxford said the amount of text being digitised was “modest in scale” and covered only out-of-copyright material. The Bodleian keeps the rights to the scans and will begin publishing them openly online within months, the spokesperson said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey rejected the suggestion that the machine-learning element had been hidden from the public and students. Digitisation was the university’s primary interest, said the spokesperson, but staff had been open that the project would also contribute training data.The Bodleian’s collections remain intact under the deal, unlike with secondhand book acquisitions elsewhere that are being pulped after scanning. Anthropic, OpenAI’s close rival, has spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents can be scanned before having them pulped. Anthropic has said it does not buy and destroy rare and antiquarian books.A tech news site, 404 Media, also placed a tracking device inside a secondhand book order and traced it to an Amazon facility in the US, where the books were also dismantled and scanned.The Oxford spokesperson said: “The material digitised through the project with OpenAI is modest in scale, out of copyright, and OpenAI’s use of the material is not exclusive.“The Bodleian libraries also retain the rights to make the digitised material available themselves, and the library will begin to publish these materials openly online in the next few months, as we do with outputs from other digitisation partnerships.“The project will in fact allow the Bodleian to make the material more accessible to a wider number for people, who might otherwise have found it difficult to access.”Explore more on these topicsOpenAIUniversity of OxfordAI (artificial intelligence)ChatGPTLibrariesUniversity partnershipsnewsShareReuse this content
