title: Look again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right success | Cas Mudde | The Guardian
description: Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right, says the political scientist Cas Mudde
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right, says the political scientist Cas Mudde
Content: Elif Eralp (front, second right), lead candidate for the Left party in the German capital, and on course for a historic win in Berlin on 20 September.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElif Eralp (front, second right), lead candidate for the Left party in the German capital, and on course for a historic win in Berlin on 20 September.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionGermanyLook again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right successCas MuddeDefeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the rightSat 26 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTShareGermany held three regional elections this month and, although each of them had a unique result, much of the media and political commentary reduced them to: “German chancellor clingsto power after latestloss to far right. Since 2016, the year of Brexit and Trump, “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” has become the overarching narrative about Europe. But while these elections were important, this reductive take both oversimplifies the complexities of contemporary European politics and drives a defeatist “end of democracy” narrative.Saxony-Anhalt’s election on 6 September wasa global news event– understandably, given Germany’s history, economy and place in Europe. The international media hadspeculated for monthsabout an outright majority for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party came close, setting arecord score with 43.8%,but it has so far failed to form a government, despite the amenable position of the “left-conservative” Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.Two weeks later, the AfD came in first again, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, with 38.2% of the vote. International media interest was much less pronounced this time, maybe because it was the second of the three ballots, but more likely because the party was not close to reaching a majority. Moreover, the far-right success was overshadowed by the dramatic defeat for the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. For the first time in the history of the Federal Republic ofGermany, the party did not make it into a state parliament. The relatively modest loss of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD), on the other hand, was barely discussed.Finally, in the Berlin state election on the same day, the Left party (Die Linke) scored a stunning victory, gaining almost twice as many new votes as the AfD, which came in only third. Berlin will most likely now be governed by a Left-Greens-SPD coalition, headed by Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish political refugees. Perhaps most striking was that a clear majority of young women (54%) voted for the “far-left” party, representing abroader leftwing trend among young womenthat continues to be ignored by most media and politics representatives.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators gather in Berlin, Germany, on 12 September 2026, to protest against the AfD.Photograph: Maria Castro/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockWhereas the Saxony-Anhalt election was oftengeneralisedas thestory of Germany, if notEurope as a whole, the Berlin election is, at best, flattened out to a story of capital cities: uniquely cosmopolitan metropoles inhabited by highly educated progressives and immigrants. No matter that Saxony-Anhalt’s population, at 2.1 million, is just slightly over half the size of Berlin’s, and is among the oldest and whitest in the country. Moreover, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a state that is much more like Saxony-Anhalt than like Berlin, will most likely also be governed by a Left-Left-Green government – a striking fact that again has gone largely undiscussed.This is not to say that the success of the far right and the defeat of the established parties in Germany are not important or alarming, but they are not the only notable features of these elections. Actually, the fact that two of the three states will have leftwing governments is in many ways more newsworthy, given that purely leftwing governments are increasingly rare in Europe. On a similar note, global media attention on Swedenwanedas soon as it was clear that the left bloc was likely to succeed in creating a new government and the far-right Sweden Democrats would not enter the government.Reducing the many complexities of contemporary politics to an “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” narrative is not only problematic because it ignores significant other developments; notably, important transformations within major cities, where multicultural electorates are moving left rather than right (seen recently in, among others,CopenhagenandNew York). But more importantly, and dangerously, it also strengthens the far-right’s populist narrative, which portrays politics as a struggle between “the elite” (that is, all the mainstream parties) and “the people” (allegedly represented by the far right).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBerlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma AydemirRead moreSimilarly, somemediahave been keen to adopt the“horseshoe” theory of politics, prominently and strategically used byMerz, in which the liberal-democratic mainstream is squeezed from both sides, by the far right and far left. This conflates two very different challenges though. While it is true that established parties are challenged by new(er) parties, particularly because younger voters vote less for the established rightandleft, this includes liberal democratic parties like the Greens, too.Moreover, while the far right does threaten liberal democracy – and the AfD even threatens democracy per se – the so-called far left rarely does. Like Die Linke, most parties that are considered “far left” are former communist parties which have become significantly more moderate over time, presenting an ideology that reflects the social democracy of the 1970s much more than the revolutionary socialism of the former communist world. In fact, few “far left” parties are still even populist these days.So, while both the far right and “far left” threaten the established parties, only the far right threatens liberal democracy. It makes political sense for established politicians such as Merz to equate liberal democracy with the established parties, but the media should not uncritically share these claims. Surveys continue to show evidence of what the US political scientist Robert Dahl termed “a democratic paradox”: where very high support for the system of democracy is combined with very high dissatisfaction with the state of real, existing democracy.By highlighting the complexities of contemporary politics, in particular the frustration of the young (women) who are looking for liberal democratic alternatives to established parties, both the far-right populist binary of “establishment versus far right” and the defeatist “end of democracy” narrative are weakened. Hopefully this will give space to liberal democratic parties, old and new, to move beyond the self-defeating strategy of catering again and again to the same stereotypical voter with“legitimate concerns”, and instead mobilise and represent different groups of dissatisfied democrats.Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author ofThe Far Right TodayExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Break Clause: two lovers flatshare during a breakup – and it makes for totally refreshing TV | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: They sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’t
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: They sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’t
Content: Will-they-won’t-they … Lara Ricote as Lil and Samuel Bottomley as Ben in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/Kerry SpicerView image in fullscreenWill-they-won’t-they … Lara Ricote as Lil and Samuel Bottomley as Ben in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/Kerry SpicerThe watcherTelevision & radioBreak Clause: two lovers flatshare during a breakup – and it makes for totally refreshing TVThey sign a rental contract, and then their relationship immediately collapses. This funny comedy-drama from Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote tackles real life in a way most sitcoms daren’tRhik SamadderSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been at more than one party where a stranger has told me they are still living with their ex, even sharing a bed. I don’t judge. I’ve experienced this myself. I remember a sad, uncanny time at the end of a relationship. Untangling our lives but not our bodies, supporting the other through their worst pain while trying to ignore the fact that the worst pain is you. But sometimes these strangers tell me they have been living this way for months, perhaps years, and my empathy flips to horror. “What the hell is going on in your house?” I think.I found answers in Break Clause (Thursday, 10pm), a new Channel 4 dramedy. It’s the story of sweethearts Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote), Leeds University graduates who decide to transplant their lives to London. On the eve of moving, there’s an incident that leads to a terrible confession in the hallway of their new flat. Ben and Lil break up – in the presence of their estate agent, who tells them the paperwork is irrevocable. They will have to live together for six months until the contract break clause. That’s awkward! But can tenancy rights correct a relationship wrong?Break Clause mines territory other shows ignore: the biting economic pressure of being young in a housing crisis. There’s no suspension of disbelief here, no twentysomethings living in loft apartments the size of a Virgin Atlantic business lounge. The couple live in south London, in an ex-council flat with grotty underpasses. Ben has a meet-cringe with a neighbour who spots him bin-diving for food. He’s copying videos posted by foraging influencers. “I think they mean the bins outside M&S, not the big ones under flats,” she replies.View image in fullscreenAll together now … Break Clause.Photograph: Channel 4Lil is an architect, Ben is a writer. It’s hard for any household to survive income inequality, by which I mean only one of them has one. Lil gets a job, at a firm, on a promotion track, while Ben volunteers to be injected with viruses for £800. Honestly, I’m not sure he is a good writer. Partly because he thought that a medical trial was a job interview, partly because he attempts to steal a YA novel idea from a teenager he tutors. Also, he’s too nice.Then there’s dating, which takes place under each other’s noses. Ben and Lil are trying to be friends. What choice do they have, forced cheek by jowl? They could illegally sublet, I suppose, but it probably wouldn’t give them both the means to live elsewhere. Perhaps their relationship isn’t over, the series teases. But should it be?‘I’m not even an actor – I was just grieving!’ Rising star Lara Ricote on the heartache behind her new breakup comedyRead moreIf a 22-year-old were to confess to me they weren’t sure their current partner was “the one”, I would tell them baldly that obviously they weren’t, and that their relationship with relationships had barely begun. There’ll be more of this pain, I’d say, harder lessons, plus a healthy whack of bad timing and cosmic injustice. It’s probably a good thing I don’t have young people who look up to me.Break Clause’s will-they-won’t-they can feel thin, and John Thomson is underused as Ben’s father. But it’s funny, there’s verve to the dialogue and direction, plus a winning performance from Mexican-American comedian Ricote, an effervescent mix of Megan Stalter and Jenny Slate. She lands the best gags – such as when Lil, seized by the romance of a moment, will jump into a game of double dutch with teenagers, or lean her head on a stranger’s shoulder as they sit on a bench by the Thames. Repulsed and confused, they all give her a dirty look. “Bad call on my part,” Lil acknowledges.Mostly, it’s refreshing to watch a show that isn’t wholly convinced love conquers all. In this economy? I’m convinced that twentysomething couples who live together now do so primarily to split rent. Certainly, no one in London is in love. They can’t access the upper tiers of the self-actualisation pyramid required, because they’re too stressed about not having a pension. Most comedies exist in a fantasy realm, where all housing is affordable. But escapism isn’t everything. Maybe rental regulation is the romance this generation needs.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe watcherTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A couple of times people walked out’: how an Anne Frank musical became the hottest theater ticket of the year | Off-Broadway | The Guardian
description: The creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapper
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapper
Content: ‘Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.’Photograph: Shawn SalleyView image in fullscreen‘Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.’Photograph: Shawn SalleyOff-Broadway‘A couple of times people walked out’: how an Anne Frank musical became the hottest theater ticket of the yearThe creators and stars of Slam Frank on their off-Broadway production - which reimagines the Holocaust victim as a pansexual rapperJuan A RamírezSat 26 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s difficult to not invoke the term “woke” when discussingSlam Frank, the 2025 musical that reimaginesAnne Frankas a pansexual Latina. Controversial even before its first performance, it giddily satirizes identity politics through its show-within-a-show structure, in which a progressive theatre company attempts to modernize the Holocaust victim’s story by paralleling it to the struggles faced by marginalized people today. Here, the mother of “Anita” is Black, her father is neurodivergent and, while hiding in Amsterdam, they are very much immigrants.Creator Andrew Fox recognizes “a temptation to categorize it as anti-woke art”, but points readily at the show’s fans and detractors, who fall across every conceivable party line, and cautions against one-note interpretations. “I think the piece is just trying to grapple with the last 15 years of cultural and intellectual upheaval and get some comedy out of it.”Following last year’s sold-out run at the Asylum NYC comedy club (now retroactively referred to as a workshop), it will premiere off-Broadway proper at the Orpheum theatre on 4 October.The idea started online, if you can believe it, when Fox stumbled across a2022 tweetdissecting Frank’s alleged white privilege. The composer-lyricist got to work on a hip-hop musical inspired by that absurd debate, and reconnected with an old school friend, writer Joel Sinensky, who suggested they implement the backstage concept. (Before then, Fox says, “it was closer toOleannathan to Waiting for Guffman.”)“We have many things that we disagree on, but the thing that we were always very united on is this feeling that we were tired of didactic theater,” Sinensky says. “A lot of the work that’s been made commercially in the last decade has been very direct about what you’re supposed to take away from it, and we wanted to write something that was a reaction to that – that was about that.”So while the current sociopolitical moment (post-#MeToo, post-Covid, post-“Woke 1.0”) is certainly a target in the musical’s line of fire, its form lampoons the art that has resulted from that zeitgeist.Hamiltonis a major inspiration – if that’s the word – with Slam Frank’s logo riffing on the blockbuster bio-musical’s own, and its musical sensibility imitates its verbose, sloganeering rap.Pre-Existing Condition review – Lupita Nyong’o is phenomenal in domestic abuse dramaRead moreWhat it doesn’t borrow from Hamilton, purposefully, is a clear ideology. The production’s social media, managed by Fox, has been a masterclass in subterfuge and trolling. (“Fasting is Fatphobic,” reads an Instagram post shared on Yom Kippur.) Fox, who is Jewish, says one of their guiding intentions was to never convey “a specific viewpoint or message”.“We committed pretty early to making something that, anytime we feel like we’re making one point and it’s starting to feel like a lecture, we swing in another direction,” he says. “It lets us focus on making the piece as effective as possible at getting reactions, getting laughs, getting shock.”Sinensky says he revels in Reddit reviews of the show, which alternately label him and Fox as pro-Zionist, antisemitic, extremist right- and leftwing: “That, to me, is one of the best indicators that we succeeded – that people can see it and love it or get angry for different reasons.”Online chatter aside, reviews have been largely positive. The show’s publicist (understandably) makes the most out of anX postby Ben Brantley, the former New York Times theater critic, arguing that it “may be the most important new show around”. Its director, Sam LaFrage, recalls avisit from Patti LuPone, who he says came backstage at Asylum NYC to mention how moved she’d been.View image in fullscreenAusten Horne, Amelia Louise Barr and Olivia Bernábe in Slam Frank.Photograph: Shawn Salley“I get really excited by something that makes me feel like art is back,” says LaFrage. “Like, wecando plays that make people uncomfortable, and say the things that have been left unsaid because we’ve been worried about getting canceled, you know? The play within the play is a great container to exercise that right, to be artists. Slam Frank is about what’s happened to art.”Like Fox and Sinensky, LaFrage feels the musical is a way to poke fun at his own “woke” past, something he thinks also legitimizes the honesty of its satirical intent. “I used to do drag queen family theater downtown,” he says with a mix of pride and chagrin.Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Read more“When Trump got elected, obviously that was awful, but I let woke get the best of me,” says Walker Stovall, who plays a character modeled after the camera operators in big-budgetJamie Lloydproductions. Like LaFrage, he speaks with an earnest tongue-in-cheek. “You should be critical about the way you think and about what you’re taught, but I think when I was letting it get in the way of connecting with other people is when it all went bad.”Fox echoes the sentiment that respectability politics have served an opposite effect. Many of the characters in Slam Frank often get bogged down in well-meaning, barely intelligible jargon. (At one point, someone wonders “through what assemblage of counter-hegemonic labor shall the scaffolding of our interlocking systems of oppression be rendered obsolete?”)“It’s a very strange way of speaking and writing that kind of detaches people from their own thoughts,” he says. “Part of what our show tries to do is represent that experience of being part of a culture that is becoming less human and more abstract, and how funny or horrifying that can be.”Ironically, the musical was previously ejected from a highbrow workshop hosted by BMI, the music licensing organization, for that un-abstracted bravado. According to Fox, “what got it kicked out was the non-binary coming out song, and as far as I know, there wasn’t a single non-binary person in that room. Then the next year, a bunch of new non-binary people joined the workshop and that was their favorite song in the show.”Olivia Bernábe, the non-binary actor who plays Anita, says they find the number “hysterical”. They first learned of the show through Fox’s TikTok videos, and thought it was “just an intense commit-to-the-bit, but with really good music”.“I know that there are people who do get offended,” says Bernábe. “There have been a couple of times where people have walked out; I don’t know if they forget that it’s satire, or it could be that everyone has a different threshold for it. Weareteasing, but not actually making fun of the identity. What the show plays with is the idea of your identity equaling your ethics, because that’s just not true.”View image in fullscreenThe cast of Slam Frank.Photograph: Shawn SalleyThere’s plenty of button-pushing atop that righteous jestering: the entrance to the Orpheum’s auditorium, for example, has been made to look like the bookcase which led to the Frank family’s hideout, with a neon sign welcoming visitors to “The Attic”. But Fox thinks “the culture was ready to move in this direction” of irreverence, paraphrasing a quote fromRick Rubin, the famous record producer, “that ideas are in the air and that somebody’s gonna get them. If you don’t go forward with it, that idea doesn’t die with you.”“There are many things in the culture reflective of things that Slam Frank is doing, so it’s clearly something in the air,” he says. “There’s certainly questions about the manipulation of the sanctity of the Holocaust in the popular imagination. I’ve gotten some emails that are like, ‘People don’t take this topic seriously anymore because of you,’ and I’m like, ‘I’ve been talking to people for the last three years; they were ready to not take it seriously anymore.’”Slam Frank’s final 20 minutes, set off by a truly audacious plot twist, are its most controversial, widening its scope from historical satire to contemporary excoriation. It was the only aspect to give Stovall any misgivings, before he recognized its value.“My gut instinct was, ‘Don’t do this to my girls,’” he says, half joking. “I had to think about it and be like, ‘Why do I have a problem with this? I don’t actually have a problem with this. This is hilarious.’ And the reason I had a problem with it is why I think it’s important to put it onstage, right?”Slam Frank is at the Orpheum theatre,New York, until 30 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOff-BroadwayUS theaterTheatreAnne FrankComedyNew YorkMusicalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper
Content: Austen translation … Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenAusten translation … Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Going out, staying inCultureFrom Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadDaisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caperSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaSense and SensibilityOut nowDaisy Edgar-Jones has a big bonnet to fill in the role Emma Thompson made her own in Ang Lee’s Oscar-winning version of Jane Austen’s romance. But let’s not compare: Blue Jean director Georgia Oakley’s take sees a fresh cast place new emphasis on the bond between sisters Marianne and Elinor.Her Private HellOut nowProfessional provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn returns with another slice of the outre, this time in a science fiction mode. It’s the tale of a young woman, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), who encounters a supernatural killer in diamond-encrusted gloves in a mist-shrouded city.RemakeOut nowTaking on the devastating subject of the death of his own son, revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee makes the film that no parent would want to make. Using his own home video and family archive, he creates a bereavement memoir that traces a life from infancy to adolescence to an adulthood marred by addiction.Heartofthe BeastOut nowTraining Day screenwriter David Ayer directs this thriller about one man and his dog attempting to survive in the wilderness after a plane crash. But not just any man and dog: he’s an ex-special forces officer and the dog is a retired combat dog. Curiously, it stars Brad Pitt where you might expect Jason Statham.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenFlava sensation … Honey Dijon joins the lineup at Homobloc.Photograph: Henrik NielsenJill ScottLondon,28 September; Birmingham,29 September; Manchester,1 October; London, 13 & 14 October; touring to 14 OctoberThe R&B and soul legend heads out on tour in support of To Whom This May Concern, her first album in 11 years. Expect classics, specifically from 2000’s Who Is Jill Scott?, alongside her dextrous, genre-hopping new material.Michael CraggWagner’s ParsifalRoyal Opera House, London,1to 17 OctoberIt grapples with good and evil, love and violence, life and death – so no wonder Parsifal lasts upwards of four hours. Acclaimed director Evgeny Titov makes his Royal Opera debut with this new production conducted by Jakub Hrůša. The high-wattage cast includes Stanislas de Barbeyrac, Christian Gerhaher and Ekaterina Gubanova.Flora WillsonXhosa ColeScarboroughSpa,26SeptemberContemporary and classic jazz sax maestro Xhosa Cole reworks the music of Thelonious Monk at the 23rd Scarborough jazz festival – Soft Machine, Alan Barnes and star vocalists Ian Shaw, Liane Carroll and Brigitte Beraha also enhance the event’s usual classy bill. Cole also plays London’s Vortex on 29 & 30 September.John FordhamHomoblocDepot Mayfield, Manchester,26 SeptemberBilled as a “Queer block party for all”, the late-night celebration returns to Manchester with a typically stellar lineup, including German pop star Kim Petras. Elsewhere, DJ-producer Honey Dijon goes back-to-back with underground house maverick Derrick Carter, while LSDXOXO, Erol Alkan and DJ Paulette will also be popping up.MCGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenSurreal thing …René Magritte’s La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), 1936.Photograph: Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkThis Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of MagritteGagosian Grosvenor Hill, London,to 12 DecemberIt may not be a pipe but it is an exhibition, one dedicated to the great surrealist master René Magritte and his enduring influence on art. Some major loans will hang alongside works on paper, photography and sculpture.Beverly BuchananSpike Island, Bristol,to 31 JanuaryFive decades’ worth of sculpture, painting and earthworks are packed into the first European survey for this artist who died in 2015, leaving behind a vast body of work about the US’s troubled south.Olivia BaxYorkshire Sculpture Park, nr Wakefield,to 14 MarchTwenty new, heavily textured, multicoloured and very strange sculptural assemblages by this young London-based artist, filled with salvaged materials and gloopy neon references to BMX parks.Evelyn Taocheng WangGoldsmith’s Centre for ContemporaryArt, London,to 13 DecemberExpect an outsider’s portrait of Britain in this debut UK institutional exhibition for Evelyn Taocheng Wang, taking a heavily conceptual look at what makes us so uniquely us (humour, reserve, period dramas) through sculpture, painting and installation.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenHome front economics … The Standard of Living.The Standard of LivingTheatre Royal Haymarket, London,to 12 DecemberJames Graham has an uncanny way of combining character and country. His latest play stars Rory Kinnear and is about the radical economist John Maynard Keynes, set against the backdrop of a Britain reeling from the first world war. Directed by Nicholas Hytner.Miriam GillinsonRhys James30 Septemberto 15 May; tour starts FolkestoneYet to achieve household-name status, 35-year-old James is widely considered one of UK standup’s master craftspeople. His new show Chop Logic combines a relentless stream of ingenious gags with the story of his circumcision.Rachel AroestiMurder Before EvensongWatermilltheatre, Newbury,to 14 NovemberRev Richard Coles’s cosy crime novel is adapted for the stage. It’s 1988 in the peaceful village of Champton, where life centres on the church, but a shocking murder changes everything and the rector is pulled into the investigation.MGThick & TightTuesday to 28 November; tour startsNewcastle upon TyneThe Guardian’s best dance show of 2025 goes on tour. A hilarious, subversive, offbeat treat from uncategorisable duo Thick & Tight and guests, Natural Behaviour mixes dance, text, lip-sync and silliness in surreal sketches. Subjects include the writer James Baldwin, lesbian seagulls and the dust in Quentin Crisp’s flat.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenArt attack … Kill Jackie.Photograph: Unai MateoKill JackiePrime Video,2 OctoberCatherine Zeta-Jones goes full madcap camp – and even gets to keep her native Welsh accent – in this big, bonkers crime caper about an ex-con art dealer whose past catches up with her. Daniel Ings, Raff Law and Sidse Babett Knudsen also star.WarSky Atlantic & Now,2 October, 9pmIt’s Sienna Miller v Dominic West in this deluxe new thriller from George Kay (Lupin, The Long Shadow). A film star and tech titan face “the biggest divorce trial in British legal history”, meaning their respective teams of lawyers, including Nick Mohammed, will stop at nothing in order to come out on top.East of EdenNetflix,1 OctoberZoe Kazan follows in her grandfather Elia’s footsteps with this adaptation of Steinbeck’s 1952 opus. Florence Pugh gets her teeth stuck into one of fiction’s most notorious antiheroines in Cathy Ames, whose author described her as having a “malformed soul”. Christopher Abbott plays her abandoned husband.Break ClauseChannel 4,1 October, 10pmA former couple – promising young architect Lil (comedian Lara Ricote) and directionless graduate Ben (Samuel Bottomley) – are forced to cohabit in a London flat due to a watertight rental contract in this sweet and goofy will-they-won’t-they (get back together) comedy from Jess Bray.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenBar work … Nivalis Nights.Photograph: ION LANDSNivalis NightsPC; out29 SeptemberA cyberpunk life-simulation where, instead of running around with a futuristic pistol and getting caught up in gang wars, you are just trying to make a living. Starting out with a food stand, you can eventually own the night through a network of bars, restaurants and clubs – and learn everything about the city from your loose-lipped patrons.The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – RemasteredAll platforms; out29 SeptemberOutcast monster hunter Geralt of Rivia gets caught up in the dark machinations of phantom huntsmen and warring kings in this updated and complete version of an all-time great role-player. If you have somehow yet to play this eastern European dark fantasy masterpiece, you really have run out of excuses.Keza MacDonaldStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenTop drawer … alt-rock riser Blondshell.Photograph: Reese LaytonBlondshell – ViolinsOut nowAfter Sabrina Teitelbaum’s first pop-leaning incarnation as BAUM imploded in 2020, the New Yorker morphed into alt-rocker Blondshell. While the musical backdrop is heavier and more guitar-based, that pop nous still runs through this third album, especially on the galloping Fur Elise.Julia Jacklin – The GemOut nowNamed after her local pub, the fourth album – and her first for the much-loved label 4AD – by Melbourne-based songwriter Julia Jacklin is full of lovingly crumpled rock. Exploring reinvention, longing and excavation, songs such as The Hardest Thing and I Wish are full of unforgettable melodic nuggets.Tinashe – PopstarOut nowAfter getting lost in the major-label system, US bop-maker Tinashe has thrived as an independent artist. On her eighth album she dabbles in hyperpop elasticity via the undulating Melatonin, while the low-slung Crash Out adds trap and R&B to the mix.M83 – I Wrote You a LetterOut nowThe French synth-pop outfit, led by Anthony Gonzalez, return with their 10th album, and first in three years. title: The Guide #262: Why laughing at the movies isn’t always funny | Culture | The Guardian
description: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?
Content: Exorcist II: The Heretic … left to right, Max von Sydow, Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher on set, directed by John Boorman.Photograph: PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenExorcist II: The Heretic … left to right, Max von Sydow, Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher on set, directed by John Boorman.Photograph: PR IMAGEThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #262: Why laughing at the movies isn’t always funnyIn this week’s newsletter: From A Space Odyssey to The Exorcist II, audiences can turn a serious film into an accidental comedy – but where does the line fall between laughing with a film, and laughing at it?Gwilym MumfordSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore every screening at the West End’s Prince Charles Cinema, a public service message is played. It’s usually oneread by John Waters, welcoming cinemagoers to the “most depraved and beautiful movie theatre in London”, before imploring them to “turn off your cellphone, asshole”. More recently, though, a new message has been played, read by none other than Timothée Chalamet, who made a guest appearance at the cinema last year. Along with the usual requests for phones to be switched off, Timmy makes an unusual plea: for audience members not tolaugh “like Max Cady”at moments in the film that aren’t supposed to be laughed at. Because the Prince Charles mostly plays older movies, there can be what Chalamet calls a “disconnect” between the time that the film was made and today: ropey scenes of sex or violence, outdated language or technology, or anything else that jars with modern sensibilities and causes people to hoot derisively.It’s a surprisingly real problem, not just at the Prince Charles but at any repertory cinema. On Reddit there are plenty of threads bemoaning people guffawing at everything fromA Space Odysseyto the films ofDavid Lynch, a phenomenon one film writer on Substack has christened ‘performative laughter’. For anyone caught in a cinema when this unwelcome cackling occurs, it can be a killer. There’s little more guaranteed to break the spell of a non-comedy film than laughter: scary movies are instantly made about 75% less scary, thrillers become less white-knuckle, dramas lose their weight.If uninvited laughter is bad enough for audiences, think about the people making the films. Surely nothing is worse for a director – aside from an absence of laughter in a film that you intended to be funny, perhaps – than people laughing at something you’ve poured your passion, creativity and hard work into. For a sense of how devastating it can be, watchBoorman and the Devil, a terrific documentary in cinemas this week about John Boorman’s Exorcist sequel, Exorcist II: The Heretic (pictured above), one of the most maligned films in movie history.Boorman wasn’t a fan of William Friedkin’s original Exorcist film, considering it sadistic and exploitative. So he sought to make a radically different follow-up, swapping out the first film’s creeping, low-lit dread for something grand, fantastical and even a little bit hopeful – an ambition that surely should have served as a massive flashing warning sign to Warner Bros execs, which bankrolled the film to the sum of a then unprecedented $14m. Boorman’s sequel hardly lacked for ambition: its sprawling plot included detours to Africa and Latin America, a device called a synchronizer that merged people’s brainwaves, and original Exorcist star Linda Blair (pictured below) tapdancing, for some reason.View image in fullscreenTap dancing extraordinaire … Linda Blair in Boorman and the Devil.Photograph: PR IMAGEWhat it didn’t have – arguably by design – was scares, precisely what those who flocked to see the film in huge numbers after the first film’s success were expecting. When they didn’t get them, they responded with confusion, boredom and finally laughter. The press soon picked up on audiences rolling in the aisles across America and the intense negative buzz around the film caused it to plummet at the box office after its first week.Things got so bad that Boorman set about frantically re-editing a film that was already in cinemas, giving it a more unhappy ending and removing some of its more guffawed-at moments. His changes came too late for the US – Warner Bros determined it would be too pricey to replace the prints of a film they already regarded as a sunk cost, though international audiences did get the new version – and too late to save its reputation: it still regularly appears on worst-of-all-time lists.Boorman and the Devil gently attempts to salvage Exorcist II’s standing, spotlighting its pioneering use of Steadicam, occasionally beautiful cinematography, and general sense of vaulting ambition. It’s notable though, that even many of the documentary’s more sympathetic talking heads – directors, film critics, industry professionals – still consider it a bad movie. It does have a very prominent defender in Boorman himself, now 93, who is interviewed at length in the film. He believes he did good work on Exorcist II, but still feels “the old wound” of its disastrous reputation, and of that mocking laughter.His reaction is understandable, but there are positive ways to respond to such a setback. Another film that regularly appears alongside Exorcist II in those damning lists isThe Room, Tommy Wiseau’s genuinely abysmal 2003 drama. It’s a film that is so bad that it achieved firm cult-classic status with a certain type of film fan. In fact the Prince Charles cinema does a roaring trade in screenings of the film, where audiences ignore Chalamet’s pre-film message to snigger en masse at its terrible dialogue, bizarre plotting and horrible wooden acting. Wiseau himself regularly turns up to introduce the film and do Q&As, and is treated with the same adulation as any A-lister. He’s turned mass mockery into cult-hero status – a presumably profitable little sideline. Proof, perhaps, that laughter can sometimes be the best medicine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rare sale of David Hockney painting of beloved dog Stanley could fetch £2.5m | David Hockney | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Dog Painting 17 is believed to be one of only six of works from Dog Series in private hands and first to be auctioned
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Exclusive: Dog Painting 17 is believed to be one of only six of works from Dog Series in private hands and first to be auctioned
Content: David Hockney’s Dog Painting 17, 1995.Photograph: David Hockney/Christie’sView image in fullscreenDavid Hockney’s Dog Painting 17, 1995.Photograph: David Hockney/Christie’sDavid HockneyRare sale of David Hockney painting of beloved dog Stanley could fetch £2.5mExclusive: Dog Painting 17 is believed to be one of only six of works from Dog Series in private hands and first to be auctionedMark BrownNorth of England correspondentSat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Hockney adored his dachshunds Stanley and Boodgie and let them run riot – so much so that after one had an accident in the LA home of the actor Dennis Hopper, the painter is said to have quipped: “It’ll be dry in the morning, luv, and you can just pick it up.”But Hockney did not just indulge his four-legged companions, he treated them as portrait subjects for a series of paintings, one of which is to be sold by Christie’s.The piece is the first from a series of dog paintings by Hockney,who died in June, ever to appear at auction. “This is such an exciting painting for us,” said Tessa Lord, Christie’s head of postwar and contemporary art. “The rarity is kind of extraordinary.”The painting is titled DogPainting17 and shows Hockney’s first dachshund, Stanley, curled up on a cushion, fast asleep. It has an estimate of £1.5m-£2.5m and is one of more than 40 works that Hockney painted in 1994-95 for his Dog Series.Stanley, named after Stan Laurel, was picked out as a puppy by Hockney in 1987 and followed him around constantly. Boodgie, more reserved, arrived later.View image in fullscreenHockney holding one of his dachshunds in 1993.Photograph: Photo Researchers/Getty ImagesAccording to Hockney’sauthorised biographer Christopher Simon Sykes, friends of the peripatetic Hockney were astonished he was getting a dog in the first place. But they soon saw how besotted he was.The feeling was mutual and the noisy dachshunds soon became an essential part of his busy friend- and visitor-filled life inhis Hollywood Hills home on Montcalm Avenue.Sykes in his biography writes that Hockney was not bothered about house training, with one friend, Jonathon Brown, recalling how the dogs used to defecate in his shoes.On a visit by Hockney for dinner at Hopper’s Frank Gehry-designed house in Venice, LA, Boodgie left a “gift” in the middle of the floor.According to Brown, Hockney did retrospectively wag his finger, telling Boodgie “no, NO!”. Then, “as Hopper’s look of a chain-gang murderer increased in intensity, Hockney added: “Oah, it’ll be dry in the morning, luv, and you can just pick it up.”Hopper, the story goes, was left with two choices: silence or murder. “He chose silence, but he looked like murder.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHockney at his Los Angeles home in 1987.Photograph: Anthony Barboza/Getty ImagesHockney embarked on his dog paintings when he needed some sunshine in his life. He had lost several friends to Aids and was devastated by the death of one of his closest, oldest friends, Henry Geldzahler, to pancreatic cancer. The artist told one journalisthe wanted“desperately to paint something loving”.Lord said: “He felt such a loss of love, this was kind of a catharsis for him.”Christie’s believes there are only six of the dog paintings in private hands, with the others owned by the David Hockney Foundation.The seller of Dog Painting 17 bought it after the dog series went on display at the LA Louver gallery, a wildly popular show that Hockney said attracted 7,000 people in four days – many with their own dogs in tow.Lord said the painting displayed “incredible spontaneity” and “fluidity of brushstrokes, but it still feels richly textured. You’ve got this sort of mottling underneath the cushion and you’ve got that slight flick of the ear that really animates Stanley.”She said the painting shone light on an important chapter in the life of one of the greatest artists of the 20th and 21st century. “I love the fact that there is this kind of innocence to it but it is so much more than that. There’s a universality to it … it’s so much more than just a portrait of a dog.”The painting will be sold on 14 October during Frieze Week, and it will go on display – anyone can see it for free – at Christie’s in London from 8 October.Explore more on these topicsDavid HockneyPaintingArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Lesley Manville returns as a murder-solving book editor | Television & radio | The Guardian

Content: A meticulous eye … Marble Hall Murders on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Eleventh Hour Films/Sony Pictures Television/Jonathan HessionView image in fullscreenA meticulous eye … Marble Hall Murders on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Eleventh Hour Films/Sony Pictures Television/Jonathan HessionTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Lesley Manville returns as a murder-solving book editorMarble Hall Murders is the final chapter of Anthony Horowitz’s hit mystery trilogy. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Priya Elan,Jack Seale,Alexi DugginsandSimon WardellSat 26 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarble Hall Murders9.35pm, BBC OneThe amateur sleuth is a well-worn archetype but Lesley Manville inhabits it more persuasively than most in this third and final adaptation of Anthony Horowitz’s mystery trilogy. Manville is book editor (and side-hustle detective) Susan Ryeland, who is persuaded to help whip a troubled young author’s manuscript into shape. She is drawn into a murder case that spans multiple timelines and circles enticingly back to a tiny coven of occult-obsessed children. Odd and intriguing.Phil HarrisonStrictly Come Dancing6.15pm, BBC OneIt might be harder to pin down who everyone is this season, beyond a few nepo babies and Delta Goodrem, but we’re still excited for the first live episode of the series. There’s no public vote this week but you can bet on Craig saying something relatively soul-destroying to one of the 15 couples strutting their stuff.Priya ElanThe Space Race in Colour8pm, Channel 4The success of Apple TV’s shows For All Mankind and Star City hint at our fascination with the “space race”. This evocative series explores the era, beginning with the origin story: Germany’s fearsome V2 rocket. Its creator passed his secrets to the Americans, who took them to the moon and back.PHParis Police 19109pm, BBC FourThe French (obviously) period drama continues to mix dark intrigue with deadpan absurdity, as accusations and regular violent deaths accumulate in the elegant wake ofla femme mystérieuseMarguerite Steinheil (Evelyne Brochu). Could the butler have done it?Jack SealeThe Golden Cobra10pm, BBC ThreeA second series of this animation set in and around Ebbw Vale’s grimmest takeaway. Events turn somewhat fantastical – for reasons that aren’t entirely clear, Ebbw Vale now has a beach. But are seaside-related accidents going to prove dangerous to Basil’s most prolific customer? Happily tasteless, grossout fun.PHSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneIt has been a patchy return for the British version of SNL so far, but might this be the night it takes off? It’s hosted by Amelia Dimoldenberg, the increasingly high-profile YouTuber behind the recently retired web series Chicken Shop Dates, while music comes from Rachel Chinouriri.Alexi DugginsFilm choiceThe Moment, 6.35am, 1.30pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenI love it? … The Moment on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: NBC Universal/SkyIt’s hard to tell whether Charli xcx’s mockumentary is a way of summing up her world-exploding “Brat summer” of 2024 or razing it all to the ground. As it counts down to a big arena tour and its accompanying concert film, Aidan Zamiri’s tale flips between the musician being overwhelmed by her sudden celebrity and a string of comically terrible Spinal Tap-ish decisions (the Brat credit card for gay people is a highlight).
