title: I hoped my children would have epiphanies while visiting my homeland; my father suggested we go swimming instead | Malaysia holidays | The Guardian
description: I brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals do
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals do
Content: Tessa Lu with her family in Penang, Malaysia.Composite: Guardian Design/Tessa LuView image in fullscreenTessa Lu with her family in Penang, Malaysia.Composite: Guardian Design/Tessa LuMalaysia holidaysI hoped my children would have epiphanies while visiting my homeland; my father suggested we go swimming insteadI brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals doTessa LuSat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 21.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I stepped out of Penang international airport, the humidity hit me like I was peering into a just-opened rice cooker. The air carried whiffs of exhaust fumes, fried food and something earthy. It felt thrilling and familiar because I was born in Penang and lived there for six years before I moved to Australia. I looked back at my three children who were visiting for the first time. They were draped over their suitcases like wilted lettuce. “Welcome to Penang,” I said, wiping sweat off my brow.It was July 2026. It had been 13 years since I last visited Penang, when my father had hosted a lavish wedding dinner featuring a champagne fountain and swan-shaped ice sculpture for me and my new husband. For my white, Australian husband, it was a trip of firsts: his first Chinese tea ceremony; his first 10-course banquet; the first time he met my extended family. But for me, it had been the last time I’d spoken Mandarin and the last time I had seen my grandmother before she died.As my parents grew older, I worried my Chinese heritage would be lost for ever. My children spoke only English and spent their Saturdays playing sport rather than attending Mandarin lessons and calligraphy classes like I had. When Gong Gong (maternal grandfather) spoke of his childhood, the children smiled indulgently but thought he was exaggerating when he said his only toy was a discarded bicycle tyre and he’d had to share one apple with his five siblings.My ‘Chinglish’ has a cringe-inducing ocker accent – but I’m determined to pass it on to my child | Monica TanRead moreI wanted to bring my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. My father, who lives in Perth but travels there frequently, booked his flight the night I floated the idea to him.On the first morning of our trip, my father met me, my husband and our children at our hotel in central George Town. He gazed at the gleaming marble floors and wood panelling of the Eastern & Oriental Hotel and said: “When I was young, I never dared to set foot in this hotel. Only rich Europeans stayed here.” Nowwewere the rich tourists – a fact that made me feel guilty and grateful – and to the man dressed in a khaki colonial outfit and safari helmet who held a door open for us, my toddler sang a cheery: “Thank you!”We began our trip gently, letting the children luxuriate in an air-conditioned mall and paw through racks of fast fashion before we ventured outside to explore George Town on foot. “It’s not every day you get to walk through a Unesco world heritage site,” I chirped. But the heat was intense and the children’s interest in colonial architecture and street art evaporated in the afternoon sun.In the evening, my father led our search for dinner through a labyrinth of alleyways, shepherding us off the road when cars and motorbikes rumbled through. At the first restaurant, there were no free seats and the air was sulfurously pungent from a nearby durian stall. In the second place, the smoke billowing from the satay grill triggered my daughter’s asthmatic cough. Finally, we found a place that dished up barbecued pork on springy egg noodles coated in a sticky soy sauce. We fell upon our food in a frenzy. Later, we walked back to the hotel along the esplanade, marvelling at the sunset that lit up the clouds like smears of mandarin sorbet across the sky.Towards the end of our trip, we visited my father’s childhood home. We drove along a winding road that hugged the contours of the hills in the island’s north. On one side, verdant rainforest towered above; on the other side, past the guard rail, was a sharp drop, with dizzying glimpses of the houses in the valley below. When we reached Tanjung Bungah, the suburb where my father had lived, the children scowled from the backseat. My 10-year-old hissed: “When can we go shopping?” The toddler pleaded to return to the hotel’s infinity pool, which was fringed by palm trees and overlooked the Andaman Sea. Undeterred, my father stopped by a truck piled high with coconuts. A shirtless man used a machete to hack one open and stuck a plastic straw in it. My father handed it to my son, who spilled it on to his lap.We continued down a narrow dirt road and stopped at a small weatherboard house with a red tin roof. The house was empty and neglected but my father still had a key. We squeezed past two bedrooms and shuffled to the kitchen at the back. The electrical wiring was exposed and the concrete floor was gouged with holes. There were no ceilings; sunlight filtered in through the holes in the roof. The toilet was outside. The entire house was smaller than our two hotel rooms. I pictured my father, who was one of six children, living there with his family.“How did you fit all eight of you in this tiny house?” I asked.“Fourteen,” he corrected me. “With my grandparents, three uncles and one aunty.”I took my daughter on a holiday to Hong Kong to visit family. I didn’t realise how hard it would be to leave | Lucille WongRead more“Woah,” my eldest daughter said, her eyes wide. Perhaps she was thinking of her bedroom at home, which was spacious enough for two bookcases and a double bass, and had a door that she slammed for privacy. The toddler began to cry and I picked her up, wondering if she finally understood the grim poverty that her Gong Gong had endured.“I want to go back to the pool,” she sobbed.My father ushered us back into the minivan and we drove back to the hotel. I thought he might be disappointed in the children’s behaviour but, instead, he urged me to take them for a swim. I realised that I’d expected too much of them; what child could resist leaping into cool water on a muggy day or lying on a sun lounger eating ice-cream? I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege and we enjoyed our final days doing as Penang locals do: shopping and eating. On one occasion, when I ordered food in faltering Mandarin, my toddler stared at me with wonder and exclaimed: “Mum, you can speak Spanish!”Our trip did not, as I had hoped, inspire epiphanies in the children about their heritage or their grandparents’ early struggles. Perhaps these will dawn on them as they grow up. For now, it was enough that they shared some experiences that featured in my earliest memories – they’d sweltered in tropical humidity and sat on red plastic stools, slurping noodles. And their Gong Gong had hugged them goodbye in a hotel lobby where he’d once believed he did not deserve to step foot.Explore more on these topicsMalaysia holidaysAustralian lifestyleFamilyAsiaParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UK | Hotels | The Guardian
description: From a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxes
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: From a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxes
Content: The Copley Arms in Hessenford in Cornwall.Photograph: Mike DaveyView image in fullscreenThe Copley Arms in Hessenford in Cornwall.Photograph: Mike DaveyHotels15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UKFrom a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxesRhiannon BattenSat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTShareThe TempusDoxford, NorthumberlandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zac+ZacFrom the chequerboard restaurant chairs to the disco ball-glittered bar and leopard print-cushioned bedrooms, this 41-bedroom hotel has more than a hint of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland about it. The 2026 winner of Visit England’s gold award for best small hotel, the Tempus recently opened eight wooden cabins overlooking the estate’s lake, and runsstargazing breaksin partnership with nearby Kielder Observatory. This month sees the launch of wellness experiences, combining gentle yoga and sound baths, while foraging workshops celebrate the estate’s wild bounty. Alnwick, Bamburgh and kipper-smoking Craster are close by.Doubles from £121B&B,thetempus.co.ukThe Old Bridge InnAviemore, the CairngormsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rupert ShanksYou can walk, cycle, swim or kayak straight from the door of this pub and bunkhouse on the banks of the River Spey in outdoorsy Aviemore. This mellow gastropub serves smoked haddock chowder and Caribbean lamb curry pies along with Cairngorm Brewery’s ales – and you’re likely to catch some live folk music too. Fresh from a recent revamp, its seven vintage-inspired bedrooms are decorated in autumnal shades of gold, green, rust and teal. Ranging from simple dorms to en suite doubles and family rooms, they come with access to a shared kitchen and dining room for DIY dinners and breakfasts.Family rooms forup to fivefrom £80room-only,oldbridgeinn.co.ukThe Black HorseAmberley, SussexView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsFood is the big draw at this new pub with rooms in the South Downs. Run by farm-to-fork restaurateurs the Gladwin brothers, the 12-bedroom inn is their first venture outside London, and their first with accommodation. One thing they are deeply familiar with is local producers – not least their own family. Beef comes from their farm, wines from their vineyard, Nutbourne, and some of the pub’s artwork has been painted by family matriarch Bridget. Stay over and you can wake to breakfasts of homemade brioche with just-laid eggs, farmhouse sausages or trout gravadlax. Stroll around the village, with itscastle hotelandpottery, orhikeover to Arundel then catch a train back to Amberley.Doubles from £125B&B,blackhorse-pub.comThe AbergwaunFishguard, PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPembrokeshire is home to spectacular beaches, but if an autumn storm blows in, it’s great to have galleries, cafes, pubs and cinemas where you can take cover. That’s where Fishguard comes in. This small harbour town has quietly blossomed over the last couple of years. The latest opening is the Abergwaun, a bistro with rooms launched in July by the folk behind the nearbyRed Onion cafe. Feast on locally line-caught seabass with kelp beurre blanc, then drift off to sleep in one of five smart, latte-coloured bedrooms. The next day, take in a pottery workshop atTŷ Clai, hike along thePembrokeshire coast pathfor a Sunday roast at theSailor’s Safety,or catch a gig atFfwrn.Doubles from £140B&B,theabergwaun.co.ukThe Lister ArmsMalham, Yorkshire DalesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jo Ritchie/The GuardianMalham is one of the Yorkshire Dales’ great hiking hubs, withMalham Tarn, the amphitheatrical cliffs ofMalham Cove, andJanet’s FossandGordale Scarwaterfalls within easy reach – and staying in the village became a little easier this summer with the opening of Lister Farmhouse. Its 13 bedrooms pair smart taupe, olive and blueberry fabrics with warm wood and leather. Part of the expanded Lister Arms, which includes rooms at theinn itselfand at a nearbybarn conversion, the new farmhouse bedrooms are two minutes’ walk away, beside sister pub theBuck Inn. For breakfast, stroll across a packhorse bridge to the pub.Doubles from £135B&B,listerarms.co.ukThe Great DecoyHurstbourne Tarrant, HampshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsFormerly the George & Dragon, when this Test valley pub with rooms opened in June, its name was changed to the Great Decoy in a nod to the area’s second world war history, when the surrounding countryside was used as part of a network of decoy sites to draw enemy bombers away from strategic targets. These days, a tempting mix of pub bangers (venisonsteak frites, wood-fired pizzas), plump-pillowed bedrooms and affordable rates is luring a more peaceful crowd. The pub is a low-beamed, candlelit haven and its eight bedrooms mix antiques with bright modern art and jauntily striped, scalloped headboards.Doubles from £90B&B,thegreatdecoy.co.ukThe Riverside InnRoss-on-Wye, HerefordshireView image in fullscreenIt was in Ross-on-Wye in the late 18th century that the artist and writer Rev William Gilpin set the blueprint for British tourism. Popularising the picturesque, he encouraged travellers to explore the local landscape for pleasure, helping to establish the idea of the British scenic escape (albeit infamously suggesting that “a mallet judiciously used” might improve the ruined charm of Tintern Abbey). More than two centuries later, five elegant new bedrooms have just opened at the Riverside Inn, giving modern-day visitors a suitably comfortable base from which to explore the area’s antiques and salvage shops, and stroll the leafy riverside pathways aroundSymonds Yat. Named afterCharlie Mackesycharacters, the rooms are decorated with finds fromBaileys Home Storeand other local businesses.Doubles from £180B&B,riversideinn-wyestreet.comThe William CecilStamford, LincolnshireView image in fullscreenOn the edge of the Burghley estate, along one of Stamford’s cute-as-a-bonnet Georgian streets, this treasured hotel underwent a major renovation two years ago. Named after Lord William Cecil, chief advisor to Elizabeth I, the 18th-century building is home to 26 bedrooms decorated in Bridgerton-meets-Babington chic, all chalky pink and sage green stripes, ginghams, velvets and chintz. The latest addition is Wild Floral, a botanical-inspired room launched this summer in collaboration with Lincolnshire designerSophie Allport. Head out to explore the copper-flecked parkland ofBurghley House, then return for pheasant kiev and blackberry tart at Milly’s, the in-house bistro.Doubles from £155B&B,thewilliamcecil.co.ukCorsham HouseCorsham, WiltshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave WattsIt was no surprise that Corsham was chosen as a backdrop for the recent TV dramatisation of Jilly Cooper’s Rivals – the market town is a primetime destination. Wild peacocks roam its Georgian streets, a “secret” garden unwinds behind statelyCorsham Court– home to one of Wiltshire’s finest private art collections – and independent shops and cafes rule. In the centre of it all is Corsham House, a new brasserie and bottle shop with rooms that opened in July. Once a bank, it’s now profiting from the town’s “Bath in miniature” credentials, serving its signature Corsham chips with chicken salt alongside fat rump cap steaks, and putting guests up in 11 small but daintily designed bedrooms painted in shades of rose, damson and beech.Doubles from£111 room-only,corshamhouse.comThe Copley ArmsHessenford, CornwallView image in fullscreenJust off the A387, between Plymouth and Looe, this riverside pub with rooms is worth detouring off the beaten Cornish track for. Recently taken over by the couple behind Lydford’s award-winningCastle Inn, its 17th-century core has been elegantly refurbished. Fill up on fish tacos or the catch of the day, then head upstairs, or into the cottage just behind the inn, to slumber in one of eight earthily coloured, softly lit bedrooms (the cottage rooms are the quietest). The following morning, wake to a full Cornish before hiking a loop through the woods of theSeaton Valleyor strolling a section of theSouth West coast pathover to Looe.Doubles from £100B&B(two nights for £160from Sept-April),copleyarms.co.ukThe Swallow Falls InnBetws-y-Coed, Eryri (Snowdonia)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tinman PhotographyJust across the road from its namesake waterfall, this former coaching inn reopened last year after a major overhaul, offering visitors a comfortable and affordable base for exploringEryri national park. Its 38 bedrooms are painted in warm, muted shades and bookended by floral wallpapers, tongue-and-groove panelling and bright, metro-tiled bathrooms. Family rooms come with sturdy wooden bunk beds and, downstairs, you can order lasagne or sausage and mash in a space framed by fringed lampshades, floral curtains and mossy green paintwork. From the inn, you can follow a riverside trail into the village of Betws-y-Coed or soak up the autumn colours on one of the waymarked paths in the nearbyGwydir forest park.Doubles from £76B&B,inncollectiongroup.comThe CrownBildeston, SuffolkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lucy TomsEstate-to-plate dining is the cornerstone of this sunshine-hued Tudor inn between Bury St Edmunds and Ipswich. One of several Suffolk pubs and hotels owned by the Nedging Hall estate, who completed a sympathetic makeover this spring, it has 13 smartly understated new bedrooms. It’s fully plugged into the estate’s homegrown supply chain; the owners also operate a butchery, kitchen garden and East Anglia’s oldest brewery, Mauldons (for which they grow malt barley). Head out on a gentlethree-mile loop walk to neighbouring Chelsworth, then take a seat by the dining room’s open fire to feast on treacle-cured pork ribeye with garlic croquettes, and deliciously wibbly Basque cheesecake.Doubles from £195B&B,thebildestoncrown.comThe Customs HouseBowling, West DunbartonshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyA hop, skip and jump (or 30-minute train ride) north-west of Glasgow, this stylish new hotel sits at the western end of the Forth and Clyde canal. Well-placed for towpath walks and cycles, it’s a grand reimagining of what was built in 1790 as the customs house for Bowling harbour. There are seven tweed-hued bedrooms in the main building, each with a view of the water and each named after a different cargo, and a floating lodge suite was added this summer, along with a sauna and cold plunge. When the restaurant opens in a neighbouring building next year, it will operate as a full-service hotel but, for now, staff are only on site during the day; evening arrivals are self check-in and continental breakfasts self-serve.Doubles from £120B&B,thecustomshousebowling.co.ukLe Strange ArmsOld Hunstanton, NorfolkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Matt Keal PhotographyClose to theRSPB reserve at Snettishamand the nature reserve atHolme Dunes, this stretch of north Norfolk coastline is a prime destination for spotting waders and waterfowl as they stop to rest on their way south, and is similarly restorative for humans. Follow a day of beach walks and sky-gazing with dinner at newly renovated gastropub theAncient Mariner– menu highlights include Barsham’s beer-battered fish and chips, and cheeseboards ripe with local favourites Norfolk Dapple and Binham Blue – before walking across to sister hotel Le Strange Arms to sleep. Its more affordable standard rooms have yet to be updated, but recently renovated self-catering lodges and apartments put a modish mustard and navy spin on seaside chic.Doubles from £91room-only,lestrangearms.co.ukWild DuckEwen, the CotswoldsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Chris TerryOpen fires? A scene-stealing, carved wood bar? Plates of buttery chicken and chips? Double Diamond ale on tap? If you were Pinterest-boarding the fantasy Cotswolds pub after a yomp through the fields (or along the river – the Thames Path starts 10 minutes’ drive away), it would be something like the Wild Duck. Just south of Cirencester, this 16th-century gardeners’ cottage turned coaching inn has been stylishly overhauled by local hospitality luminaries Sam and Georgie Pearman. Reopened in March, it now has five bedrooms above the pub and 14 others in a new wing, each decorated with heritage wallpapers, Edward Bulmer paints, antique finds and custom-designed rugs.Doubles from £150B&B,countrycreatures.comPrices are for October-November and were correct at time ofpublication

title: Henry Harris’ vegetarian recipe for French onion and parsley soup | Food | The Guardian
description: A thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbs
Content: Henry Harris’ French onion and parsley soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ French onion and parsley soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFoodHenry Harris’ vegetarian recipe for French onion and parsley soupA thick and creamy, flavourful onion soup topped with grated cheese and herbsHenry HarrisSat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was a child, my mother often made onions in white sauce to serve with roast lamb. I loved their thick, velvety texture and how they brought richness, sweetness and even more savouriness to a good Sunday lunch. A similarly thick tangle of onions features in the classicsoupe à l’oignon gratinée,which can’t really be mimicked without a deep, dark, beefy stock, so rather than even try, it’s best to introduce another layer of flavour entirely. The parsley here yields a very different end result that also proves to be rather comforting.Onion and parsley soupPrep15 minCook1 hr 15 minServes4-6125g unsalted butter6 large onions, peeled and finely slicedSalt and black pepper2 bay leaves1 litre vegetable stock250ml double cream1 large bunchflat-leaf parsley, picked75gemmental(suitable for vegeatarians), finely grated4 tbsp croutonsMelt the butter in a large, heavy pan on a medium heat, then add the sliced onions. Season generously with pepper and a little salt, add the bay leaves, then cover and leave to cook gently for 45 minutes to an hour, stirring regularly, until the onions have sweated down to the softest vegetable mass – you want to take them to the point when, were you to squeeze them in your hands, they would turn to a pulp.Add the stock, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir in the cream and cook for another five minutes. Taste and add more salt and pepper if needed.At the very last minute, finely chop the parsley, stir it into the soup and ladle immediately into warmed bowls. Serve topped with the grated cheese and a few croutons.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodSoupStarterMain courseFrench food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wonderful, full-fat indulgence’: the best (and worst) supermarket lemon cheesecake, tasted and rated | Dessert | The Guardian
description: We sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: We sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?
Content: Best of the zest: our taster took into account the lemon content – and the additives – as he put cheesecake to the test.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenBest of the zest: our taster took into account the lemon content – and the additives – as he put cheesecake to the test.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterDessertReview‘Wonderful, full-fat indulgence’: the best (and worst) supermarket lemon cheesecake, tasted and ratedWe sift through the sweet and the sour of the creamy citrus dessert, but which ones are overloaded with additives and which are more generous with the juice?The best supermarket party cakesTom HuntSat 26 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLemon cheesecake is traditionally made by whipping cream, cream cheese, sugar and lemon, then pouring that on to a base made from melted butter and crushed biscuits (butter, flour, oats, sugar), before putting it in the fridge to set. That’s eight ingredients max, yet the average for today’s store-bought versions is 24.Every cake in today’s test falls firmly into the ultra-processed food category and typically contains at least five ingredients that aren’t found in domestic kitchens. Although real lemon juice or concentrate features in every one, lemon oil and acidity regulators are used to ensure that tart, lemony flavour.Although every cheesecake is edible and delicious in some way, and made so by that ultimate trio of salt, sugar and fat, the quality of taste and texture differs greatly. The best ones have a wonderful fattiness, a tart, lemony complexity and a good ratio of biscuit to topping; the worst tasted of stale biscuits, acidity regulators and plastic packaging.The best supermarket lemon cheesecakesBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Sicilian lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£7.50 for 580g at Waitrose (£1.29/100g)★★★★☆A pale lemon cheesecake topped with a spoon of lemon marmalade and a thick, sweet and firm but still crumbly base. Dangerously moreish. Not too sweet (19.2% sugar), full-fat indulgence and a wonderful, bitter lemon edge. No emulsifiers, preservatives, acidity regulators, colours or flavourings, but does contain seven additives, including certified sustainable palm oil, palm kernel oil, palm fat and invert sugar syrup.Best bargain:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5.50 for 500g at Sainsbury’s (£1.10/100g)★★★★☆A very deep mascarpone cheesecake with a layer of set curd on top, a spoon of lemon rind marmalade in the centre, a thick base and a 60:40 cheese-to-biscuit ratio.Verysweet (25.3% total sugars), plus the lemon curd in the cheese mix gives it a dense texture. Four additives – palm oil and potassium citrates, carotenes, invert sugar syrup – though no emulsifiers, preservatives, stabilisers or thickeners.And the rest …Tesco Finest lemon & mascarpone cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5.50 for 500g at Tesco (£1.10/100g)★★★★☆A pale cheesecake with candied lemon peel garnish and blobs of lemon curd throughout. A light, moussey texture, quite sweet (21% sugar) with a strong lemon flavour, a nice, compact base and a 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. No emulsifiers, preservatives or acidity regulators, but six additives nonetheless, including palm oil, amidated pectin, algal carotenes and invert sugar syrup.Morrisons the Best Sicilian lemon cheesecakesView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 192g at Morrisons (£1.82/100g)★★★☆☆Two small individual cheesecakes topped with a zesty lemon curd, a dash of white chocolate and a good ratio of moist biscuit base to topping. Made with British milk and Sicilian lemons, this is super-sweet (27.7% sugar), but there are no preservatives, colours or stabilisers, and only four additives (palm oil, invert sugar syrup, soya lecithins, flavouring).M&S Sicilian lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£5 for 585g at Ocado (86p/100g)★★★☆☆A light, moussey and quite sweet (20.5% sugar) deep-dish cheesecake with bitter lemon curd on top. A 65:35 cheese-to-biscuit ratio, but the base tastes a bit stale. Emulsifier- and preservative-free, but still nine additives including palm oil, palm kernel oil, sodium citrates and invert sugar syrup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnglish Cheesecake Company lemon & mascarpone cheesecake slicesView image in fullscreen£4 for 180g at Ocado (£2.22/100g)£4 for 180g at Tesco (£2.22/100g)★★☆☆☆Two large slices with a nice, firm base and a 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. An odd synthetic acidic aroma (probably from the citric acid and potassium sorbate), but a good, strong lemon flavour and moussey texture. The least sweet cake in the test (17.7% sugars), but eight additives including palm oil, modified starch, soya lecithins and flavouring. A Great Taste one-star winner in 2024.Gü Spanish lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£3.95 for 170g at Ocado (£2.32/100g)£3.95 for 170g at Sainsbury’s (£2.32/100g)★★☆☆☆Moussey and saucy with a crumbly, moist base (thanks to the ramekin format). Super-sweet (26% sugars), and less lemony than most, with a synthetic, sour flavour. Emulsifier-free, but six additives including RSPO-certified palm oil, invert sugar syrup and modified starch.The Bakery at Asda zingy lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£4.78 for 500g at Asda (96p/100g)★★☆☆☆Super-rich, cheesy, creamy and not too sweet (19% sugars), with lemon coulis swirled into the top and a good 70:30 cheese-to-biscuit ratio. Low actual lemon content (2%) with a distinct lemon oil flavour. Seven additives, including palm oil, polyglycerol esters of fatty acids, mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids and potassium metabisulphite.Co-op Irresistible lemon cheesecakeView image in fullscreen£4 for 160g at Co-op (£2.50/100g)★★☆☆☆Noticeably rich and creamy, with a lemon curd layer on top and a moist base. Very sweet (23% sugars), tart and lemony, with a distinctive lemon oil intensity. No preservatives or stabilisers beyond modified starch, but there are seven additives including palm oil, glucose syrup, invert sugar syrup and citric acid.Aldi Specially Selected lemon & white chocolate cheesecake slicesView image in fullscreen£2.09 for 180g at Aldi (£1.16/100g), in store only★☆☆☆☆A very sweet (20.8% sugars), fluffy cheesecake with a powerful, bitter lemon flavour, a soft digestive biscuit base and extra sweetness from the white chocolate topping. Eight additives, including palm oil, modified starch, soya lecithins and potassium sorbate.For more, read thebest (and worst) supermarket dark chocolateExplore more on these topicsDessertThe FilterFoodCakeFruitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Athens on a plate – a food-lover’s guide to the Greek capital | Athens holidays | The Guardian
description: Top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the city
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the city
Content: Highlight: Tucking in at Epta Martyres wine bar, Athens.Photograph: Angelos GiotopoulosView image in fullscreenHighlight: Tucking in at Epta Martyres wine bar, Athens.Photograph: Angelos GiotopoulosEat your way around...Athens holidaysAthens on a plate – a food-lover’s guide to the Greek capitalAthens-born chef Nick Molyviatis and Greek restaurant supremo David Carter share their top tips to the best cafes, bars and restaurants in the cityDavid Carter and Nick Molyviatis, as told to Joanna TaylorSat 26 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoffeeNormally we stay around Plaka, soAnanais the coffee shop I go to most often. There’s alsoBehold The Manin Exarchia, which is one of the coolest coffee shops I’ve been to. Exarchia has a really rebellious, anti-establishment feel and this place completely fits that – it has great music, great coffee and it’s just very cool. I don’t think there’s a coffee shop in London that’s quite like it. DCView image in fullscreen‘Casual and low-key’: Anäna Cafe, Plaka, Athens.My favourite is also Anana; It’s casual and low-key, with somewhere to sit down and relax. I’ll have a freddo espresso (espresso shaken over ice), which is basically the Greek national coffee now. NMAthens: a new, confident Greek cuisineBakeriesFor pastries,Akrais one of the best places in Athens. The food itself is rustic, simple and delicious, and the pastries are unbelievably technical. There’s something almost incongruous about it – you eat very simple savoury food and then a dessert arrives that’s incredibly elaborate. It shouldn’t necessarily work, but it does. DCView image in fullscreenRoll up! No Crumbs bakery.No Crumbsopened this year and I’ve already been a few times. It’s a little outside the centre, but it’s where I’d go for breakfast or something to eat on the move. In central Athens, I also likeFillo, which specialises in traditional pies from around Greece. Last time I went, they had three differentspanakopitas from three different regions. NMBreakfastI don’t really do breakfast in Athens. We’ll normally get coffee, then at about 11am go toDiporto, which is usually our first proper stop. It’s this incredible, old, rundown restaurant near the market: cash only, orders taken with a pen, massive wine barrels in the room, no choice of wine. They just put wine and water on the table. The food is incredibly simple: chickpeas, beans, vegetables cooked down slowly, sometimes grilled sardines or fish from the market. You could recreate a Greek taverna in London, but you could never recreate Diporto. There’s such magic in it. DCView image in fullscreen‘Such magic’: Diporto restaurant, Athens.Photograph: Hector Christiaen/AlamyIf I want to start the day properly, I go to Ipiros inside the meat market, at about 10.30am. It’s not really breakfast; it’s a proper meal. They serve slow-cooked dishes in huge pots and we usually get the tripe soup, which is good for a hangover, with loads of bread. Then we walk around the corner to Diporto and have the opposite: braised beans, chickpeas, salad and, whatever time it is, wine. NMTraditional tavernasWhenever we fly into Athens, we try to go straight toTaverna To Trigonoin Kalyvia, out by the airport. It’s as magic as a taverna gets. One side of the menu is salads, tzatziki, cheeses and breads; the other is grilled meat such as sausage, spit-roast lamb, offal, lamb chops, sheep chops. Everything is cooked to order and served with incredible abundance and generosity. It’s very simple: good produce, salt, oregano and lemon; nothing is over-embellished. I wouldn’t go to Athens without going there. DCView image in fullscreenChop-chop! Manári restaurant, Athens.Manáriis a proper meat chop house in central Athens. It’s relatively new, but it feels as traditional as possible, and you don’t need to travel into the mountains outside the city to find meat that good. I order the lamb chops, pasta with meat juices and tomato salad. The lamb chops are as good as – if not better than – a good dry-aged steak. Another favourite isTavern Spanosin Kato Patisia, for lamb chops and meats cooked slowly on the spit. Once they run out, they run out. NMNew-wave restaurantsLinou Soumpasis & Siais probably the most forward-thinking restaurant in Athens right now, and probably one of the best in Greece. It takes quite humble, seafood-led food and gives it a fine edge without losing its simplicity. The room is incredibly simple and every detail is really considered. Last time I went, they served a version ofkakavia, the traditional fish soup, which was essentially a beautiful fish and vegetable broth with olive oil. Something that simple, done that well, is incredible. DCView image in fullscreen‘Restrained and modern’: Linou Soumpasis and Sia restaurant, Athens.Linou is one of my go-tos, too. It reminds me a bit ofLyle’smeetsBrat. It has a restrained approach to food that still feels very modern. I’d also go toPharaoh, particularly for the vegetables and whatever they’re doing with fermented wheat, andAteno, which we went to twice in two days on my last trip. Get the Greek salad, stuffed vegetables and fries with mushrooms and eggs. I also really likeEx Machina: their saganaki is fried cheese but served cold, and I always want to see what [the chef] Adam Kodovas is doing with the seafood broth because the dish changes every few months, while the formula remains the same. I go toAkrafor lunch because they serve smaller portions and I can order as many dishes as possible. NMSeafoodTravoltais banging; it’s old-school and a bit likeBentley’sin London. You get huge plates of crudo and whole fish, and they have an amazing prawn and squid skewer with squid ink and olive oil that they mix at the table. It can get expensive (fish is incredibly expensive in Greece), but if you’re really into seafood it’s very cool.Phitais another good seafood place, a little further out. DCView image in fullscreen‘Old school’: Travolta restaurant, Athens.Photograph: Monika KritikouTravolta would be my choice for more classic seafood, too. If you want something more elevated, I’d go toIodionear Kolonaki. There’s one dish I’ll always remember, which is raw fish served cold with a crisp sheet of rice paper on top and a warm avgolemono sauce – a classic Greek sauce made with egg and lemon. You grab everything together in one bite and it’s great. NMCheap eatsFor souvlaki, the best is often at little roadside or market stalls. Last time we were in Exarchia, we found a tiny souvlaki stall mainly serving the market vendors. Forsouvla, the bigger rotisserie-style meats, we go toPsitopoleio Peloponnhsos. They serve huge pieces of meat, lamb heads; all sorts of pretty gnarly stuff cooking on the rotisserie. DCGyros are a dangerous subject for Greeks because everyone has their favourite.Achilleasin Neos Kosmos is one of the few places that still makes their own [meat rotisserie] (rather than buying it ready-made). In the centre, I really likeHoocut. They aren’t technically gyros because they slice the meat raw, cook it and then chop it again into small strips, but the mentality is similar. For a late-night version, go toMandrakiin Kaisariani. They’re open until about 2am and cook meat on spits late into the night. Their gyros are huge and often sell out. It’s cheap, traditional and the sort of thing people actually eat every day. NMWine and cocktailsWine is Fineis really good for a pre-dinner drink, and I also loveEpta Martyres, from the people behindLoggia[on Sifnos]; I’d been to both loads of times before I even realised they were connected. In Greece, I tend to want wines that are light and bright.Assyrtikois the obvious one; in that climate you want something really zippy. DCView image in fullscreenBaba Au Rum, Athens.Pharaohhas a great wine list, andTanini Agapi Mouis an amazing wine bar. A Greek grape I discovered this year is Vidiano. Vidiano can lean quite dry but still feels really pleasant and crisp; depending on where it’s grown, the fruit and minerality change a lot. It’s easygoing but complex at the same time. NMLine Athensis quite molecular and it’s the kind of place you stay for the night. The cocktails are some of the best I’ve ever had in my life, let alone Athens.Baba au Rumis right in the mix, too. There’s alsoRumble in the Junglebehind The Bar in Front of the Bar. The first is a bar where you walk in and think, “This is cool,” then go through another door into the second, even cooler bar hidden behind it. It’s very Athens. DCYou have to mention Line and The Bar in Front of the Bar. At Bar in Front, they’re trying to be as zero waste as possible, and you basically order through a window in a wall and sit drinking in the street. I choose what to drink according to the weather – last time I had a frozen martini that was almost like a slushie. At Line, the Paloma is usually my go-to, although on my last two visits I had one of their punches, which changes regularly. NMMarkets and food shoppingWe always go to Athens’ central fish and meat markets. I particularly recommend being in Athens on a Saturday because that’s when you find all these farmers’ markets around the city. Some of my best times in Athens have been wandering around those. DCView image in fullscreenPreparing fish ahead of a busy day at the central fish market.Photograph: Image Professionals GmbH/AlamyNear Diporto there’sMiran, a charcuterie shop with a huge range of cheeses and cured meats that they make themselves. Buy something there, pick up some bread and take it home. There’s also a huge farmers’ market every Saturday around Exarchia with outstanding produce. NMOut of townI really likeVouliagmeni, down on the coast where the Four Seasons is. We used to drive down there in the morning for sunrise, or chase the sunset if we were filming. Lake Vouliagmeni is there, too. It’s much more suburban, with huge houses and tree-lined boulevards, and it’s absolutely beautiful. You probably need a car. I don’t have one particular restaurant to send you to; for me it’s the area itself. DCView image in fullscreenLake Vouliagmeni, near Athens.Photograph: Nito/ShutterstockFor meat, go out towards the airport to Kalyvia. There are two enormous tavernas,Christoforosand To Trigono. During the week they can be completely empty, but at the weekend you’ll struggle to get a table. People tend to swear allegiance to one or the other; I don’t have a favourite. It normally depends on who’s driving me and where they want to go. Although the last few times I’ve been to Christoforos. NMDavid Carter is the founder of London hospitality groupDCCO, whose restaurants includeOmaandAgora, and Nick Molyviatis is co-founder ofZylia, also in London.Explore more on these topicsAthens holidaysEat your way around...FoodGreek food and drinkGreece holidaysRestaurants (Food)Restaurants (Travel)ShareReuse this content

title: Cooking with Tom Kerridge, the Michelin ‘meatfluencer’ | Tom Kerridge | The Guardian
description: The star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilli
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilli
Content: ‘Practically orchestral’: Tom Kerridge at work on a venison chilli.Photograph: Jenny Zarins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Practically orchestral’: Tom Kerridge at work on a venison chilli.Photograph: Jenny Zarins/The GuardianCooking with...Tom KerridgeInterviewCooking with Tom Kerridge, the Michelin ‘meatfluencer’Zoe WilliamsThe star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilliSat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Kerridge is the king of meat: first as a chef, transforming pub classics like pork belly into Michelin-starred fare atThe Hand and Flowersin Marlow 20 years ago, and later openingThe Butcher’s Tap and Grillin the same village; then as a cookery writer: hisOutdoor Cooking– The Ultimate Modern Barbecue Bibleof 2021 is well named, being both as comprehensive and as worshipful as a holy book; and recently as a “meat-fluencer”, making gorgeous skills videos on Instagram andYouTube.That was just destiny, he says (more or less). “When you’re cooking in a classic brigade system, the sections are like a larder: you’ve got starters, you’ve got garnish, you’ve got meat and fish, you’ve got pastry. The meat is the lead section, where the most experienced chef is, because that’s where you land when you’ve learned to treat vegetables with love and respect. If you fuck up cabbage, it doesn’t cost a lot.” It’s true, it doesn’t, but if you saw the care Kerridge puts into dicing an onion – peeling its layers apart like he’s making a mosaic, assiduous even about half an inch of waste – of anonion– you’d know that love and respect aren’t really about money.View image in fullscreenTreated with respect: the veggie ingredients for venison chilli.Kerridge is in his hideaway, also in Marlow, making a venison chilli, which flies off his menu for reasons I am shortly to discover. Even though itisSeptember, he is passionate that people should stop thinking of venison as an autumn-only meat – it’s available all year round. You could definitely become a connoisseur by knowing the difference in flavour profile between a red deer and a muntjac, but not by consigning it to some perfect season. You have to “drive flavour into it,” he says: “it sits there with beef but it’s much leaner, so it’s harder in some ways, because there’s no fat content.” The flipside is that it takes on spice really well, and by the time this dish is done – slow-roasted loin, a ragu made separately, everything cooked for hours, combined at the end with some fat chunks of salami – there’s a lot going on, and it is practically orchestral.Part of that experimentation and complexity is driven by necessity. When Kerridge started in his first kitchen, it was at theCalcot Manorin Tetbury, a classic posh hotel restaurant – one Michelin star, many layers of tablecloth, a food sensibility that was all about fine dining and being somewhat French: “the best ingredients, all racks of lamb and fillets of beef.” That was 1991, and he was 18 – it became quite a racy and experimental decade, in food as well as everything else, and tastes changed to incorporate the rest of the animal. In 2001, Kerridge became head chef ofBellamy’sin London, but that wasn’t as formative asAdlards: “amazing restaurant, small space, really busy, right in the middle of Norwich. That was the first time that I thought: ‘Maybe I could do this’.”View image in fullscreen‘If you saw the care Kerridge puts into dicing an onion ...’At The Hand and Flowers, Kerridge could stamp the place with his ambition: Michelin-starred food for people who didn’t want to dress like they were going to the opera. It’s hard even to remember the atmosphere of the hushed formality Kerridge ushered away. It’s no accident that his was the first ever pub to get its second Michelin star; helovespubs. “Wintertime walks across the Lake District, ending up in a pub with an open fire, that smell of crackling wood, beer and steamed puddings; summertime beer gardens; city-centre pubs; London pubs, where loads of city workers are all stood outside, packed together like fish: all of them are amazing, and the one thing they all have in common is a sense that it doesn’t matter where you come from – irrespective of your educational background, financial background, they’re warm. Everybody understands how a pub works, and everyone’s welcome.”The financial crash took a bit of weathering for Kerridge, and he didn’t start expanding his slate of restaurants until 2015. But by that time, after two series ofGreat British Menu,the BBC had started to hang whole concepts off his name –Proper Pub Food,Spring Kitchen,Best Ever Dishes– and he had name recognition, but never as a panto personality; he always came across on screen exactly as he does off it: a decent, practical-minded, funny bloke who would follow a flavour to the ends of the earth but never make a soliloquy about it. By 2020, he had three restaurants in Marlow, two in London including at theCorinthia Hotel,and one in Manchester. “Then, when Covid came, it was terrifying. We lost an awful lot of money: an event company we had closed, and the restaurant in Manchester ended up closing too – but everybody was in the same boat.”‘I’ve never known fear like it’: Tom Kerridge on booze, bad-boy chefs and the crisis for pubs and restaurantsRead moreThe financial pressures facing the industry at the moment are of a different order of magnitude, Kerridge says. “Six or seven years ago, a good restaurant might make 10% profit – not big numbers but you could make that work. Now, a lot of great places are making a fraction of that, and some aren’t breaking even.”Foodand energy costs have gone up massively, business rates are high, and the minimum wage and national insurance changes hit this industry particularly hard because it’s quite staff-intensive. “The cost of employing a young person over the last four years has gone up by a third. There’s no way you can put those costs on to the punter – they just won’t go out, or they’ll go to other places that aren’t putting them on. Then it becomes a race to the bottom; a competition to see who can lose the least money.”Kerridge is very active in the campaign to cut VAT on the sector from 20 to 10%, which seemed to be falling on deaf ears, but then the prime minister changed and the mood changed, and before long a business rate cut was announced, but just for pubs. Restaurants may yet see a slice of government largesse, but at the moment it feels to Kerridge like “there’s no help, there’s no cavalry coming over the hill”, and this is corroding creativity everywhere, because chefs don’t have the headroom to take risks and mess about: 21 hospitality venues are closing every week in the UK.View image in fullscreenTom Kerridge making venison chilli: ‘roast the hell out of the mince before you do anything else.’But back to that chilli. The venison haunch, which has been braising for three hours already, has gone into the ragu and the whole thing is a rich and sheeny mahogany, which is the daunting bit for the home cook – how to avoid a grey mess without the cheap win of a can of tomatoes? And Kerridge is anti chucking-in-a-can of tomatoes.There are cheffy touches at the end. Coriander oil actually couldn’t be simpler – you just whizz coriander with olive oil – but it looks so chic against a splodge of sour cream it’s unreal. A bit of grated chocolate, a bit of lime; I guess we would once have called this fusion – French and Mexican – but now it feels like the satisfyingly inevitable result of anyone blessed with a deer. “I was a kid who grew up in the 1980s,” Kerridge says. “It was crispy pancakes and potato waffles, in a single-parent family on an estate in Gloucester. We weren’t cooking tea every night. But my mum would do Sunday lunch, and she’d do it for everyone we brought back from the rugby club. She didn’t have any money – we never really had a joint; she just used to roast sausage meat and then do all the vegetables. There was always enough, and it was always delicious.” It’s not the obvious origin story for Kerridge, but in a way, it is.View image in fullscreenTipping point: venison ‘takes on spice really well’.A tip that will change your cookingWhen making chilli or bolognese, roast the hell out of the mince before you do anything else. Do this on the hob: put the meat in a pan with a bit of oil, high heat, and roast it for much longer than you would ever have dreamt. Take it way past the point of just having a bit of colour. When it starts to leave its charred remnants on the bottom of the pan, don’t worry – the onions going in afterwards will deglaze all that with their natural juices. When it starts to look very dark – pretty nubbly and dry – again, don’t fret; it will rehydrate later when you add the stock. Don’t trouble yourself over whether it’s lean mince or not: you can sieve off the rendered fat after this first stage, then you get all the benefits of fattier meat with none of the grease. “When you think of the flavour profile you get from a barbecue, or the outside bits of roast beef – that’s the bit everyone likes. And that’s what you’ll get from this ragu.” I tried this myself when I got home, and it was hands down the best bolognese I’ve ever made.Tom’s favourite utensil: the cast-iron panView image in fullscreenTom Kerridge – ‘This is absolutely chef-proof,” he says, “indestructible.”The famous lacquered versions – Le Creuset and whatnot – are the ones that look good in the interiors magazines, but matte black and unvarnished as the day it was born is Tom’s preference (Kerridge has developed a range for M&S, which I wouldn’t normally mention except it’s very good value). “This is absolutely chef-proof,” he says, “indestructible.” If you think of all pans as quite hard to destroy, that’s because you only use yours once or twice a week. A pan that can survive life in a restaurant, 10 uses a service, with outrageous heat (both direct and indirect), rambunctious cheffy fireworks, and still last a lifetime is a higher-order pan.Venison chilliView image in fullscreenVenison chilli as made by Tom Kerridge, with some soured cream and coriander oil on the side..I love a regular beef chilli, but this venison version is something else! Using a combination of diced haunch and venison mince gives the dish a real depth of flavour and a great texture. Although it takes a bit more time, it’s pretty straightforward, and the result is well worth it. Finishing the rich dish with dark chocolate, red wine and a zing of lime perks it up beautifully.Serves6-8For the venison haunchVegetable oil,for cooking1kg venison haunch,diced2 carrots,halved4 celery sticks,trimmed and cut in half1 onion,peeled and quartered1bouquet garni(sprig each of thyme and rosemary and a bay leaf, tied together with kitchen string)2 garlic cloves,peeled and sliced1 litredark rich beef or venison stockFor the chilli2 tbsp cumin seeds2 tbsp coriander seeds2 tsp chilli powder2 tsp cracked black pepper400g minced venisonVegetable oil,for cooking2 onions,peeled and diced4 garlic cloves,peeled and finely grated150g Milano salami or chorizo,diced400g tin kidney beans,drained and rinsed150ml red wineFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lime75g dark chocolate(70% cocoa solids),grated, plus extra to serveSalt and freshly ground black pepperCreme fraiche, to serveHeat the oven to 140C (120C fan)/275F/gas 1. Heat a glug of oil in a large, heavy-based, flameproof casserole over a high heat. Sear the diced venison, in batches to avoid overcrowding the pan, for a few minutes until well coloured on all sides. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside in a bowl.Lower the heat, add the carrots to the pan and saute until they have taken on plenty of colour. Now add the celery, onion and bouquet garni and fry for a few minutes, then add the garlic and cook for another minute or two.Return the meat to the pan, pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Put the lid on and transfer to the oven to braise for three hours, until the meat is succulent and deliciously tender.Remove the meat from the oven and cool slightly. Put a colander over a bowl, and tip the venison braise into the colander to strain off the stock. Reserve the stock and separate the meat from the vegetables. Transfer the meat to a bowl and set aside;discardthe vegetables and bouquet garni.For the chilli, put a small frying pan over a medium heat and add the cumin and coriander seeds. Toast for two to three minutes, rattling the pan, until fragrant. Let it all cool slightly, then grind to a powder using an electric spice grinder or pestle and mortar. Tip into a bowl and mix in the chilli powder and black pepper.Heat a large, nonstick frying pan over a medium heat. Add the minced venison and dry-fry, stirring frequently, for 20–25 minutes, until it is nicely browned and has a tasty, nutty flavour. It should be very crisp. Drain the mince in a colander to remove any excess fat and set aside.While the mince is cooking, heat a dash of oil in a large, deep, nonstick saute pan over a medium heat and fry the onions and garlic for eight to 10 minutes, until softened. Stir in the ground spices and cook for two to three minutes to release their flavour.Stir in the cooked mince and salami or chorizo, cook for two to three minutes, then pour in the reserved stock from the braised haunch. Add the kidney beans, give it a stir and bring to a boil. Lower the heat to a simmer and reduce the sauce until it’s thick and stew-like – about 20 minutes.Stir in the venison haunch and heat through for five minutes. Pour in the red wine, bring to a boil and add the lime zest, then lower the heat, season to taste and warm for a few minutes.Remove from the heat and stir in the chocolate. Serve the venison chilli on warmed plates, with a dollop of creme fraiche and a little more chocolate grated over the top.This is an edited extract from Tom’s Table, published by Bloomsbury at £25.
